## Introductory Remarks

In undertaking a discussion of the interpretation of dreams, I do not believe I have strayed beyond the proper bounds of neuropathology. When examined psychologically, the dream proves to be the first link in a chain of abnormal mental formations whose other links, namely the hysterical phobia, the obsession, and the delusion, must for practical reasons command the physician's attention. The dream, as will become clear, has no comparable claim to practical significance. Its theoretical value as a model case, however, is all the greater, and anyone who cannot explain how dream images arise will try in vain to understand phobias, obsessive ideas, and delusions, or to grasp their therapeutic importance.

Yet the same connection that gives our subject its importance is also responsible for the shortcomings of the present work. The reader will often find places where the discussion seems to break off abruptly, like the jagged edges of a fractured surface. Each of these marks a point of contact at which the problem of how dreams are formed meets the broader problems of psychopathology. Those problems cannot be treated here, but I intend to take them up in future work, should I have sufficient time and energy and should further material become available.

The particular nature of the material I have used to explain the interpretation of dreams has made this publication difficult. The work itself will show why all the dreams recorded in the existing literature or collected by others were useless for my purpose. For my examples, I had to choose between my own dreams and those of my patients undergoing psychoanalytic treatment. I hesitated to use the patients' dreams because, in them, the dream processes were complicated in an unwelcome way by the admixture of neurotic traits. My own dreams, on the other hand, carried an unavoidable drawback: I was obliged to reveal more of the intimate details of my inner life than I would have liked, and more than is usually required of an author who is not a poet but a scientist investigating nature. This was painful, but it could not be helped. I had to accept the inevitable rather than give up altogether on demonstrating the truth of my psychological findings. Admittedly, I could not resist the temptation to disguise some of my indiscretions through omissions and substitutions, and each time I did so, it seriously diminished the value of the examples I was using. I can only hope that readers of this work will put themselves in my difficult position and show forbearance, and that anyone inclined to take offense at any of the dreams reported here will grant that, in the life of dreams at least, thought must be free.

## Preface to the Second Edition

If a second edition of this rather difficult book has been called for before ten years have passed, I owe no thanks for it to the professional circles to whom I appealed in the preceding pages. My colleagues in psychiatry have apparently made no effort to overcome the initial surprise that my new conception of the dream provoked. The professional philosophers, who are accustomed to treating the problem of dream life as one aspect of the states of consciousness and to dispatching it in a few sentences, most of them identical from one author to the next, have apparently failed to notice that this field contains all sorts of things that must inevitably lead to a thorough transformation of our psychological theories. The conduct of the scientific reviewers could only justify the expectation that this work was destined to sink into oblivion. Nor would the small band of courageous pupils who follow my lead in the medical application of psychoanalysis, and who follow my example in analyzing dreams in order to use those analyses in treating neurotic patients, have been enough by themselves to exhaust the first edition. I am therefore indebted to that wider circle of intelligent seekers after truth whose interest has earned me the invitation to return, after nine years, to this difficult and in so many respects fundamental work.

I am glad to say that I have found little to change. Here and there I have inserted new material, added new observations drawn from my wider experience, and tried to revise certain points. But everything essential about the dream and its interpretation, together with the psychological propositions derived from it, has remained unchanged; at least from my own point of view, it has stood the test of time. Readers familiar with my other writings on the causes and mechanism of the psychoneuroses know that I have never presented anything unfinished as though it were complete, and that I have always tried to revise my assertions as my understanding advanced. In the realm of dream life, however, I have been able to stand by what I first declared. Throughout the long years of my work on the problems of the neuroses, I have repeatedly been beset by doubts and have often made mistakes, yet it was always in the interpretation of dreams that I found my bearings again. My many scientific opponents therefore show an especially sure instinct when they refuse to follow me into this territory of dream investigation.

The material I used in this book to illustrate the rules of dream interpretation, drawn chiefly from my own dreams, has likewise resisted any substantial change in this revision, even though events have since overtaken many of those dreams and diminished their significance. For me, indeed, the book holds a further personal meaning, one I could grasp only after I had finished it. It proved to be part of my self-analysis, a reaction to the death of my father, which is the most significant event and the deepest loss in a man's life. Once I recognized this, I felt unable to erase the traces of its influence. For the reader, however, it makes no difference from what material he learns to value and interpret dreams.

Berchtesgaden, Summer of 1908.

## Preface to the Third Edition

Nine years passed between the first and second editions of this book, yet the demand for a third edition has arisen after little more than one. I have reason to be pleased by this change. But just as I never took readers' earlier neglect of my work as proof that it lacked merit, I cannot take the interest it now attracts as proof of its excellence.

The advance of scientific knowledge has left its mark on *The Interpretation of Dreams*. When I wrote the book in 1899, my "Sexual Theories" had not yet been written, and the analysis of the more complicated forms of psychoneurosis was still in its infancy. Dream interpretation was meant to assist in the psychological analysis of the neuroses, but since then our deeper understanding of the neuroses has in turn reshaped our conception of the dream. The study of dream interpretation has also continued to develop in a direction the first edition did not sufficiently emphasize. From my own experience, and from the work of Wilhelm Stekel and others, I have since learned to assign greater importance to the extent and significance of symbolism in dreams, or more precisely, in unconscious thinking.

A great deal has therefore accumulated over the past year that demands attention. I have tried to do justice to this new material through numerous insertions in the text and the addition of footnotes. These supplements may at times threaten to distort the original discussion, and even with their help I may not have succeeded in raising the original text to the level of our present views. If so, I ask the reader's indulgence for the gaps in the book, since they are simply the consequences and signs of the rapid development our knowledge is now undergoing. I will also venture to predict the other directions in which later editions of *The Interpretation of Dreams*, should any be called for, will differ from this one. On the one hand, they will need to draw on the rich material of poetry, myth, linguistic usage, and folklore; on the other, they will need to examine more deeply the relationship of the dream to the neuroses and to mental illness.

Mr. Otto Rank has given me valuable help in selecting the additions and in reading the proofs. I am grateful to him, and to many others, for their contributions and corrections.

Vienna, Spring 1911.

## I The Scientific Literature on the Problems of the Dream

In the pages that follow, I will demonstrate that there exists a psychological technique by which dreams can be interpreted, and that when this method is applied, every dream reveals itself to be a meaningful psychological structure, one that can be assigned a definite place in the mental activity of waking life. I will further attempt to explain the processes that give dreams their strangeness and obscurity, and through those processes to discover the nature of the psychic forces that work, sometimes together and sometimes against one another, to produce the dream. Once this is accomplished, my investigation will end, because it will have reached the point where the problem of the dream meets broader problems, whose solution must be sought through other material.

I must assume that the reader is familiar with the work of earlier authors and with the present standing of the dream problem in science, since in the course of this treatise I will seldom have occasion to return to them. Despite the efforts of several thousand years, little progress has been made toward a scientific understanding of dreams. The authors themselves acknowledge this so universally that there seems no need to quote individual opinions. In the writings listed at the end of this book, the reader will find many stimulating observations and a good deal of interesting material bearing on our subject, but little or nothing that touches the true nature of the dream or definitively solves any of its riddles. Still less, of course, has reached the knowledge of the educated general public.

The first book to treat the dream as an object of psychology appears to be Aristotle's *On Dreams and Their Interpretation*. Aristotle holds that the dream is daemonic rather than divine in nature. It belongs, that is, to the order of nature and its spirits, not to the gods, and yet it carries deep meaning when correctly interpreted. He was also familiar with some of the characteristics of dream life. He knew, for example, that the dream magnifies slight sensations perceived during sleep into great ones: "One imagines that one is walking through fire and feels hot, when this or that part of the body becomes slightly warmed." From this he concluded that dreams might readily reveal to the physician the first signs of a change in the body that had begun but gone unnoticed during the day. I have been unable to study the Aristotelian treatise more deeply, owing to insufficient preparation and a lack of expert assistance.

As is generally known, the ancients before Aristotle did not regard the dream as a product of the dreaming mind, but as a divine inspiration. Even in those early times, the two opposing currents that run throughout all later assessments of dream life were already apparent. The ancients distinguished between true and valuable dreams, sent to warn the dreamer or to foretell the future, and vain, deceptive, and empty dreams, whose purpose was to mislead him or lead him to ruin. This pre-scientific conception of the dream was entirely in keeping with the ancients' general view of life, which habitually projected into the outer world, as reality, what possessed reality only within the mind. It also accounted for the chief impression that the memory of a dream makes on waking life the next morning, for in that memory the dream seems, compared with the rest of the mind's contents, something foreign, as if it came from another world.

It would also be a mistake to suppose that the theory of the supernatural origin of dreams has no followers today. Setting aside all bigoted and mystical writers, who are perfectly entitled to cling to the remnants of the once vast realm of the supernatural until scientific explanation has swept them away, one still encounters shrewd men who are averse to anything fanciful and who nonetheless go so far as to base their religious belief in the existence and intervention of superhuman forces on the inexplicability of dream phenomena, as Haffner does. The validity that certain schools of philosophy, such as the school of Schelling, attribute to dream life is a clear echo of the undisputed divinity of dreams in antiquity. Nor is the debate closed on the prophetic power of dreams. This is because the psychological explanations so far attempted are too inadequate to master the accumulated material, however strongly everyone devoted to a scientific way of thinking may feel that such claims ought to be rejected.

Writing a history of our scientific knowledge of dream problems is especially difficult because, however valuable some parts of that knowledge may have been, no steady progress in any definite direction can be discerned. No foundation of secure results has been laid on which later investigators could continue to build. Instead, each new author takes up the same problems afresh, starting from the very beginning. If I were to follow the authors in chronological order and review the opinions each has held on the problems of the dream, I would be unable to draw a clear and complete picture of the present state of knowledge. I have therefore chosen to organize my treatment by theme rather than by author, and for each problem of the dream I will cite the material the literature offers toward its solution.

Since I have not succeeded in mastering the entire literature, which is widely scattered and entangled with writings on other subjects, I must ask my readers to be satisfied so long as no fundamental fact or important point of view has been lost in my account.

Until recently, most authors treated sleep and dreams together, and alongside them they regularly discussed analogous states in psychopathology, as well as other dreamlike states such as hallucinations and visions. More recent works, by contrast, have tended to keep more closely to the theme and to take up a single question of dream life as their subject. This change, I believe, expresses the conviction that clarity and agreement on such obscure matters can be reached only through a series of detailed investigations. What I offer here is precisely such a detailed investigation, and one of a specifically psychological nature. I have little occasion to examine the problem of sleep, since it is essentially a physiological problem, although the character of sleep must include a change in the functional conditions of the mental apparatus. The literature on sleep will therefore not be considered here.

A scientific interest in the phenomena of dreams as such leads to the following inquiries, which are partly dependent on one another.

**(a) The Relation of the Dream to the Waking State.** The naïve judgment of a person on waking assumes that the dream, if it did not actually originate in another world, has at least carried the dreamer into one. The old physiologist Burdach, to whom we owe a careful and discerning description of dream phenomena, expressed this conviction in an often-quoted passage: "Waking life, with its trials and joys, its pleasures and pains, never repeats itself in the dream. On the contrary, the dream aims to free us from these. Even when our whole mind is filled with one subject, when deep sorrow has torn our hearts, or when a task has claimed the full power of our minds, the dream either gives us something entirely foreign, or takes only a few elements from reality for its combinations, or merely enters into the key of our mood and symbolizes reality."

L. Strümpell, in his *Nature and Origin of Dreams*, a study justly held in high regard everywhere, expresses himself to the same effect: "He who dreams turns his back on the world of waking consciousness." And again: "In the dream, the memory of the orderly content of waking consciousness and of its normal behavior is as good as entirely lost." And: "The almost complete isolation of the mind in the dream from the regular, normal content and course of the waking state...."

The overwhelming majority of authors, however, have taken the opposite view of the dream's relation to waking life. Haffner writes: "First of all, the dream is the continuation of the waking state. Our dreams always attach themselves to ideas that were in our consciousness shortly before. Careful examination will nearly always find a thread by which the dream has connected itself with the experience of the previous day." Weygandt flatly contradicts Burdach's statement quoted above: "For it may often be observed, apparently in the great majority of dreams, that they lead us directly back into everyday life instead of releasing us from it." Maury puts it in a concise formula: "We dream of what we have seen, said, desired, or done." Jessen, in his *Psychology*, published in 1855, is somewhat more explicit: "The content of dreams is more or less determined by the individual personality, by age, sex, station in life, education, and habits, and by the events and experiences of one's whole past life."

The ancients held the same idea about the dependence of dream content on life. Radestock writes: "When Xerxes, before his march against Greece, had been dissuaded from this resolution by sound advice, but was urged again and again by dreams to undertake it, Artabanus, one of the old rational dream interpreters of the Persians, told him very aptly that dream images mostly contain what one has been thinking about while awake."

In Lucretius's didactic poem *On the Nature of Things*, there occurs this passage: "Whatever pursuit a person is most devoted to, whatever matters we have long dwelt on, and whatever the mind has been most intently occupied with, these same things we generally seem to engage in during sleep: lawyers plead their cases and draft laws, generals fight and go into battle," and so on.

Cicero, in his treatise *On Divination*, says much the same, as Maury did much later: "Above all, the remnants of those things we have thought about or done while awake stir and move about in our minds."

The contradiction between these two views of the relation between dream life and waking life does seem insoluble. It is therefore worth mentioning the account of F. W. Hildebrandt, writing in 1875, who believes that the peculiarities of the dream can generally be described only as "a series of contrasts which apparently shade off into contradictions." "The first of these contrasts is formed, on the one hand, by the strict isolation or seclusion of the dream from true and actual life, and, on the other, by the continual encroachment of each upon the other and their constant dependence on one another. The dream is something absolutely separate from the reality experienced in the waking state. One may call it an existence hermetically sealed off and separated from real life by an impassable chasm. It frees us from reality, extinguishes our normal recollection of reality, and places us in another world and an entirely different life, which at bottom has nothing in common with reality...."

Hildebrandt then asserts that when we fall asleep, our whole being, with all its forms of existence, vanishes "as through an invisible trapdoor." In a dream, one may be sailing to St. Helena to offer the imprisoned Napoleon some exquisite Moselle wine. The former emperor receives one most cordially, and one feels almost sorry when the pleasant illusion is destroyed on waking. But now compare the situation of the dream with reality. The dreamer has never been a wine merchant and has no wish to become one. He has never made a sea voyage, and St. Helena is the last place he would choose as the destination for one. He feels no sympathy for Napoleon but, on the contrary, a strong patriotic hatred. And finally, the dreamer was not yet born when Napoleon died on the island, so it was beyond all possibility for him to have had any personal dealings with Napoleon. The dream experience thus appears as something foreign, inserted between two periods of life that follow one another in perfect harmony.

"Nevertheless," Hildebrandt continues, "the opposite seems just as true and correct. I believe that alongside this seclusion and isolation there can still exist the most intimate relation and connection. We may rightly say that whatever the dream offers, it finds its material in reality and in the mental life arranged around that reality. However strange the dream may seem, it can never detach itself from reality, and its most sublime as well as its most absurd creations must always borrow their raw material either from what we have seen with our own eyes in the outer world, or from what has previously found a place somewhere in our waking thoughts. It must be taken, that is, from what we have already experienced, whether objectively or subjectively."

**(b) The Material of the Dream: Memory in the Dream.** That all the material making up the content of a dream originates in some way in experience, and is reproduced or recalled in the dream, may at least be taken as an indisputable truth. Yet it would be wrong to assume that the connection between dream content and reality will readily reveal itself as the obvious result of comparing the two. On the contrary, the connection must be carefully sought, and in many cases it manages to escape discovery for a long time. The reason lies in a number of peculiarities displayed by memory in dreams, which, though universally known, have until now entirely escaped explanation. It will be worthwhile to investigate these characteristics thoroughly.

It often happens that material appears in a dream which, in the waking state, one cannot afterward recognize as belonging to one's own knowledge and experience. One remembers well enough having dreamed about the matter in question, but cannot recall when or whether one actually experienced it. The dreamer is thus left in the dark about the source from which the dream has drawn, and is even tempted to credit the dream with an independent productive power, until, often long afterward, some new event brings back the memory of an earlier experience given up as lost, and so reveals the dream's source. One is then forced to admit that something was known and remembered in the dream that had been withdrawn from memory in the waking state.

Delbœuf relates from his own experience an especially striking example of this kind. In his dream he saw the courtyard of his house covered with snow, and found two small lizards, half-frozen and buried in it. Being a lover of animals, he picked them up, warmed them, and put them back into a crevice in the wall set aside for them. He also gave them some small fern leaves that grew on the wall, which he knew they were fond of. In the dream he knew the name of the plant: *Asplenium ruta muralis*. The dream went on, and after a digression returned to the lizards. To his astonishment, Delbœuf saw two more little animals descending on what remained of the ferns. Turning his eyes to the open field, he saw a fifth and a sixth lizard running into the hole in the wall, and finally the whole street was covered with a procession of lizards, all moving in the same direction, and so on.

In his waking state, Delbœuf knew only a few Latin names of plants, and nothing of *Asplenium*. To his great surprise, he found that a fern by this name really existed, and that its correct name was *Asplenium ruta muraria*, which the dream had slightly distorted. Coincidence could hardly be considered, yet it remained a mystery to Delbœuf where in the dream he had acquired his knowledge of the name *Asplenium*.

The dream occurred in 1862. Sixteen years later, while visiting one of his friends, the philosopher noticed a small album of dried plants, of the kind sold as souvenirs to visitors in many parts of Switzerland. A sudden memory came to him. He opened the herbarium, found in it the *Asplenium* of his dream, and recognized his own handwriting in the Latin name beneath it. Now the connection could be traced. In 1860, two years before the lizard dream, a sister of this friend had visited Delbœuf while on her honeymoon. She had with her this album, which was intended for her brother, and Delbœuf had taken the trouble to write the Latin name beneath each of the dried plants, as a botanist dictated them to him.

The same fortunate chance that made it possible to report this valuable example also allowed Delbœuf to trace another part of the dream to its forgotten source. One day in 1877 he came across an old volume of an illustrated magazine and found pictured in it the entire procession of lizards exactly as he had dreamed it in 1862. The volume was dated 1861, and Delbœuf recalled that he had subscribed to the magazine from its first issue.

That the dream has at its disposal memories inaccessible to the waking state is so remarkable and theoretically important a fact that I wish to draw further attention to it by reporting several other "hypermnesic dreams," that is, dreams that display a heightened power of memory. Maury relates that for some time the word *Mussidan* kept coming into his mind during the day. He knew it was the name of a French town, but nothing more. One night he dreamed of a conversation with a certain woman who told him she came from Mussidan, and when he asked where the town was, she answered: "Mussidan is a district town in the Département of the Dordogne." On waking, Maury put no faith in the information he had received in his dream, but a geographical dictionary showed it to be perfectly correct. In this case the dream's superior knowledge is confirmed, but the forgotten source of that knowledge was never traced.

Jessen tells of a very similar dream from earlier times. Among others, we may mention here the dream of the elder Scaliger, as recounted by Hennings. Scaliger had written a poem in praise of the famous men of Verona, and a man named Brugnolus appeared to him in a dream, complaining that he had been left out. Although Scaliger could not remember ever having heard of him, he wrote some verses in his honor, and his son later discovered in Verona that a Brugnolus had once been renowned there as a critic.

Myers is said to have published a whole collection of such hypermnesic dreams in the *Proceedings of the Society for Psychical Research*, which unfortunately are not available to me. I believe that anyone who occupies himself with dreams will recognize as a very common phenomenon the fact that the dream shows evidence of knowing and remembering things unknown to the waking person. In my psychoanalytic investigations of nervous patients, which I will discuss later, I am in a position more than once every week to convince my patients, from their own dreams, that they are well acquainted with quotations, obscene expressions, and the like, and that they make use of these in their dreams even though they have forgotten them in waking life. I will cite here a simple case of dream hypermnesia, because the source that made the knowledge available to the dream was easy to trace.

A patient dreamed, in the course of a long dream, that he ordered a "Kontuszówka" in a café. After telling me the dream, he asked what the word might mean, since he had never heard it before. I was able to tell him that Kontuszówka was a Polish liqueur, and that he could not have invented the name in his dream, since I had long known it from advertisements. At first the patient would not believe me. But some days later, after he had acted out his dream in a café, he noticed the name on a sign at a street corner that he had been obliged to pass at least twice a day for months.

I have learned from my own dreams how much the discovery of the origin of certain dream elements depends on chance. For years before writing this book, I was haunted by the image of a very simply shaped church tower that I could not remember ever having seen. Then I suddenly recognized it, with absolute certainty, at a small station between Salzburg and Reichenhall. This was in the late 1890s, and I had first traveled that route in 1886. In later years, when I was already deeply engaged in the study of dreams, I was quite annoyed by the frequent recurrence of a dream image of a certain peculiar place. I saw it in a definite spatial relation to myself: to my left, a dark space from which many grotesque sandstone figures stood out. A faint glimmer of memory, which I did not quite trust, told me it was the entrance to a beer cellar, but I could explain neither the meaning nor the origin of the image.

In 1907 I happened to come to Padua, which, to my regret, I had been unable to visit since 1895. My first visit to this beautiful university city had been disappointing. I had been unable to see Giotto's frescoes in the church of the Madonna dell'Arena, having turned back on the way there when told that the little church was closed that day. On my second visit, twelve years later, I meant to make up for this, and before anything else I set out for the Madonna dell'Arena. On the street leading to it, on my left, probably at the very spot where I had turned back in 1895, I found the place I had so often seen in my dream, with its sandstone figures. It was, in fact, the entrance to a restaurant garden.

One of the sources from which the dream draws material for reproduction, material that is partly neither recalled nor used in waking thought, is childhood. I will simply cite some of the authors who have observed and emphasized this.

Hildebrandt writes: "It has already been expressly admitted that the dream sometimes brings back to the mind, with remarkable reproductive power, remote and even forgotten experiences from the earliest periods of life."

Strümpell writes: "The subject becomes more interesting when we remember how the dream sometimes brings forth, from beneath the deepest and heaviest layers that later years have piled upon the experiences of earliest childhood, the images of certain places, things, and persons, entirely undamaged and with all their original freshness. This is not confined to impressions that were vividly conscious when they arose, or that were stamped with strong psychic significance and later return in the dream as genuine memories, giving pleasure to the awakened mind. On the contrary, the depths of dream memory also hold images of persons, things, places, and early experiences that either had little consciousness and no psychic value at all, or have long since lost both, and that therefore appear completely strange and unfamiliar, both in the dream and in the waking state, until their earlier origin is revealed."

Volkelt writes: "It is particularly noteworthy how easily memories of childhood and youth enter into the dream. What we long ago stopped thinking about, what has long since lost all importance for us, the dream recalls again and again."

The dream's command over this childhood material, which, as is well known, mostly fills the gaps in conscious memory, gives rise to some interesting hypermnesic dreams, dreams in which memory reaches beyond its waking limits. I will report a few of them here.

Maury relates that as a child he often traveled from his native town of Meaux to nearby Trilport, where his father was supervising the construction of a bridge. One night a dream carried him back to Trilport, and he was once again playing in its streets. A man wearing some kind of uniform came up to him. Maury asked his name, and the man introduced himself as C——, a guard on the bridge. When he woke, Maury still doubted that the memory was real, so he asked his old servant, who had been with him since childhood, whether she remembered a man by that name. "Certainly," she answered. "He used to be the watchman on the bridge your father was building back then."

Maury reports another example that shows just as neatly how reliable the childhood memories that surface in dreams can be. A Mr. F——, who had spent his childhood in Montbrison, decided after an absence of twenty-five years to visit his hometown and the old friends of his family. The night before he left, he dreamed that he had already arrived, and that near Montbrison he met a man he did not recognize by sight, who told him he was Mr. F., a friend of his father's. The dreamer remembered that as a child he had known a gentleman of that name, but once awake he could no longer recall the man's face. Several days later, having actually arrived in Montbrison, he found the place from his dream, which he had supposed was unknown to him, and there he met a man whom he immediately recognized as the Mr. F. of the dream. The real man was simply older than the figure in the dream.

I can add one of my own dreams, in which the remembered impression was replaced by an association. In the dream I saw a person whom I recognized, while still dreaming, as the doctor from my hometown. His features were indistinct and blended with the image of one of my teachers, a colleague whom I still see now and then. When I woke I could find no connection between the two men. But when I asked my mother about the doctor of my early childhood, I learned that he had been blind in one eye. My teacher, whose figure had covered over the doctor's in the dream, was also blind in one eye. I have not seen that doctor in thirty-eight years, and so far as I know I have never thought of him while awake, even though a scar on my chin might have reminded me of his care.

As if to offset the enormous role assigned to childhood impressions in dreams, many writers maintain that most dreams contain elements from the very recent past. Robert, for instance, declares that the normal dream is generally concerned only with impressions from the last few days. Robert's theory of the dream, as we will see, absolutely requires that old impressions be pushed into the background and recent ones brought forward. All the same, the fact he describes is real, and my own investigations confirm it. Nelson, an American writer, believes that the impressions found most often in dreams date from two or three days earlier, as though the impressions of the day immediately before the dream were not yet faint and distant enough.

Many writers who are convinced of a close connection between the content of dreams and waking life have been struck by the fact that impressions which have absorbed the waking mind intensely appear in dreams only after they have been pushed, to some degree, out of the work of waking thought. As a rule, for example, we do not dream of someone we loved who has died while we are still overwhelmed by grief. Yet Miss Hallam, one of the most recent observers, has collected examples of exactly the opposite pattern, and she defends this point as a matter of individual psychology.

The third peculiarity of memory in dreams, and the most remarkable and baffling, lies in how it selects the material it reproduces. The dream gives weight not only to the most significant memories but also to the most trivial and superficial ones. On this point I will quote the writers who have voiced their surprise most forcefully.

Hildebrandt: "It is a remarkable fact that dreams do not, as a rule, draw their elements from great and deep-rooted events, or from the powerful and pressing concerns of the previous day, but from unimportant matters, from the most worthless scraps of recent experience or of the more distant past. The most shocking death in our family, whose impressions keep us awake far into the night, is wiped from our memory until the first moment of waking brings it back with crushing force. Meanwhile, the wart on the forehead of a passing stranger, whom we did not think about for a single second once he was out of sight, plays its part in our dreams."

Strümpell: "...cases in which the analysis of a dream brings to light elements that, though they come from the events of the previous day or the day before that, prove so unimportant and worthless to the waking mind that they slip into oblivion soon after they occur. They may be remarks by others overheard by chance, actions observed in passing, fleeting glimpses of things or people, single phrases from books, and so on."

Havelock Ellis: "The profound emotions of waking life, the questions and problems on which we spend our chief voluntary mental energy, are not the ones that usually present themselves at once to dream-consciousness. So far as the immediate past is concerned, it is mostly the trifling, incidental, 'forgotten' impressions of daily life that reappear in our dreams. The mental activities that are most intensely awake are those that sleep most profoundly."

Binz takes these features of memory in dreams as an occasion to express his dissatisfaction with explanations of dreams that he himself had endorsed: "And the normal dream raises similar questions. Why do we not always dream of memories from the preceding days, instead of reaching back, for no apparent reason, to an almost forgotten past that lies far behind us? Why in dreams does consciousness so often revive the impressions of indifferent memory images, while the brain cells that carry the most sensitive records of experience remain for the most part inert and numb, unless some sharp revival during waking life has stirred them shortly before?"

It is easy to see how the dream memory's strange preference for the indifferent, and therefore unnoticed, details of daily experience usually leads us to overlook entirely the dream's dependence on waking life, or at least makes that dependence hard to prove in any particular case. This is how Miss Whiton Calkins, in her statistical study of her own dreams and those of a friend, came to find that 11 percent of all the dreams showed no connection to waking life. Hildebrandt was surely right to assert that every one of our dream images could be explained by its origins if we devoted enough time and material to tracing them. He does, admittedly, call this "a most tedious and thankless job." At best, he says, it would lead us to dig out all sorts of worthless mental material from the remotest corners of the memory, and to bring to light trivial moments from the distant past that were perhaps buried within an hour of occurring. I must say, however, that I regret this perceptive writer declined to follow a road whose beginning looked so unpromising, because it would have led him straight to the heart of the dream problem.

The behavior of memory in dreams is certainly of the greatest significance for any theory of memory in general. It teaches us that "nothing we have once possessed mentally is ever entirely lost," as Scholz puts it; or, in Delbœuf's words, that "every impression, even the most insignificant, leaves an unalterable trace, capable of reappearing at any time." Many other pathological phenomena of mental life push us toward the same conclusion. We should keep this extraordinary capacity of memory in dreams firmly in mind, so that we can see clearly the contradictions that certain dream theories, to be discussed later, are forced to put forward when they try to explain the absurdity and incoherence of dreams by a partial forgetting of what we knew during the day.

One might even think of reducing dreaming to a phenomenon of memory, treating the dream as the expression of a reproductive activity that never rests, even at night, and that exists for its own sake. Views like those of Pilcz would seem to support this. According to Pilcz, close relations can be demonstrated between the time at which we dream and the content of the dream: the impressions a dream reproduces in deep sleep belong to the most distant past, while those reproduced toward morning are recent. But the way the dream actually handles the material it remembers makes such a conception unlikely from the start. Strümpell rightly points out that experiences are not repeated in dreams. The dream does make an attempt in that direction, but the next link is missing, or it appears in altered form, or it is replaced by something entirely new. The dream offers only fragments of reproduction, and this is so consistently the rule that it can be put to theoretical use. Still, there are exceptions, in which a dream repeats an episode as completely as waking memory would. Delbœuf tells of a university colleague who relived in a dream, in every detail, a dangerous carriage ride from which he had escaped injury as if by a miracle. Miss Calkins mentions two dreams whose content exactly reproduced incidents from the previous day, and I will later have occasion to report an example that came to my attention, in which a childhood experience returned unchanged in a dream.

**(c) Dream Stimuli and Dream Sources.** What is meant by dream stimuli and dream sources can be explained by way of the popular saying, "Dreams come from the stomach." Behind this notion lies a theory that sees the dream as the result of a disturbance of sleep. We would not have dreamed if something disturbing had not arisen during sleep, and the dream is the reaction to that disturbance.

The question of what provokes dreams takes up more space than any other in the writers' accounts. It goes without saying that this problem could arise only once the dream had become an object of biological investigation. The ancients, who regarded the dream as divinely inspired, had no need to look for its source; for them the dream came from the will of divine or demonic powers, and its content was the product of what those powers knew or intended. Science, however, soon raised the question of whether the stimulus to dreaming is always the same or whether it can take many forms, and this in turn led to the question of whether the causal explanation of the dream belongs to psychology or to physiology. Most writers seem to assume that the causes of disturbed sleep, and therefore the sources of dreams, can be of various kinds, and that physical as well as mental stimuli can act as instigators of dreams. Opinions differ widely over which of these sources deserves preference, how they should be ranked, and indeed how important each is for the origin of dreams.

Wherever the list of dream sources is complete, it comes down in the end to four types, which are also used to classify dreams:

I. External (objective) sensory stimuli.

II. Internal (subjective) sensory stimuli.

III. Internal (organic) physical stimuli.

IV. Purely mental sources of stimulation.

**I. External Sensory Stimuli.** The younger Strümpell, son of the philosopher whose writings on dreams have already guided us more than once, has reported, as is well known, his observations of a patient who suffered from a general loss of sensation in the skin and from paralysis of several of the higher sense organs. This man fell asleep whenever the few sensory channels still connecting him to the outside world were closed off. When we want to sleep, we usually try to bring about a situation much like the one in Strümpell's case. We close off the most important sensory channel, the eyes, and we try to shield the other senses from every stimulus and from every change in the stimuli acting on them. Then we fall asleep, even though our preparations never fully succeed. We can neither keep all stimuli away from our sense organs nor entirely extinguish the sensitivity of those organs. The fact that a strong enough stimulus can wake us at any moment should prove to us "that the mind remains in constant contact with the material world even during sleep." The sensory stimuli that reach us while we sleep can easily become the sources of dreams.

There are a great many stimuli of this kind. They range from the unavoidable ones, which the state of sleep itself brings with it or at least occasionally produces, to accidental stimuli that are suited, or even designed, to end sleep. A strong light may force its way into the eyes, a noise may become audible, or some odor may irritate the lining of the nose. In the spontaneous movements of sleep we may uncover parts of the body and expose them to the cold, or by shifting position we may produce sensations of pressure and touch. A fly may bite us, or some small accident in the night may strike more than one sense at once. Observers have drawn attention to a whole series of dreams in which the stimulus, verified on waking, corresponded so closely to part of the dream's content that it could be identified as the dream's source.

I will cite here a number of such dreams, collected by Jessen, that can be traced to more or less accidental objective sensory stimuli. "Every dimly perceived noise gives rise to corresponding dream images. The rolling of thunder puts us in the thick of battle, the crowing of a rooster may be transformed into human screams of terror, and the creaking of a door may conjure up dreams of burglars breaking into the house. When one of our blankets slips off in the night, we may dream that we are walking around naked or falling into water. If we lie diagonally across the bed with our feet sticking out past the edge, we may dream that we are standing at the brink of a terrifying precipice, or falling from a great height. If our head happens to slip under the pillow, we may imagine a huge rock hanging over us, about to crush us beneath its weight. A buildup of semen produces erotic dreams, and local pain produces the idea of being mistreated, of hostile attacks, or of accidental injury."

"Meier, in his *Attempt at an Explanation of Sleepwalking* (Halle, 1758), once dreamed that he was set upon by several people who threw him flat on the ground and drove a stake into the earth between his big toe and the next. While he was imagining this in the dream, he suddenly woke and felt a piece of straw stuck between his toes. On another occasion, according to Hemmings in *On Dreams and Sleepwalking* (Weimar, 1784), the same writer dreamed he was being hanged when his shirt had been pinned somewhat tightly around his neck. Hauffbauer dreamed in his youth that he had fallen from a high wall, and on waking found that the bedframe had come apart and he had actually fallen to the floor.... Gregory relates that he once put a hot-water bottle at his feet and dreamed that he was climbing to the summit of Mount Etna, where he found the ground almost unbearably hot. Another man, after a blistering plaster had been applied to his head, dreamed that he was being scalped by Indians; a third, whose shirt was damp, dreamed he was being dragged through a stream. An attack of gout led one patient to believe that he was in the hands of the Inquisition, suffering the pains of torture (Macnish)."

The argument from the resemblance between stimulus and dream content gains strength if, by deliberately applying stimuli, we can produce dreams that correspond to them. According to Macnish, Giron de Buzareingues had already carried out such experiments. "He left his knee uncovered and dreamed that he was traveling at night by mail coach. He remarked in this connection that travelers would know well how cold one's knees get in a coach at night. Another time he left the back of his head uncovered and dreamed that he was taking part in an open-air religious ceremony. In the region where he lived, it was the custom to keep the head covered at all times except on such occasions."

Maury reports new observations of dreams he induced in himself. (A number of other attempts produced no result.)

1. He was tickled with a feather on his lips and on the tip of his nose. He dreamed of a horrible torture: a mask of pitch was stuck to his face and then ripped off, taking the skin with it.

2. Scissors were sharpened against a pair of pincers. He heard bells ringing, then the sounds of an alarm, which carried him back to the June Days of 1848, the uprising in Paris that year.

3. Eau de Cologne was held under his nose. He found himself in Cairo, in the shop of Johann Maria Farina, the maker of the original cologne. This was followed by wild adventures that he could not reconstruct.

4. His neck was lightly pinched. He dreamed that a blistering plaster was being applied to him, and he thought of a doctor who had treated him as a child.

5. A hot iron was brought close to his face. He dreamed that *chauffeurs*, the bands of robbers who terrorized the French countryside in the revolutionary period and were named for their practice of "heating" their victims, had broken into the house and were forcing the occupants to hand over their money by thrusting their feet into burning coals. Then the Duchess of Abrantès entered, whose secretary he imagined himself to be in the dream.

6. A drop of water was let fall on his forehead. He imagined himself in Italy, sweating heavily and drinking the white wine of Orvieto.

7. When light from a burning candle was repeatedly directed onto him through red paper, he dreamed of the weather, of heat, and of a storm at sea that he had once lived through in the English Channel.

D'Hervey, Weygandt, and others have made further attempts to produce dreams experimentally.

Many observers have remarked on the dream's striking skill at weaving sudden impressions from the outside world into its structure, so that they appear as the climax of a gradually prepared and long-anticipated catastrophe. Hildebrandt relates: "In earlier years I occasionally used an alarm clock to wake regularly at a certain hour in the morning. It must have happened hundreds of times that the sound of this device fitted into what seemed a very long and connected dream, as if the whole dream had been designed especially for it, as if it found in that sound its proper and logically necessary climax, its inevitable conclusion."

I will cite three of these alarm-clock dreams for another purpose shortly.

Volkelt relates: "A composer once dreamed that he was teaching school and was in the middle of explaining something to his pupils. He had nearly finished when he turned to one of the boys and asked, 'Did you understand me?' The boy shouted back like a man possessed, 'Ya!' Annoyed, the teacher scolded him for shouting. But now the whole class was screaming 'Orya!', then 'Euryo!', and finally 'Feueryo!', the old German cry of 'Fire!' He was then woken by an actual fire alarm in the street."

Garnier, in his *Treatise on the Faculties of the Soul* (1865), as reported by Radestock, relates that Napoleon I, while asleep in a carriage, was woken from a dream by an explosion. The dream had carried him back to the crossing of the Tagliamento and the bombardment of the Austrians, so that he started up, crying, "We are undermined!"

The following dream of Maury's has become famous. He was ill and confined to bed, with his mother sitting beside him. He dreamed of the Reign of Terror during the Revolution. He witnessed terrible scenes of murder, and was finally summoned before the Revolutionary Tribunal himself. There he saw Robespierre, Marat, Fouquier-Tinville, and all the grim heroes of that cruel era. He had to give an account of himself, and after all sorts of incidents that did not stay in his memory, he was sentenced to death. Accompanied by an enormous crowd, he was led to the place of execution. He climbed the scaffold, the executioner strapped him to the board, the board tipped forward, and the blade of the guillotine fell. He felt his head separate from his body and woke in terrible anguish, only to find that the top rail of the bed had fallen and struck the back of his neck exactly as the blade of a guillotine would have.

This dream prompted a lively discussion in the *Revue Philosophique*, begun by Le Lorrain and Egger. The question was whether, and how, the dreamer could have compressed so much apparent dream content into the brief interval between perceiving the stimulus and waking up.

Examples like these make objective stimuli during sleep seem the most firmly established of all dream sources; indeed, they are the only source that figures at all in the layman's understanding. If we ask an educated person who is unfamiliar with the literature on dreams how dreams arise, he is sure to answer by pointing to some case he knows of, in which a dream was explained after waking by an identifiable objective stimulus. Scientific inquiry cannot stop there, however. It is driven to look further by the observation that the stimulus acting on the senses during sleep never appears in the dream in its true form, but is replaced by some other image that is related to it in one way or another. The relation between the stimulus and the resulting dream is, in Maury's words, "some affinity or other, but one that is neither unique nor exclusive." If we read, for example, three of Hildebrandt's alarm-clock dreams, we are bound to ask why the same stimulus produced such different results, and why it produced these particular results and no others.

"I am taking a walk on a beautiful spring morning. I stroll through the green fields toward a neighboring village, where I see the villagers, dressed in their Sunday clothes and carrying their hymnbooks under their arms, heading to church in great numbers. I remember that it is Sunday and that the morning service will soon begin. I decide to attend, but since I am somewhat overheated, I also decide to cool off first in the churchyard that surrounds the church. While I am reading the various epitaphs, I hear the sexton climb the tower, and I see, high in the belfry, the small village bell that is about to signal the start of the service. For a little while longer it hangs motionless; then it begins to swing, and suddenly its notes ring out so clearly and piercingly that my sleep comes to an end. But the sound of bells is coming from the alarm clock."

"A second combination. It is a bright day, and the streets lie under deep snow. I have promised to join a sleigh ride, but I have had to wait some time before word comes that the sleigh is at my door. Now the preparations for climbing in are made: I put on my furs, adjust my muff, and at last I am in my seat. Yet the departure is still delayed, until the reins give the impatient horses their unmistakable signal. They set off, and the sleigh bells, now shaken hard, strike up their familiar Janissary music, the clashing, jingling din of the old Turkish military bands, with a force that instantly tears through the gossamer of my dream. Again it is only the shrill sound of my alarm clock."

And a third example: "I see the kitchen maid walking down the corridor to the dining room with several dozen plates piled in her arms. The column of porcelain seems to me in danger of losing its balance. 'Be careful,' I cry, 'you'll drop the whole stack.' The usual retort is, of course, not long in coming: she is used to such things. Meanwhile I keep following her with an anxious eye, and sure enough, at the threshold the fragile dishes fall, tumble, and scatter across the floor in hundreds of pieces. But I soon notice that the noise, which goes on and on, is not really a clatter at all but a genuine ringing, and with this ringing the dreamer now realizes that the alarm clock has done its job."

Why does the dreaming mind misjudge the nature of the objective sensory stimulus? Strümpell, and Wundt in nearly identical terms, have answered that the mind reacts to the stimuli that assail it during sleep by forming illusions. We recognize a sensory impression and interpret it correctly, that is, we assign it to the group of memories where all our previous experience tells us it belongs, provided the impression is strong, clear, and lasting enough, and provided we have the time needed for this reflection. When these conditions are not met, we mistake the object that gives rise to the impression, and on that basis we form an illusion. "If someone walking in an open field makes out a distant object indistinctly, he may at first take it for a horse." On closer inspection the image of a cow lying down may press itself upon him, and the impression may finally resolve itself, with certainty, into a group of people sitting together. The impressions the mind receives during sleep from external stimuli are similarly indistinct. They give rise to illusions because the impression calls up a greater or smaller number of memory images, and it is through these that the impression acquires its psychic value. Which of the many relevant regions of memory supplies the corresponding images, and which of the possible associative links come into play, remains, even by Strümpell's own account, impossible to determine. It is left, so to speak, to the whims of mental life.

Here we have a choice. We may concede that the laws of dream formation really cannot be traced any further, and so refrain from asking whether the interpretation of the illusion called up by the sensory impression depends on still other conditions. Or we may suppose that the objective sensory stimulus that breaks in upon sleep plays only a modest part as a source of dreams, and that other factors determine which memory image is called up. Indeed, if we examine closely the dreams Maury produced experimentally, which I have deliberately reported in detail, we are inclined to think that the experiment really explains the origin of only one element in each dream. The rest of the dream content seems too independent, too precisely determined in its details, to be explained by the single requirement that it fit the element introduced by the experiment. One even begins to doubt the illusion theory, and the power of the objective impression to shape the dream, on learning that during sleep this impression sometimes receives the strangest and most far-fetched interpretations. M. Simon, for instance, describes a dream in which he saw people of gigantic size seated at a table and distinctly heard the dreadful clatter of their jaws snapping together as they chewed. On waking, he heard the hoofbeats of a horse galloping past his window. Suppose the sound of the hoofs had called up ideas from the memory sphere of *Gulliver's Travels*, from the visit to the giants of Brobdingnag and from the virtuous horse-creatures, as I might perhaps interpret it without any help from the author. Should not the choice of a memory sphere so remote from the stimulus be further illuminated by other motives?

II. Internal (Subjective) Sensory Stimuli. Whatever objections may be raised, we must grant that the role of objective sensory stimuli in producing dreams has been established beyond dispute. If these stimuli nevertheless seem insufficient, in kind and frequency, to explain all dream images, we are led to look for other sources of dreams that act in a similar way. I do not know where the idea first arose that internal, subjective stimuli should be considered alongside external sensory stimuli, but in fact this is done more or less thoroughly in all the more recent accounts of the causes of dreams. "An important part in dream illusions," writes Wundt, "is played by those subjective sensations of sight and hearing that we know in the waking state as the luminous chaos in the dark field of vision, the ringing or buzzing in the ears, and so on, and especially by irritation of the retina. This explains the dream's remarkable tendency to dazzle the eyes with multitudes of similar or identical objects. We see spread out before us countless birds, butterflies, fish, colored beads, flowers, and the like. Here the luminous dust in the dark field of vision has taken on fantastic shapes, and the dream embodies each of the many points of light that make it up as a separate image, which is perceived as a moving object because the luminous chaos is itself in motion. This is also the root of the dream's great fondness for the most elaborate animal forms, since the multiplicity of shapes readily follows the form of the subjective light images."

As a source of dreams, subjective sensory stimuli have the obvious advantage that, unlike objective stimuli, they do not depend on external accident. They are available to the explanation, so to speak, whenever it needs them. They are inferior to objective stimuli, however, in that their role as instigators of dreams, which observation and experiment have demonstrated for objective stimuli, can be verified only with difficulty, if at all. The chief evidence for the dream-producing power of subjective sensory excitation comes from the so-called hypnagogic hallucinations, which Johannes Müller described as "fantastic visual phenomena." These are the very vivid and shifting images that appear regularly to many people as they fall asleep, and that may linger for a while even after the eyes have been opened. Maury, who was much troubled by them, studied them thoroughly and maintained that they are related to, or rather identical with, the images of dreams, as Müller had already asserted. Maury states that a certain mental passivity is necessary for them to arise: the strain of attention must slacken. But in an ordinary state of mind one can produce a hypnagogic hallucination by sinking for a second into such lethargy, after which one may wake again, until this oft-repeated process ends in sleep. If one wakes shortly afterward, Maury reports, it is often possible to find in the dream the same images that appeared as hypnagogic hallucinations before one fell asleep. This once happened to him with a group of grotesque figures, with distorted features and strange headdresses, which forced themselves upon him with incredible persistence as he was falling asleep and which, on waking, he remembered having dreamed. On another occasion, when he was hungry because he was keeping to a rather strict diet, he saw hypnagogically a plate and a hand holding a fork that was taking food from it. In his dream he found himself at a table laden with food and heard the clatter of the diners' forks. On yet another occasion, having fallen asleep with irritated and painful eyes, he had the hypnagogic hallucination of microscopically small characters, which he was forced to decipher one by one with great effort. When he was awakened an hour later, he recalled a dream of an open book in very small print, which he had been obliged to read through with laborious effort.

Just as with these images, auditory hallucinations of words, names, and so forth may also appear hypnagogically and then recur in the dream, like an overture announcing the principal theme of the opera to follow.

A more recent observer of hypnagogic hallucinations, George Trumbull Ladd, has followed the path taken by Müller and Maury. Through practice he acquired the ability to rouse himself abruptly, without opening his eyes, two to five minutes after gradually falling asleep. This gave him the opportunity to compare the retinal sensations that were just fading with the dream images still in his memory. He assures us that a close relation between the two can always be recognized, in the sense that the luminous dots and lines of the retina's spontaneous light furnished, as it were, the sketched outline or framework for the dream figures perceived by the mind. A dream, for example, in which he saw clearly printed lines in front of him, which he read and studied, corresponded to an arrangement of the luminous dots and lines in the retina into parallel rows. In his own words: "The clearly printed page that he was reading in the dream resolved itself into an object that appeared to his waking perception like part of a real printed sheet seen through a small hole in a piece of paper, from too great a distance to be made out distinctly." Without in any way underestimating the central, mental part of the phenomenon, Ladd believes that hardly any visual dream arises in our minds that is not based on material supplied by this internal state of stimulation in the retina. This is especially true of dreams that occur shortly after one falls asleep in a dark room, whereas dreams that occur in the morning, near the time of waking, draw their stimulation from the objective light that enters the eye from the brightening room. The shifting, endlessly variable character of the retina's spontaneous luminous excitation corresponds exactly to the restless succession of images our dreams present. If we give any weight to Ladd's observations, we cannot underestimate how productive this subjective source of excitation is for the dream, since visual images apparently form the principal ingredient of our dreams. The contribution of the other senses, apart from hearing, is slighter and less constant.

III. Internal (Organic) Physical Stimulation. If we are inclined to look for the sources of dreams not outside the organism but within it, we must remember that almost all our internal organs, which in health scarcely remind us of their existence, can, in states of excitation, as we call them, or in disease, become sources of the most painful sensations, which must be placed on the same footing as external causes of pain and sensory stimuli. It is on the strength of very old experience that Strümpell, for example, declares that "during sleep the mind becomes far more deeply and broadly aware of its connection with the body than in the waking state, and it is compelled to receive, and be influenced by, stimulating impressions that arise from parts and changes of the body of which it is unaware while awake." Even Aristotle considered it quite possible that the dream might draw our attention to the first signs of illness, which we had not noticed at all while awake, because the dream exaggerates the impressions. Some medical writers, who were certainly far from believing in any prophetic power of dreams, have granted dreams this significance at least for the forecasting of disease, as M. Simon and many older authors attest.

Even in our own time there seems to be no shortage of well-documented examples of such diagnostic feats on the part of the dream. Tissié, for instance, cites from Artigues's *Essai sur la valeur séméiologique des rêves* (Essay on the Symptomatic Value of Dreams) the case of a forty-three-year-old woman who, during several years of apparently perfect health, was troubled by anxiety dreams. A medical examination later revealed an incipient heart disease, to which she soon succumbed.

Serious disorders of the internal organs evidently act as instigators of dreams in a considerable number of people. Writers quite generally note the frequency of anxiety dreams in diseases of the heart and lungs; indeed, so many authors, among them Radestock, Spitta, Maury, M. Simon, and Tissié, give this aspect of dream life such prominence that I shall content myself here with simply referring to them. Tissié even supposes that diseased organs stamp their own characteristic features on the content of the dream. The dreams of people with heart disease are generally very brief and end in a terrified awakening, and the situation of dying under dreadful circumstances almost always figures in their content. People with lung disease dream of suffocation, of being crushed in a crowd, and of flight, and a great many of them suffer from the familiar nightmare, which, incidentally, Boerner succeeded in producing experimentally by lying face down and blocking the openings of the airways. In digestive disorders the dream contains ideas drawn from the sphere of pleasure and disgust. Finally, the influence of sexual excitement on the content of dreams is plain enough in everyone's experience, and it lends the strongest support to the whole theory that dreams are stimulated by organic sensation.

Moreover, in reading through the literature on dreams, it becomes quite obvious that some of the authors, Maury and Weygandt among them, were led to study the problems of the dream by the influence that their own pathological conditions exerted on the content of their dreams.

Yet these undoubtedly established facts add less to our stock of dream sources than one might suppose. The dream is a phenomenon that occurs in healthy people, perhaps in everyone and every night, and a diseased state of the organs is clearly not one of its necessary conditions. For our purposes, the question is not where particular dreams come from, but what the stimulating source of the ordinary dreams of normal people might be.

We need go only one step further, however, to find a source of dreams more abundant than any mentioned so far, one that promises indeed to be inexhaustible in every case. If it is established that the bodily organs in illness become a stimulating source of dreams, and if we grant that the mind, turned away from the outer world during sleep, can devote more attention to the interior of the body, then we may readily assume that the organs need not become diseased in order to send the sleeping mind stimuli that somehow grow into dream images. In the waking state we perceive, in a broad and diffuse way, a general feeling of the body, distinguishable only by its quality, to which, in the view of physicians, every organic system contributes its share. At night this general feeling would gain powerful force and become active through its individual components, and it would naturally provide both the most powerful and the most common source for the production of dream images. It still remains to be examined, however, by what rule organic sensations are transformed into dream images.

The theory of the origin of dreams just described has been the favorite of all medical writers. The obscurity that hides the core of our being, the *moi splanchnique*, or "visceral self," as Tissié calls it, from our knowledge, and the obscurity surrounding the origin of dreams, match each other too well not to be linked. The line of thought that makes organic sensation the instigator of dreams has a further appeal for the physician: it supports a common causal origin for dreams and mental illnesses, which resemble each other in so many of their manifestations, since changes in organic feeling and stimuli arising from the internal organs are both widely held to be of great importance in the origin of the psychoses. It is therefore not surprising that the theory of bodily sensation can be traced to more than one originator, each of whom proposed it independently.

A number of authors have been influenced by the line of thought developed by the philosopher Schopenhauer in 1851. Our picture of the universe, in his view, arises because our intellect recasts the impressions that reach it from outside in the molds of time, space, and causality. Sensations from the interior of the organism, conveyed by the sympathetic nervous system, exert during the day an influence on our mood that is for the most part unconscious. At night, however, when the overwhelming effect of the day's impressions is no longer felt, the impressions pressing upward from within can win attention, just as at night we hear the murmur of a spring that the noise of the day had drowned out. How else, then, could the intellect respond to these stimuli than by performing its characteristic function? It will transform them into figures that occupy space and time and move along the thread of causality, and so the dream comes into being. Scherner, and Volkelt after him, attempted to trace closer connections between physical sensations and dream images, but we shall reserve discussion of these attempts for the chapter on the theory of the dream.

In a study notable for its logical rigor, the psychiatrist Krauss located the origin of dreams, as well as of delirium and delusions, in the same element: organically determined sensation. According to Krauss, there is hardly a spot in the organism that might not become the starting point of a dream or a delusion. Organically determined sensations, he writes, "may be divided into two classes: first, those of the total feeling, or general sensations; and second, specific sensations inherent in the principal systems of the vegetative organism, which fall into five groups: the muscular, the respiratory, the gastric, the sexual, and the peripheral sensations." Krauss conceives the origin of the dream image from physical sensation as follows. The aroused sensation calls up an idea related to it according to some law of association and combines with that idea to form an organic structure. Toward this structure, however, consciousness does not take its normal attitude: it pays no attention to the sensation itself and concerns itself entirely with the accompanying idea. This, he holds, is also why the true state of affairs has been misunderstood for so long. Krauss coins a specific term for the process: the "transubstantiation of feeling into dream images."

That organic bodily sensations exert some influence on the formation of dreams is almost universally acknowledged today, but the question of what law governs the relation between the two receives various answers, often couched in obscure terms. Under the theory of bodily stimulation, the particular task of dream interpretation is to trace the content of a dream back to the organic stimulus that caused it. Unless we accept the rules of interpretation proposed by Scherner, we are often confronted with the awkward fact that the organic source of stimulation reveals itself only in the content of the dream.

A certain consensus does appear, however, in the interpretation of the various forms of dream called "typical" because they recur in so many people with nearly the same content. Among these are the familiar dreams of falling from a height, of teeth falling out, of flying, and of embarrassment at being naked or scantily dressed. This last dream is said to be caused simply by the perception, during sleep, that one has thrown off the bedcovers and lies exposed. The dream of teeth falling out is explained by "dental irritation," which need not, however, imply any morbid state of excitation in the teeth. According to Strümpell, the flying dream is the fitting image the mind uses to interpret the sum of stimuli arising from the rise and fall of the lungs, once the skin of the chest has become insensible; it is this latter circumstance that produces a sensation akin to the idea of flying. Falling from a height in a dream is said to occur because, after awareness of the pressure on the skin has lapsed, either an arm drops away from the body or a bent knee is suddenly straightened, so that the feeling of pressure on the skin returns to consciousness, and this passage into consciousness takes mental form as a dream of falling. The weakness of these plausible attempts at explanation clearly lies in the fact that, without any further justification, they allow one or another group of organic sensations to vanish from mental perception or to force itself upon it, until the combination of circumstances needed for the explanation has been arranged. I shall have occasion later, however, to return to typical dreams and their origin.

By comparing a series of similar dreams, M. Simon tried to formulate certain rules for how organic sensations influence the character of the resulting dream. He writes: "If any organic apparatus that normally takes part in the expression of an emotion enters, for whatever reason, during sleep into the state of excitation to which that emotion usually rouses it, the resulting dream will contain ideas appropriate to that emotion."

Another of his rules reads: "If an organic apparatus is in a state of activity, excitation, or disturbance during sleep, the dream will bring forth ideas related to the exercise of the organic function that apparatus performs."

Mourly Vold has undertaken to prove experimentally the influence that the theory of bodily sensation assumes for a single domain. He altered the positions of sleepers' limbs and then compared the resulting dreams with the changes he had made. From these experiments he reports the following propositions:

1. The position of a limb in a dream corresponds approximately to its position in reality; that is, we dream of the limb in a static condition that matches its actual condition.

2. When we dream of a limb in motion, one of the positions passed through in carrying out that movement always corresponds to the limb's real position.

3. In the dream, the position of one's own limb may be attributed to another person.

4. One may also dream that the movement in question is obstructed.

5. A limb in some particular position may appear in the dream as an animal or a monster, in which case a certain analogy is established between the two.

6. The position of a limb may prompt ideas in the dream that bear some relation or other to that limb. If our fingers are occupied, for example, we dream of numbers.

Results like these would lead me to conclude that even the theory of bodily sensation cannot entirely eliminate the apparent freedom with which the dream determines which image is to be called up.

**IV. Psychic Sources of Stimulation.** In discussing how the dream relates to waking life and where dream material comes from, we learned that investigators, the earliest as well as the most recent, agreed that people dream about what they do during the day and about what interests them while they are awake. This interest, carried over from waking life into sleep, is more than a psychic bond joining the dream to life. It also supplies a source of dreams that should not be underestimated, one that, taken together with the stimuli that become interesting and active during sleep, suffices to explain the origin of every dream image. Yet we have also heard the opposite claim: that the dream draws the sleeper away from the concerns of the day, and that in most cases we do not dream of the things that have occupied our attention during the day until they have lost, for waking life, the stimulus of immediacy. At every step in the analysis of dream life, then, we are reminded that it is not permissible to lay down general rules without making room for qualifications such as "frequently," "as a rule," and "in most cases," and without allowing for the validity of the exceptions.

If conscious interest, together with the inner and outer stimuli of sleep, were enough to account for the causes of dreams, we ought to be able to give a satisfactory account of the origin of every element in a dream. The riddle of dream sources would then be solved, leaving only the task of separating the parts played by psychic and by somatic stimuli in individual dreams. In fact, however, no such complete solution of a dream has ever been achieved in any case. What is more, everyone who has attempted one has found that, in most cases, a great many components of the dream remained whose source he could not explain. The interests of the day, as a psychic source of dreams, plainly do not reach far enough to justify the confident assertion that we all carry on our waking affairs in our dreams.

No other psychic sources of dreams are known. With the possible exception of the explanation offered by Scherner, which will be discussed later, every account in the literature therefore shows a large gap when it comes to deriving the material for the visual images that are most characteristic of the dream. Faced with this dilemma, most authors have tended to play down as far as possible the psychic factor in the stimulation of dreams, since it is so difficult to approach.
