They do, of course, divide dreams into two main classes, the nerve-stimulus dream and the association dream, and they assert that the latter springs exclusively from the reproduction of earlier material, as Wundt does. But they still cannot dispel the doubt, voiced by Volkelt, whether such dreams "do not appear without being impelled by a psychic stimulus." The distinctive quality of the pure association dream also proves elusive. In Volkelt's words: "In association dreams proper we can no longer speak of such a firm nucleus. Here the loose grouping penetrates into the very center of the dream. Ideation, already set free from reason and intellect, is no longer held together here by the more important psychic and mental stimuli, but is left to its own aimless shifting and utter confusion."

Wundt, too, attempts to diminish the psychic factor in the stimulation of dreams. He declares that "the phantasms of the dream are certainly wrongly regarded as pure hallucinations," and that "most dream ideas are probably in reality illusions, since they proceed from faint sensory impressions that are never extinguished during sleep." Weygandt adopts this view but extends it to every case, asserting that "the first source of all dream ideas is a sensory stimulus, to which reproductive associations are then attached." Tissié goes further still in suppressing the psychic sources of stimulation: "Dreams of absolutely psychic origin do not exist," he writes, and elsewhere, "The thoughts of our dreams come to us from outside...."

Those authors who, like the influential philosopher Wundt, take a middle course do not fail to point out that in most dreams the somatic stimuli work together with the psychic instigators of the dream, the latter being either unknown or recognized as the interests of the day.

We shall learn later that the riddle of dream formation can be solved by uncovering an unsuspected psychic source of stimulation. For the present, we need not be surprised that the stimuli of non-psychic origin have been overestimated as factors in forming the dream. This is not only because they alone are easy to find and can even be confirmed by experiment; it is also because the somatic conception of the origin of dreams corresponds thoroughly to the mode of thought now prevailing in psychiatry. The brain's mastery over the organism is, to be sure, strongly emphasized. But anything that might demonstrate an independence of psychic life from verifiable organic changes, or a spontaneity in its manifestations, alarms the psychiatrist of today, as if acknowledging it would inevitably bring back the era of the philosophy of nature and the metaphysical conception of the soul's essence. The psychiatrist's distrust has placed the psyche under guardianship, so to speak, and now requires that none of its impulses reveal any capacity of its own. Such an attitude, however, shows little confidence in the strength of the causal chain that runs between the material and the psychic. Even where investigation shows the psychic to be the primary cause of a phenomenon, deeper inquiry will one day succeed in tracing the path further, to the organic determination of the psychic. But where the psychic must be taken, for now, as the limit of our knowledge, that is no reason to deny it.

**(d) Why the Dream Is Forgotten After Waking.** That a dream "fades away" in the morning is proverbial. It can, of course, be remembered, since we know the dream only by recalling it after we wake. But very often we believe that we remember it only incompletely, and that there was more of it during the night. We can watch the memory of a dream that was still vivid in the morning vanish over the course of the day, leaving only a few small fragments. We often know that we have dreamed, but not what. And we are so accustomed to dreams being forgotten that we do not reject as absurd the possibility that a person may have dreamed even when he knows nothing in the morning of either the content or the fact of the dream. On the other hand, dreams sometimes show an extraordinary persistence in memory. I have had occasion to analyze with my patients dreams they had had twenty-five years or more before, and I can remember a dream of my own that lies at least thirty-seven years in the past and yet has lost none of its freshness. All this is very remarkable, and for the present incomprehensible.

The forgetting of dreams is treated in greatest detail by Strümpell. It is evidently a complex phenomenon, for Strümpell explains it not by a single cause but by a considerable number of them.

In the first place, all the factors that produce forgetting in waking life also govern the forgetting of dreams. When awake, we tend quickly to forget a great many sensations and perceptions because they are too faint and carry too little emotional feeling. The same holds for many dream images: they are forgotten because they are too weak, while stronger images near them are remembered. Intensity alone, however, is not the only factor determining whether dream images are preserved. Strümpell, like other authors such as Calkins, concedes that dream images are often forgotten quickly even though they are known to have been vivid, while many of those retained in memory are very shadowy and indistinct. Second, in waking life we tend to forget easily what has happened only once and to notice more readily what recurs. Most dream images, however, are unique experiences, and this peculiarity contributes equally to the forgetting of all dreams. A third reason for forgetting is of greater importance. For feelings, ideas, thoughts, and the like to become memorable to any degree, it matters that they not remain isolated, but that they enter into connections and associations of a suitable kind. If the words of a short verse are taken and jumbled together, they will be very difficult to remember. "Arranged in a fitting sequence, one word helps another, and the whole, as meaning, stays easily and firmly in the memory for a long time. Contradictions we usually retain with as much difficulty, and as rarely, as things that are confused and disordered." Now, dreams in most cases lack sense and order. Dream compositions are by their very nature incapable of being remembered, and they are forgotten because they usually fall apart the very next moment. These conclusions, it should be said, do not entirely agree with Radestock's observation that we retain best precisely those dreams that are most peculiar.

According to Strümpell, still other factors in the forgetting of dreams arise from the relation of the dream to the waking state. Waking consciousness forgets dreams, evidently, as the counterpart of a fact already mentioned: the dream (almost) never takes over orderly sequences of memories from waking life, but only particular details, which it tears loose from the habitual psychic connections in which they are recalled while we are awake. The dream composition therefore has no place among the sequences of ideas that fill the mind, and it lacks every aid to memory. "In this way the dream structure rises, as it were, from the soil of our psychic life and floats in psychic space like a cloud in the sky, which the next breath of air soon disperses." The same effect is reinforced by the fact that on waking, our attention is immediately seized by the onrushing world of the senses, and very few dream images can withstand its force. They fade before the impressions of the new day as the light of the stars fades before the sun.

A final factor favoring the forgetting of dreams is that most people take little interest in them. Someone who studies dreams for a time and takes a special interest in them usually dreams more during that period than at any other; that is, he remembers his dreams more easily and more often.

Two further reasons for the forgetting of dreams, which Bonatelli added to Strümpell's list and which Benini reports, are already contained in Strümpell's account: first, that the change in general bodily feeling between sleeping and waking is unfavorable to the reproduction of one state's contents in the other; and second, that the different arrangement of ideational material in the dream makes it, so to speak, untranslatable for waking consciousness.

As Strümpell observes, it is all the more remarkable that, despite all these reasons for forgetting, so many dreams are retained in memory. The authors' persistent efforts to formulate laws for the remembering of dreams amount to an admission that here, too, something remains puzzling and unsolved. Certain peculiarities of dream memory have attracted particular notice in recent years: for instance, that a dream believed forgotten in the morning may be recalled during the day through some perception that happens to touch on its forgotten content, as Radestock and Tissié have noted. The whole of our memory of dreams, moreover, is open to an objection that, in critical eyes, sharply reduces its value. One may doubt whether our memory, which leaves out so much of the dream, does not also falsify what it retains.

Strümpell expresses such doubts about the accuracy with which dreams are reproduced: "It therefore easily happens that active consciousness involuntarily inserts a great deal into the recollection of the dream; one imagines that one has dreamed all sorts of things that the actual dream did not contain."

Jessen puts the matter very decidedly: "Moreover, we must not lose sight of a fact that has so far received little attention: in investigating and interpreting orderly and logical dreams, we almost always take liberties with the truth when we recall a dream to memory. Unconsciously and unintentionally we fill in the gaps and supplement the dream images. Rarely, perhaps never, has a connected dream been as connected as it appears to us in memory. Even the most truth-loving person can hardly recount a dream without exaggerating and embellishing it. The human mind's tendency to see everything as connected is so strong that, if a dream is recalled somewhat disconnectedly, the mind unwittingly supplies the missing connections."

The observations of V. Eggers, though surely arrived at independently, read almost like a translation of Jessen's words: "The observation of dreams has its own special difficulties, and the only way to avoid all error in such matters is to commit to paper, without the slightest delay, what one has just experienced and noticed. Otherwise forgetting comes quickly, whether total or partial. Total forgetting is of no consequence; but partial forgetting is treacherous. For if one then sets out to recount what one has not forgotten, one is liable to complete by imagination the incoherent and disjointed fragments supplied by memory.... One becomes an artist without knowing it, and the story, told again and again, imposes itself on the belief of its author, who in good faith presents it as an authentic fact, duly established by sound methods...."

Spitta makes a similar point. He seems to think that only in our attempt to reproduce the dream do we impose order on its loosely associated elements: "to make connection out of disconnection, that is, to add the process of logical connection that is absent from the dream."

Since we possess at present no other objective check on the reliability of our memory, and since such a check is in fact impossible when we examine a dream that is our own experience, with memory as its only source, the question arises of what value we can attach to our recollections of dreams at all.

**(e) The Psychological Peculiarities of Dreams.** In the scientific investigation of dreams, we start from the assumption that the dream is a product of our own psychic activity. Yet the finished dream strikes us as something alien, its authorship so little forced upon us that we can say "a dream came to me" as readily as "I dreamed." Where does this "psychic strangeness" of the dream come from? Judging from our discussion of the sources of dreams, we may suppose that it does not depend on the material that enters the dream content, since that material is largely shared by dream life and waking life. We may ask, then, whether it is changes in the psychic processes themselves that produce this impression in the dream, and in this way put a psychological characteristic of the dream to the test.

No one has emphasized more strongly the essential difference between dreaming and waking life, or drawn more far-reaching conclusions from it, than G. Th. Fechner, in some remarks in his *Elements of Psychophysics*. He holds that neither "the mere sinking of conscious psychic life below the main threshold" nor the withdrawal of attention from the influences of the outer world suffices to explain the peculiarities of dream life as compared with waking life. He believes, rather, that the scene of action of dreams is different from that of waking ideational life. "If the scene of psychophysical activity were the same during sleep and waking, the dream, in my view, could only be a continuation of waking ideation at a lower degree of intensity, and would have to share its material and its form. But the state of affairs is quite different."

What Fechner really meant has never been made clear, nor, to my knowledge, has anyone else followed the road whose starting point he indicated in this remark. An anatomical interpretation, in the sense of physiological localization in the brain or even with reference to the histological layers of the cerebral cortex, must surely be ruled out. The idea may yet prove ingenious and fruitful, however, if it can be applied to a psychic apparatus built out of a number of agencies arranged one behind another.

Other authors have been content to single out one or another of the tangible psychological peculiarities of dream life, and perhaps to use these as a starting point for more ambitious attempts at explanation.

It has rightly been observed that one of the chief peculiarities of dream life appears already in the state of falling asleep and may be called a sleep-onset phenomenon. According to Schleiermacher, what characterizes the waking state is that psychic activity takes place in concepts rather than in images. The dream, by contrast, thinks in images, and one can observe that as sleep approaches, voluntary activities become difficult in the same measure as involuntary ones appear, the latter belonging entirely to the class of images. The inability to perform the kind of mental work we experience as intentionally willed, and the appearance of images that regularly accompanies this lapse, are two qualities that persist throughout the dream, and in analyzing it psychologically we must recognize them as essential features of dream life. As for the images themselves, the hypnagogic hallucinations, we have found that even in content they are identical with the images of dreams.

The dream, then, thinks predominantly, though not exclusively, in visual images. It also makes use of auditory images and, to a lesser extent, of impressions from the other senses. Much in it is also simply thought or conceived, probably represented by remnants of verbal ideas, just as in the waking state. What is characteristic of the dream, however, is only those elements of its content that behave like images, that is, that resemble perceptions more than they resemble memories. Setting aside all the debates on the nature of hallucinations, familiar to every psychiatrist, we may say, with all authorities on the subject, that the dream hallucinates: it replaces thoughts with hallucinations. In this respect visual and auditory ideas behave alike. It has been observed that the memory of a sequence of musical sounds with which one falls asleep turns, as one sinks into sleep, into a hallucination of the same melody, only to give way again on waking, and this may alternate repeatedly with dozing off, to the softer and qualitatively different memory-ideas.

The transformation of an idea into a hallucination is not the only way in which the dream departs from a waking thought that might correspond to it. Out of these images the dream forms a situation; it presents something as happening now; it dramatizes an idea, as Spitta puts it. But this side of dream life is fully characterized only when we remember that while dreaming we do not, as a rule, imagine that we are thinking but rather that we are living through an experience; that is, we accept the hallucination in full belief. The exceptions require a special explanation. The critical recognition that we have not experienced anything, but have only thought it in a peculiar way, that we have dreamed it, comes to us only when we wake. This feature distinguishes the true dream of sleep from the daydream, which is never mistaken for reality.

Burdach has summed up the characteristics of dream life considered so far in the following sentences: "As characteristic features of the dream we may add (a) that the subjective activity of our mind appears as objective, inasmuch as our faculty of perception perceives the products of fantasy as if they were sensory impressions ... (b) that sleep abolishes self-command, so that falling asleep requires a certain passivity.... The images of slumber are conditioned by the relaxation of self-command."

The task now is to explain the mind's credulity toward dream hallucinations, which can appear only after a certain voluntary activity has been suspended. Strümpell asserts that in this respect the mind behaves correctly and in accordance with its own mechanism. Dream elements are by no means mere ideas; they are true and real experiences of the mind, like those that arise in the waking state through the senses. Whereas in waking life the mind represents and thinks in verbal images and language, in the dream it represents and thinks in real, tangible images. The dream also displays a consciousness of space, projecting sensations and images into an external space just as in the waking state. It must therefore be granted that in the dream the mind stands in the same relation to its images and perceptions as it does when awake. If it is nonetheless led astray, this is because in sleep it lacks the critical faculty that alone can distinguish between sense perceptions arising from within and those arising from without. It cannot submit its images to the tests that alone could prove their objective reality. It further neglects to distinguish between images that are arbitrarily interchanged and others where no free choice is involved. It errs because it cannot apply the law of causality to its contents. In short, the mind's estrangement from the outer world also explains why it believes in the subjective world of the dream.

Delbœuf reaches the same conclusion by a somewhat different route. We grant dream images the credence of reality, he argues, because in sleep we are cut off from the outer world and have no other impressions to compare them with. Yet perhaps we do not believe in our hallucinations simply because we are unable to test them while asleep. The dream can deceive us despite all such tests: it can make us believe that we touch the rose we see, and still we are only dreaming. According to Delbœuf, there is no valid criterion for deciding whether something is a dream or waking reality except the fact of awakening, and even that holds only as a practical generality. "I declare everything I have experienced between falling asleep and waking to be illusion," he writes, "if on waking I notice that I am lying undressed in my bed." And again: "During sleep I took the dream images to be real because of a mental habit that cannot be put to sleep, the habit of perceiving an outer world against which I can set my own self."

Since this turning away from the outer world is taken as the mark of the dream's most striking characteristics, it is worth recalling some ingenious observations by the elder Burdach. They clarify how the sleeping mind relates to the outer world, and they also guard us against overrating the conclusions just drawn. "Sleep occurs only on condition that the mind is not excited by sensory stimuli," Burdach writes, "but it is not the absence of sensory stimuli that brings on sleep so much as a lack of interest in them. Some sensory impressions are even necessary, insofar as they calm the mind. The miller can fall asleep only when he hears the clatter of his mill, and a person who, as a precaution, has made a habit of keeping a light burning at night cannot fall asleep in the dark."

"During sleep the mind isolates itself from the outer world and withdraws from the periphery. Nevertheless, the connection is not entirely broken. If we did not hear and feel during sleep, but only after waking, we would never wake at all. The persistence of sensation is shown still more plainly by the fact that what wakes us is not always the sheer physical force of an impression, but its significance for the mind. An indifferent word does not rouse the sleeper, but if he is called by name, he wakes. The mind, then, distinguishes among sensations even during sleep. For the same reason, we may be woken by the absence of a sensory stimulus, if that stimulus bears on something important to us. We wake when the light goes out, and the miller wakes when his mill comes to a standstill. In such cases waking is caused by the cessation of a sensory activity, which presupposes that the activity was perceived all along, and that it did not disturb the mind because it was indifferent or even soothing."

Even if we set aside these objections, which should not be taken lightly, we must still concede that the qualities of dream life considered so far, those arising from withdrawal from the outer world, cannot fully account for the strangeness of dreams. If they could, it would be possible to convert the hallucinations of the dream back into ideas and its situations back into thoughts, and so accomplish the task of dream interpretation. That is precisely what we do when, after waking, we reproduce a dream from memory. Yet whether this retranslation succeeds fully or only in part, the dream remains as mysterious as before.

Moreover, all the authors assume without hesitation that the material of waking ideas undergoes still other, more far-reaching changes in the dream. Strümpell puts it this way: "With the cessation of active, objective perception and of normal consciousness, the mind loses the ground in which its feelings, desires, interests, and actions were rooted. The mental states, feelings, interests, and valuations that cling to memory images in waking life also succumb to an obscure pressure, which severs their connection with those images. The perceptual images of things, persons, places, events, and actions from waking life are reproduced individually and in great abundance, but none of them brings its mental value along with it. That value has been stripped from them, and so they drift about in the mind, left to their own resources."

According to Strümpell, this loss of mental value, which in turn derives from the mind's withdrawal from the outer world, is chiefly responsible for the impression of strangeness that the dream makes on us when we remember it.

We have seen that even the act of falling asleep entails giving up one mental activity, namely the voluntary direction of the flow of ideas. This suggests, as other considerations also do, that the sleeping state may extend its influence to the mental functions themselves. Perhaps one or another of these functions is suspended altogether. Whether the remaining ones continue to work undisturbed, and whether they can perform normally under these conditions, is the next question. It occurs to us that the peculiarities of the dream might be explained by a lowered level of mental activity during sleep, and the impression the dream makes on our waking judgment seems to support this view. The dream is disconnected. It combines the worst contradictions without hesitation, admits impossibilities, ignores the knowledge on which we rely by day, and displays ethical and moral dullness. Anyone who behaved in waking life as people do in dreams would be considered insane. Anyone who, while awake, spoke in the manner of a dream or reported the kinds of things a dream contains would strike us as confused and feeble-minded. We therefore believe we are simply stating the facts when we place little value on mental activity in dreams, and especially when we declare that the higher intellectual faculties are suspended in the dream, or at least badly impaired.

With unusual unanimity (the exceptions will be dealt with elsewhere), the authors have passed judgments on the dream of a kind that leads directly to a definite theory or explanation of dream life. It is time to supplement the summary I have just given with a collection of statements by various authors, philosophers and physicians alike, on the psychological character of the dream.

According to Lemoine, the incoherence of dream images is the one essential characteristic of the dream. Maury agrees: "There are no dreams that are entirely reasonable and do not contain some incoherence, some anachronism, some absurdity." Hegel, as quoted by Spitta, held that the dream lacks any objective, intelligible coherence.

Dugas writes: "The dream is psychic anarchy, both emotional and mental. It is the play of functions left to themselves, operating without control and without aim. In the dream the mind is a spiritual automaton."

Even Volkelt, according to whose theory mental activity during sleep is by no means aimless, concedes "the relaxation, dissolution, and confusion of the life of ideas, which is ordinarily held together by the logical force of the central self."

The absurdity of the connections between ideas in dreams could hardly be condemned more strongly than it was by Cicero, in his treatise *On Divination*: "Nothing can be imagined so preposterous, so disordered, so monstrous that we cannot dream it."

Fechner says: "It is as if mental activity had been transferred from the brain of a rational being into the brain of a fool."

Radestock says: "It seems impossible to discern any fixed law in this absurd activity. Having escaped the strict policing of the rational will and of attention, which govern the waking life of ideas, the dream whirls everything about in a mad, kaleidoscopic play."

Hildebrandt says: "What astonishing leaps the dreamer permits himself in his chains of reasoning! With what indifference he sees the most familiar laws of experience turned upside down! What ridiculous contradictions in the order of nature and society he will tolerate before, as we say, things go too far, and the sheer overload of nonsense wakes him! We multiply with perfect composure that three times three makes twenty. We are not in the least surprised when a dog recites poetry to us, when a dead man walks to his own grave, or when a rock floats on water. In all seriousness, and on high command, we travel to the duchy of Bernburg or the principality of Liechtenstein to inspect the country's navy, or we let ourselves be enlisted as volunteers by Charles XII shortly before the Battle of Poltava."

Binz points to a theory of dreams that follows from these impressions: "Of every ten dreams, at least nine have absurd content. In them we join together persons or things that bear not the slightest relation to one another. The next moment, as in a kaleidoscope, the arrangement shifts, if possible into one still more nonsensical and irrational than before. So the changing play of the imperfectly sleeping brain continues until we wake, press a hand to our forehead, and ask ourselves whether we really still possess the capacity for rational imagination and thought."

Maury finds a comparison for the relation between dream images and waking thought that a physician will find especially telling: "The production of these images, which in the waking person is usually called forth by the will, corresponds in the realm of the intellect to what certain involuntary movements seen in chorea and in paralytic disorders are in the realm of motor function." Beyond this, Maury regards the dream as "a whole series of degradations of the faculty of thinking and reasoning."

There is little need to cite the authors who repeat Maury's assertion for each of the higher mental activities in turn. According to Strümpell, certain logical operations based on relations and connections disappear in the dream, even, of course, at points where the nonsense is not obvious. According to Spitta, ideas in the dream are entirely exempt from the laws of causality. Radestock and others stress the weakness of judgment and decision in dreams. According to Jodl, the dream exercises no critical faculty and does not correct a series of perceptions by reference to the whole content of consciousness. The same author states that "all forms of conscious activity occur in the dream, but they are imperfect, inhibited, and isolated from one another." Stricker, along with many others, explains the contradictions between dreams and our conscious knowledge by saying that facts are forgotten in the dream and the logical relations between ideas are lost.

Yet the authors who speak so unfavorably of the mind's capacities in dreams nevertheless admit that the dream retains a certain remnant of mental activity. Wundt, whose teaching has influenced so many other researchers on the problem of dreams, explicitly acknowledges this. One might ask what kind of mental life these remnants represent and how they behave in the dream. It is now almost universally agreed that the reproductive faculty, memory, appears to be the least affected in dreams. As noted earlier, it may even display a certain superiority over the same function in waking life, although some of the dream's absurdities are to be explained precisely by the forgetfulness of dream life. According to Spitta, it is the emotional life of the mind that sleep does not overtake, and that then directs the dream. "By emotion (*Gemüt*)," he writes, "we understand the constant unity of the feelings as the innermost subjective essence of the human being."

Scholz sees mental activity at work in the "allegorizing interpretation" to which the material of the dream is subjected. Siebeck likewise finds in the dream the "supplementary interpretive activity" that the mind exercises on everything it perceives and observes.

The status of what appears to be the highest mental function, consciousness, poses a special difficulty for the dream. Since we can know anything only through consciousness, there can be no doubt that it is retained. Spitta, however, believes that only consciousness is preserved in the dream, not self-consciousness. Delbœuf confesses that he cannot conceive of such a distinction.

The laws of association that govern the connection of ideas also hold for dream images; indeed, their dominance shows itself in the dream more purely and forcefully than anywhere else. Strümpell says: "The dream follows either, as it seems, solely the laws of bare ideas, or the laws of organic stimuli together with such ideas, that is, without being influenced by reflection and reason, aesthetic sense, or moral judgment." The authors whose views I am presenting here conceive of dream formation roughly as follows. The sum of sensory stimuli that act on the sleeper from the various sources discussed elsewhere first awakens in the mind a set of ideas, which present themselves as hallucinations (or, as Wundt says more precisely, as illusions, since they originate in external and internal stimuli). These ideas combine with one another according to the familiar laws of association, and by the same rules they call up a fresh series of ideas and images. The whole of this material is then worked over as well as possible by whatever remains active of the mind's organizing and reasoning faculties, as Wundt and Weygandt describe. So far, however, no one has succeeded in discovering the motive that determines whether the arousal of images not originating in external objects follows one law of association or another.

It has repeatedly been observed, though, that the associations linking dream ideas to one another are of a particular kind, different from those found in waking thought. Volkelt says: "In the dream, ideas chase and hunt one another on the strength of chance resemblances and barely perceptible connections. All dreams are shot through with such loose, unbound associations." Maury attaches great importance to this way of connecting ideas, which allows him to draw a closer analogy between dream life and certain mental disorders. He identifies two main characteristics of delirium: "first, a spontaneous and, as it were, automatic action of the mind; second, a faulty and irregular association of ideas." Maury gives two excellent examples from his own dreams in which mere similarity of sound forms the link between dream ideas. Once he dreamed that he was making a pilgrimage (in French, *pèlerinage*) to Jerusalem or Mecca. After many adventures he found himself with the chemist Pelletier, who, after some conversation, handed him a zinc shovel (*pelle*), which in the dream fragment that followed became his great battle sword. On another occasion he dreamed he was walking along a highway, reading the kilometers on the milestones. Presently he was with a spice merchant who had large scales on which to weigh Maury, and the merchant said to him, "You are not in Paris, but on the island of Gilolo." A string of images followed, in which he saw the lobelia flower and then General Lopez, whose death he had read about shortly before. He finally woke up while playing a game of lotto.

We are fully prepared, however, to learn that this low estimate of the dream's mental activity has not gone unchallenged. Admittedly, a challenge seems difficult here. Nor does it carry much weight when one of the detractors of dream life, Spitta, assures us that the same psychological laws that govern waking life also govern the dream, or when another, Dugas, declares that "the dream is neither unreason nor even pure irrationality," so long as neither has made any effort to reconcile this verdict with the mental anarchy and dissolution of all functions that they themselves describe in the dream.

Others, however, seem to have glimpsed the possibility that the madness of the dream may not be without method, that it may be only feigned, like the madness of the Danish prince, Hamlet, of whom Polonius observes, "Though this be madness, yet there is method in't." These authors must have refused to judge by appearances, or else the dream appeared to them quite differently.

Without dwelling on its apparent absurdity, Havelock Ellis regards the dream as "an archaic world of vast emotions and imperfect thoughts," whose study might acquaint us with primitive stages in the development of mental life. A thinker such as Delbœuf asserts, though without offering any proof against the contrary evidence, and therefore without justification: "In sleep, all the faculties of the mind except perception (intelligence, imagination, memory, will, and morality) remain intact in their essence. They are simply applied to imaginary and shifting objects. The dreamer is an actor who plays at will the madmen and the sages, the executioners and the victims, the dwarfs and the giants, the demons and the angels." The Marquis d'Hervey, whom Maury sharply disputes and whose work I was unable to obtain despite every effort, seems to have opposed the underestimation of the mind's capacity in dreams most vigorously of all. Maury describes his position as follows: "The Marquis d'Hervey grants the intellect, during sleep, its full freedom of action and attention. He seems to regard sleep as consisting solely in the closing of the senses, their shutting out of the external world, so that in his view the sleeping man is scarcely distinguishable from the man who lets his thoughts wander while stopping up his senses. The entire difference between ordinary thought and the thought of the sleeper is that in the latter the idea takes on a visible, objective form and resembles, to the point of being mistaken for it, the sensation produced by external objects. Memory takes on the appearance of a present event."

Maury adds, however, "that there is a further and fundamental difference, namely that the intellectual faculties of the sleeping man do not maintain the balance they keep in the waking man."

The range of opinion in the literature on the dream as a mental product is wide. It extends from the deepest disparagement, examples of which we have just seen, through the notion of a value not yet disclosed, to an overestimation that ranks the dream far above the capacities of waking life. Hildebrandt, who, as we know, sets out the psychological characteristics of the dream in three antinomies, or paired contradictions, sums up the extreme ends of this range in the third of them. The dream, he says, moves "between a heightening, often an intensification that rises to virtuosity, and on the other hand a marked diminution and weakening of mental life, often sinking below the human level."

"As for the first, who cannot confirm from his own experience that, in the creations and weavings of the genius of the dream, there sometimes appear a depth and sincerity of emotion, a tenderness of feeling, a clarity of vision, a delicacy of observation, and a quickness of wit that we would modestly have to deny possessing as constant traits in waking life? The dream has a wonderful poetry, a superb gift for allegory, an incomparable humor, and a delightful irony. It sees the world in the light of a peculiar idealization, and often heightens the effect of its appearances into the most penetrating grasp of the essence that underlies them. It shows us earthly beauty in true heavenly radiance, the sublime in its highest majesty, the truly frightening in its most gruesome form, and the ridiculous in indescribably broad comedy. At times, after waking, we are so filled with one of these impressions that we imagine the real world has never offered us anything like it."

One may well ask whether the disparaging remarks and these inspired tributes are really aimed at the same object. Have the admirers overlooked the foolish dreams, and the detractors the thoughtful and ingenious ones? And if both kinds occur, dreams that deserve to be judged one way and dreams that deserve to be judged the other, is it not idle to seek a psychological character of the dream at all? Would it not be enough to say that anything is possible in a dream, from the deepest degradation of mental life to an elevation of it rarely seen in waking life? Convenient as this solution would be, it has one thing against it: the efforts of all dream researchers seem to presuppose that the dream does have a definable character, one that holds universally in its essential features and that must resolve these contradictions.

There is no question that the mental capacities of the dream won quicker and warmer recognition in the intellectual era now behind us, when philosophy rather than exact natural science governed educated minds. Statements like Schubert's, that the dream frees the mind from the power of external nature and releases the soul from the chains of the senses, and similar views expressed by the younger Fichte and others, who portray the dream as a soaring of mental life to a higher plane, hardly seem conceivable to us today. They are now repeated only by mystics and the devout. With the advance of scientific thinking, a reaction set in against this high estimate of the dream. It is above all the medical authors who tend to dismiss mental activity in dreams as trivial and worthless, whereas philosophers and lay observers, amateur psychologists whose contributions to this field certainly cannot be ignored, have for the most part upheld the mental value of the dream, in closer agreement with popular belief. Whoever is inclined to underrate the mind's capacity in dreams will naturally favor bodily sources of stimulation in explaining their origin. Whoever leaves the dreaming mind the greater part of its capacities has, by the same token, no reason not to admit that it also has independent stimuli for dreaming.

Among the superior activities that, even on sober comparison, one is tempted to attribute to dream life, memory is the most striking; we have already discussed at length the frequent experiences that demonstrate it. Another advantage of dream life, often praised by the older authors, is that it can consider itself sovereign with respect to distance in time and space, is easily recognized as an illusion. As Hildebrandt has observed, this superiority is purely illusory: the dream pays as much heed to time and space as waking thought does, for the simple reason that it is only a form of thinking. The dream is said to enjoy yet another advantage with regard to time, being independent of its passage in a further sense. Dreams like Maury's guillotine dream, reported above, seem to show that a dream can pack more perceptual content into a very brief interval than the waking mind could master in the same span. These conclusions, however, have been disputed on many grounds. The essays of Le Lorrain and Egger, "On the Apparent Duration of Dreams," set off a long and interesting debate, which has probably not yet had the last word on this delicate and far-reaching question.

That the dream can take up the intellectual work of the day and bring to a conclusion what was left unsettled, that it can resolve doubts and problems, and that it can become a source of fresh inspiration for poets and composers appears indisputable, as many reports attest, along with the collection compiled by Chabaneix. Yet even if the facts are beyond dispute, their interpretation remains open in principle to a great many doubts.

Finally, the alleged prophetic power of the dream is contested ground, where hard, unyielding reflection meets stubborn and persistent faith. It is only fair that we refrain from denying everything factual in this area, since a number of such cases may well admit of explanation on natural psychological grounds.

**(f) Ethical Feelings in the Dream.** For reasons that will become clear only after the reader has become acquainted with my own investigations of the dream, I have separated from the psychology of the dream the narrower problem of whether, and to what extent, the moral dispositions and feelings of waking life carry over into dreams. Here we meet again the same contradictions that surprised us in the authors' descriptions of every other mental capacity. Some assert flatly that the dream knows nothing of moral obligation; others assert just as flatly that man's moral nature persists in his dream life.

An appeal to our own experience of dreaming, night after night, seems to place the first assertion beyond doubt. Jessen writes: "Nor does one become better or more virtuous in dreams. On the contrary, conscience seems to fall silent there, for one feels no pity and can commit the worst crimes, such as theft, murder, and assassination, with perfect indifference and without any remorse afterward."

Radestock says: "It is worth noting that in dreams associations run their course and ideas combine without any influence from reflection and reason, aesthetic taste, or moral judgment; judgment is extremely weak, and ethical indifference reigns supreme."

Volkelt puts it this way: "As everyone knows, sexual relations in dreams are especially unbridled. Just as the dreamer is himself shameless in the extreme and wholly lacking in moral feeling and judgment, so he also sees others, even the people he most respects, engaged in acts that, awake, he would blush to associate with them even in thought."

Statements like Schopenhauer's, that in dreams everyone acts and speaks in accordance with his character, stand in the sharpest contrast to these. R. P. Fischer maintains that subjective feelings and desires, affects and passions, show themselves in the willful freedom of dream life, and that a person's moral qualities are mirrored in his dreams.

Haffner writes: "With rare exceptions . . . a virtuous person will be virtuous in his dreams as well; he will resist temptation and show no sympathy for hatred, envy, anger, or any other vice, while the sinful person will, as a rule, find in his dreams the same images he keeps before him when awake."

Scholz writes: "In dreams there is truth: despite every mask of pride or humility, we still recognize our own self. . . . The honest man commits no dishonorable act even in a dream, or, if he does, he is horrified by it as by something alien to his nature. The Roman emperor who had one of his subjects executed because the man had dreamed of cutting off the emperor's head was not wrong to justify the sentence on the ground that whoever has such dreams must harbor similar thoughts while awake. That is why, of something that can find no place in our minds, we say so pointedly: 'I would never dream of such a thing.'"

Pfaff, varying a familiar proverb, says: "Tell me your dreams for a while, and I will tell you what you are inside."

The short work by Hildebrandt, from which I have already quoted so often, and which is the most complete and thought-provoking contribution to the problem of the dream that I found in the literature, places the question of morality in dreams at the center of its interest. For Hildebrandt, too, it is a firm rule that the purer the life, the purer the dream, and the more impure the one, the more impure the other.

Man's moral nature, he holds, persists even in dreams: "But while we are neither offended nor made suspicious by an arithmetical error, however obvious, by a reversal of scientific fact, however romantic, or by an anachronism, however witty, we never lose sight of the difference between good and evil, right and wrong, virtue and vice. However much of what accompanies us through the day may vanish in the hours of sleep, Kant's categorical imperative clings to our heels as an inseparable companion whom we cannot shake off even in slumber. . . . This can be explained only by the fact that the foundation of human nature, its moral essence, is too firmly fixed to be caught up in the kaleidoscopic shaking to which fantasy, reason, memory, and the other faculties of the same rank succumb in dreams."

In the further discussion of the subject, both groups of authors display remarkable distortion and inconsistency. Strictly speaking, all those who assert that the moral personality crumbles in dreams should have no further interest in immoral dreams. They could reject the attempt to hold the dreamer responsible for his dreams, and to infer from their wickedness some evil strain in his nature, just as calmly as they rejected the seemingly similar attempt to prove the worthlessness of his waking intellectual life from the absurdity of his dreams. The others, for whom "the categorical imperative" extends into dreams as well, would have to accept full responsibility for their immoral dreams; one could only hope, for their own sake, that their own objectionable dreams would not lead them to abandon an otherwise firmly held estimate of their own morality.

Yet it seems that no one knows for certain how good or how bad he is, and that no one can deny remembering immoral dreams of his own. For beyond the opposition already noted in judging the morality of dreams, both groups of authors try to explain where immoral dreams come from, and here a new opposition arises, depending on whether their origin is sought in the functions of mental life or in physically determined impairments of that life. The pressing force of the facts then allows the advocates of responsibility and of irresponsibility in dream life alike to agree in recognizing a special psychic source for the immorality of dreams.

All those who allow morality to persist in dreams nevertheless take care not to accept full responsibility for their dreams. Haffner says: "We are not responsible for dreams, because the basis on which alone our life has truth and reality is withdrawn from our thoughts. . . . Hence there can be no dream-willing and dream-acting, no virtue or sin." Still, a person is responsible for a sinful dream insofar as he brings it about indirectly. Just as in waking life, it is his duty to cleanse his moral mind, and particularly so before going to sleep.

Hildebrandt pursues the analysis of this mixture of rejected and acknowledged responsibility for the moral content of dreams much further. He grants that the dramatic mode of representation in dreams, the compression of the most complicated processes of deliberation into the briefest span of time, and the devaluation and confusion of the dream's representational elements, all of which he concedes, must be counted in mitigation of the immoral aspect of dreams. He nevertheless confesses that, after the most earnest reflection, he is inclined to deny that responsibility for faults and sins committed in dreams can simply be dismissed.

"When we wish to reject an unjust accusation emphatically," he writes, "especially one touching our intentions and convictions, we naturally use the expression: 'I would never have dreamed of such a thing.' By this we mean, of course, that we regard the realm of dreams as the last and remotest place where we could be held responsible for our thoughts, because there these thoughts are so loosely and incoherently connected with our real being that we would hardly count them as our own. Yet because we feel compelled to deny expressly that such thoughts exist even in this realm, we indirectly admit at the same time that our justification would be incomplete if it did not reach that far. And I believe that here, though unconsciously, we speak the language of truth."

And further: "No dream thought can be imagined whose first motive has not already passed through the waking mind as some wish, desire, or impulse." Of this original impulse, he argues, we must say that the dream did not discover it. The dream has only copied and extended it, only worked up into dramatic form a bit of historical material it found already in us; it enacts the words of the apostle, "Whoever hates his brother is a murderer." And while, after we wake and become conscious of our moral strength, we may smile at the boldly built structure of a depraved dream, the original material from which it was formed has nothing laughable about it. One feels responsible for the dreamer's transgressions, not for the whole sum, but still for a certain percentage. "In this sense, which is hard to contest, we understand the words of Christ, 'Out of the heart proceed evil thoughts,' for we can hardly avoid the conviction that every sin committed in a dream carries with it at least a faint minimum of guilt."

Hildebrandt thus locates the source of immorality in dreams in the germs and hints of evil impulses that pass through our minds during the day as tempting thoughts, and he sees fit to include these immoral elements in the moral assessment of the personality. These are the same thoughts, and the same assessment of them, that have led devout and holy men of every age to lament that they are wicked sinners.

There is certainly no reason to doubt that such contrasting ideas occur generally, in most people and in spheres other than the ethical as well. They have not always been judged very seriously. Spitta quotes a relevant remark by A. Zeller from the article "Irre" in Ersch and Gruber's *Allgemeine Encyklopädie der Wissenschaften*: "The mind is rarely so fortunately constituted as to possess at all times enough strength not to be disturbed by ideas that run counter to the usual clear course of thought, and not merely by inessential ideas but by perfectly ridiculous ones. Indeed, the greatest thinkers have had cause to complain of this dreamlike, disturbing, and tormenting rabble of ideas, which wrecks their deepest reflection and their most sacred and earnest mental work."

Another observation of Hildebrandt's sheds clearer light on the psychological status of these contrasting ideas: the dream sometimes lets us glimpse the deep, innermost recesses of our being, which in waking life are generally closed to us. Kant expresses the same insight in his *Anthropology* when he says that dreams exist to lay bare our hidden dispositions and to reveal to us not what we are, but what we might have become had we been raised differently. Radestock says that dreams often reveal to us only what we do not wish to admit to ourselves, and that we therefore wrongly condemn them as liars and deceivers. Observations like Benini's remind us that the emergence of impulses foreign to our consciousness is merely analogous to the way dreams make use of other ideational material that is either absent from waking life or plays only an insignificant part there. Benini writes: "Certain inclinations of ours that we believed long since stifled and extinguished reawaken; old, buried passions come back to life; things and people we never think of appear before us." Volkelt expresses himself in a similar way: "Even ideas that entered our consciousness almost unnoticed, and have perhaps never been retrieved from oblivion, often announce their presence in the mind through dreams." Finally, it is worth mentioning here that, according to Schleiermacher, the process of falling asleep is accompanied by the appearance of undesirable ideas, or images.

We may group under the heading "undesirable ideas" the whole body of ideational material whose appearance arouses our wonder in immoral and absurd dreams alike. The only significant difference is that undesirable ideas in the moral sphere stand in opposition to our other feelings, while the rest merely strike us as strange. So far, nothing has been done that would allow us to dissolve this difference through deeper understanding.

But what is the significance of undesirable ideas appearing in dreams? What conclusions about the psychology of the waking and dreaming mind can be drawn from these nocturnal manifestations of contrary ethical impulses? Here we encounter a new divergence of opinion, and once again a different grouping of the authors.

The line of thought followed by Hildebrandt, and by others who share his basic view, can be carried forward only by ascribing to immoral impulses a certain force even in waking life, a force that is, to be sure, inhibited from advancing into action, and by asserting that something falls away during sleep which, acting as an inhibition, had kept us from noticing that such an impulse existed. The dream thus shows the real, if not the entire, nature of man, and offers a means of making hidden mental life accessible to our understanding. Only on this assumption can Hildebrandt assign the dream the role of a monitor that alerts us to moral ravages in the soul, just as, in the view of physicians, it can announce a physical illness that has so far gone unnoticed. Spitta, too, can be guided by no other conception when he refers to the surge of excitement that pours into the psyche during puberty, for example, and consoles the dreamer by saying that he has done all in his power if he has led a strictly virtuous life while awake, has tried to suppress sinful thoughts whenever they arise, and has kept them from ripening into actions. On this conception, we might call the "undesirable" ideas those that are "suppressed" during the day, and we would have to recognize in their appearance a genuine psychic phenomenon.

If we followed other authors, we would have no right to this last inference. For Jessen, undesirable ideas in dreams, as in waking life, in fever, and in other deliria, have merely "the character of a voluntary activity put to rest, and of a somewhat mechanical procession of images and ideas produced by inner impulses." An immoral dream proves nothing about the dreamer's mental life except that he has somehow become acquainted with the ideas in question; it is certainly not a psychic impulse of his own.

Another author, Maury, leaves us wondering whether he, too, does not credit the dream state with the capacity to break mental activity down into its components rather than destroying it at random. He writes of dreams in which one oversteps the bounds of morality: "It is our inclinations that speak and make us act, without conscience holding us back, though at times it warns us. I have my faults and my vicious inclinations; in the waking state I try to struggle against them, and I quite often manage not to give in. But in my dreams I always give in, or, to put it better, I act on their impulse, without fear and without remorse. . . . Evidently the visions that unfold before my mind and make up the dream are suggested to me by the urges I feel, which my absent will makes no effort to repress."

Anyone who believes that dreams can reveal an actually existing but repressed or concealed immoral disposition in the dreamer could not state his view more forcefully than in Maury's words: "In dreams, then, man reveals himself wholly to himself, in his native nakedness and wretchedness. As soon as he suspends the exercise of his will, he becomes the plaything of all the passions against which, in the waking state, conscience, the sense of honor, and fear defend us." Elsewhere he puts it in these striking terms: "In dreams it is above all instinctive man who reveals himself. . . . Man returns, so to speak, to the state of nature when he dreams; and the less acquired ideas have penetrated his mind, the more the inclinations at odds with them retain their influence over him in dreams." He then offers as an example that his dreams often show him as the victim of precisely those superstitions he attacks most vehemently in his writings.

The value of all these perceptive observations for a psychological understanding of dream life is spoiled, however, by Maury's refusal to see in the phenomena he observed so accurately anything more than proof of the "psychological automatism" that, in his opinion, governs dream life. He conceives of this automatism as the complete opposite of psychic activity.

A passage in Stricker's studies on consciousness reads: "Dreams do not consist merely of delusions. If, for example, one is afraid of robbers in a dream, the robbers are of course imaginary, but the fear is real. This draws our attention to the fact that the development of affect in dreams does not admit of the judgment we pass on the rest of the dream content, and the question arises which part of the mental processes in dreams may be real, that is, which part may claim a place among the mental processes of waking life."

**(g) Dream Theories and the Function of the Dream.** A statement about the dream that attempts to explain as many of its observed characteristics as possible from a single point of view, and that at the same time defines the dream's relation to a wider sphere of phenomena, may be called a theory of dreams. Individual theories will differ from one another in that they single out one characteristic of the dream or another and attach their explanations and connections to it. It is not strictly necessary for a theory to yield a function for the dream, that is, some use or other activity it performs. Still, our expectations, which are usually attuned to teleology, to explanation by purpose, will welcome theories that promise an understanding of the dream's function.

We have already encountered many conceptions of the dream that deserve, to a greater or lesser degree, to be called dream theories in this sense. The ancient belief that dreams were sent by the gods to guide human action was a complete theory of the dream, supplying information on everything about it worth knowing. Since the dream became an object of biological investigation, we have acquired a larger number of theories, though some of them are very incomplete.

Setting aside any claim to completeness, we may attempt the following loose grouping of dream theories, based on their fundamental conception of the degree and kind of mental activity in dreams:

1. Theories, like Delbœuf's, that allow the full mental activity of waking life to continue into the dream. Here the mind does not sleep; its apparatus remains intact, but because it is placed under conditions different from those of waking, its normal operation must produce results different from those of waking. The question for these theories is whether they can derive the differences between dreaming and waking thought entirely from the conditions of the sleeping state. They also lack any possible access to a function of the dream: one cannot see why we dream at all, why the complicated mechanism of the mental apparatus keeps running even when placed under conditions for which it is evidently not suited. Only two sensible responses would remain, to sleep without dreaming or to wake when disturbing stimuli approach, instead of the third, which is to dream.

2. Theories that, on the contrary, assume for the dream a reduction of mental activity, a loosening of connections, and an impoverishment of available material. According to these theories, sleep must be assigned a psychological character entirely different from the one Delbœuf gives it. Sleep reaches far beyond the mind. It does not consist merely in shutting the mind off from the outer world; it penetrates the mind's very mechanism and at times renders it unusable. If I may borrow a comparison from psychiatry, the first group of theories constructs the dream on the pattern of paranoia, in which the intellect remains intact but works on distorted material, while the second models it on dementia or amentia, in which the intellect itself is weakened or thrown into confusion.

The theory that only a fragment of mental activity, paralyzed by sleep, finds expression in the dream is by far the favorite among medical writers and in the scientific world generally. Insofar as one can assume a broader interest in explaining dreams, it may fairly be called the reigning theory of the dream. It is worth stressing how easily this particular theory avoids the worst reef that threatens every explanation of dreams: running aground on one of the contradictions the dream embodies. Because it regards the dream as the result of a partial waking, or, in the words of Herbart's psychology of dreams, "a gradual, partial, and at the same time highly anomalous waking," it manages to cover the entire range of the dream's inferior performances, revealed in its absurdities, up to the full concentration of mental activity, by tracing a sequence of states that grow steadily more wakeful until they arrive at full awakening.

Those who find the language of psychology indispensable, or who prefer a more scientific mode of thought, will find this theory of the dream set out in Binz's discussion:

"This state of numbness, however, gradually draws to a close in the early hours of the morning. The fatigue products accumulated in the albumen of the brain steadily diminish; they are slowly broken down or carried off by the constantly flowing circulation. Here and there, certain masses of cells can be distinguished as awake, while everything around them remains torpid. The isolated work of these individual groups now appears before our clouded consciousness, which lacks the control of those other parts of the brain that govern association. Hence the images produced, which for the most part correspond to objective impressions from the recent past, fit together in a wild and irregular way. As the number of liberated brain cells steadily grows, the irrationality of the dream steadily diminishes."

The conception of the dream as an incomplete, partial waking, or at least traces of its influence, can surely be found in every modern physiologist and philosopher. Its fullest expression is in Maury. He often seems to imagine waking and sleeping as conditions that belong to particular anatomical regions; at any rate, he appears to believe that each anatomical province is tied to a definite psychic function. I will simply note here that even if the theory of partial waking were confirmed, a great deal would remain to be done in working it out.

Naturally, this conception of dream life leaves no room for any function of the dream. On the contrary, its verdict on the status and importance of dreaming is consistently expressed in Binz's statement: "All the facts, as we see, compel us to characterize the dream as a physical process that is in every case useless, and in many cases actually morbid."

The term "physical" as applied to the dream, which owes its prominence to Binz, points in more than one direction. First, it refers to the dream's causation, a matter that was especially clear to Binz, since he studied the experimental production of dreams through the administration of poisons. It is certainly in keeping with this kind of theory to attribute the instigation of dreams exclusively to bodily sources wherever possible. In its most extreme form, the argument runs as follows: once we have put ourselves to sleep by shutting out stimuli, there would be no need and no occasion to dream until morning, when our gradual awakening under the influx of new stimuli would be reflected in the phenomenon of dreaming. In practice, however, sleep cannot be kept free of stimuli. Just as Mephistopheles, in Goethe's *Faust*, complains that the germs of life spring up from every quarter and defeat all his efforts to destroy it, so stimuli reach the sleeper from every side: from without, from within, and even from bodily regions that never trouble us in waking life. Sleep is thus disturbed. The mind is roused now by this trifle, now by that, functions for a while with its awakened portion, and is glad to fall asleep again. The dream is a reaction to the stimulus that disturbs sleep, though admittedly a wholly superfluous one.

To call the dream a physical process, even though it remains an activity of the mental organ, carries yet another meaning. It is meant to deny the dream the dignity of a psychic process. The esteem in which representatives of exact science have held dream activity is perhaps best illustrated by their application to the dream of a very old comparison: "the ten fingers of a person ignorant of music, running over the keys of an instrument." Understood this way, the dream becomes something entirely untranslatable, for how could the ten fingers of an unmusical player produce music?

The theory of partial wakefulness did not go unchallenged, even in earlier times. In 1830, Burdach wrote: "If we say that the dream is a partial wakefulness, then, in the first place, we explain neither the waking nor the sleeping state; and secondly, we express nothing more than that certain forces of the mind are active in the dream while others are at rest. But irregularities of this kind occur throughout life...."

Among the existing theories that regard the dream as a "physical" process, there is one especially interesting conception, first put forward by Robert in 1866, which is attractive because it assigns the dream a function, a useful end. Robert bases his theory on two observed facts that we have already discussed in considering the material of dreams: that we very often dream about the trivial impressions of the day, and that we rarely carry the day's absorbing interests over into our dreams. Robert maintains, as exclusively correct, that matters which have been fully dealt with never instigate dreams; only matters that remain incomplete in the mind, or that touched it only fleetingly, can do so. "We usually cannot explain our dreams because their causes lie in sensory impressions from the previous day that did not receive sufficient recognition from the dreamer." The conditions under which an impression can enter a dream are therefore either that its processing has been disturbed, or that it was too insignificant to claim any processing at all.

Robert accordingly conceives of the dream as "a physical process of elimination that has come to our awareness through the psychic manifestation of its reaction." Dreams are the elimination of thoughts nipped in the bud. "A man deprived of the capacity to dream would surely, in time, become mentally unbalanced, because an immense number of unfinished, unresolved thoughts and superficial impressions would accumulate in his brain, and under their pressure everything that ought to be incorporated into memory as a finished whole would be crushed." The dream acts as a safety valve for the overburdened brain. Dreams have healing and unburdening properties.

It would be a mistake to ask Robert how mere representation in a dream can unburden the mind. He apparently concluded from these two peculiarities of dream material that during sleep the ejection of worthless impressions is carried out as a bodily process, and that dreaming is not a distinct psychic process at all, but merely the awareness we receive of that elimination. Elimination is not, of course, the only thing that happens in the mind during sleep. Robert himself adds that the stimuli of the day are also worked over, and that "whatever cannot be eliminated from the undigested thought material lying in the mind is bound together, by threads of thought borrowed from fantasy, into a finished whole, and thus entered into memory as a harmless fantasy picture."

But it is in his critique of the sources of dreams that Robert sets himself most bluntly against the prevailing theory. According to that theory, there would be no dream at all if external and internal sensory stimuli did not repeatedly rouse the mind; Robert, by contrast, places the impulse to dream within the mind itself. It lies in an overload that demands discharge. With perfect consistency, he holds that those determining causes of the dream which depend on the physical state are of secondary rank, and could never provoke dreams in a mind that held no material for dream formation drawn from waking consciousness. He does concede, however, that the fantasy images arising in the depths of the mind can be influenced by nervous stimuli. For Robert, then, the dream is not quite so dependent on the bodily element. Yet it is still not a psychic process, and it has no place among the psychic processes of waking life. It is a nocturnal bodily process within the apparatus devoted to mental activity, and it has a function to perform: to protect that apparatus from overstrain, or, to change the metaphor, to cleanse the mind.

Another author, Yves Delage, builds his theory on the same features of the dream, those that become evident in the selection of dream material, and it is instructive to see how a slight shift in the understanding of the same facts yields a conclusion of quite different import.

After losing someone very dear to him to death, Delage discovered from his own experience that we do not dream of what preoccupies us intensely during the day, or that we begin to dream of it only once it has been overshadowed by other daily concerns. His inquiries among other people confirmed that this holds universally. He makes an apt observation of this kind, if it should prove generally true, about the dreams of newlyweds: "If they were deeply in love, they almost never dreamed of each other before the wedding or during the honeymoon; and if they dreamed of love, it was to be unfaithful with some person who was indifferent or odious to them." But what, then, do we dream of? Delage recognizes that the material of our dreams consists of fragments and remnants of impressions from the preceding days and from earlier times. Everything that appears in our dreams, which we might at first be inclined to regard as creations of dream life, proves on closer investigation to be unrecognized reproduction, "unconscious memory." Yet this material shares a common character: it originates in impressions that probably struck our senses more forcefully than our minds, or from which our attention was diverted soon after they appeared. The less conscious an impression is, and at the same time the stronger, the better its chance of playing a part in the next dream.

These are essentially the same two categories of impressions that Robert emphasized, the insignificant and the unresolved. But Delage alters the connection between them by assuming that these impressions become the subject of dreams not because they are trivial but because they are unresolved. Insignificant impressions, too, are in a sense not fully settled; by their very nature as new impressions they are "so many tightened springs," which will relax during sleep. Still more entitled to a role in the dream than the faint, scarcely noticed impression is a strong one whose processing has been accidentally held up or deliberately repressed. The psychic energy accumulated during the day through inhibition or suppression becomes, at night, the mainspring of the dream.

Unfortunately, Delage stops at this point in his train of thought. He can attribute only the smallest share of the dream to independent psychic activity, and so his theory falls back on the prevailing doctrine of a partial sleep of the brain: "In sum, the dream is the product of wandering thought, without aim or direction, fixing itself in turn on those memories that have kept enough intensity to place themselves in its path and halt it as it passes, establishing between them a link that is sometimes weak and indecisive, sometimes stronger and tighter, according to how far the present activity of the brain is suspended by sleep."

A third group comprises those theories that credit the dreaming mind with the capacity and inclination for a special psychic activity which, in the waking state, it can carry out either not at all or only imperfectly. The exercise of these capacities usually yields a useful function for the dream. The dignity that older psychological writers conferred upon the dream belongs chiefly to this category. In place of a survey of these writers, however, I shall content myself with quoting Burdach, according to whom the dream "is the natural activity of the mind, not limited by the force of individuality, not disturbed by self-consciousness, and not directed by self-determination, but the life of the sensitive central point indulging in free play."

Burdach and others evidently regard this reveling in the free use of one's own powers as a state in which the mind refreshes itself and gathers new strength for the day's work, much in the manner of a holiday. Burdach therefore quotes with approval the admirable words in which the poet Novalis praises the reign of the dream: "The dream is a bulwark against the regularity and commonness of life, a free recreation of the fettered imagination, in which it mixes together all the images of life and interrupts the unbroken seriousness of grown men with a child's joyous play. Without dreams we would surely age sooner, and so the dream may be regarded, if not as a gift directly from above, then as a delightful task, a friendly companion on our pilgrimage to the grave."

Purkinje depicts the refreshing and curative work of the dream more vividly still. "Productive dreams in particular would perform these functions. They are light plays of the imagination, with no connection to the events of the day. The mind does not wish to prolong the tension of waking life, but to release it and recover from it. Above all, it creates conditions opposed to those of the waking state. It cures sadness with joy, worry with hope and cheerful, distracting images, hatred with love and friendliness, and fear with courage and confidence; it calms doubt with conviction and firm belief, and vain expectation with fulfillment. Many sore places in the mind, which the day keeps continually open, sleep heals by covering them over and guarding them against fresh irritation. The healing effect of time rests partly on this." We all feel that sleep benefits the life of the mind, and the vague intuition of popular opinion apparently cannot be talked out of the idea that dreaming is one of the ways in which sleep bestows its benefits.

The most original and far-reaching attempt to explain the dream as a special activity of the mind, one that can display itself freely only in sleep, was undertaken by Scherner in 1861. His book is written in a heavy, bombastic style and inspired by an almost intoxicated enthusiasm for its subject, which is bound to repel us unless it sweeps us along with it. It places so many obstacles in the way of analysis that we gladly turn to the clearer and shorter account in which the philosopher Volkelt presents Scherner's theories. "From these mystical agglomerations, from all these gorgeous and magnificent billows, there does indeed flash and radiate an ominous gleam of meaning, but the philosopher's path is not made any clearer by it." Such is the judgment passed on Scherner's account by one of his own followers.

Scherner is not among those authors who let the mind carry its capacities undiminished into dream life. He explains, in fact, how in dreams the centrality and spontaneous energy of the ego are weakened, how cognition, feeling, will, and imagination are altered by this decentralization, and how what remains of these psychic forces has no true mental character but only the nature of a mechanism. In their place, however, the activity of the mind called fantasy, freed from all rational control and therefore entirely unchecked, rises in the dream to absolute supremacy. It does take its last building blocks from the memory of waking life, but with them it erects structures as different from those of waking life as day is from night. In the dream it proves itself not merely reproductive but productive, and its peculiarities give dream life its strange character. It favors the unlimited, the exaggerated, and the prodigious; but, freed from the hampering categories of thought, it gains greater flexibility, agility, and a new delight. It is exquisitely sensitive to the delicate emotional stirrings of the mind and to agitating feelings, and it swiftly recasts the inner life into the clear, sculptural forms of the outer world. Dream fantasy lacks the language of concepts: whatever it wants to say, it must depict in images, and because the idea now acts with such force, it depicts it with all the richness, power, and immensity of that pictorial mode. Its language, however simple, therefore becomes roundabout, cumbersome, and heavy. Clarity is made especially difficult by the fact that fantasy dislikes representing an object by its own image and prefers an alien one, provided that image can express the particular aspect of the object it wishes to convey. This is the symbolizing activity of fantasy.... It is also highly significant that dream fantasy reproduces objects not in detail but only in outline, and even that in the broadest strokes. Its paintings therefore appear brilliantly light and graceful. Yet dream fantasy does not stop at merely representing the object; it is driven from within to involve the dreaming ego with the object to a greater or lesser degree, and so to produce an action.
