A visual dream, for example, shows gold coins lying in the street; the dreamer picks them up, rejoices, and carries them away.

According to Scherner, the material on which dream fantasy exercises its artistry consists predominantly of the organic sensory stimuli that remain so obscure during the day. Thus Scherner's fanciful theory and the perhaps overly sober theories of Wundt and other physiologists, though otherwise diametrically opposed, agree entirely in their assumptions about the sources and instigators of dreams. But in the physiological theory, the psychic reaction to internal physical stimuli is exhausted once ideas suited to those stimuli have been awakened; these ideas then summon other ideas by association, and at that stage the chain of psychic processes appears to end. According to Scherner, by contrast, the physical stimuli merely supply the psychic force with material that it can bend to its fantastic purposes. For Scherner, the formation of the dream only begins where, in the view of others, it comes to an end.

The way dream fantasy treats physical stimuli can hardly be considered purposeful. Fantasy plays a teasing game with them, representing the organic source of the stimuli in the corresponding dream through some form of vivid, concrete symbolism. Indeed, Scherner holds, though Volkelt and others do not share the view, that dream fantasy has a favorite representation for the organism as a whole: the house. Fortunately, however, it does not seem to confine itself to this material. It may also, conversely, use a whole series of houses to designate a single organ, such as very long rows of houses for intestinal stimulation. On other occasions, particular parts of the house stand for particular parts of the body. In a dream caused by headache, for example, the ceiling of the room, which the dreamer sees covered with loathsome, reptile-like spiders, represents the head.

Quite apart from house symbolism, any other suitable object may be used to represent the parts of the body that provoke the dream. As Volkelt summarizes: "Thus the breathing lungs find their symbol in the blazing stove with its roaring draft, the heart in hollow boxes and baskets, the bladder in round, bag-shaped, or simply hollow objects. In the male dream of sexual excitement, the dreamer finds in the street the upper part of a clarinet, next to it the same part of a tobacco pipe, and beside that a piece of fur. The clarinet and the tobacco pipe represent the approximate shape of the male sexual organ, while the fur represents the pubic hair. In the female sexual dream, the tightness of the closely pressed thighs may be symbolized by a narrow courtyard enclosed by houses, and the vagina by a very narrow, slippery, soft footpath running through the courtyard, along which the dreamer must walk, perhaps to deliver a letter to a gentleman." It is particularly noteworthy that at the end of such a physically stimulated dream, fantasy, as it were, drops its mask and represents the stimulating organ or its function openly. The "tooth-stimulated dream," for instance, usually ends with the dreamer taking a tooth out of his mouth.

Dream fantasy may direct its attention not only to the shape of the stimulating organ but also to the substance it contains, making that substance the object of symbolization. A dream of intestinal stimulation, for example, may lead us through muddy streets, and a dream of bladder stimulation to foaming water. Or the stimulus itself, the manner of its excitation, and the object it craves may be represented symbolically; or the dreaming ego may enter into a concrete relationship with the symbols of its own state, as when, under painful stimuli, we struggle desperately with vicious dogs or raging bulls, or when, in a sexual dream, the dreamer sees herself pursued by a naked man. Whatever elaboration the details may receive, a symbolizing, fantastic activity remains the central force of every dream. In his finely and fervently written book, Volkelt then attempted to penetrate further into the nature of this fantasy and to assign the psychic activity so identified its place in a system of philosophical ideas, a system that, however, remains far too difficult to grasp for anyone not prepared by prior schooling to enter sympathetically into philosophical modes of thought.

Scherner attaches no useful function to the activity of the symbolizing fantasy in dreams. In the dream, the psyche plays with the stimuli at its disposal. One might suspect that it plays in an improper manner. One might also ask whether our careful study of Scherner's theory, whose arbitrariness and departure from the rules of all investigation are only too obvious, can lead to any useful results. It would then be right for us to forestall any dismissal of Scherner's theory without examination by answering that such a dismissal would be too arrogant. The theory is built on the impressions a man received from his own dreams, a man who paid them close attention and who seems to have been personally well suited to tracing obscure psychic events. Furthermore, it deals with a subject that for thousands of years has struck humanity as mysterious, yet rich in content and connections, and toward whose explanation rigorous science, by its own admission, has contributed nothing beyond attempting, in flat opposition to popular feeling, to deny the subject any substance or significance. Finally, let us frankly admit that we apparently cannot avoid the fantastic in our attempts to explain the dream. There are fantastic ganglion cells, too: the passage quoted earlier from so sober and exact an investigator as Binz, which depicts the dawn of awakening spreading across the dormant cell masses of the cerebrum, is no less fanciful and improbable than Scherner's attempts at interpretation. I hope to be able to show that something real lies beneath Scherner's ideas, though it has been perceived only dimly and lacks the universality that would entitle it to be called a theory of dreams. For now, Scherner's theory, set against the medical theory, may at least show us between what extremes the explanation of dream life still wavers.

**(h) Relations between the Dream and Mental Diseases.** When we speak of the relation between dreams and mental disorders, we may mean three different things. First, there are etiological and clinical relations, as when a dream represents or sets off a psychotic condition, or lingers on after such a condition has passed. Second, there are the changes that dream life undergoes in mental illness. Third, there are inner relations between dreams and the psychoses, analogies that point to a close kinship between them. These many connections between the two kinds of phenomena were a favorite theme of medical writers in earlier periods of medicine, and they have become so again in recent times, as the literature collected by Spitta, Radestock, Maury, and Tissié shows. Sante de Sanctis has lately turned his attention to the same relationship. For the purposes of our discussion, a brief glance at this important subject will be enough.

On the clinical and etiological relations between dreams and the psychoses, I will report the following observations as representative examples. Hohnbaum asserts, as Krauss reports, that the first attack of insanity frequently originates in an anxious and terrifying dream, and that the patient's ruling idea is connected with this dream. Sante de Sanctis cites similar observations in paranoiacs and declares that in some of them the dream is the *vraie cause déterminante de la folie*, "the true determining cause of the madness." The psychosis may spring to life all at once, with the dream causing the mental disturbance and containing its explanation, or it may develop slowly through further dreams that must still struggle against the patient's doubt. In one of de Sanctis's cases, the disturbing dream was accompanied by mild hysterical attacks, which were followed in turn by an anxious, melancholic state. Féré, as cited by Tissié, describes a dream that caused a hysterical paralysis. In these cases the dream is presented to us as the cause of the mental disturbance, although we would describe the facts just as well if we said that the disturbance first manifests itself in dream life, that it first breaks out in the dream. In other instances the morbid symptoms were contained in dream life, or the psychosis remained confined to it. Thomayer, for example, draws attention to anxiety dreams that must be understood as equivalent to epileptic attacks. Allison, as Radestock reports, has described a "nocturnal insanity" in which the patients seem perfectly well during the day, while hallucinations, fits of frenzy, and the like regularly appear at night. De Sanctis and Tissié report similar observations, among them a paranoid dream-equivalent in an alcoholic, in which voices accused his wife of infidelity. Tissié reports numerous recent observations in which actions of a pathological character, based on delusions or obsessive impulses, originated in dreams. Guislain describes a case in which sleep was replaced by an intermittent insanity.

There can be little doubt that physicians will one day concern themselves not only with the psychology of dreams but with their psychopathology as well.

In patients recovering from insanity, it is often especially clear that while their daytime functions have returned to normal, their dream life may still belong to the psychosis. Gregory, according to Krauss, is said to have been the first to draw attention to such cases. Macario, as Tissié reports, describes a manic patient who, a week after his complete recovery, again experienced in his dreams the flight of ideas and the passionate impulses of his illness.

Very few investigations have yet been made into the changes that dream life undergoes in people suffering from chronic psychoses. The inner kinship between dreams and mental disturbance, on the other hand, which shows itself in a broad agreement between the manifestations of the two, was noticed early. According to Maury, Cabanis was the first to point it out, in his *Rapports du physique et du moral*; he was followed by Lelut, J. Moreau, and above all the philosopher Maine de Biran. The comparison is, to be sure, still older. Radestock opens the chapter devoted to it with a collection of sayings that express the analogy between dreams and insanity. Kant says somewhere: "The lunatic is a dreamer in the waking state." According to Krauss, "Insanity is a dream with the senses awake." Schopenhauer calls the dream a brief madness and madness a long dream. Hagen describes delirium as a dream life brought on not by sleep but by disease. And Wundt declares in his *Physiological Psychology*: "As a matter of fact, we may in our dreams live through almost all the symptoms we encounter in insane asylums."

Spitta lists the specific points of agreement that make such an identification seem reasonable, and Maury groups them in very similar fashion: "(1) Suspension, or at least slowing, of self-consciousness; hence ignorance of one's condition as such, and therefore an inability to feel astonishment and an absence of moral awareness. (2) Altered perception by the sense organs: perception is diminished in dreams and generally heightened in insanity. (3) The combination of ideas solely according to the laws of association and reproduction; hence the automatic formation of groups of ideas, and for this reason a disproportion in the relations between them, producing exaggerations and phantasms. And as a result of all this: (4) A change or transformation of the personality, and at times of particular traits of character, amounting to perversities."

Radestock adds some further features, or analogies in the material itself: "Most hallucinations and illusions occur in the sphere of sight, hearing, and general bodily sensation. As in dreams, the fewest elements are supplied by the senses of smell and taste. The fever patient, like the dreamer, is assailed by memories from the remote past; what the waking and healthy person seems to have forgotten is recalled in sleep and in illness." The analogy between dream and psychosis acquires its full weight only when, like a family resemblance, it extends to the finer gestures and the individual peculiarities of facial expression.

"To one who is tormented by physical and mental suffering, the dream grants what reality has denied him, namely physical well-being and happiness; so, too, the insane see bright pictures of happiness, greatness, sublimity, and wealth. The imagined possession of estates and the imaginary fulfillment of wishes, whose denial or destruction has served as the psychic cause of the insanity, often form the main content of the delirium. The woman who has lost a dearly loved child experiences the joys of motherhood in her delirium; the man who has suffered financial ruin believes himself immensely rich; and the jilted girl pictures herself in the bliss of tender love."

This passage, in which Radestock summarizes a perceptive discussion by Griesinger, shows with the greatest clarity that wish fulfillment is a characteristic of the imagination common to both the dream and the psychosis. My own investigations have taught me that here lies the key to a psychological theory of the dream and of the psychosis alike.

"Absurd combinations of ideas and weakness of judgment are the chief characteristics of both dreams and insanity." In both we find an overestimation of one's own mental powers that seems absurd to sober judgment, and the rapid sequence of ideas in the dream corresponds to the flight of ideas in the psychosis. Neither has any sense of the measure of time. The dissociation of personality in dreams, which may, for instance, divide one's own knowledge between two persons, so that one of them, the stranger, corrects the dreamer's own ego, corresponds exactly to the well-known splitting of personality in hallucinatory paranoia; the dreamer, too, hears his own thoughts spoken by strange voices. Even fixed delusions have their analogue in the stereotyped, recurring pathological dream, the *rêve obsédant*. After recovering from a delirium, patients often declare that the illness seemed to them like an unpleasant dream; indeed, they tell us that occasionally, even in the course of their illness, they felt they were only dreaming, just as frequently happens in the dreams of sleep.

In view of all this, it is not surprising that Radestock sums up his own opinion, and that of many others, as follows: "Insanity, an abnormal phenomenon of disease, is to be regarded as an intensification of the periodically recurring normal dream states."

Krauss tried to ground the relationship between dreams and insanity in their etiology, or rather in their exciting causes, and thereby perhaps made the connection even closer than the analogy between their manifestations could. According to him, the fundamental element common to both is, as we have seen, the organically determined sensation: the sensation of physical stimuli, the general bodily feeling produced by contributions from all the organs. Peise's view, as cited by Maury, may be compared with this.

The undeniable agreement between dreams and mental disturbance, reaching even into characteristic details, is one of the strongest supports of the medical theory of dream life, which represents the dream as a useless and disruptive process and as the expression of diminished psychic activity. We cannot expect, however, to find the final explanation of dreams in the mental disorders, since it is well known how unsatisfactory our understanding of their origin remains. It is very probable, on the other hand, that a revised conception of the dream must also affect our views of the inner mechanism of mental disorders, and so we may say that in trying to solve the mystery of the dream, we are also working toward an understanding of the psychoses.

I owe the reader an explanation for not having extended my survey of the literature on dream problems to cover the period between the first appearance of this book and its second edition. However unsatisfying this explanation may seem, it was nonetheless what guided me. The motives that chiefly led me to summarize how dreams have been treated in the literature were exhausted by the foregoing introduction; to continue the work would have cost me extraordinary effort and yielded little benefit or knowledge. The nine intervening years have produced nothing new or valuable, either in actual material or in points of view, for the understanding of dreams. In most of the publications that have since appeared, my work has gone unmentioned and unregarded; least attention of all has been paid to it by the so-called "investigators of dreams," who have thereby furnished a splendid example of the aversion to learning anything new that is characteristic of scientific men. *Les savants ne sont pas curieux*, "Scholars are not curious," as the mocking Anatole France put it. If there were such a thing in science as a right of retaliation, I in turn would be justified in ignoring the literature published since this book appeared. The few reviews that have appeared in scientific journals are so full of folly and misunderstanding that my only possible answer to my critics would be to ask them to read this book again. Perhaps I should also ask them to read it as a whole.

In the works of physicians who use the psychoanalytic method of treatment, among them Jung, Abraham, Riklin, Muthmann, Stekel, and Rank, a great many dreams have been reported and interpreted according to my instructions. Where these works go beyond confirming my assertions, I have noted their results at the relevant points in my discussion. A supplement to the bibliography at the end of this book gathers the most important of these new publications. The lengthy book on dreams by Sante de Sanctis, which appeared in German translation soon after its original publication, came out at almost the same moment as mine, so that, like two letters crossing in the mail, neither could take account of the other: I could take as little notice of him as the Italian author could of me. Unfortunately, I am further obliged to state that this laborious work is exceedingly poor in ideas, so poor that one could never guess from it that the problems I have dealt with even exist.

Finally, I must mention two publications that come close to my own treatment of dream problems. A younger philosopher, H. Swoboda, who has set out to extend Wilhelm Fliess's discovery of biological periodicity, in cycles of twenty-three and twenty-eight days, into the psychic realm, has produced an imaginative work in which, among other things, he uses this key to solve the riddle of the dream. Under his scheme, the interpretation of dreams would fare badly: the content of dreams would be explained by the coincidence of all those memories that, on a given night, complete one of the biological periods for the first or the nth time. A personal communication from the author led me to assume that he no longer wished to defend this theory seriously. But it seems I was mistaken in that conclusion. Elsewhere I shall report some observations bearing on Swoboda's claim, though I remain unconvinced by its conclusions. It gave me far greater pleasure to come upon, by chance and in an unexpected place, a conception of the dream that agrees in all essentials with my own. The dates rule out any possibility that this conception was influenced by a reading of my book, and I must therefore welcome it as the only demonstrable instance in the literature of independent agreement with the essence of my theory of dreams. The book containing the passage on dreams that I have in mind was published in a second edition in 1900 by Lynkeus, under the title *Phantasien eines Realisten*, "Fantasies of a Realist."

## II Method of Dream Interpretation

### The Analysis of a Sample Dream

The title I have given this treatise signals the tradition from which I intend to begin my discussion of dreams. I have set myself the task of showing that dreams can be interpreted. Whatever I contribute toward solving the dream problems just discussed can come only as a by-product of settling this particular problem of my own. The moment I assume that dreams are interpretable, I find myself at odds with the prevailing science of dreams, and indeed with every dream theory except Scherner's. To "interpret a dream" means to state its meaning: to replace it with something that takes its place in the chain of our mental activities as a link of full weight and value. But as we have seen, the scientific theories of the dream leave no room for any problem of interpretation, because they hold that the dream is not a mental act at all. It is a physical process that announces itself to the mental apparatus through signs. Popular opinion has always held otherwise. Claiming its privilege to proceed illogically, it concedes that the dream is incomprehensible and absurd, yet it cannot bring itself to deny the dream all significance. Guided by a dim intuition, it seems instead to assume that the dream does have a meaning, though a hidden one. It assumes that the dream stands in for some other process of thought, and that one need only uncover this substitute correctly to arrive at the dream's concealed sense.

Laypeople have therefore always tried to "interpret" dreams, and they have used two fundamentally different methods. The first takes the dream's content as a whole and seeks to replace it with another content that is intelligible and in certain respects analogous. This is symbolic dream interpretation, and it naturally breaks down from the start with dreams that seem not merely unintelligible but confused. The biblical Joseph's reading of Pharaoh's dream illustrates the procedure. Seven fat cows, followed by seven lean ones that devour them, are a symbolic substitute for a prophecy: seven years of famine will come upon the land of Egypt and consume the entire surplus produced by seven years of plenty. Most of the artificial dreams that poets invent are designed for this kind of symbolic interpretation. They present the poet's thought in a disguise that matches the characteristics of dreaming as we know them from experience. The notion that dreams are chiefly concerned with future events, whose course they foresee, is a remnant of the prophetic significance once attributed to them. It now becomes the motive for projecting the meaning found by symbolic interpretation into the future, by means of an "it shall come to pass."

There is, of course, no way to demonstrate how such a symbolic interpretation is reached. Success remains a matter of clever guesswork and direct intuition. For this reason dream interpretation has naturally been elevated into an art that seems to depend on extraordinary gifts. The second popular method renounces any such claims. It might be called the "cipher method," because it treats the dream as a kind of secret code in which each sign is translated into another sign of known meaning according to a fixed key. Suppose I have dreamed of a letter and also of a funeral or something similar. I consult a "dream book" and find that "letter" is to be translated as "vexation," and "funeral" as "marriage, engagement." It then remains for me to string the jumble I have decoded into some connected meaning, which once again I am to take as referring to the future. An interesting variant of this cipher procedure appears in the work on dream interpretation by Artemidorus of Daldis, and it partly corrects the method's purely mechanical character. Artemidorus takes into account not only the content of the dream but also the dreamer's personality and station in life. The same dream content therefore means one thing for a rich man, a married man, or an orator, and another for a poor man, a bachelor, or, say, a merchant. The essential feature of this procedure is that the work of interpretation is directed not at the dream as a whole but at each part of its content separately, as though the dream were a conglomerate in which every fragment requires its own particular handling. It was surely the incoherent and confused dreams that prompted the invention of the cipher method.

Neither of these popular procedures can be of the slightest value for the scientific treatment of the subject. The symbolic method is limited in its application and admits of no general demonstration. In the cipher method everything depends on whether the key, the dream book, is reliable, and there is no guarantee of that whatsoever. One might be tempted to concede the point to the philosophers and psychiatrists and dismiss the problem of dream interpretation as a fanciful one.

I have come, however, to think otherwise. I have been compelled to recognize that this is another of those fairly common cases in which an ancient and stubbornly held popular belief seems to have come closer to the truth than the verdict of present-day science. I must insist that dreams really do have meaning and that a scientific method of interpreting them is possible. I arrived at knowledge of this method in the following way.

For several years I have been working to resolve certain psychopathological formations, such as hysterical phobias and obsessional ideas, for therapeutic purposes. I took up this work after becoming acquainted with an important report by Joseph Breuer, which showed that in these formations, regarded as morbid symptoms, resolution and treatment go hand in hand. Wherever it has been possible to trace such a pathological idea back to the elements in the patient's mental life from which it arose, the idea has crumbled away and the patient has been freed of it. Our other therapeutic efforts have failed, and these conditions remain mysterious. I therefore find it tempting, despite every difficulty, to press forward along the path Breuer opened until the subject is fully understood. I shall have to report in detail elsewhere on the form the technique of this procedure has finally taken and on the results of the work done so far. It was in the course of these psychoanalytic studies that I came upon dream interpretation. I required my patients to tell me every idea and thought that occurred to them in connection with a given theme, and they would then relate their dreams. In doing so they taught me that a dream can be woven into the chain of mental associations that must be traced backward through memory, starting from the pathological idea. The next step was to treat the dream itself as a symptom and to apply to it the method of interpretation that had been developed for symptoms.

This requires a certain psychological preparation of the patient. Two things are attempted at once. The first is to sharpen his attention to his own mental perceptions. The second is to eliminate the critical judgment with which he normally screens the thoughts that rise up in him. For self-observation with concentrated attention, it helps if the patient lies in a restful position with his eyes closed. He must be explicitly instructed to give up criticizing the thoughts he perceives. He must also be told that the success of the psychoanalysis depends on his noticing and reporting everything that passes through his mind. He must not suppress one idea because it seems unimportant or irrelevant to the subject, or another because it seems nonsensical. He must remain impartial toward his ideas, for this critical habit is precisely what would be to blame if he failed to find the desired solution to the dream, the obsession, or whatever the problem may be.

In the course of my psychoanalytic work I have noticed that the state of mind of a person who is reflecting is entirely different from that of a person who is observing his own mental processes. Reflection involves more mental activity than even the most attentive self-observation, as the tense posture and furrowed brow of reflection show, in contrast with the relaxed features of self-observation. Both require concentrated attention, but in reflection one also exercises criticism. One rejects some of the ideas that arise. One cuts others short so as not to follow the trains of thought they would open. Toward still others one may act in such a way that they never become conscious at all; they are suppressed before they are perceived. In self-observation, by contrast, one's only task is to suppress this criticism. If one succeeds, a limitless number of ideas that would otherwise have remained beyond reach rise into consciousness. With the help of this newly obtained material, both pathological ideas and dream images can be interpreted. The aim is evidently to bring about a mental state that resembles the state just before falling asleep, and indeed the hypnotic state as well, in the way it distributes psychic energy, which is to say mobile attention. As we fall asleep, "unwanted ideas" come to the fore because a certain deliberate and certainly also critical activity relaxes, an activity we ordinarily allow to steer the course of our thoughts. We usually attribute this relaxation to "fatigue," and the unwanted ideas that emerge are transformed into visual and acoustic images, as Schleiermacher and others have observed. In the state used for analyzing dreams and pathological ideas, this activity is deliberately and willfully set aside. The psychic energy thus saved, or some part of it, is devoted to attentively following the unwanted thoughts that now surface. These thoughts retain their character as ideas, and in this lies the difference from the state of falling asleep. In this way "unwanted ideas" are turned into "wanted" ones.

The method demands that we suspend the criticism we usually apply to these apparently "freely rising" ideas, and for some people this is not easy. The "unwanted ideas" habitually provoke the most violent resistance, which tries to keep them from surfacing. Yet if we can trust our great poet-philosopher Friedrich Schiller, a very similar tolerance is the precondition of poetic creation. Otto Rank drew my attention to a passage in Schiller's correspondence with Körner in which Schiller replies to a friend who complains of his lack of creativity:

"The reason for your complaint lies, it seems to me, in the constraint that your intellect imposes on your imagination. I must make an observation here and illustrate it with an allegory. It does not seem beneficial, and it is actually harmful to the creative work of the mind, if the intellect examines too closely the ideas already pouring in, as it were, at the gates. Taken by itself, an idea may be quite trivial and quite far-fetched, yet it may become important because of one that follows it. Perhaps, in a certain combination with others that may seem equally absurd, it can form a very useful structure. The intellect cannot judge any of this unless it holds onto the idea long enough to see it in connection with the others. In a creative mind, however, the intellect has withdrawn its watchmen from the gates. The ideas rush in pell-mell, and only then does the intellect survey and critically examine the great heap. You gentlemen critics, or whatever else you call yourselves, are ashamed or afraid of the momentary, passing madness found in all true creators, whose longer or shorter duration distinguishes the thinking artist from the dreamer. Hence your complaints of barrenness, for you reject too soon and discriminate too severely."

Schiller wrote this in a letter dated December 1, 1788.

And yet such a "withdrawal of the watchmen from the gates of the intellect," as Schiller calls it, such a shift into uncritical self-observation, is by no means difficult.

Most of my patients manage it after their first instructions. I can do it quite completely myself, if I help the process along by writing down whatever occurs to me. The amount of psychic energy by which critical activity is reduced in this way, and by which the intensity of self-observation can be increased, varies widely depending on the subject on which attention is to be fixed.

The first step in applying this procedure teaches us that we can make only the separate parts of the dream's content the object of our attention, not the dream as a whole. Suppose I ask a patient who is still unpracticed, "What occurs to you in connection with this dream?" He is usually unable to fix on anything in his mental field of vision. I have to present the dream to him piece by piece. Then, for each fragment, he offers a series of associations, which may be called the "background thoughts" of that part of the dream. In this first and important respect, then, my method departs from the popular, traditional method of symbolic interpretation made famous in legend and approaches the second, the "cipher method." Like the cipher method, it interprets in detail rather than en masse. Like it, it treats the dream from the start as something composite, a conglomerate of mental images.

In the course of psychoanalyzing neurotic patients I have already interpreted many thousands of dreams, but I do not wish to use this material in introducing the technique and theory of dream interpretation. I would certainly be open to the objection that these are the dreams of neuropathic subjects, and that conclusions drawn from them cannot be carried over to the dreams of healthy people. But another reason also compels me to set them aside. The theme of these dreams is naturally always the history of the illness underlying the neurosis. Using them would require a very long introduction and an inquiry into the nature and logical conditions of the psychoneuroses. These matters are new and unfamiliar in the highest degree, and they would divert attention from the problem of dreams. My purpose lies rather in the opposite direction: I mean to use the solution of dreams to prepare the ground for solving difficult problems in the psychology of the neuroses. But if I exclude the dreams of neurotics, I cannot afford to be too selective with what remains. All that is left are the dreams occasionally told to me by healthy acquaintances and those cited as examples in the literature on dream life. Unfortunately, none of these dreams comes with an analysis, and without one I cannot discover a dream's meaning. My procedure is, of course, not as simple as the popular cipher method, which translates the dream content according to a fixed key. On the contrary, I fully expect the same dream to conceal a different meaning in different persons and in different contexts. I must therefore fall back on my own dreams. They offer an abundant and convenient body of material, supplied by a person of roughly normal health and bearing on many incidents of everyday life. I shall certainly meet with doubts about the reliability of such "self-analyses," and it will be said that they leave the door wide open to arbitrariness. In my judgment, conditions are actually more favorable in self-observation than in the observation of others. In any case, it is legitimate to see how much can be achieved through self-analysis. I must also overcome further difficulties that arise within myself. One has an understandable reluctance to expose so many intimate details of one's own mental life, and one does not feel safe from being misunderstood by strangers. But one must be able to rise above this. "Every psychologist," writes Delbœuf, "is obliged to confess even his own weaknesses if he believes that by doing so he may shed light on some obscure problem." And I may assume that the reader's initial interest in the indiscretions I am bound to commit will soon give way to complete absorption in the psychological problems they illuminate.

I shall therefore choose one of my own dreams and use it to demonstrate my method of interpretation. Every such dream requires a preliminary account. I must now ask the reader to make my interests his own for a considerable stretch, and to become absorbed with me in the most trivial details of my life, for an interest in the hidden meaning of dreams absolutely demands this kind of transference.

Preliminary account: In the summer of 1895 I had given psychoanalytic treatment to a young woman who was on close terms of friendship with me and my family. Such a tangle of relationships can easily stir up a variety of feelings in the physician, and especially in the psychotherapist. His personal stake is greater and his authority smaller. A failure threatens to undermine his friendship with the patient's family. The treatment ended in partial success: the patient was rid of her hysterical anxiety, but not of all her physical symptoms. At that time I was not yet certain of the criteria that mark the final resolution of a case of hysteria, and I expected her to accept a solution that did not seem acceptable to her. Since we disagreed, we broke off the treatment for the summer holidays. One day a younger colleague, one of my closest friends, came to see me. He had visited the patient, Irma, and her family at their country resort. I asked him how he had found her and received the answer: "She is better, but not entirely well." I realize that these words of my friend Otto, or the tone of voice in which he spoke them, angered me. I thought

I heard a reproach in his words, perhaps a suggestion that I had promised the patient too much, and, rightly or wrongly, I attributed Otto's apparent siding against me to the influence of the patient's relatives, who, I assumed, had never approved of my treatment. Still, my unpleasant impression did not become clear to me, and I said nothing about it. That same evening I wrote out Irma's case history so that I could hand it, as though in self-justification, to Dr. M., a mutual friend who was then a leading figure in our circle. During the night that followed, or perhaps toward morning, I had the following dream, which I recorded immediately on waking.

**Dream of July 23–24, 1895**

*A great hall, with many guests whom we are receiving. Among them is Irma, whom I at once take aside, as though to answer her letter and to reproach her for not yet accepting the "solution." I say to her: "If you still have pains, it is really only your own fault." She answers: "If you only knew what pains I have now in my neck, stomach, and abdomen; I am all drawn together." I am frightened and look at her. She looks pale and bloated, and I think that I must be overlooking some organic illness after all. I take her to the window and look down her throat. She shows some resistance to this, like a woman who wears false teeth. I think that she does not need them anyway. Then the mouth opens properly, without difficulty, and I find a large white patch on the right, and elsewhere I see extensive grayish-white scabs attached to curious curling structures, plainly shaped like the turbinate bones, the scroll-like bones inside the nose. I quickly call Dr. M., who repeats the examination and confirms what I found. Dr. M. looks quite unlike himself: he is very pale, he limps, and his chin is clean-shaven. My friend Otto is now also standing beside her, and my friend Leopold percusses her small body, tapping on her chest to listen to the sound, and says: "She has some dullness low on the left." He also points out an infiltrated patch of skin on her left shoulder, which I can feel just as he does, in spite of her dress. M. says: "There's no doubt it's an infection, but it doesn't matter; dysentery will follow, and the poison will be excreted." We also know directly where the infection came from. Not long ago, when she was feeling unwell, my friend Otto gave her an injection of a propyl preparation, propyls … propionic acid … trimethylamine, the formula of which I see printed before me in heavy type. Injections like that should not be given so carelessly. And probably the syringe was not clean.*

This dream has an advantage over many others. It is immediately clear which events of the previous day it connects to and what subject it addresses, since the preliminary account supplies both. The news about Irma's health I had received from Otto, and the case history I had been writing late into the night, continued to occupy my mind even in sleep. Even so, no one who has read the preliminary account and knows the content of the dream has been able to guess what the dream means. Nor do I know myself. I am puzzled by the symptoms Irma complains of in the dream, since they are not the ones for which I treated her. I smile at the consultation with Dr. M. I smile at the absurd idea of an injection of propionic acid, and at the consolation Dr. M. attempts to offer. Toward the end, the dream seems more obscure and more compressed than at the beginning. To learn what all this means, I have no choice but to undertake a thorough analysis.

**Analysis**

*The hall, with many guests whom we are receiving.*

That summer we were living at the Bellevue, an isolated house on one of the hills near the Kahlenberg. The house had originally been built as a place of entertainment, and for that reason it has unusually high, hall-like rooms. The dream also took place at the Bellevue, a few days before my wife's birthday. During the day my wife had said she expected several friends, Irma among them, to come to us as guests for her birthday. My dream, then, anticipates this situation: it is my wife's birthday, and we are receiving many people, Irma among them, as guests in the great hall of the Bellevue.

*I reproach Irma for not having accepted the solution. I say: "If you still have pains, it is your own fault."*

I could have said this while awake, and perhaps I did. At that time I held the opinion, which I later recognized to be wrong, that my task was limited to informing patients of the hidden meaning of their symptoms. Whether they then accepted the solution on which success depended was not my responsibility. I am grateful to this error, now happily overcome, for making life easier for me at a time when, with all my unavoidable ignorance, I was expected to produce successful cures. But in the speech I make to Irma in the dream, I see that above all I do not want to be blamed for the pains she still feels. If they are Irma's own fault, they cannot be mine. Should the purpose of the dream be sought in this direction?

*Irma's complaints: pains in the neck, abdomen, and stomach; she is drawn together.*

Stomach pains were part of my patient's set of symptoms, but they were not very prominent; she complained more of nausea and disgust. Pains in the neck and abdomen, and tightness in the throat, played almost no part in her case. I wonder why I settled on this particular selection of symptoms, and for the moment I cannot find the reason.

*She looks pale and bloated.*

My patient always had a ruddy complexion. I suspect that someone else is being substituted for her here.

*I am frightened at the thought that I must have overlooked some organic illness.*

As the reader will readily believe, this is a constant fear for a specialist who sees almost nothing but neurotics and who is used to attributing to hysteria so many symptoms that other physicians treat as organic. At the same time, I am troubled by a faint doubt, though I cannot say where it comes from, about whether my fear is entirely honest. If Irma's pains really are organic in origin, then I am not obliged to cure them, since my treatment removes only hysterical pains. It seems to me, in fact, that I *want* to find a mistake in the diagnosis, because then I could no longer be reproached for failing.

*I take her to the window to look down her throat. She resists a little, like a woman who has false teeth. I think she does not need them anyway.*

I had never had occasion to examine Irma's mouth. This episode in the dream reminds me of an examination I had made some time before of a governess who at first gave an impression of youthful beauty but who, on opening her mouth, took certain pains to hide her teeth. Other memories of medical examinations, and of the small secrets they uncover to the discomfort of both examiner and examined, attach themselves to this case. "She does not need them anyway" may at first be a compliment to Irma, but I suspect another meaning. In a careful analysis, one can sense whether or not the underlying thoughts one expects to find have been exhausted. The way Irma stands at the window suddenly reminds me of another experience. Irma has a close woman friend of whom I think very highly. One evening, when I paid her a visit, I found her standing at the window in exactly the position reproduced in the dream, and her physician, this same Dr. M., declared that she had a diphtheritic membrane. Both Dr. M. and the membrane reappear later in the dream. It now occurs to me that over the past few months I have been given every reason to suppose that this lady, too, is hysterical. Indeed, Irma herself let this slip to me. But what do I actually know about her condition? Only one thing: that, like Irma, she suffers from hysterical choking in her dreams. In the dream, then, I have replaced my patient with her friend. I now remember that I have often toyed with the hope that this lady might also engage me to relieve her of her symptoms. But even at the time I thought it unlikely, because she is very reserved by nature. She resists, as the dream shows. Another explanation might be that she does not need it; so far, in fact, she has proved strong enough to manage her condition without outside help.

Only a few features now remain that I can assign neither to Irma nor to her friend: pale, bloated, false teeth. The false teeth lead me to the governess, and I now feel inclined to settle for bad teeth. Then another person occurs to me to whom these features might refer. She is not my patient, and I do not wish her to become one, because I have noticed that she is not at ease with me, and I do not think she would make a compliant patient. She is usually pale, and once, during a spell when she was particularly well, she looked bloated. I have thus compared my patient Irma with two other women, both of whom would likewise resist treatment. What can it mean that I have exchanged her for her friend in the dream? Perhaps that I *wish* to exchange her: either the other woman arouses stronger sympathy in me, or I think more highly of her intelligence. For I consider Irma foolish because she does not accept my solution. The other woman would be more sensible and so more likely to give in. *Then the mouth opens properly, without difficulty*: she would tell me more than Irma does.

*What I see in the throat: a white patch and scabby nostrils.*

The white patch recalls diphtheria, and so Irma's friend, but it also recalls the grave illness of my eldest daughter two years earlier and all the anxiety of that unhappy time. The scabs in the nose remind me of a worry about my own health. At that time I frequently used cocaine to reduce troublesome swelling in my nose, and a few days before, I had heard that a woman patient who did the same had developed extensive necrosis, a dying-off of tissue, in the mucous membrane of her nose. My recommendation of cocaine in 1885 had also brought serious reproaches upon me. A dear friend, who had already died by 1895, had hastened his end through the misuse of this drug.

*I quickly call Dr. M., who repeats the examination.*

This would simply reflect the position M. held among us. But the word "quickly" is striking enough to call for a particular explanation. It reminds me of a painful episode in my medical practice. By repeatedly prescribing a drug, sulfonal, a sedative that was still considered harmless at the time, I had once caused severe poisoning in a woman patient, and I had turned in great haste to an older, more experienced colleague for help. A further detail confirms that I really did have this case in mind. The patient, who died of the poisoning, bore the same name as my eldest daughter. This had never occurred to me until now, but now it seems almost like fate's retribution, as though the substitution of persons in the dream were to be continued in another sense: this Mathilde for that Mathilde, an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth. It is as if I were seizing every opportunity to reproach myself for a lack of medical conscientiousness.

*Dr. M. is pale, without a beard on his chin, and he limps.*

This much is accurate: his unhealthy appearance often worries his friends. The other two characteristics must belong to someone else. I think of an elder brother living abroad who keeps his chin clean-shaven and whom, if I remember rightly, the M. of the dream rather resembles on the whole. A few days earlier, news had arrived that this brother was lame because of an arthritic disease of the hip. There must be a reason why the dream fuses the two men into one. I remember that I was in fact on bad terms with both of them, and for similar reasons: both had recently rejected a certain proposal I had put to them.

*My friend Otto is now standing next to the sick woman, and my friend Leopold examines her and points out a dullness low on the left.*

My friend Leopold is also a physician and a relative of Otto. Because the two practice the same specialty, fate has made them rivals who are constantly being compared with each other. Both of them assisted me for years while I was still running a public clinic for children with nervous disorders, and scenes like the one in the dream often took place there. While I was debating a diagnosis with Otto, Leopold would examine the child again and make an unexpected contribution to the decision. The difference in temperament between the two resembled that between Inspector Bräsig and his friend Karl in Fritz Reuter's novel: one was distinguished by his quickness, the other was slow and deliberate but thorough. If I set Otto against the careful Leopold in the dream, I apparently do so in order to praise Leopold. The comparison is similar to the earlier one between the disobedient patient Irma and her friend, whom I consider more sensible. I now become aware of one of the tracks along which the dream's chain of associations runs: from the sick child to the children's clinic. The dullness low on the left recalls a particular case that matched it in every detail, in which Leopold astonished me with his thoroughness. Beyond this, I have a vague notion of something like a metastatic illness, one that spreads from its original site to other parts of the body, but this might rather be a reference to the woman patient I would like to have in place of Irma. For this lady, as far as I can tell, resembles a woman suffering from tuberculosis.

*An infiltrated patch of skin on the left shoulder.*

I see at once that this is my own rheumatism of the shoulder, which I always feel when I have stayed up late into the night. The wording in the dream also sounds ambiguous: "which I can feel … in spite of her dress." What is meant is "feel in my own body." I am struck, too, by how unusual the phrase "infiltrated patch of skin" sounds. "An infiltration at the upper left, behind" is the expression we are accustomed to; it would refer to the lung, and so, once again, to tuberculosis patients.

*In spite of her dress.*

This, admittedly, is only an insertion. At the clinic, of course, we examined the children undressed, which stands in some contrast to the way adult women patients have to be examined. The story used to be told of a prominent clinician that he always examined his patients physically only through their clothes. The rest is obscure to me, and, frankly, I have no wish to pursue the matter further.

*Dr. M. says: "It's an infection, but it doesn't matter. Dysentery will follow, and the poison will be excreted."*

At first this strikes me as ridiculous, yet it must be analyzed as carefully as everything else. Looked at more closely, it does seem to have a kind of meaning. What I had found in the patient was local diphtheritis. I remember the discussion of diphtheritis and diphtheria at the time of my daughter's illness: diphtheria is the general infection that develops from local diphtheritis. Leopold demonstrates the presence of such a general infection by means of the dullness, which thus suggests a metastatic lesion, a secondary site of disease. I believe, however, that this kind of metastasis does not occur in diphtheria. It recalls pyemia instead, a form of blood poisoning in which abscesses spread through the body.

*It doesn't matter* is meant as a consolation. I believe it fits in as follows. The preceding part of the dream has produced the idea that the patient's pains are the result of a serious organic illness. I begin to suspect that in this way I am merely trying to shift the blame away from myself. Psychological treatment cannot be held responsible for a diphtheritic illness that persists. But now, in turn, I am troubled at having invented such serious suffering for Irma solely to clear myself. It seems cruel. I therefore need an assurance that the outcome will be a happy one, and it seems a reasonable choice to put the words of consolation into the mouth of Dr. M. But here I regard myself as standing above the dream, a fact that itself requires explanation.

Yet why is this consolation so absurd?

*Dysentery.*

There is some far-fetched theoretical notion that diseased matter can be removed through the intestines. Am I making fun, in this way, of Dr. M.'s large stock of far-fetched explanations and his habit of discovering curious connections between diseases? Dysentery suggests something else as well. A few months ago I had in my care a young man who suffered remarkable pains when moving his bowels, a case that colleagues had treated as "anemia with malnutrition." I recognized that it was a matter of hysteria, but I was unwilling to try my psychotherapy on him and sent him off on a sea voyage instead. A few days before the dream, I had received a despairing letter from him in Egypt, saying that he had suffered a new attack there, which the local physician had diagnosed as dysentery. I suspect that the diagnosis was simply a mistake by an ignorant colleague who lets hysteria make a fool of him. Still, I cannot help reproaching myself for having placed the patient where he might contract an organic disease of the bowels on top of his hysteria. Moreover, "dysentery" sounds like "diphtheria," a word that does not appear in the dream.

It must indeed be the case that with the consoling prognosis "Dysentery will follow," and so on, I am making fun of Dr. M., for I remember that years ago he jokingly told a very similar story about another colleague. He had been called in to consult with this colleague on the case of a woman who was gravely ill, and he had felt obliged to point out to the other physician, who seemed very optimistic, that he had found albumen in the patient's urine, a sign of kidney disease. The colleague was not in the least troubled and answered calmly: "That doesn't matter, doctor; the albumen will certainly be excreted." I can therefore no longer doubt that this part of the dream contains derision for those colleagues who know nothing of hysteria. As if in confirmation, a question now arises in my mind: "Does Dr. M. know that the symptoms of his patient, our friend Irma, which give reason to fear tuberculosis, are also based on hysteria? Has he recognized the hysteria, or has he foolishly overlooked it?"

But what could be my motive for treating this friend so badly? The answer is very simple: Dr. M. agrees with my solution no more than Irma herself does. In this dream, then, I have already taken revenge on two people: on Irma, with the words "If you still have pains, it is your own fault," and on Dr. M., with the absurd consolation I have put into his mouth.

*We know directly where the infection came from.*

This direct knowledge within the dream is very remarkable. Only a moment before, we did not know it, since the infection was first demonstrated by Leopold.

*Not long ago, when she was feeling unwell, my friend Otto gave her an injection.*

Otto had in fact mentioned that during his short visit to Irma's family he had been called to a nearby hotel to give an injection to someone who had suddenly fallen ill. Injections also bring back the memory of my unfortunate friend who poisoned himself with cocaine. I had recommended the drug to him only for oral use, to ease his withdrawal from morphine, but he once gave himself injections of cocaine.

*With a propyl preparation ... propyls ... propionic acid.* How did this ever occur to me? On the same evening on which I had written up part of the case history, before I had the dream, my wife opened a bottle of liqueur labeled "Ananas," the German word for pineapple. It was a present from our friend Otto, who has a habit of giving presents on every possible occasion; I hope that a wife will one day cure him of it. The liqueur gave off such a smell of fusel oil, the harsh, oily by-product of poor distillation, that I refused to taste it. My wife suggested, "We'll give this bottle to the servants," but I, more prudent still, forbade it, adding the philanthropic remark, "They mustn't be poisoned either." The smell of fusel oil, which consists largely of amyl alcohol, has evidently awakened in my memory the whole chemical series of propyl, methyl, and so on, and this series supplied the propyl preparation of the dream. I have, it is true, made a substitution here: I dreamt of propyl after smelling amyl. But substitutions of this kind are perhaps permissible, especially in organic chemistry.

*Trimethylamine.* In the dream I see the chemical formula of this substance, which probably shows a great effort on the part of my memory. The formula is printed in heavy type, as though to set apart something of particular importance from its context. Where does this trimethylamine, so forcefully brought to my attention, lead? It leads to a conversation with another friend, who for years has known all my ideas while they were still taking shape, as I have known his. At that time he had just told me some of his thoughts about the chemistry of sexuality, and had mentioned, among other things, that he believed trimethylamine to be one of the products of sexual metabolism. The substance thus leads me to sexuality, the factor to which I attribute the greatest significance in the origin of the nervous disorders I try to cure. My patient Irma is a young widow. If I am anxious to excuse the failure of her treatment, I suppose I could best do so by pointing to this condition, which her admirers would gladly change. And how remarkably such a dream is put together! The other woman, whom I take as my patient in the dream in place of Irma, is also a young widow.

I suspect I know why the formula for trimethylamine has made itself so prominent in the dream. So many important things are gathered up in this one word. Trimethylamine alludes not only to the overpowering factor of sexuality but also to a person whose sympathy I remember with satisfaction whenever I feel myself abandoned in my opinions. Should not this friend, who plays so large a part in my life, appear again in the dream's chain of thought? Of course he must. He is particularly familiar with the consequences of disorders of the nose and its adjoining cavities, and he has revealed to science several highly remarkable connections between the turbinate bones, the thin, scroll-shaped plates of bone inside the nasal passages, and the female sexual organs. Hence the three curly formations in Irma's throat. I had Irma examined by him to see whether her stomach pains might be of nasal origin. But he himself suffers from a suppurative rhinitis, a festering inflammation of the nose, which worries him, and perhaps there is an allusion to this in the pyemia, the blood poisoning that hovers before me in the dream's talk of metastases.

*Such injections are not made so rashly.* Here the charge of carelessness is hurled directly at my friend Otto. I have the impression that I had some thought of this kind in the afternoon, when his words and looks seemed to show that he had taken sides against me. It was perhaps: "How easily he is influenced; how carelessly he passes judgment." The sentence also points once more to my deceased friend, who so lightly took refuge in cocaine injections. As I have said, I had never intended the drug to be injected at all. I see that in reproaching Otto I touch again on the story of the unfortunate Matilda, from which the same reproach arises against me. Clearly I am collecting here examples of my own conscientiousness, but also of its opposite.

*Probably the syringe was not clean, either.* This is another reproach aimed at Otto, but it originates elsewhere. The day before, I happened to meet the son of an eighty-two-year-old lady to whom I am obliged to give two injections of morphine every day. She is in the country at present, and I had heard that she was suffering from an inflammation of the veins. I immediately thought that it must be an infection caused by a contaminated syringe. It is my pride that in two years I have not given her a single infection; I am constantly concerned, of course, to see that the syringe is perfectly clean. For I am conscientious. From the inflammation of the veins I return to my wife, who suffered from emboli, or blood clots, during one of her pregnancies. Three related situations now rise to the surface of my memory, involving my wife, Irma, and the dead Matilda, and the sameness of these situations plainly justifies my letting the three women stand in for one another.

I have now completed the interpretation of the dream. In the course of it I have taken great pains to capture every idea that a comparison between the dream's content and the dream thoughts hidden behind it must have prompted. Meanwhile, the "meaning" of the dream has dawned on me. I have become aware of a purpose that the dream carries out, and that purpose must have been the motive for dreaming. The dream fulfills several wishes that were stirred in me by the events of the previous evening: Otto's news and my writing down of the case history. For the upshot of the dream is that I am not to blame for the suffering Irma still endures, and that Otto is. Otto had annoyed me with his remark about Irma's incomplete cure, and the dream takes my revenge on him by turning the reproach back upon himself. The dream frees me of responsibility for Irma's condition by attributing it to other causes, and it supplies a whole array of them. The dream represents a certain state of affairs as I would wish it to be. Its content is therefore the fulfillment of a wish, and its motive is a wish.

This much is apparent at first glance. But many details of the dream also become intelligible when they are viewed as wish fulfillments. I take revenge on Otto not only for hastily siding against me, by accusing him of a careless medical procedure, the injection, but also for the bad liqueur that smells of fusel oil, and I find an expression in the dream that unites both reproaches: the injection with a preparation of propyl. Still I am not satisfied, and I continue my revenge by comparing him with his more reliable colleague, as if to say, "I like him better than you." But Otto is not the only one who must feel the force of my anger. I take revenge on my disobedient patient by exchanging her for a more sensible, more docile one. Nor do I let Dr. M.'s contradiction pass unnoticed; I express my opinion of him in an obvious allusion, to the effect that his attitude to the question is that of an ignoramus ("dysentery will follow," and so on).

Indeed, it seems to me as though I were appealing over his head to someone better informed, namely my friend who told me about trimethylamine, just as I have turned from Irma to her friend and from Otto to Leopold. Take these three people away, replace them with three others of my choosing, and I shall be released from the reproaches I do not wish to have deserved! The dream goes to the most elaborate lengths to prove to me that these reproaches are unfounded. Irma's pains are not to be charged to me, because she herself is to blame for them by refusing to accept my solution. Irma's pains are none of my business, because they are organic in nature and cannot possibly be healed by a psychological cure. Irma's sufferings are adequately explained by her widowhood (trimethylamine!), which I naturally cannot alter. Irma's illness was caused by a careless injection on Otto's part, with an unsuitable substance, of a kind I would never have given. Irma's suffering is the result of an injection made with a dirty syringe, like the inflammation of the veins in my old lady, whereas I never do any such harm with my injections.

I am well aware that these explanations of Irma's illness, which unite in acquitting me, do not agree with one another; they even exclude one another. The whole plea, for this dream is nothing else, vividly recalls the defense of a man accused by his neighbor of having returned a borrowed kettle in damaged condition. In the first place, he said, he had returned the kettle undamaged; in the second place, it already had holes in it when he borrowed it; and in the third place, he had never borrowed the kettle from his neighbor at all. So much the better: if even one of these three lines of defense is accepted as valid, the man must be acquitted.

Still other subjects mingle in the dream whose connection to my release from responsibility for Irma's illness is less transparent: my daughter's illness and that of a patient with the same name, the harmfulness of cocaine, the illness of my patient traveling in Egypt, concern for the health of my wife, my brother, and Dr. M., my own physical ailments, and concern for my absent friend who suffers from suppurative rhinitis. But if I keep all these things in view, they combine into a single train of thought, which might be labeled: concern for the health of myself and others, or professional conscientiousness. I recall a vague, unpleasant sensation when Otto brought me the news of Irma's condition. I would like, finally, to record the expression of this fleeting sensation, since it belongs to the train of thought woven into the dream. It is as though Otto had said to me: "You do not take your duties as a physician seriously enough; you are not conscientious; you do not keep your promises." This train of thought then placed itself at my service, so that I might show how thoroughly conscientious I am and how deeply I care about the health of my relatives, friends, and patients. Curiously enough, this body of thought also contains some painful memories, which bear out the blame assigned to Otto rather than the accusation against me. The material appears to be impartial, yet the connection between this broader material, on which the dream rests, and the narrower theme of the dream, which gives rise to the wish to be innocent of Irma's illness, is unmistakable.

I do not claim to have uncovered the meaning of the dream completely, or that my interpretation is without gaps. I could spend much more time on it, draw further explanations from it, and raise new problems that it invites us to consider. I even know the points from which further chains of association could be followed. But considerations of the kind that attach to every dream of one's own hold me back from the work of interpretation. Whoever is quick to condemn such reserve is welcome to try being more candid than I. For now, I am content with the discovery just made. If the method of dream interpretation outlined here is followed, it will be found that the dream really does have meaning, and is by no means the expression of fragmentary brain activity, as the authorities would have us believe. When the work of interpretation is complete, the dream can be recognized as the fulfillment of a wish.

## III The Dream Is the Fulfilment of a Wish

When a traveler has made his way through a narrow mountain pass and reached a high point where the roads divide and the view opens broadly in several directions, he may reasonably stop for a moment to consider which way to turn next. Something similar happens to us now that we have mastered this first dream interpretation. We stand in the clear light of a sudden insight. The dream is not like the random noise of a musical instrument struck by some external force rather than played by the musician's hand. It is not senseless or absurd, and it does not require us to suppose that one part of our store of ideas lies dormant while another begins to awaken. It is a fully valid psychic phenomenon, and in fact the fulfilment of a wish. It takes its place in the chain of intelligible mental acts that make up our waking life, and it has been constructed by a highly complex intellectual activity.

Yet at the very moment we are inclined to celebrate this discovery, we are overwhelmed by a crowd of questions. If the dream, as interpretation shows, represents a wish as fulfilled, why does it express this fulfilment in such a peculiar and unfamiliar way? What changes have the dream thoughts undergone before being transformed into the manifest dream we remember on waking? How did this transformation take place? Where does the material worked into the dream come from? What accounts for the peculiarities we observe in the dream thoughts, such as their capacity to contradict one another? Recall the analogy of the kettle: the man accused of returning a borrowed kettle damaged replies that he returned it undamaged, that it already had a hole when he borrowed it, and that he never borrowed it at all. Each defense would be valid on its own, but together they cancel one another out. And finally, can the dream teach us something new about our inner mental processes, and can its content correct opinions we have held during the day?

For the present, I suggest that we set all these questions aside and follow a single path. We have found that the dream represents a wish as fulfilled. Our next concern must be to determine whether this is a universal characteristic of dreams, or merely the incidental content of the particular dream, the dream "of Irma's injection," with which we began our analysis. Even if we resolve that every dream has a meaning and a psychic value, we must still allow for the possibility that this meaning is not the same in every dream. The first dream we considered was the fulfilment of a wish; another might prove to be a fear realized; a third might have a reflection as its content; a fourth might simply reproduce a memory. Are there, then, other wish dreams? Or are there perhaps no dreams but wish dreams?

It is easy to show that dreams often display their character as wish fulfilments openly and recognizably, so much so that one may wonder why the language of dreams was not understood long ago. There is, for example, a dream I can produce as often as I like, almost as an experiment. If I eat anchovies, olives, or other heavily salted foods in the evening, I become thirsty during the night and wake up. But the waking is preceded by a dream that always has the same content: I am drinking. I gulp down water in long draughts, and it tastes as sweet as only a cool drink can when one's throat is parched. Then I wake and feel an actual desire to drink. The occasion for this dream is thirst, which I perceive upon waking. The wish to drink arises from this sensation, and the dream shows me that wish as fulfilled. In doing so, it performs a function whose nature I soon guess. I sleep well and am not used to being awakened by a bodily need. If I can quench my thirst by dreaming that I am drinking, I need not wake up to satisfy it. It is, in short, a dream of convenience. The dream substitutes itself for action, as happens elsewhere in life. Unfortunately, the need for water to quench thirst cannot be satisfied by a dream, as my thirst for revenge against Otto and Dr. M. could be, but the intention is the same.

This same dream recently appeared in a modified form. On this occasion I became thirsty before going to bed and emptied the glass of water that stood on the little chest beside my bed. Several hours later in the night came a fresh attack of thirst, accompanied by discomfort. To get water, I would have had to get up and fetch the glass standing on my wife's night table. I therefore dreamed, quite appropriately, that my wife was giving me a drink from a vase. The vase was an Etruscan cinerary urn, a funeral vessel of the kind once used to hold the ashes of the dead, which I had brought home from a journey to Italy and had since given away. But the water in it tasted so salty, apparently from the ashes, that I had to wake up. One can see how conveniently the dream is able to arrange matters. Since its only purpose is the fulfilment of a wish, it can be perfectly selfish. Love of comfort is truly incompatible with consideration for others. The appearance of the cinerary urn is probably itself another wish fulfilment: I regret that I no longer own the vase, and it, like the glass of water at my wife's side, is out of my reach. The urn also suits the salty taste, which had by now grown stronger and which I knew would force me to wake.

Such convenience dreams were very frequent with me in my youth. Having always been accustomed to work late into the night, I found it difficult to wake early. I used to dream that I was already out of bed and standing at the washstand. Eventually I could no longer conceal from myself that I had not yet got up, but in the meantime I had managed to sleep a while longer. I know the same dream of laziness from a young colleague of mine who seems to share my fondness for sleep. The landlady with whom he lodged near the hospital had strict orders to wake him on time every morning, but she certainly had a great deal of trouble carrying them out. One morning, sleep was particularly sweet. The woman called into the room: "Mr. Joe, get up, you have to go to the hospital." At this the sleeper dreamed of a hospital ward, a bed in which he was lying, and a chart pinned above his head that read: "Joe H., cand. med., 22 years old," the standard designation for a medical student. He said to himself in the dream, "If I'm already in the hospital, I don't have to go there," turned over, and went on sleeping. He had thus openly admitted to himself his motive for dreaming.

It is no harder to discover wish fulfilments in several dreams I have collected from healthy people. A friend who knew my theory of dreams and had explained it to his wife said to me one day: "My wife asked me to tell you that yesterday she dreamed she was having her period. You'll know what that means." Of course I know. If a young wife dreams that she is menstruating, her periods have stopped. I can understand that she would have liked to enjoy her freedom a little longer before the burdens of motherhood began. It was a clever way of announcing her first pregnancy. Another friend writes that his wife recently dreamed she noticed milk stains on the front of her blouse. This too indicates pregnancy, but not a first one this time: the young mother wishes to have more milk for her second child than she had for the first.

A young woman who for weeks had been cut off from all company while nursing a child through an infectious illness dreamed, after the illness had ended safely, of a social gathering at which Alphonse Daudet, Paul Bourget, Marcel Prévost, and others were present. All of them were very pleasant to her and entertained her delightfully. The various authors in the dream had the features their portraits give them. But Prévost, whose portrait she did not know, looked like the disinfecting man who had cleaned the sickrooms the day before and had been the first visitor to enter them after a long interval. The dream might evidently be translated perfectly as follows: "It's about time for something more entertaining than this endless nursing."

Perhaps this selection will be enough to show that dreams are often found, and under the most varied and complicated circumstances, that can be understood only as wish fulfilments and that present their content without disguise. For the most part these are short, simple dreams, which stand in pleasant contrast to the confused and crowded dream compositions that have chiefly attracted the attention of other writers on the subject. Still, it will be worthwhile to spend some time on these simple dreams. We may expect to find the simplest dreams of all in children, whose mental activities are certainly less complicated than those of adults. In my opinion, child psychology should perform a service similar to the one that the study of the anatomy and development of the lower animals performs for research into the structure of the higher ones. Until now, only a few deliberate efforts have been made to use child psychology for this purpose.

The dreams of small children are simple wish fulfilments and are therefore, compared with the dreams of adults, not at all interesting. They pose no problem to be solved, but they are naturally invaluable as proof that the dream, in its essence, signifies the fulfilment of a wish. I have been able to collect several examples of such dreams from material furnished by my own children.

For two dreams, one by my daughter, then eight and a half years old, and the other by a boy of five and a quarter, I am indebted to an excursion to the beautiful village of Hallstatt in the summer of 1896. I should explain first that during that summer we were living on a hill near Aussee, from which, in good weather, we had a splendid view of the Dachstein from the roof of our house. With a telescope one could easily make out the Simony Hut, a mountain shelter near the summit. The children often tried to see it through the telescope, though I do not know with what success. Before the excursion I had told them that Hallstatt lay at the foot of the Dachstein, and they looked forward to the day with great joy. From Hallstatt we went into the valley of Eschern, whose changing scenery delighted the children. One of them, however, the boy of five, gradually grew discontented. Each time a mountain came into view he would ask, "Is that the Dachstein?" and I would have to answer, "No, only a foothill." After he had asked this several times he fell completely silent, and he flatly refused to come with us up the flight of steps to the waterfall. I assumed he was worn out. But the next morning he came to me beaming with joy and said: "Last night I dreamed we were at the Simony Hut." Now I understood him. When I had spoken of the Dachstein, he had expected that on the excursion to Hallstatt he would climb the mountain and come face to face with the hut that had been so much discussed at the telescope. When he discovered that he was to be treated to foothills and a waterfall instead, he was disappointed and became discontented. The dream compensated him. I tried to learn some details of it, but they were meager: "You have to climb steps for six hours," as he had heard.

On this same excursion, wishes destined to be satisfied only in dreams had also arisen in the mind of the eight-and-a-half-year-old girl.
