We had taken along to Hallstatt our neighbor's twelve-year-old son, a perfect little gentleman who, it seems to me, already enjoyed the full affection of the young lady. The next morning she told the following dream: "Just think, I dreamed that Emil was one of us, that he called you papa and mamma, and slept at our house in the big room like our boys. Then mamma came into the room and threw a big handful of chocolate bars under our beds." The girl's brothers, who had evidently not inherited a talent for dream interpretation, declared, just like the authorities: "That dream is nonsense." The girl defended at least part of the dream, and from the standpoint of the theory of the neuroses it is worth knowing which part: "The part about Emil belonging to us is nonsense, but the part about the chocolate bars isn't." It was precisely this latter part that was obscure to me, and my wife supplied the explanation. On the way home from the railway station, the children had stopped in front of a coin-operated vending machine and had wanted exactly the kind of chocolate bars, wrapped in shiny metallic paper, that they knew from experience such machines sold. But their mother had rightly judged that the day had brought enough wish fulfilment and had left this wish to be satisfied in dreams. This little scene had escaped me. The part of the dream my daughter had condemned I understood at once. I had myself heard our well-mannered guest telling the children to wait until papa or mamma caught up. For the little girl, the dream turned this temporary relationship into a permanent adoption. Her affectionate nature did not yet know any form of living together other than those mentioned in the dream, which are taken from her relationship with her brothers. Why the chocolate bars were thrown under the beds could not, of course, be explained without questioning the child.

From a friend I have learned of a dream very similar to my boy's. It concerned an eight-year-old girl. Her father had taken the children on a walk to Dornbach, intending to visit the Rohrerhütte, but turned back because it had grown too late, and promised to make up for their disappointment another time. On the way home they passed a signpost pointing the way to the Hameau. The children now asked to be taken there as well, but for the same reason had to be content with a postponement to another day. The next morning the eight-year-old came to her father, satisfied, and said: "Papa, last night I dreamed you were with us at the Rohrerhütte and on the Hameau." Her impatience had anticipated in the dream the fulfilment of her father's promise.

Another dream, inspired in my daughter, then three and a quarter years old, by the picturesque beauty of Aussee, is equally straightforward. The little one had crossed the lake for the first time, and the trip had passed too quickly for her. She did not want to leave the boat at the landing and cried bitterly. The next morning she told us: "Last night I was sailing on the lake." Let us hope that the length of this dream voyage was more satisfactory to her.

My eldest boy, then eight years old, was already dreaming of the realization of his fantasies. He had ridden in a chariot with Achilles, with Diomedes as his charioteer. The day before, of course, he had shown a lively interest in a book of Greek myths that had been given to his older sister.

If we may grant that children's talking in their sleep also belongs to the category of dreaming, I can report the following as one of the most recent dreams in my collection. My youngest daughter, then nineteen months old, had vomited one morning and had therefore been kept without food all day. During the night that followed this day of hunger, she was heard calling out excitedly in her sleep: "Anna Feud, strawberry, huckleberry, omelette, pap!" She used her own name in this way to express the idea of possession. The menu apparently included just about everything that would have seemed to her a desirable meal. The fact that berries appeared on it twice was a demonstration against the household's health regulations, and it rested on a circumstance she had by no means overlooked: the nurse had blamed her indisposition on eating too many strawberries. In the dream, she took revenge for this opinion, which she found distasteful.

If we call childhood happy because it does not yet know sexual desire, we must not forget how abundant a source of disappointment and self-denial, and therefore of dream stimulation, the other great drive of life, hunger, can become for it. Here is a second example of this. My nephew, then twenty-two months old, had been given the task of congratulating me on my birthday and presenting me with a little basket of cherries, which at that time of year were not yet in season. He seemed to find this hard, for he kept repeating, "Cherries in it," and could not be persuaded to let the basket out of his hands. But he knew how to secure compensation. Until then he had been in the habit of telling his mother every morning that he had dreamed of the "white soldier," an officer of the guard in a white cloak whom he had once admired in the street. On the day after the birthday, he woke up joyfully with a piece of news that could only have come from a dream: "He(r)man eat up all the cherries!"

What animals dream of, I do not know. But a proverb, which one of my readers called to my attention, claims to know. It asks, "What does the goose dream of?" and answers, "Of maize!" The whole theory that the dream is the fulfilment of a wish is contained in these two lines.

We now see that we could have arrived at our theory of the hidden meaning of dreams by the shortest route had we simply consulted everyday speech. The wisdom of proverbs, it is true, sometimes speaks contemptuously enough of dreams, and seems to support the scientific opinion that "Dreams are mere froth." Yet in ordinary usage the dream is the gracious fulfiller of wishes. "I would never have imagined that in my wildest dreams," exclaims someone who finds his expectations surpassed by reality.

## IV Distortion in Dreams

If I claim that wish fulfilment is the meaning of every dream, so that there can be no dreams except wish dreams, I can be sure of meeting the most emphatic contradiction from the start. The objections will run something like this: "That some dreams must be understood as fulfilments of wishes is nothing new. Writers on the subject recognized it long ago: Radestock, Volkelt, Tissié, and M. Simon, who discusses the hunger dreams of the imprisoned Baron Trenck, as well as a passage in Griesinger. But the claim that there can be no dreams except those of wish fulfilment is another of the unjustified generalizations with which you have lately chosen to distinguish yourself. Dreams with the most painful content, and without a trace of wish fulfilment, are common enough. The pessimistic philosopher Eduard von Hartmann perhaps stands furthest from the theory of wish fulfilment. In his *Philosophy of the Unconscious*, Part II, he writes: 'As regards the dream, it carries all the troubles of waking life over into the sleeping state; the one thing it does not carry over is the one thing that can in some measure reconcile a cultivated person to life, namely scientific and artistic enjoyment.'

"Even less discontented observers have stressed that pain and disgust occur in dreams more often than pleasure. Scholz and Volkelt, among others, say so. Two women, Sarah Weed and Florence Hallam, have even worked out from their own dreams a mathematical expression for the predominance of displeasure: they classify 58 per cent of their dreams as disagreeable and only 28.6 per cent as positively pleasant. Besides the dreams that carry the painful feelings of waking life on into sleep, there are dreams of fear, in which this most terrible of all unpleasant sensations torments us until we wake. And it is precisely children who are so often haunted by these fear dreams, as Debacker has shown in his study of night terrors, the *pavor nocturnus*, even though it was in children that you claimed to find wish dreams in their undisguised form."

Anxiety dreams do seem to rule out any generalization of the thesis, established through the examples of the last section, that the dream is a wish fulfilment. They even seem to brand that thesis as absurd. Yet these apparently conclusive objections are not hard to escape. Our doctrine does not rest on taking the manifest content of the dream at face value. It refers to the thought content that interpretation reveals behind the dream. We must therefore distinguish between the manifest and the latent content of the dream. Certainly there are dreams whose content is extremely painful. But has anyone ever tried to interpret these dreams and uncover the latent thoughts within them? If not, then neither objection holds against us. The possibility remains that even painful and frightening dreams, once interpreted, will turn out to be wish fulfilments.

In scientific work, when one problem proves difficult to solve, it often helps to take up a second problem alongside it, just as two nuts are easier to crack by pressing them together than one at a time. So we face not only the question of how painful and frightening dreams can be fulfilments of wishes. Our discussion so far also raises another: why do dreams with indifferent content, which turn out to be wish fulfilments, not display their meaning openly? Consider the dream of Irma's injection, which I reported in full. It is not painful in any way, and interpretation shows it to be a striking wish fulfilment. But why should interpretation be needed in the first place? Why does the dream not say directly what it means? In fact, even the dream of Irma's injection does not at first strike us as showing one of the dreamer's wishes fulfilled. The reader will not have had that impression, and I myself did not know it until I had carried out the analysis. If we call this peculiarity of dreams, the fact that they need explaining, the distortion of dreams, then a second question follows: where does this distortion come from?

Going by first impressions, one might arrive at several possible answers, for example that during sleep we are unable to find adequate expression for the dream thoughts. The analysis of certain dreams, however, compels us to explain distortion differently. I shall show this with a second dream of my own. It again involves a number of indiscretions, but it repays that personal sacrifice by shedding thorough light on the problem.

**Preliminary statement.** In the spring of 1897 I learned that two professors at our university had proposed me for appointment as *Professor extraordinarius*, roughly the rank of assistant professor. The news came unexpectedly and pleased me a good deal, since it expressed the regard of two eminent men and could not be explained by any personal interest on their part. But I told myself at once that I must not build any expectations on it. For the past several years the university administration had left proposals of this kind unacted upon, and several colleagues who were older than I and at least my equals in merit had waited in vain for their appointments all that time. I had no reason to suppose I would fare any better, and so I resolved to console myself. I am not, so far as I know, ambitious, and I practise medicine with satisfying results even without the recommendation of a title. Besides, it was not a question of whether I thought the grapes sweet or sour, as the fox in the fable did; they plainly hung far too high for me.

One evening a friend of mine came to see me, one of those colleagues whose fate I had taken as a warning for myself. He had long been a candidate for promotion to professor, a title which in our society raises a physician to a demigod in the eyes of his patients. Being less resigned than I was, he made a habit of calling now and then at the offices of the university administration to press his case. He came to me straight from one of these visits. This time, he said, he had driven the exalted gentleman into a corner and asked him outright whether it was not really considerations of religious creed that were holding up his appointment. The reply had been that, to be sure, in the present state of public opinion, His Excellency was not in a position to, and so on. "Now at least I know where I stand," my friend said as he finished his story. It told me nothing new, but it was calculated to confirm me in my resignation, for the same considerations of creed applied to my own case.

On the morning after this visit I had the following dream, which was notable for its form. It consisted of two thoughts and two images, with thought and image alternating. I record here only the first half, because the second half has nothing to do with the purpose for which I am citing the dream.

I. *My friend R. is my uncle. I feel great affection for him.*

II. *I see his face before me, somewhat altered. It seems elongated, and a yellow beard surrounding it stands out with peculiar distinctness.*

Then come the other two parts, again a thought and an image, which I omit.

The interpretation of this dream proceeded as follows.

When the dream came back to me in the course of the morning, I laughed outright and said, "The dream is nonsense." But I could not get it out of my head; it pursued me all day, until at last, in the evening, I reproached myself: "If one of your patients, in the course of interpreting a dream, had nothing better to say than 'That is nonsense,' you would take him to task and suspect that some disagreeable matter lay hidden behind the dream, something he wished to spare himself from exposing. Apply the same rule to yourself. Your opinion that the dream is nonsense probably signifies nothing more than an inner resistance to interpreting it. Do not let yourself be put off." Then I set about the interpretation.

"R. is my uncle." What could that mean? I have had only one uncle, my Uncle Joseph. His story was a sad one. More than thirty years earlier he had yielded to the temptation of engaging in dealings that the law punishes severely, and on that occasion the law did punish him. My father, whose hair turned grey with grief within a few days, always used to say that Uncle Joseph had never been a wicked man, only a simpleton; those were his words. If, then, my friend R. is my Uncle Joseph, that amounts to saying, "R. is a simpleton." Hardly credible, and very unpleasant! But there is the face I see in the dream, with its long features and its yellow beard. My uncle really did have such a face, long and framed by a handsome blond beard. My friend R. was quite dark, but when dark-haired people begin to go grey, they pay for the splendour of their youth. Their black beards undergo an unpleasant change of colour, hair by hair: first reddish brown, then yellowish brown, and only at last a definite grey. My friend R.'s beard is now at this stage, and so, I notice with regret, is my own. The face I see in the dream is at once my friend R.'s and my uncle's. It resembles one of Galton's composite photographs: to bring out family resemblances, Galton photographed several faces one over another on the same plate, so that a single blended face emerged. There can be no doubt, then. I really do hold the opinion that my friend R. is a simpleton, like my Uncle Joseph.

I still have no idea why I have constructed this connection, to which I must object in the strongest terms. But it does not reach very far, for my uncle was a criminal, while my friend R. is innocent, except perhaps for having been punished for knocking down an apprentice with his bicycle. Could I mean that offence? That would be a ridiculous comparison. At this point I remember another conversation, with another colleague, N., on the very same subject. I met N. in the street. He too has been nominated for a professorship, and having heard of the honour paid to me, he congratulated me on it. I emphatically declined the congratulations, saying, "You are the last person to make a joke like that, since you know from your own case what such a nomination is worth." To which he replied, though probably not in earnest, "You can't be sure of that. There is a very particular objection against me. Don't you know that a woman once brought a legal complaint against me? I hardly need assure you that the matter was investigated. It was a contemptible attempt at blackmail, and it was all I could do to keep the complainant herself from being punished. But perhaps the affair will be used against me at the ministry to keep me from being appointed. You, on the other hand, are above reproach."

Here I have found my criminal, and with him the interpretation and drift of the dream. My Uncle Joseph stands for both colleagues who have not been appointed to professorships, the one as a simpleton, the other as a criminal. I now also know why I need this representation. If considerations of creed are a deciding factor in the delay of my friends' appointments, then my own appointment is also in doubt. But if I can attribute their rejection to other causes that do not apply to me, my hopes remain intact. This is how my dream proceeds. It makes the one friend, R., a simpleton and the other, N., a criminal. Since I am neither, what we had in common is dissolved; I am entitled to look forward to my appointment as professor, and I have escaped applying to my own case the painful information that the high official gave R.

I must pursue the interpretation of this dream further, for to my mind it is not yet fully cleared up. I am still troubled by the ease with which I degrade two respected colleagues in order to clear my own path to the professorship. My dissatisfaction with my conduct has, it is true, lessened since I learned how to assess the statements dreams make. I would dispute anyone who claimed that I really consider R. a simpleton, or that I disbelieve N.'s account of the blackmail affair. Nor do I believe that Irma was made seriously ill by an injection of a propyl preparation given her by Otto. Here, as there, what the dream expresses is only my wish that things might be so. The statement in which my wish is realized sounds less absurd in the second dream than in the first. It makes more skilful use of actual facts as points of attachment, rather like a well-constructed slander, of which people say "there's something in it." For at that time my friend R. did have the vote of one professor in the faculty against him, and my friend N. had himself, all unsuspecting, supplied me with the material for slander. Nevertheless, I repeat, the dream still seems to me to need further explanation.

I now recall that the dream contains another element that our interpretation has so far left out of account. After it occurs to me that my friend R. is my uncle, I feel great affection for him. To whom does this feeling belong? I never had any affection for my Uncle Joseph. My friend R. has been dear to me for years, but if I went to him and expressed my feelings in terms anywhere near as strong as the affection in the dream, he would certainly be surprised. My affection for him seems false and exaggerated, much like my opinion of his mental qualities, which I express by fusing his personality with my uncle's, except that it is exaggerated in the opposite direction. And now a new state of affairs becomes clear to me. The affection in the dream does not belong to the hidden content, to the thoughts behind the dream. It stands in opposition to that content and is designed to conceal what interpretation might reveal. That is probably its very purpose.

I remember how reluctantly I set to work on the interpretation, how long I tried to put it off, and how I declared the dream to be sheer nonsense. I know from my psychoanalytic practice how such a verdict is to be understood. It has no value as information; it is simply the registering of an emotion. When my little daughter does not want an apple she is offered, she says it tastes bitter without having tasted it at all. When my patients behave like the little girl, I know that a notion is at stake which they want to suppress. The same is true of my dream. I do not want to interpret it because it contains something I object to. Once the interpretation is complete, I discover what that was: the assertion that R. is a simpleton. I may trace the affection I feel for R. not to the hidden dream thoughts but to this unwillingness of mine. If my dream is distorted at this point compared with its hidden content, and distorted into its very opposite, then the apparent affection in the dream exists for the sake of the distortion. The distortion here proves to be intentional; it is a means of dissimulation. My dream thoughts contain an unfavourable judgment of R., and so that I may not become aware of it, its opposite, a feeling of affection for him, makes its way into the dream.

The fact recognized here may well hold universally. As the examples in Section III have shown, there are dreams that are undisguised wish fulfilments. Wherever a wish fulfilment is concealed and unrecognizable, there must be some aversion to the wish, and because of this aversion the wish can find expression only in distorted form. Let me look for a parallel in social life to this event in the inner life of the mind. Where in social life do we find a similar distortion of a mental act? Only where two people are involved, one of whom holds a certain power while the other must show a certain regard for that power. The second person will then distort his mental acts; he will, as we say, dissimulate. The politeness I practise every day is largely dissimulation of this kind. When I interpret my dreams for the reader, I am forced to make distortions of the same sort. The poet, too, complains of the need for such disguise:

"The best that you know, you may not tell the youngsters."

The political writer who has unwelcome truths to tell the government finds himself in the same position. If he states them without reserve, the government will suppress them: after the fact, in the case of something spoken, and in advance, if they are to appear in print. The writer must fear the censor, and so he moderates and distorts the expression of his opinion. Depending on how sensitive the censorship is, he finds himself forced either to refrain from certain particular forms of attack or to speak in allusions rather than direct terms. Or he must dress his objectionable statement in some harmless-looking guise. He may, for instance, describe an incident between two mandarins in the East while having the officials of his own country in mind. The stricter the censor's rule, the more thorough the disguise becomes, and often the more ingenious and humorous the means used to put the reader back on the track of the real meaning.

The correspondence between the workings of the censor and the phenomena of dream distortion can be traced in detail, and it justifies us in assuming similar conditions behind both. We should then assume that in every human being there are, as the fundamental cause of dream formation, two psychic forces, or currents, or systems. One of them forms the wish that the dream expresses; the other acts as a censor on this dream wish and, through its censorship, forces a distortion of the wish's expression. The only question is what gives this second instance, or agency, the authority to exercise its censorship. If we remember that the hidden dream thoughts are not conscious before analysis, while the manifest dream content is remembered as conscious, we easily arrive at the assumption that the privilege of admitting things to consciousness belongs to the second instance. Nothing from the first system can reach consciousness without first passing the second instance, and the second instance lets nothing through without exercising its rights and forcing on the candidate for admission whatever changes suit it. Here we are forming a very definite conception of the "essence" of consciousness. For us, becoming conscious is a particular mental act, distinct from and independent of the process by which an idea is formed or fixed, and consciousness appears to us as a sense organ that perceives a content presented to it from elsewhere. It can be shown that psychopathology cannot possibly do without these fundamental assumptions. A more thorough examination of them must wait for a later occasion.

If I keep in mind the idea of the two psychic instances and their relation to consciousness, I find in politics a very exact analogy for the extraordinary affection I feel in the dream for my friend R., who is so degraded in the course of its interpretation. I turn my attention to a political state in which a ruler, jealous of his prerogatives, is locked in conflict with an alert and active public opinion. The people are indignant at an official they despise and demand his dismissal. Rather than reveal that he has been forced to bow to the public will, the autocrat pointedly bestows some great honor on the official, an honor for which there would otherwise have been no occasion. In just this way, the second instance, the one that controls access to consciousness, lavishes an extraordinary tenderness on my friend R., because the wishful impulses of the first system, pursuing a particular interest of their own at that moment, are inclined to dismiss him as a simpleton.

We may now begin to suspect that the interpretation of dreams can give us hints about the structure of our psychic apparatus, hints we have so far waited for in vain from philosophy. We will not follow that path, however. Instead, once we have cleared up the subject of dream distortion, we will return to our original problem. The question was how dreams with disagreeable content could be analyzed as the fulfillment of wishes. We now see that this is possible wherever dream distortion has taken place, wherever the disagreeable content is merely a disguise for what is wished. Bearing in mind our assumption of two psychic instances, we can now say that disagreeable dreams do in fact contain something disagreeable to the second instance, but something that at the same time fulfills a wish of the first. They are wish dreams in the sense that every dream originates in the first instance, while the second acts upon the dream only by repelling, never by creating. If we confine ourselves to what the second instance contributes to the dream, we can never understand it, and all the riddles that earlier writers have found in dreams will remain unsolved.

That a dream really does have a secret meaning, and that this meaning turns out to be the fulfillment of a wish, must be proved afresh in every case through analysis. I therefore select several dreams with painful content and attempt to analyze them. Some are the dreams of hysterical patients, which require lengthy preliminary explanation and, now and then, an examination of the psychic processes at work in hysteria. I cannot, however, spare the reader this added difficulty in the exposition.

When I treat a psychoneurotic patient analytically, dreams are invariably, as I have said, a subject of our discussion. I must therefore give the patient all the psychological explanations that helped me understand his symptoms, and in doing so I face criticism perhaps no less keen than what I can expect from my colleagues. My patients contest the thesis that all dreams are wish fulfillments with perfect regularity. Here are several examples of the dream material offered to me in order to refute it.

"You always tell me that a dream is a fulfilled wish," begins a clever woman patient. "Now I'll tell you a dream whose content is exactly the opposite, a dream in which a wish of mine is not fulfilled. How do you reconcile that with your theory? Here is the dream:

"I want to give a supper party, but I have nothing in the house except some smoked salmon. I think of going out to shop, but then I remember that it is Sunday afternoon, when all the shops are closed. Next I try to telephone some caterers, but the telephone is out of order. So I have to give up my wish to give a supper party."

I answer, naturally, that only analysis can decide what this dream means, though I admit that at first glance it seems sensible and coherent and looks like the very opposite of a wish fulfillment. "But what occurrence gave rise to this dream?" I ask. "You know that the stimulus for a dream always lies among the experiences of the previous day."

Analysis. The patient's husband, an upright and conscientious wholesale butcher, had told her the day before that he was getting too fat and must therefore begin a treatment for obesity. He would rise early, take exercise, keep to a strict diet, and above all accept no more invitations to supper. Laughing, she goes on to tell how her husband, dining at the common table of an inn, had made the acquaintance of a painter who insisted on painting his portrait because he had never come across such an expressive head. Her husband had answered in his blunt way that he was most grateful for the honor, but was quite convinced that a piece of a pretty young girl's backside would please the artist more than his whole face. She said she was very much in love with her husband at the time and teased him a great deal. She had also asked him not to send her any caviar. What does that mean?

In fact, she had long wanted to eat a caviar sandwich every morning but had begrudged herself the expense. Of course, her husband would have gotten her the caviar at once had she asked for it. Instead, she had begged him not to send it, so that she could go on teasing him about it.

This explanation strikes me as far-fetched. Unacknowledged motives habitually hide behind such unsatisfying explanations. We are reminded of the subjects hypnotized by Bernheim who carried out a posthypnotic command and who, when later asked their motives, did not answer, "I don't know why I did that," but felt obliged to invent a reason that was plainly inadequate. Something similar is probably true of my patient's caviar. I see that she feels compelled to create an unfulfilled wish in her actual life. Her dream, too, presents this denied wish as an accomplished fact. But why does she need an unfulfilled wish?

The associations produced so far are not enough to interpret the dream. I ask for more. After a short pause, which corresponds to the overcoming of a resistance, she reports that the day before she had visited a woman friend of whom she is genuinely jealous, because her husband is forever praising this woman. Fortunately, the friend is very lean and thin, and her husband likes full figures. And what had this thin friend talked about? Naturally, about her wish to put on a little weight. She had also asked my patient, "When are you going to invite us again? You always set such a good table."

Now the meaning of the dream is clear. I can say to the patient: "It is just as if, when she made that request, you had thought: 'Of course! I'm to invite you so you can eat yourself fat at my house and become even more attractive to my husband. I'd rather never give another supper.' The dream then tells you that you cannot give a supper, and so fulfills your wish to contribute nothing toward filling out your friend's figure. Your husband's resolve to decline supper invitations in order to lose weight has taught you that people grow fat on the food served at social gatherings." All that remains is a little conversation to confirm the solution. The smoked salmon in the dream has not yet been accounted for. "How did the smoked salmon in the dream come to mind?" "Smoked salmon is this friend's favorite dish," she answered. I happen to know the lady and can confirm that she begrudges herself salmon just as my patient begrudges herself caviar.

The dream admits of yet another, more precise interpretation, one made necessary only by a subsidiary detail. The two interpretations do not contradict each other; rather, they overlap, and together they furnish a neat example of the ambiguity common to dreams and to all other psychopathological formations. We have seen that at the very time she dreams of a wish being denied, the patient is busy in real life securing an unfulfilled wish for herself, namely the caviar sandwiches. Her friend, too, had voiced a wish, to get fatter, and it would not surprise us if our patient had dreamed that her friend's wish went unfulfilled. For it is her own wish that her friend's wish to gain weight should not be fulfilled. Instead, however, she dreams that one of her own wishes is not fulfilled. The dream takes on a new interpretation if in it she means not herself but her friend: if she has put herself in her friend's place, or, as we may say, has identified herself with her friend.

I believe she has done exactly this, and as a sign of the identification she has created an unfulfilled wish in reality. But what is the meaning of this hysterical identification? Clearing it up requires a thorough exposition. Identification is a highly important factor in the mechanism of hysterical symptoms. Through it, patients can express in their symptoms not only their own experiences but those of a great many other people. They can suffer, as it were, for a whole crowd, and fill every role in a drama with nothing but the resources of their own personality. It will be objected that this is simply the familiar phenomenon of hysterical imitation, the ability of hysterical subjects to copy any symptoms that impress them when they appear in others, as though their pity were stirred to the point of reproducing them. But this describes only the path along which the psychic process is discharged in hysterical imitation, and the path a psychic act takes and the act itself are two different things. The act is somewhat more complicated than one tends to imagine hysterical imitation to be: it corresponds to an unconscious process of reasoning carried through to its conclusion, as an example will show. A physician who has a female patient with a particular kind of twitching, lodged with other patients in the same hospital ward, is not surprised to learn one morning that this peculiar hysterical attack has found imitators. He simply tells himself that the others saw her and did the same, and calls it psychic infection. True enough, but psychic infection proceeds roughly as follows. As a rule, patients know more about one another than the physician knows about any one of them, and they go on concerning themselves with one another after the doctor's visit is over. One of them has an attack today, and soon the others learn that its cause was a letter from home, a renewed lovesickness, or the like. Their sympathy is aroused, and a syllogism that never reaches consciousness completes itself within them: "If one can have an attack like this from such causes, then I too may have such an attack, for I have the same reasons." Were this a train of thought capable of becoming conscious, it might express itself as a fear of having the same attack. But it takes place in another psychic sphere, and so it ends in the actual appearance of the dreaded symptom. Identification, then, is not simple imitation but a sympathy founded on the same etiological claim. It expresses an "as though," and refers to some shared quality that has remained in the unconscious.

In hysteria, identification is most often used to express a sexual bond. A hysterical woman identifies most readily, though not exclusively, with people with whom she has had sexual relations, or who have sexual relations with the same people she does. Language itself takes account of this idea: two lovers are said to be "one." In hysterical fantasy, as in dreams, it is enough for identification that one thinks of sexual relations, whether or not they ever become real. The patient, then, is merely following the rules of hysterical thinking when she gives expression to her jealousy of her friend, a jealousy she herself admits is unjustified, by putting herself in her friend's place and identifying with her through the creation of a symptom: the denied wish. I might clarify the process more specifically as follows. In the dream she puts herself in her friend's place because her friend has taken her own place with respect to her husband, and because she would like to take her friend's place in her husband's esteem.

The contradiction to my theory raised by another woman patient, the wittiest of all my dreamers, was resolved more simply, though along the same pattern: the non-fulfillment of one wish signifies the fulfillment of another. One day I had explained to her that dreams are wish fulfillments. The next day she brought me a dream in which she was traveling with her mother-in-law to the summer resort they were to share. I knew that she had fought fiercely against spending the summer near her mother-in-law, and I also knew that she had happily escaped her by renting an estate at a resort far away. The dream reversed this longed-for solution. Was this not the flattest contradiction of my theory that dreams fulfill wishes? Certainly, and one had only to draw the inference from this dream to arrive at its interpretation. According to the dream, I was wrong. It was therefore her wish that I should be wrong, and the dream showed her that wish as fulfilled. But the wish that I be wrong, fulfilled here in the matter of the summer residence, actually concerned something more serious. At the time, I had concluded from the material of her analysis that something significant for her illness must have happened at a particular period of her life. She had denied it, because she had no memory of it. We soon came to see that I was right. Her wish that I be wrong, transformed into the dream, thus corresponded to the understandable wish that those things, at that point merely suspected, had never happened at all.

Without any analysis, merely by way of conjecture, I ventured to interpret a small incident involving a friend who had been my classmate through all eight years of the Gymnasium, the classical secondary school. He once heard me lecture to a small gathering on the novel subject of the dream as a wish fulfillment. He went home, dreamed that he had lost all his cases (he was a lawyer), and then complained to me about it. I took refuge in an evasion: "One can't win every case." But privately I thought: "If for eight years I sat as Primus, the head of the class, on the first bench, while he drifted somewhere around the middle, isn't it natural that he should have carried a wish from his boyhood that I, too, might for once thoroughly disgrace myself?"

In the same way, a female patient offered me another, gloomier dream as a contradiction of my theory of the wish dream. The patient, a young girl, began: "You remember that my sister now has only one boy, Charles. She lost the elder one, Otto, while I was still living in her house. Otto was my favorite; it was really I who brought him up. I like the other little one too, but of course not nearly as much as the one who died. Last night I dreamed that I saw Charles lying dead before me. He was lying in his little coffin with his hands folded, there were candles all around, and, in short, it was just like the time of little Otto's death, which shook me so deeply. Now tell me, what does this mean? You know me. Am I really wicked enough to wish that my sister would lose the only child she has left? Or does the dream mean that I would rather Charles had died than Otto, whom I love so much more?"

I assured her that this interpretation was impossible. After some reflection, I was able to give her the interpretation of the dream, which she subsequently confirmed.

Orphaned at an early age, the girl had been raised in the home of a much older sister, and among the friends and visitors who came to the house she had met a man who made a lasting impression on her heart. For a time it seemed as though this barely acknowledged attachment would end in marriage, but the happy outcome was thwarted by the sister, whose motives have never been fully explained. After the break, the man our patient loved stayed away from the house. Some time after little Otto's death, to whom her affection had meanwhile turned, she became independent. But she did not succeed in freeing herself from her attachment to her sister's friend. Her pride commanded her to avoid him, yet she found it impossible to transfer her love to the other suitors who presented themselves one after another. Whenever the man she loved, who belonged to the literary profession, announced a lecture anywhere, she was sure to be in the audience, and she seized every other opportunity to see him from a distance without being seen. I remembered that the day before, she had told me the Professor was going to a certain concert and that she was going too, for the pleasure of seeing him. That was the day of the dream, and the concert was to take place on the day she told me the dream. I could now easily see the correct interpretation, and I asked her whether she could recall anything that had happened after little Otto's death. She answered at once: "Certainly. The Professor came back then after a long absence, and I saw him once again beside little Otto's coffin." It was exactly as I had expected. I interpreted the dream as follows: "If the other boy were to die now, the same thing would happen again. You would spend the day with your sister, the Professor would certainly come to offer his condolences, and you would see him again under the same circumstances as before. The dream signifies nothing but this wish of yours to see him again, a wish you are struggling against inwardly. I know that you are carrying the ticket for today's concert in your bag. Your dream is a dream of impatience; it has anticipated by several hours the meeting that is to take place today."

To disguise her wish, she had evidently chosen a situation in which wishes of that sort are ordinarily suppressed, a situation so filled with sorrow that no one thinks of love. And yet it is quite possible that even in the actual scene at the bier of the second, more dearly loved boy, which the dream copied faithfully, she had been unable to suppress her tender feelings for the visitor she had missed for so long.

A different explanation emerged in the case of a similar dream reported by another woman patient, who in her earlier years had been known for her quick wit and cheerful manner, and who still displayed these qualities, at least in the notions that occurred to her during treatment. In the course of a longer dream, this lady seemed to see her fifteen-year-old daughter lying dead before her in a box. She was strongly inclined to turn this dream image into an objection to the theory of wish fulfillment, though she herself suspected that the detail of the box must lead to a different understanding of the dream. During the analysis it occurred to her that on the previous evening the conversation among the company had turned to the English word "box" and its many German translations: a box, a box at the theater, a chest, a box on the ear, and so on. From other components of the same dream we can add that she had guessed the relationship between the English word "box" and the German *Büchse*, and had then been haunted by the memory that *Büchse*, like "box," is used in vulgar speech for the female genitals. Making some allowance for her notions of topographical anatomy, it was therefore possible to assume that the child in the box signified a child in the mother's womb. At this stage of the explanation she no longer denied that the dream image really corresponded to one of her wishes. Like so many other young women, she was by no means happy when she became pregnant, and more than once she admitted to me that she had wished the child might die before it was born. Once, in a fit of anger after a violent scene with her husband, she had even struck her abdomen with her fists in order to hit the child inside. The dead child, then, really was the fulfillment of a wish, but of a wish that had been set aside fifteen years earlier, and it is hardly surprising that she no longer recognized its fulfillment after so long an interval. Much had changed in the meantime.

The group of dreams to which these last two examples belong, dreams whose content is the death of a beloved relative, will be taken up again under the heading of "Typical Dreams." There I will be able to show, with new examples, that despite their unwelcome content, all of these dreams must be interpreted as wish-fulfillments.

The following dream, which was again told to me in order to dissuade me from generalizing too hastily about wishing in dreams, I owe not to a patient but to an intelligent lawyer of my acquaintance. "I dream," he told me, "that I am walking in front of my house with a lady on my arm. A closed carriage is waiting there. A gentleman walks up to me, identifies himself as a police officer, and demands that I come with him. I ask only for time to put my affairs in order. Can you possibly suppose that I wish to be arrested?"

"Of course not," I had to concede. "Do you happen to know what charge you were arrested on?"

"Yes. I believe it was for infanticide."

"Infanticide? But you know that only a mother can commit that crime, against her newborn child?"

"That is true."

"And what were the circumstances of the dream? What happened the evening before?"

"I would rather not tell you that. It is a delicate matter."

"But I must know, or we will have to give up interpreting the dream."

"Well, then, I will tell you. I spent the night not at home but at the house of a lady who means a great deal to me. When we woke in the morning, there was intimacy between us again. Then I fell back asleep and dreamt what I have told you."

"The woman is married?"

"Yes."

"And you do not want her to conceive a child?"

"No. That might give us away."

"Then you do not have intercourse in the normal way?"

"I take the precaution of withdrawing before ejaculation."

"May I assume that you used this method several times during the night, and that by morning you were not entirely sure you had succeeded?"

"That may be so."

"Then your dream is the fulfillment of a wish. Through it you obtain the assurance that you have not fathered a child, or, which amounts to the same thing, that you have killed one. I can easily show you the connecting links. Do you remember that a few days ago we were talking about the hardships of marriage, and about the inconsistency of permitting intercourse so long as no pregnancy results, while any interference after the egg and the sperm have met and a fetus has formed is punished as a crime? In that connection we also recalled the medieval controversy over the precise moment at which the soul actually enters the fetus, since the concept of murder can apply only from that point onward. And you no doubt know the gruesome poem by Lenau that places infanticide and the prevention of children on the same footing."

"Strangely enough, I happened to think of Lenau that very afternoon."

"Another echo in your dream. And now I will show you a second, subordinate wish-fulfillment in it. You are walking in front of your house with the lady on your arm. So you are bringing her home with you, instead of spending the night at her house as you actually do. That the wish-fulfillment at the heart of the dream should disguise itself in so unpleasant a form may have more than one cause. In my essay on the causes of anxiety neurosis, you will find that I list interrupted intercourse as one of the factors that produce neurotic anxiety. It would be consistent with this if, after repeated intercourse of that kind, you were left in an uneasy mood, which then became an element in the construction of your dream. You also use this unpleasant state of mind to conceal the wish-fulfillment. There is still the matter of the infanticide, which we have not yet explained. Why should this crime, which is peculiar to women, occur to you?"

"I will confess that I was involved in such an affair years ago. Through my fault, a girl tried to protect herself from the consequences of a liaison with me by obtaining an abortion. I had nothing to do with carrying out the plan, but naturally I was worried for a long time that the affair might be discovered."

"I understand. That memory supplied a second reason why the thought that you had performed your precaution badly must have been painful to you."

A young physician who heard my colleague recount this dream must have felt that it touched him personally, for he promptly imitated it in a dream of his own, applying the same pattern of thought to a different subject. The day before, he had submitted his income declaration, which was perfectly honest, since he had little to declare. He dreamt that an acquaintance came from a meeting of the tax commission and told him that all the other income declarations had passed without objection, but that his own had aroused general suspicion and he would be punished with a heavy fine. The dream is a thinly disguised fulfillment of the wish to be known as a physician with a large income. It also recalls the story of the young woman who was advised not to accept her suitor because he had a quick temper and would surely beat her once they were married. Her answer was: "I wish he would beat me!" Her wish to be married is so strong that she accepts into the bargain the misery said to come with that marriage, the misery predicted for her, and even elevates it into a wish.

These dreams occur very frequently, and they seem flatly to contradict my theory, since they contain the denial of a wish or some event that is decidedly unwished for. If I group them together under the heading of "counter-wish dreams," I find that all of them can be traced to two principles, one of which I have not yet mentioned, although it plays a large part in human dreaming. One of the motives behind these dreams is the wish that I should be proved wrong. Such dreams occur regularly during treatment whenever a patient is in a state of resistance toward me, and once I have explained to a patient my theory that the dream is a wish-fulfillment, I can count with considerable certainty on provoking one. I may even expect a dream to take this form merely in order to fulfill the wish that I be proved wrong. The last dream I will report from those that arose in the course of treatment shows exactly this. A young woman who had fought hard to continue her treatment with me, against the will of her relatives and the authorities she had consulted, dreamt as follows: *She is forbidden at home to come to me any longer. She then reminds me of my promise to treat her for nothing if necessary, and I say to her: "I can show no consideration in money matters."*

In this case it is not at all easy to demonstrate the fulfillment of a wish. But in every case of this kind there is a second problem, and solving it helps to solve the first. Where does she get the words she puts into my mouth? I have of course never said anything of the sort to her. One of her brothers, however, the very one who has the greatest influence over her, had been kind enough to make this remark about me. The purpose of the dream, then, is that this brother should be proved right. And she does not seek to vindicate him only in her dream; it is her purpose in life and the motive for her illness.

The other motive behind counter-wish dreams is so obvious that it is in danger of being overlooked, as it was for some time in my own case. In the sexual constitution of many people there is a masochistic component, which has arisen through the conversion of the aggressive, sadistic component into its opposite. Such people are called "ideal" masochists when they seek pleasure not in physical pain inflicted on them but in humiliation and in the chastisement of the soul. Such people can plainly have counter-wish dreams and unpleasant dreams that are nonetheless, for them, nothing but wish-fulfillments, since they satisfy their masochistic inclinations. Here is one such dream. A young man who in earlier years had tormented his older brother, toward whom he felt a homosexual attraction, but who had since undergone a complete change of character, had a dream in three parts. In the first, *he is "insulted" by his brother.* In the second, *two adults are caressing each other with homosexual intent.* In the third, *his brother has sold the business that the young man had intended to manage himself in the future.* He woke from this last part with the most unpleasant feelings, and yet it is a masochistic wish-dream, which might be translated: *It would serve me right if my brother made that sale against my interests, as punishment for all the torments he suffered at my hands.*

I hope that the foregoing discussion and examples will be enough, until some further objection is raised, to make it credible that even dreams with painful content are to be analyzed as wish-fulfillments. Nor will it seem a matter of chance that in the course of interpretation one always comes upon subjects that one would rather not speak or think about. The unpleasant feeling these dreams arouse is simply identical with the aversion that tries, usually with success, to keep us from taking up or discussing such subjects, and which all of us must overcome whenever, despite its unpleasantness, we find it necessary to address the matter. But this unpleasant feeling, which also appears in dreams, does not rule out the existence of a wish. Everyone has wishes he would not like to tell others, wishes he does not care to admit even to himself. We are justified on other grounds in linking the unpleasant character of all these dreams with the fact of dream distortion, and in concluding that these dreams are distorted, and their wish-fulfillment disguised beyond recognition, for no other reason than that there exists a repugnance, a will to suppress, directed against the subject matter of the dream or against the wish the dream creates. Dream distortion, then, turns out to be in reality an act of the censor. We will take into account everything that the analysis of unpleasant dreams has brought to light if we restate our formula as follows: *The dream is the (disguised) fulfillment of a (suppressed, repressed) wish.*

There still remains one particular species of dream with painful content: the anxiety dream, whose inclusion among wish-dreams will meet with the least acceptance from the uninitiated. But I can dispose of the problem of anxiety dreams very briefly, for what they reveal is not a new aspect of the dream problem. In their case the question is one of understanding neurotic anxiety in general. The fear we experience in a dream is only apparently explained by the dream's content. If we analyze that content, we find that the fear in the dream is no more justified by it than the fear in a phobia is justified by the idea on which the phobia rests. It is true, for example, that a person can fall out of a window, and that some care is called for near one. But it remains inexplicable why the anxiety in the corresponding phobia is so intense, and why it pursues its victims so much further than its origin would warrant. The same explanation that applies to the phobia, then, applies to the anxiety dream as well. In both cases the anxiety is only superficially attached to the idea that accompanies it; it comes from another source.

Because dream anxiety is so closely related to neurotic anxiety, any discussion of the former obliges me to refer to the latter. In a short essay on "The Anxiety Neurosis," I argued that neurotic anxiety originates in sexual life and corresponds to a libido that has been diverted from its object and has failed to find an outlet. From this formula, which has since proved its validity ever more clearly, we may conclude that the content of anxiety dreams is sexual in nature, and that the libido belonging to that content has been transformed into fear. Later I will have the opportunity to support this claim by analyzing several dreams of neurotic patients. I will also return to the factors that determine anxiety dreams, and to their compatibility with the theory of wish-fulfillment, when I make another attempt to approach the theory of dreams.

## V The Material and Sources of Dreams

Once the analysis of the dream of Irma's injection had shown me that a dream is the fulfillment of a wish, my interest turned to whether I had discovered a universal characteristic of dreams, and for the time being I set aside every other question that the interpretation might have raised. Having now reached the goal along one of these paths, I can turn back and choose a new starting point for exploring the problems of the dream, even if this means losing sight for a while of the theme of wish fulfillment, which is still far from exhausted.

My method of interpretation now allows me to uncover a latent dream content whose significance far exceeds that of the manifest content. This compels me to take up the individual problems of the dream afresh, to see whether the riddles and contradictions that seemed beyond reach, so long as we had only the manifest content, can now be solved satisfactorily.

The views of earlier writers on the relation of the dream to waking life, and on the source of dream material, were set out at length in the introductory chapter. Three peculiarities of memory in dreams have often been noted but never explained:

1. The dream distinctly prefers impressions from the few days immediately preceding it, as Robert, Strümpell, Hildebrandt, and Weed-Hallam have observed.

2. The dream selects its material by principles different from those of waking memory: it recalls not what is essential and important, but what is subordinate and overlooked.

3. The dream has at its disposal the earliest impressions of childhood, and brings to light details from that period of life which, once again, seem trivial to us and which in waking life we had long believed forgotten.

These writers, of course, observed these peculiarities in the selection of dream material only in connection with the manifest content.

### (a) Recent and Indifferent Impressions in the Dream

When I consult my own experience about the sources of the elements that appear in dreams, I must state at once that every dream contains some reference to the events of the day just past. Whatever dream I take up, my own or someone else's, this finding is confirmed. Knowing this, I can usually begin the work of interpretation by trying to discover which experience of the previous day stimulated the dream, and in many cases this is the quickest route. In the two dreams I analyzed closely in the preceding chapter, the dream of Irma's injection and the dream of my uncle with the yellow beard, the reference to the previous day is so plain that it needs no further comment. But to show that such a reference can be demonstrated regularly, I will examine a portion of my own record of dreams, reporting each one only as far as is necessary to identify the stimulus in question.

1. I pay a visit to a house where I am admitted only with difficulty, and meanwhile I keep a woman waiting for me.

Source: A conversation that evening with a female relative, in which I told her she would have to wait for some help she had asked for until a certain time.

2. I have written a monograph about a certain (unspecified) species of plant.

Source: In the window of a bookshop I had seen a monograph on the genus *Cyclamen*.

3. I see two women in the street, a mother and her daughter, the latter of whom is my patient.

Source: A woman under my treatment had told me what obstacles her mother was putting in the way of her continuing the treatment.

4. At the bookshop of S. and R. I subscribe to a periodical that costs twenty florins a year.

Source: During the day my wife had reminded me that I still owed her twenty florins of her weekly household allowance.

5. I receive a communication from the Social Democratic Committee in which I am addressed as a member.

Source: I had received communications at the same time from the Liberal Election Committee and from the president of the Humanitarian Society, of which I really am a member.

6. A man standing on a steep rock in the middle of the sea, in the manner of the painter Böcklin.

Source: Dreyfus on Devil's Island; at the same time, news from my relatives in England.

One might ask whether the dream is invariably tied to the events of the previous day, or whether the reference can extend to impressions from a somewhat longer stretch of the recent past. The question is probably not of the first importance, but I am inclined to decide in favor of the exclusive priority of the day before the dream, which I call the dream-day. Whenever I thought I had found a case in which an impression from two or three days earlier was the source of a dream, careful investigation convinced me that the impression had been remembered on the day before. A demonstrable reproduction of it had intervened between the day of the event and the night of the dream, and I could point to the recent occasion on which the old impression had come back to mind. On the other hand, I could not persuade myself that any regular interval of biological significance separates the stimulating impression from its repetition in the dream. H. Swoboda puts the first such interval at eighteen hours.

I conclude, therefore, that the stimulus for every dream is to be found among those experiences "on which one has not yet slept" for a night.

It follows that impressions from the immediate past, other than those of the day before the dream, stand in no different relation to the dream content than impressions from any period, however remote. The dream may draw its material from any time of life, provided only that a chain of thought leads back to these earlier impressions from one of the experiences of the dream-day, one of the "recent" impressions.

But why this preference for recent impressions? We can arrive at some conjectures by analyzing one of the dreams just mentioned more closely. I choose the dream of the monograph.

*Content of the dream.* I have written a monograph on a certain plant. The book lies before me, and I am just turning over a folded colored plate. Bound into each copy is a dried specimen of the plant, as though taken from a herbarium, a collection of pressed botanical samples.

*Analysis.* That morning I had seen in a bookshop window a book titled *The Genus Cyclamen*, evidently a monograph on that plant.

The cyclamen is my wife's favorite flower. I reproach myself for remembering so seldom to bring her flowers, as she would like. The theme of "bringing flowers" reminds me of a story I recently told among friends to support my claim that forgetting very often carries out a purpose of the unconscious, and that it always permits an inference about the hidden attitude of the person who forgets. A young woman, accustomed to receiving a bunch of flowers from her husband on her birthday, finds that this token of affection is missing one year and bursts into tears. Her husband comes in and cannot account for her tears until she tells him, "Today is my birthday." He strikes his forehead and exclaims, "Why, I had completely forgotten," and offers to go out at once and buy her flowers. But she will not be consoled, for she sees in his forgetfulness proof that she no longer occupies the place in his thoughts that she once did. This Mrs. L. had met my wife two days before, told her she was feeling well, and asked after me. She had been my patient some years earlier.

Some supplementary facts: I once did write something like a monograph on a plant, an essay on the coca plant, which drew Karl Koller's attention to the anesthetic properties of cocaine. I had hinted at this use of the alkaloid in my publication, but I had not been thorough enough to pursue the matter further. This reminds me that on the morning of the day after the dream (I found no time to interpret it until the evening) I had thought about cocaine in a kind of daydream. If I should ever suffer from glaucoma, I imagined, I would travel to Berlin and have myself operated on incognito at the house of my Berlin friend, by a surgeon he would recommend. The surgeon, not knowing whom he was operating on, would boast as usual of how easy such operations had become since the introduction of cocaine, and I would not betray by a single sign that I had had a share in the discovery. Connected with this fantasy were thoughts about how awkward it really is for a physician to ask a colleague for medical care for himself. The Berlin eye specialist, who did not know me, I could simply pay like anyone else.

Only after recalling this daydream do I realize that a memory of a definite experience lies concealed behind it. Shortly after Koller's discovery my father did in fact fall ill with glaucoma. He was operated on by my friend the eye specialist Dr. Koenigstein; Dr. Koller administered the cocaine anesthesia, and remarked afterward that all three of the men who had shared in the introduction of cocaine had been brought together on a single case.

I now try to recall the last time I was reminded of this business with cocaine. It was a few days earlier, when I received a *Festschrift*, a commemorative volume in which grateful pupils had marked an anniversary of their teacher and laboratory director. Among the achievements credited to people associated with the laboratory, I found a note stating that K. Koller had made the discovery of cocaine's anesthetic properties there. Now I suddenly realize that the dream is connected with an experience of the previous evening. I had just walked Dr. Koenigstein home and had been talking with him about a matter that stirs me deeply whenever it comes up. While we were talking in the entrance hall, Professor Gärtner and his young wife joined us, and I could not resist congratulating them both on how healthy they looked. Professor Gärtner happens to be one of the contributors to the *Festschrift* I have just mentioned, and he may well have brought it back to my mind. Likewise Mrs. L., whose disappointment on her birthday I described above, had come up in my conversation with Dr. Koenigstein, though in a different connection.

I will now try to explain the other elements of the dream content. A dried specimen of the plant accompanies the monograph, as though from a herbarium. The herbarium is linked to a memory of my gymnasium, the academic secondary school I attended. The headmaster once called the pupils of the upper classes together to inspect and clean the school's herbarium. Small worms had been found in it, bookworms. The headmaster seemed to have little confidence in my help, for he gave me only a few sheets. I remember to this day that they held crucifers, plants of the mustard family. My interest in botany was never great. In my preliminary examination in botany I was asked to identify a crucifer and failed to recognize it; I would have fared badly if my theoretical knowledge had not rescued me. Crucifers suggest composites, the daisy family. The artichoke is in fact a composite, and it is the one I might call my own favorite flower. My wife, who is more thoughtful than I am, often brings this favorite of mine home from the market.

I see the monograph I have written lying before me. This, too, has its reference. My friend in Berlin, whom I pictured in the daydream, wrote to me yesterday: "I think a great deal about your dream book. I see it lying before me, finished, and I am turning its pages." How I envied him that gift of prophecy! If only I could see it lying finished before me!

*The folded colored plate.* As a medical student I was much afflicted by a fondness for studying only from monographs. Despite my limited means, I subscribed to a number of medical journals whose colored plates delighted me, and I was proud of this inclination toward thoroughness. When I began to publish on my own account, I had to draw the plates for my own papers, and I remember that one of them came out so badly that a well-meaning colleague mocked me for it. This leads, though I cannot say exactly how, to a very early memory. My father once thought it would be amusing to hand a book with colored plates, an account of a journey through Persia, to me and my eldest sister to destroy. This was hardly defensible as a matter of education. I was five years old at the time and my sister three, and the image of the two of us blissfully tearing the book to pieces (leaf by leaf, I must add, like an artichoke) is almost the only one from that period of my life that has stayed fresh in my memory. Later, as a student, I developed a marked passion for collecting and owning books, analogous to my taste for studying from monographs, a hobby that appears in the dream thoughts in connection with the cyclamen and the artichoke. I became a bookworm, which links back to the herbarium. Looking back, I have always traced this first passion of my life to that childhood impression; or rather, I have recognized in the childish scene a "concealing recollection," a memory that stands in for and screens my later love of books. Of course, I also learned early that our passions are often our sorrows. When I was seventeen I had run up a considerable bill at the bookshop and had no means of paying it, and my father would hardly accept the excuse that my inclinations had not settled on something worse. But the mention of this episode from my youth brings me straight back to my conversation that evening with Dr. Koenigstein, for our talk on the dream-day had raised the same old reproach: that I am too fond of my hobbies.

For reasons that do not belong here, I will not carry the interpretation of this dream further, but will simply indicate the path that leads to its meaning. In the course of the interpretation I was reminded of my conversation with Dr. Koenigstein, and indeed of more than one part of it. When I consider the subjects that conversation touched on, the meaning of the dream becomes clear to me. Every chain of association that has been set going, about my wife's hobbies and my own, about cocaine, about the difficulty of obtaining medical treatment from one's colleagues, about my preference for monographic study and my neglect of certain subjects such as botany, continues into and connects with some branch of that widely ramifying conversation. Once again the dream takes on the character of a self-justification, a plea for my rights, like the first dream I analyzed, the dream of Irma's injection. It even continues the theme that dream began, discussing it with the new material that had accumulated in the interval between the two. Even the apparently indifferent phrasing of the dream acquires new significance. Its meaning is now: "I am, after all, the man who wrote that valuable and successful treatise on cocaine," just as I asserted in my own defense in the earlier case, "I am a thorough and industrious student." In both cases the upshot is: "I can afford to allow myself this."

But I can dispense with further interpretation, since my only purpose in reporting the dream was to examine how its content relates to the experience of the previous day that provoked it. So long as I know only the manifest content, just one connection to an impression of the day is evident. Once I have carried out the interpretation, a second source of the dream appears in another experience of the same day. The first impression to which the dream refers is an indifferent one, a minor circumstance: I see a book in a shop window whose title catches my eye for a moment and whose contents could hardly interest me. The second experience has great psychic value. I talked earnestly with my friend the eye specialist for about an hour; I made allusions in that conversation that must have touched both of us closely and that awakened memories revealing the most varied feelings within me. Moreover, the conversation was broken off unfinished because acquaintances joined us. What, then, is the relation of these two impressions of the day to each other, and to the dream that followed the next night?

In the manifest content I find only an allusion to the indifferent impression, and so I can confirm that the dream prefers to take nonessential experiences into its content. In the interpretation, by contrast, everything converges on an important event that rightly demands attention. If I judge the dream in the only correct way, by its latent content as brought to light through analysis, I have come without intending to upon a new and important fact. The notion that the dream concerns itself only with the worthless scraps of daily experience collapses. I am also compelled to contradict the claim that our waking mental life does not continue into the dream, and that the dream instead squanders psychic activity on trivial material. The opposite is true. What has occupied our minds during the day also dominates our dream thoughts, and we take the trouble to dream only about matters that have given us food for thought during the day.

The most obvious explanation for why I dream about an indifferent impression of the day, while the impression that has justly stirred me supplies the actual occasion for dreaming, is perhaps that this is yet another instance of dream distortion, which I traced earlier to a psychic force acting as a censor. The memory of the monograph on the genus *Cyclamen* is used as though it were an allusion to the conversation with my friend, much as, in the dream of the deferred supper, the friend is represented by the allusion "smoked salmon." The only question is by what intermediate steps the impression of the monograph comes to stand as an allusion to the conversation with the eye specialist, since no such relation is immediately apparent. In the case of the deferred supper, the relation is given from the outset: smoked salmon, as the friend's favorite dish, belongs directly to the set of associations that the friend's person would call up in the lady who dreamed. In the new example we have two separate impressions that at first sight seem to share nothing except that they occurred on the same day. The monograph catches my eye in the morning; I take part in the conversation in the evening.

The analysis supplies the following answer. Such connections between the two impressions do not exist at first; they are established afterward, between the ideational content of the one impression and the ideational content of the other. I have already emphasized the components of this connection in recording the analysis. I would probably have linked the idea of the monograph on cyclamen with the thought that the cyclamen is my wife's favorite flower only under some outside influence, perhaps the further memory of the flowers Mrs. L. went without. I do not believe these underlying thoughts alone would have been enough to produce a dream. As Hamlet says:

> There needs no ghost, my lord, come from the grave
> To tell us this.

But now the analysis reminds me that the name of the man who interrupted our conversation was Gärtner, which means "gardener," and that I had found his wife in blooming health. I even recall that one of my patients, who bears the pretty name of Flora, was for a time the main subject of our conversation. It must be that I completed the connection between the two events of the day, the indifferent one and the stirring one, through these links drawn from the cluster of associations belonging to the idea of botany. Further connections were then established, among them cocaine, which can with complete accuracy act as a go-between linking the person of Dr. Koenigstein with the botanical monograph I wrote. These strengthened the fusion of the two sets of associations into one, so that part of the first experience could be used as an allusion to the second.

I expect this explanation to be attacked as arbitrary or contrived. What would have happened if Professor Gärtner and his blooming wife had not come along, and if the patient we discussed had been named not Flora but Anna? The answer is simple. Had these connections of thought been absent, others would probably have been chosen. Connections of this kind are easy to establish, as the joking riddles and puns we amuse ourselves with every day are enough to show; the scope of wit is unlimited. To go a step further: had it been impossible to establish sufficiently abundant connections between the two impressions of the day, the dream would simply have turned out differently. Another of the day's indifferent impressions, which reach us in great numbers and are promptly forgotten, would have taken the monograph's place in the dream, formed a connection with the content of the conversation, and represented it in the dream. Since it was the impression of the monograph and no other that met this fate, that impression was probably the best suited to forming the connection. There is no need to marvel, like Hänschen Schlau in Lessing's epigram, who was astonished to discover that "it is the rich people of the world who have the most money."

Still, the psychological process by which, on our view, an indifferent experience is substituted for a psychologically important one seems strange and open to doubt. In a later chapter I will try to make this apparently faulty operation more intelligible. Here I am concerned only with its consequences, since the regularly recurring findings of dream analysis have forced me to assume it. The process appears to be that, over the course of these intermediate steps, a displacement takes place, a displacement, let us say, of psychic emphasis. Ideas initially charged with only weak intensity take over the charge of ideas whose initial intensity was stronger, until they reach a degree of strength that enables them to force their way into consciousness. Such displacements do not surprise us at all when it is a question of where feelings are bestowed or of motor actions in general. The unmarried woman who transfers her affection to animals, the bachelor who becomes a passionate collector, the soldier who defends a scrap of colored cloth, his flag, with his life's blood, the lover for whom a momentary clasp of hands brings bliss, or Othello, in whom a lost handkerchief provokes an explosion of rage: all of these are examples of psychic displacement that strike us as beyond question.

But when a decision about what is to reach our consciousness and what is to be withheld from it (that is, about what we are to think) is made in the same way and according to the same fundamental principles, the result strikes us as morbid, and if it happens in waking life we call it an error of thought. Here we may anticipate the outcome of a discussion that will be undertaken later: the psychic process we have identified as dream displacement will prove to be not a morbid disturbance but a process that differs from the normal only in being more primitive in nature.

The fact that the dream content takes up remnants of trivial experiences is therefore a manifestation of dream disfigurement, achieved by means of displacement.
