We may recall that we have already recognized this disfigurement as the work of a censor that controls the passage between two psychic instances. We accordingly expect dream analysis to reveal, as a rule, the genuine and significant source of the dream in the life of the day, a source whose recollection has transferred its emphasis onto some indifferent recollection. This view places us in complete opposition to Robert's theory, which consequently loses all value for us. The fact Robert was trying to explain simply does not exist. His assumption rests on a misunderstanding: the failure to put the dream's real meaning in place of its apparent content. A further objection may be raised against Robert's doctrine. If it were truly the task of the dream, through a special psychic activity, to clear our memory of the "slag" left by the day's recollections, our sleep would have to be more troubled, and more strenuously occupied, than our waking experience gives us reason to suppose. The number of indifferent impressions received during a single day, against which our memory would need protection, is obviously immense; the night would not be long enough to finish the task. It is far more probable that indifferent impressions are forgotten without any active intervention on the part of our psychic powers.

Still, something warns us against dismissing Robert's idea without further thought. We have left unexplained the fact that one of the indifferent impressions of the day, and specifically one from the previous day, regularly contributes something to the dream content. Connections between this impression and the dream's true source do not always exist from the outset. As we have seen, they are established only afterward, in the course of the dream-work, as though in order to accomplish the intended displacement. There must, then, be some necessity to form connections in this particular direction, toward the recent though indifferent impression, and that impression must owe its special fitness for the purpose to some property of its own. Otherwise it would be just as easy for the dream thoughts to transfer their emphasis onto some inessential link within their own chain of associations.

The following experiences point toward an explanation. When a day has brought two or more experiences capable of stimulating a dream, the dream fuses references to them into a single whole; it obeys an impulse to make a unity out of them. One summer afternoon, for instance, I stepped into a railway compartment and found there two friends of mine who did not know each other. One was an influential colleague; the other belonged to a distinguished family whose physician I was. I introduced the two gentlemen, but throughout the long journey I acted as go-between in the conversation, so that I had to take up a topic now with one, now with the other. I asked my colleague to recommend a mutual friend who had just begun his medical practice. He replied that he was convinced of the young man's thoroughness, but that his plain appearance would make it difficult for him to gain entry into households of rank. I answered, "That is precisely why he needs a recommendation." Shortly afterward I asked my other fellow traveler about the health of his aunt, the mother of one of my patients, who was at that time prostrated by a serious illness. On the night after this journey I dreamed that my young friend, on whose behalf I had asked for help, was in a splendid drawing room, delivering a funeral oration before a select company with the air of a man of the world. The oration concerned the old lady, now dead for the purposes of the dream, who was my second fellow traveler's aunt. (I will frankly confess that I had not been on good terms with this lady.) My dream had thus found connections between the two impressions of the day and used them to compose a single, unified situation.

On the strength of many similar experiences, I am driven to conclude that the dream function operates under a kind of compulsion that forces it to combine all the available sources of dream stimulation into a unified whole within the dream. In a later chapter, on the dream function, we shall come to know this impulse toward combination as a part of condensation, another primary psychic process.

I shall now take up the question of whether the source from which a dream originates, and to which our analysis leads us back, must always be a recent and significant event, or whether a subjective experience can play the part of dream stimulus. By a subjective experience I mean the recollection of a psychologically valuable experience, or a chain of thought. Numerous analyses yield an unequivocal answer: the stimulus for a dream may be a subjective occurrence that has been made recent, so to speak, by mental activity during the day. It may be useful at this point to set out the various conditions that can be recognized as sources of dreams.

The source of a dream may be:

(a) A recent and psychologically significant experience that is directly represented in the dream.

(b) Several recent, significant experiences that the dream unites into a whole.

(c) One or more recent and significant experiences that are represented in the dream by reference to a contemporaneous but indifferent experience.

(d) A significant subjective experience (a recollection or train of thought) that is regularly represented in the dream by reference to a recent but indifferent impression.

As can be seen, dream interpretation holds firmly throughout to the condition that every component of the dream repeats a recent impression of the day. The element destined for representation in the dream may belong to the group of ideas surrounding the actual dream stimulus itself, either as an essential or as an inessential part of it. Alternatively, it may originate in the vicinity of an indifferent impression that, through associations of greater or lesser richness, has been brought into relation with the thoughts surrounding the dream stimulus. The apparent multiplicity of conditions here arises simply from the alternative of whether displacement has or has not taken place. We may note that this alternative explains the contrasts among dreams just as readily as does the ascending series of brain cells, from partially awake to fully awake, proposed by the medical theory of dreams.

It is further worth noting, with regard to this series, that the element which is psychologically valuable but not recent (a train of thought, a recollection) may be replaced, for the purposes of dream formation, by an element that is recent but psychologically indifferent. Only two conditions need be met: first, that the dream contain a reference to something recently experienced; and second, that the dream stimulus remain a psychologically valuable train of thought. In a single case, (a), both conditions are fulfilled by the same impression. We may add that the same indifferent impressions that can be used in dreams while they are recent lose this availability as soon as they are a day old, or at most a few days. We must therefore assume that the sheer freshness of an impression gives it a certain psychological value for dream formation, a value somewhat equivalent to that of emotionally charged memories or trains of thought. We shall be able to see the basis of this value only with the help of certain psychological considerations that will appear later.

In passing, our attention is drawn to the fact that important changes in the material of our ideas and memories may come about unconsciously and at night. The advice that one should sleep on a matter for a night before reaching a final decision is evidently fully justified. But we notice that at this point we have stepped from the psychology of dreaming into the psychology of sleep, a step we shall often have occasion to take.

Now an objection arises that threatens to invalidate the conclusions we have just reached. If indifferent impressions can enter the dream only when they are recent, how is it that we also find in dream content elements from earlier periods of our lives? These elements, as Strümpell puts it, possessed no psychic value even when they were recent. They ought therefore to have been forgotten long ago, and they are consequently neither fresh nor psychologically significant.

This objection can be fully answered if we rely on the results furnished by the psychoanalysis of neurotics. The solution is this: the process of displacement, which substitutes indifferent material for material of psychic significance (in thinking as well as in dreaming), had already taken place during those earlier periods of life and has since become fixed in memory. Those elements that were originally indifferent are in fact no longer so, because they have acquired the value of psychologically significant material. What has genuinely remained indifferent can never be reproduced in a dream.

From the foregoing discussion, the reader will rightly suppose that I maintain there are no indifferent dream stimuli, and consequently no harmless dreams. This I believe to be true, thoroughly and without exception, allowing only for the dreams of children and perhaps for brief dream reactions to sensations during the night. Whatever one dreams is either manifestly recognizable as psychically significant, or else it is disfigured and can be judged correctly only after a complete interpretation, whereupon it too can be recognized as possessing psychic significance. The dream never concerns itself with trifles; we do not allow matters of slight importance to disturb our sleep. Dreams that appear harmless turn out to be sinister when one takes the trouble to interpret them; if I may be permitted the expression, they all bear "the mark of the beast." Since this is another point on which I can expect opposition, and since I welcome an opportunity to show dream disfigurement at work, I shall now analyze a number of dreams from my collection.

I. An intelligent and refined young woman, who in her conduct belongs to the type we call reserved, the "still waters," relates the following dream:

Her husband asks, "Shouldn't the piano be tuned?" She replies, "It won't pay; the hammers would have to be newly buffed as well." This repeats an actual event from the previous day. Her husband had asked such a question, and she had given a similar answer. But what is the meaning of her dreaming it? She says of the piano, to be sure, that it is a disgusting old box with a bad tone, that it is one of the things her husband owned before they were married, and so on. But the key to the true solution lies in the phrase "It won't pay." This phrase originated in a visit she had paid the day before to a woman friend. There she had been asked to take off her coat, but she declined, saying, "It won't pay. I have to leave in a moment." At this point I recall that during the previous day's analysis she had suddenly taken hold of her coat, one of whose buttons had come undone. It is therefore as though she had said, "Please don't look this way; it won't pay." So "box" develops into "chest," or breast-box, the bust, and the interpretation of the dream leads directly back to a period in her physical development when she was dissatisfied with her figure. It leads to still earlier periods, too, if we take into account "disgusting" and "bad tone," and remember how often, in allusions and in dreams, the two small hemispheres of the female body stand in for the large ones, both as a substitute and as an antithesis.

II. I may interrupt this dream to insert a short, harmless dream of a young man. He dreamed that he was putting on his winter overcoat again, which was terrible. The occasion for the dream is apparently the cold weather, which had recently set in again. On closer examination, however, we notice that the two short parts of the dream do not fit together well: what is so "terrible" about wearing a heavy or thick coat in the cold? Unfortunately for the harmlessness of this dream, the first idea that analysis brings up is the memory that on the previous day a lady had secretly confided to him that her last child owed its existence to a burst condom. He now reconstructs his thoughts in light of this clue: a thin condom is dangerous, a thick one is bad. The condom is an "overcoat" because it is pulled over something; the German word *Überzieher* means literally "that which is pulled over," and it is also the ordinary German name for a light overcoat. An experience like the one the lady described would indeed be "terrible" for an unmarried man. We may now return to our other harmless dreamer.

III. She puts a candle into a candlestick; but the candle is broken, so that it does not stand straight. The girls at school say she is clumsy; the young lady replies that it is not her fault.

Here too there is an actual occasion for the dream: the day before, she really had put a candle into a candlestick, though that candle was not broken. A transparent symbolism has been used here. The candle is an object that excites the female genitals; its being broken, so that it does not stand straight, signifies impotence on the man's part, hence "it is not her fault." But does this carefully raised young woman, a stranger to all obscenity, know of this application of the candle? As it happens, she can say exactly how she came by the knowledge. While she was boating on the Rhine, another boat passed carrying students who were singing, or rather bellowing with great glee: "When the Queen of Sweden, with closed shutters and the candles of Apollo...." She did not hear or understand the last word, and her husband had to supply the explanation she needed. In the dream content these verses are replaced by the harmless memory of a task she once performed clumsily at a girls' boarding school, the link between the two being their common feature of closed shutters. The connection between the theme of masturbation and that of impotence is clear enough. "Apollo," in the latent dream content, links this dream to an earlier one in which the virgin Pallas appeared. None of this is harmless.

IV. Lest it seem too easy a matter to draw conclusions about the dreamer's actual circumstances from her dreams, I add another dream from the same person, one that likewise appears harmless. "I dreamed of doing something," she relates, "that I actually did during the day: I filled a little trunk so full of books that I had trouble closing it. My dream was exactly like what really happened." Here the dreamer herself places the chief emphasis on the correspondence between dream and reality. All such judgments and remarks about a dream, even though they have found a place in waking thought, regularly belong to the latent dream content, as later examples will further show. We are told, then, that what the dream relates actually happened during the day. It would lead us too far afield to explain how we arrived at the idea of using the English language to help interpret this dream. It is enough to say that once again it is a question of a little box, as in the earlier dream of the dead child in the box, which has been filled so full that nothing more can go into it. Nothing in the least sinister this time.

In all these "harmless" dreams, the sexual factor stands out strikingly as the motive for the censor's intervention. But this is a matter of primary importance, and we must postpone it.

### (b) Infantile Experiences as the Source of Dreams

As the third peculiarity of dream content, we have cited from all the authorities except Robert the fact that impressions from the earliest period of our lives, which seem not to be available to waking memory, may appear in dreams. It is naturally difficult to judge how often or how rarely this happens, because after waking we do not recognize the origin of the dream elements in question. Proof that we are dealing with childhood impressions must therefore be established objectively, and the conditions required for this coincide only in rare cases. A. Maury tells, as an especially conclusive case, the story of a man who decided to visit his birthplace after an absence of twenty years. On the night before his departure, he dreams that he is in an entirely unfamiliar district, where he meets a stranger and has a conversation with him. After he had returned to his home, he was able to satisfy himself that this unfamiliar district really existed near his home town, and the stranger in the dream turned out to be a friend of his late father who lived there. This is surely conclusive proof that he had seen both the man and the district in childhood. The dream, moreover, is to be interpreted as a dream of impatience, like that of the girl who carries her ticket for that evening's concert in her pocket, or of the child whose father had promised him an excursion to the Hameau, and others of the kind. The motives that explain why this particular childhood impression is reproduced for the dreamer cannot, of course, be discovered without an analysis.

One of those who attended my lectures, who boasted that his dreams were very seldom subject to disfigurement, told me that some time earlier he had seen in a dream his former tutor in bed with his nurse, who had been part of the household until he was eleven years old. In the dream it did not occur to him where this scene took place. Being much interested, he told the dream to his elder brother, who laughingly confirmed that it was real. The brother said he remembered the affair very well, since he had been six years old at the time. Whenever circumstances favored a night together, the lovers used to make him, the older boy, drunk on beer. The younger child, our dreamer, who was then three years old and slept in the same room as the nurse, was not considered an obstacle.

There is yet another case in which it can be established with certainty, without the help of dream interpretation, that a dream contains elements from childhood: namely, when it is a so-called recurrent dream, one first dreamed in childhood that later appears again and again after the dreamer has reached adulthood. I may add a few examples of this kind to those already familiar, although I have never encountered such a recurrent dream in my own case. A physician in his thirties tells me that a yellow lion, which he can describe in the minutest detail, has appeared often in his dream life from his earliest childhood to the present day. One day this lion, known to him from his dreams, was discovered in reality as a long-forgotten porcelain object. On that occasion the young man learned from his mother that it had been his favorite toy in early childhood, a fact he himself could no longer remember.

If we now turn from the manifest dream content to the dream thoughts that are revealed only through analysis, we may find childhood experiences at work even in dreams whose content would never have led us to suspect anything of the kind. I owe an especially charming and instructive example of such a dream to my esteemed colleague of the "yellow lion." After reading Nansen's account of his polar expedition, he dreamed that he was giving the bold explorer electrical treatment on an ice field for an ischemia the explorer had complained of. In analyzing this dream, he recalled a story from his childhood without which the dream remains completely unintelligible. When he was three or four years old, he had been listening intently to the grown-ups talking about voyages of exploration, and presently asked his papa whether exploration was a serious illness. He had evidently confused "trips" with "rips," and the ridicule of his brothers and sisters ensured that he never forgot the humiliating experience.

The case is much the same when, in analyzing the dream of the monograph on the genus Cyclamen, I come upon a memory, preserved from childhood, of my father allowing me to destroy a book with colored plates when I was a little boy of five. It may be doubted whether this memory actually played a part in shaping the dream content, and it may be suggested that the process of analysis established the connection after the fact. But the abundance and intricacy of the associative links vouch for the truth of my explanation: cyclamen, favorite flower, favorite dish, artichoke; to pick something to pieces like an artichoke, leaf by leaf (a phrase that rang constantly in our ears at the time, in connection with the carving up of the Chinese Empire); herbarium; bookworm, whose favorite dish is books. I may add that the ultimate meaning of the dream, which I have not given here, is most intimately connected with the content of the childhood scene.

In another series of dreams, analysis teaches us that the wish itself which gave rise to the dream, and whose fulfillment the dream turns out to be, originated in childhood. One is astonished to find the child, with all its impulses, living on in the dream.

I shall now continue the interpretation of a dream that has already proved instructive: the dream in which my friend R. is my uncle. We carried its interpretation far enough for the wish motive, the wish to be appointed professor, to assert itself unmistakably. We explained the affection shown toward my friend R. in the dream as a fiction born of opposition and spite, directed against the slight cast upon the two colleagues who appear in the dream thoughts. The dream was my own, and I may therefore continue the analysis by stating that my feelings were not altogether satisfied by the solution reached. I know that in waking life I would have expressed my opinion of these colleagues, who are treated so badly in the dream thoughts, in quite different terms. The force of my wish not to share their fate in the matter of appointment seemed too slight to account for the discrepancy between my judgment in the dream and my judgment when awake. If my desire to be addressed by a new title is really so strong, it proves a morbid ambition that I did not know existed in me and that I believe is far from my thoughts. I do not know how others who believe they know me would judge me. Perhaps I really have been ambitious. But if so, my ambition long ago moved on to objects other than the title and rank of assistant professor.

Where, then, does the ambition that the dream attributed to me come from? I recall a story I heard often as a child: at my birth, an old peasant woman told my happy mother, whose first-born I was, that she had brought a great man into the world. Such prophecies must be very common. There are many mothers full of happy expectation, and many old peasant women whose influence in the world has faded and who have therefore turned their eyes toward the future. Nor was the prophetess likely to suffer for her prediction. Could my hunger for greatness have come from this source?

A memory from later in my childhood offers a better explanation. When I was eleven or twelve, my parents used to take me in the evenings to an inn in the Prater, Vienna's large public park. One evening we noticed a man going from table to table, improvising verses on any subject he was given. I was sent to bring the poet to our table, and he was grateful for the invitation. Before asking for his subject, he dashed off a few rhymes about me and declared that, if his inspiration could be trusted, I would probably one day become a "minister." I still remember clearly the impression this second prophecy made on me. It was the time of the election of the liberal "municipal ministry." My father had recently brought home portraits of the men chosen for the cabinet, Herbst, Giskra, Unger, Berger, and others, and we had lit up the house in their honor. There were even some Jews among them, so every hardworking Jewish schoolboy carried a minister's portfolio in his satchel. Even the fact that, until shortly before I entered the university, I intended to study law, and changed my plans only at the last moment, must be connected with the impressions of that time, because a medical man can never become a minister.

And now for my dream. I begin to see that it carries me from the gloomy present back to the hopeful days of that election, and that it fulfills my wish of that time completely. In treating my two estimable and learned colleagues so badly because they are Jews, calling one a simpleton and the other a criminal, I behave as if I were the minister of education. I put myself in his place. What thorough revenge I take on his Excellency! He refuses to appoint me *professor extraordinarius*, an associate professor, and in return I take his place in my dream.

Another case shows that although the wish that drives a dream belongs to the present, it can draw great intensity from memories of childhood. I am thinking of a series of dreams based on my longing to go to Rome. I suspect I will have to satisfy this longing through dreams for a long time yet, because during the season when I am free to travel, a stay in Rome must be avoided for reasons of health. Once I dreamed that I saw the Tiber and the Bridge of Sant'Angelo from the window of a railway compartment. Then the train pulled away, and it occurred to me that I had never entered the city at all. The view in the dream was modeled on an engraving I had noticed in passing the day before in the parlor of one of my patients.

On another occasion, someone leads me up a hill and shows me Rome, half shrouded in mist and so far away that I am astonished at how clearly I can see it. The content of this dream is too rich to report in full here, but the motive, "to see the promised land from afar," is easy to recognize. The city is actually Lübeck, which I first saw in mist, and the original of the hill is the Gleichenberg.

In a third dream, I am at last in Rome, as the dream informs me. To my disappointment, the scenery is anything but urban: a little river of black water, with black rocks on one bank and large white flowers on the other. I notice a certain Mr. Zucker, whom I know slightly, and decide to ask him the way into the city. Plainly I am trying in vain to see in my dream a city I have never seen while awake. If I break the scene down into its elements, the white flowers point to Ravenna, which I know, and which for a time displaced Rome as the capital of Italy. In the marshes around Ravenna we had seen the most beautiful water lilies floating in pools of black water. The dream makes them grow in meadows, like the narcissi of our own Aussee, because at Ravenna it had been such tedious work to fish them out of the water. The black rock so close to the water vividly recalls the valley of the Tepl at Karlsbad.

"Karlsbad" now lets me explain the odd detail that I ask Mr. Zucker the way. The material from which the dream is built also includes two of those amusing Jewish anecdotes that hide so much deep and often bitter worldly wisdom, and that we love to quote in conversation and in letters. One is the story of the "constitution." A poor Jew sneaks onto the express train to Karlsbad without a ticket. He is caught, and at each ticket inspection the conductor treats him more harshly. At one station on his miserable journey he meets a friend, who asks where he is going. "To Karlsbad," he answers, "if my constitution holds out." Linked with this in my memory is another story, about a Jew who speaks no French and has been told expressly to ask, in Paris, for the way to the Rue Richelieu. For many years Paris was itself the object of my longing, and I took the great satisfaction I felt when I first set foot on its pavements as a pledge that my other wishes would also be fulfilled. Asking the way is, again, a direct allusion to Rome, since all roads lead there. Moreover, the name Zucker, which means "sugar," points once more to Karlsbad, where we send everyone suffering from the constitutional disease diabetes, called in German *Zuckerkrankheit*, "sugar sickness." The occasion for this dream was a proposal from my friend in Berlin that we meet in Prague at Easter. A further allusion to sugar and diabetes could be found in the matters I had to discuss with him.

A fourth dream, which came shortly after the last, brings me back to Rome. I see a street corner before me and am astonished at how many German placards are posted there. The day before, I had written to my friend, with prophetic foresight, that Prague would probably not be a comfortable place for German travelers. The dream therefore expressed two wishes at once: to meet him in Rome instead of in the Bohemian city, and a desire, probably dating from my student days, that the German language might be treated with more tolerance in Prague. Besides, I must have understood Czech during the first three years of my life, because I was born in a small Moravian village inhabited by Slavs. A Czech nursery rhyme that I heard at seventeen fixed itself in my memory without any effort on my part, and I can still recite it today, though I have no idea what it means. These dreams, too, are full of connections to impressions from my earliest years.

On my last journey to Italy, which took me past Lake Trasimene among other places, I finally discovered how much my longing for the Eternal City had been reinforced by impressions from my youth. I had seen the Tiber and had turned back, with painful feelings, when I was within eighty kilometers of Rome. I was just forming the plan of traveling to Naples by way of Rome the following year when a sentence came to mind, which I must have read in one of our classical authors: "It is an open question which of the two paced his room more impatiently after deciding to go to Rome: Assistant Headmaster Winckelmann or the great general Hannibal." I had in fact followed in Hannibal's footsteps. Like him, I seemed fated never to see Rome, and he too had turned aside into Campania when the whole world expected him at Rome's gates. Hannibal, whom I now resembled in this respect, had been my favorite hero during my years at the Gymnasium, the classical secondary school. Like many boys my age, I gave my sympathies in the Punic Wars not to the Romans but to the Carthaginians. Later, when I came to understand what it meant to belong to an alien race, and the anti-Semitism of my classmates forced me to take a definite stand, the Semitic general grew still larger in my eyes. To me as a youth, Hannibal and Rome symbolized the opposition between the tenacity of the Jews and the organization of the Catholic Church. The importance the anti-Semitic movement has since taken on in our emotional lives helped to fix the thoughts and impressions of that earlier time. So the wish to reach Rome has become, in my dream life, the cover and symbol for several deeply cherished wishes, wishes one might work toward with the perseverance and single-mindedness of the Carthaginian general, and whose fulfillment sometimes seems as little favored by fortune as Hannibal's lifelong wish to enter Rome.

Only now do I come upon the experience of my youth that still shows its power in all these emotions and dreams. I may have been ten or twelve when my father began taking me with him on his walks and telling me his views on the things of this world. Once, to show me how much better the times I had been born into were than his own, he told me this: "When I was a young man, I was walking one Saturday along a street in the village where you were born. I was well dressed and had a new fur cap on my head. A Christian came up, knocked my cap into the mud with one blow, and shouted, 'Jew, get off the sidewalk!'" "And what did you do?" I asked. "I stepped into the street and picked up my cap," he answered calmly. This did not strike me as heroic on the part of the big, strong man who was holding my small hand. I set this scene, which displeased me, against another that suited my feelings better: the scene in which Hannibal's father, Hamilcar Barca, made his son swear at the household altar to take vengeance on the Romans. Ever since then, Hannibal has had a place in my fantasies.

I think I can trace my enthusiasm for the Carthaginian general still further back into childhood, so that what we have here may be an emotional attachment, already formed, transferred onto a new vehicle. One of the first books to fall into my hands after I learned to read was Thiers's *Consulate and Empire*. I remember pasting little labels with the names of Napoleon's marshals on the flat backs of my wooden soldiers, and even then my declared favorite was Masséna, whom I took to be a Jew named Menasse. Napoleon himself, of course, follows Hannibal in crossing the Alps. And perhaps the growth of this martial ideal can be traced back even further, to the wishes that must have been stirred in the weaker of two playmates by my relationship, sometimes friendly and sometimes hostile, during my first three years with a boy a year older than I.

The deeper one goes in analyzing dreams, the more often one is led to childhood experiences that act as dream sources within the latent dream content.

We have seen that a dream very rarely reproduces an experience so that it forms, unabridged and unchanged, the entire manifest content. Still, some authentic examples of this process have been reported, and I can add a few new ones, which again concern scenes from childhood. In one of my patients, a dream once gave a scarcely distorted reproduction of a sexual incident, which was immediately recognized as an accurate memory. The memory had never been entirely lost in waking life, but it had been greatly obscured, and its revival was the result of the analytic work that preceded the dream. At the age of twelve, the dreamer had visited a bedridden schoolmate who, probably by accident, had uncovered himself while moving in bed. At the sight of the boy's genitals, the dreamer was seized by a kind of compulsion: he exposed himself and took hold of the other boy's member. The other boy looked at him with surprise and indignation, and he grew embarrassed and let go. Twenty-three years later, a dream repeated this scene with every detail of the emotions it had involved, changing it only in two respects: the dreamer took the passive role instead of the active one, and the schoolmate was replaced by someone from the present.

As a rule, of course, a childhood scene appears in the manifest dream content only as an allusion and must be extracted from the dream by interpretation. Examples of this kind cannot be very convincing, because there is no guarantee that they really are experiences of childhood; if they belong to the earliest years of life, memory no longer recognizes them. The conclusion that such childhood experiences are generally present in dreams rests on a great many factors that emerge in psychoanalytic work and that appear reliable enough when taken together. But when these links between dreams and childhood experiences are torn from their context for the purpose of interpreting a dream, they may not make much of an impression, especially since I never present all the material on which an interpretation depends. Still, I will not let this stop me from giving some examples.

I. The following dream comes from another woman patient: *She is in a large room full of all kinds of machines, perhaps, as she imagines, an orthopedic institute. She hears that I have no time and that she must take the treatment together with five others. But she resists and refuses to lie down on the bed, or whatever it is, that is meant for her. She stands in a corner and waits for me to say, "It isn't true." Meanwhile the others laugh at her and say it is all foolishness on her part. At the same time, it is as if she were supposed to make a lot of little squares.*

The first part of this dream alludes to the treatment and to a transference onto me. The second alludes to a childhood scene, and the two parts are joined by the mention of the bed. The orthopedic institute refers to a conversation in which I had compared the length and nature of the treatment to orthopedic treatment. At the start, I had to tell her that for the present I had little time for her, but that later I would give her a full hour every day. This roused in her the old sensitivity that is the chief trait of children destined to become hysterical: their craving for love is insatiable. My patient was the youngest of six children, hence "with five others," and as such her father's favorite, yet she seems to have felt that her beloved father gave her too little time and attention.

Her waiting for me to say "It isn't true" has the following explanation. A tailor's apprentice had delivered a dress to her, and she had paid him. She then asked her husband whether she would have to pay again if the boy lost the money. To tease her, he said yes; this is the teasing in the dream. She asked again and again, waiting for him to say "It isn't true." The latent thought of the dream can now be reconstructed: Will she have to pay me double if I give her twice as much time? This is a stingy thought, or, in the German idiom, a "dirty" one, since the same word covers both. The uncleanliness of childhood is often replaced in dreams by greed for money, and the word "dirty" supplies the bridge. If all that business of waiting for me to say, and so on, is the dream's roundabout way of expressing the word "dirty," then standing in the corner and refusing to lie down on the bed fit in as well. Both are parts of a childhood scene in which she had soiled her bed and was made to stand in the corner as punishment, with the warning that Papa would not love her anymore, while her brothers and sisters laughed at her. The little squares refer to her young niece, who had shown her the arithmetical trick of writing numbers in nine squares, I believe it is, so that they add up to fifteen in every direction.

II. Here is a man's dream: *He sees two boys scuffling, and from the tools lying about he concludes that they are coopers' boys, apprentices to a barrel maker. One boy has thrown the other down, and the boy on the ground is wearing earrings with blue stones. He hurries after the culprit with his cane raised to punish him. The boy takes refuge with a woman standing by a wooden fence, as though she were his mother. She is a day laborer's wife, and she has her back to the dreamer. At last she turns around and stares at him with a horrible look, so that he runs away in fright. In her eyes, the red flesh of the lower lids seems to stand out.*

The dream has made generous use of trivial events from the previous day. The day before, he had actually seen two boys in the street, one of whom threw the other down. When he hurried over to settle the fight, both ran off. The coopers' boys are explained only by a later dream, in whose analysis he used the expression "to knock the bottom out of the barrel." Earrings with blue stones, in his experience, are worn mainly by prostitutes. A familiar bit of doggerel about two boys also came to mind: "The other boy, his name was Mary," meaning that he was a girl. As for the woman standing there: after the scene with the two boys, he had walked along the bank of the Danube and, taking advantage of being alone, had urinated against a wooden fence. A little later on the same walk, a respectably dressed elderly lady smiled at him very pleasantly and wanted to give him her card with her address.

Since the woman in the dream stood as he had stood while urinating, the dream concerns a woman urinating. This explains the "horrible look" and the prominent red flesh, which can only refer to the genitals gaping open in a squatting position. He had seen female genitals as a child, and in later memory they had appeared as "proud flesh," the raw, swollen tissue of a healing wound, and as a "wound." The dream combines two occasions on which, as a little boy, the dreamer had a chance to see the genitals of little girls: once when he threw a girl down, and once when another girl was urinating. Another association shows that he had also kept in memory a punishment, or a threat of one, from his father, provoked by the sexual curiosity he displayed on these occasions.

III. Behind the following dream of a young woman lies a great mass of childhood memories, hastily fused into a fantasy.

*She goes out anxiously to do some shopping. On the Graben, one of Vienna's main streets, she sinks to her knees as if broken down. Many people gather around her, especially cab drivers, but no one helps her up. She makes many unsuccessful attempts to rise; finally she must have managed it, because she is put into a cab that is to take her home. A large, heavily loaded basket, something like a market basket, is thrown in after her through the window.*

This is the same woman who is always harassed in her dreams, just as she was harassed as a child. The first situation in the dream evidently comes from seeing a horse that had fallen, just as "broken down" points to horse racing. She rode in her early years, and earlier still she probably played at being a horse. Her first childhood memory, of the porter's seventeen-year-old son, who had an epileptic fit in the street and was brought home in a cab, is connected with the idea of falling down. She only heard about this incident, of course, but the idea of epileptic fits and falling has gained great power over her fantasies and later shaped the form of her own hysterical attacks. When a woman dreams of falling, it almost always has a sexual meaning: she becomes a "fallen woman." In this dream, that interpretation is probably the least doubtful, because she falls on the Graben, the place in Vienna known as the gathering ground of prostitutes.

The market basket can be interpreted in more than one way. The German word *Korb* means both "basket" and "rebuff," so it reminds her of the many rebuffs she first gave her suitors and later, as she believes, received herself. This connects with the detail that no one helps her up, which she herself interprets as being scorned. The market basket also recalls fantasies that had already come up in the analysis, in which she imagines she has married far beneath her station and must now do the marketing herself. Finally, the market basket might be taken as the mark of a servant. This brings up further childhood memories: of a cook who was dismissed for stealing and who also sank to her knees and begged for mercy, when the dreamer was twelve; and of a chambermaid who was dismissed for having an affair with the family's coachman, who incidentally married her afterward. This memory gives us a clue to the cab drivers in the dream, who, unlike what happened in reality, do not take the side of the fallen woman.

There remains the throwing of the basket, and its being thrown through the window. This leads her to the handling of baggage on the railway; to the country custom called *Fensterln*, in which a young man courts his sweetheart at night through her bedroom window; and to minor impressions from a summer stay in the country: a gentleman tossing blue plums to a lady through her window, and her little sister being frightened when a passing cretin looked in at the window. From behind all this emerges an obscure memory from her tenth year, of a nursemaid at the country resort who made love with one of the household servants, something the child had a chance to witness, and who was then "fired," thrown out of the house. In the dream this is reversed into "thrown in." We had approached this story along several other paths as well. Moreover, in Vienna a servant's baggage or trunk is contemptuously called "seven plums": "Pack up your seven plums and get out."

My collection naturally contains a large supply of such dreams from patients, whose analysis leads back to childhood impressions that are remembered dimly or not at all, and that often date from the first three years of life. But it would be a mistake to draw from them conclusions meant to apply to dreams in general. In every case we are dealing with neurotic, and especially hysterical, persons, and the part played by childhood scenes in these dreams might be determined by the nature of the neurosis rather than by the nature of the dream. Yet I am struck just as often, when interpreting my own dreams (which I do not undertake because of any obvious symptoms of illness), by how I come quite unsuspectingly upon a childhood scene in the latent dream content, and how a whole series of dreams suddenly falls into line with conclusions drawn from childhood experiences. I have already given examples of this and shall give more on various occasions. Perhaps I cannot close this chapter more fittingly than by citing several of my own dreams in which recent events and long-forgotten childhood experiences appear together as sources of the dream.

I. After traveling, when I have gone to bed hungry and tired, the great necessities of life begin to press their claims during sleep, and I dream the following: *I go into a kitchen to order some pastry. Three women are standing there, one of whom is the hostess; she is turning something over in her hands as though she were making dumplings. She answers that I must wait until she has finished (this is not distinctly spoken). I grow impatient and leave, feeling insulted. I put on an overcoat, but the first one I try is too long. I take it off and am somewhat surprised to find that it is trimmed with fur. A second coat has a long strip of cloth with Turkish designs sewn into it. A stranger with a long face and a short, pointed beard comes up and stops me from putting it on, declaring that it belongs to him. I now show him that it is embroidered all over in the Turkish style. He asks, "What business are the Turkish (designs, strips of cloth . . .) of yours?" But then we become quite friendly with each other.*

In analyzing this dream, I unexpectedly recall a novel that I read, or rather began reading at the end of its first volume, when I was perhaps thirteen. I have never known the title of the novel or the name of its author, but its ending remains vivid in my memory. The hero goes mad and keeps calling out the names of the three women who had brought him the greatest happiness and the greatest misfortune of his life. One of these names is Pélagie. I still do not know what to make of this name in the analysis. In connection with the three women, the three Parcae now come to the surface, the Fates who spin the destiny of man, and I know that one of the three women, the hostess in the dream, is the mother who gives life and who, moreover, as in my own case, gives the living creature its first nourishment. Love and hunger meet at the mother's breast. An anecdote tells of a young man who became a great admirer of feminine beauty: once, when the conversation turned to the beautiful wet nurse who had suckled him as an infant, he remarked that he was sorry he had not made better use of his opportunity at the time. I often use this anecdote to illustrate the factor of subsequence in the mechanism of the psychoneuroses, the way an experience acquires its significance only after the fact. . . . One of the Parcae, then, is rubbing the palms of her hands together as though making dumplings. This is a strange occupation for one of the Fates, and it urgently demands an explanation! The explanation is found in another, still earlier childhood memory. When I was six years old and receiving my first lessons from my mother, I was expected to believe that we are made of earth and must therefore return to earth. This did not suit me, and I doubted her teaching. My mother then rubbed the palms of her hands together, just as in making dumplings except that there was no dough between them, and showed me the blackish scales of skin that came off as proof that we are made of earth. My astonishment at this demonstration before my very eyes knew no bounds, and I resigned myself to the idea I would later hear expressed in the words: "Thou owest nature a death." So the women really are the Fates, whom I visit in the kitchen as I so often did in childhood when I was hungry and my mother told me to wait until lunch was ready. And now for the dumplings! At least one of my teachers at the university, the very one to whom I owe my knowledge of histology (epidermis), would be reminded by the name Knödl (*Knödel* is German for dumplings) of a man he had to prosecute for plagiarizing his writings. To plagiarize, to take whatever one can get even if it belongs to someone else, clearly leads to the second part of the dream, in which I am treated like a certain overcoat thief who for a time plied his trade in the lecture halls. I wrote down the word "plagiarism" for no apparent reason, simply because it occurred to me; now I see that it must belong to the latent dream content, because it forms a bridge between different parts of the manifest content. The chain of associations (Pélagie, plagiarism, plagiostomi or sharks, fish bladder) connects the old novel with the Knödl affair and with the overcoats. The German *Überzieher*, literally "something drawn over," means both an overcoat and a condom, and so clearly refers to an object belonging to the technique of sexual life. This is admittedly a very forced and irrational connection, but it is one I could never have made in waking life had the activity of the dream not already made it. Indeed, as though nothing were sacred to this impulse to force connections, the cherished name Brücke (German for "bridge," recalling the bridge of words just mentioned) now reminds me of the institute where I spent my happiest hours as a student, entirely free of care ("So will you find, at wisdom's breasts, a pleasure growing day by day"), in the most complete contrast to the urgent desires that torment me as I dream. Finally there surfaces the memory of another beloved teacher whose name again sounds like something to eat (Fleischl, from the German *Fleisch*, meat, like Knödl). With it comes a painful scene in which scales of skin play a part (mother, hostess), and madness (the novel), and a remedy from the "Latin kitchen," the pharmacy, that numbs the sensation of hunger: namely, cocaine.

I could follow these tangled trains of thought further still and fully explain the part of the dream that is missing from the analysis, but I must refrain, because the personal sacrifices this would demand are too great. I shall take up just one of the threads, which will lead us directly to the dream thoughts lying beneath the confusion. The stranger with the long face and pointed beard who wants to prevent me from putting on the overcoat has the features of a merchant in Spalato from whom my wife bought a good many Turkish fabrics. His name was Popović, a suspicious name (*Popo* being nursery German for the backside), which incidentally gave the humorist Stettenheim occasion for a pointed remark: "He told me his name, and blushingly shook my hand." Here again is the same abuse of names as before with Pélagie, Knödl, Brücke, and Fleischl. No one could dispute that such playing with names is childish nonsense; if I indulge in it, the indulgence is an act of retaliation, for my own name has countless times fallen victim to such feeble attempts at wit. Goethe once remarked how sensitive a man is about his name, which he feels he has grown into as into his own skin. On that occasion Herder composed these lines on Goethe's name:

"You who are born of gods, of Goths, or of *Kot* (mud),
your godlike images, too, are dust."

I see that this digression about the abuse of names was meant only to prepare the way for this complaint. But let us stop here. . . . The purchase in Spalato reminds me of another in Cattaro, where I was too cautious and missed the chance to make some desirable acquisitions. (Missing an opportunity at the nurse's breast; see above.) Another dream thought, prompted in the dreamer by the sensation of hunger, runs as follows: *One should let nothing slip that one can have, even if it means doing a small wrong; no opportunity should be missed; life is so short, and death inevitable.* Because this thought also has a sexual meaning, and because desire is reluctant to stop short of wrongdoing, this philosophy of *carpe diem*, of seizing the day, has reason to fear the censor and must hide behind a dream. This in turn gives voice to counter-thoughts of every kind: memories of a time when spiritual nourishment alone was enough for the dreamer, hints of repressions of every sort, and even threats of disgusting sexual punishments.

II. A second dream requires a longer preliminary account. I have taken a cab to the West Station to begin a vacation trip to Aussee, and I reach the station in time for the train to Ischl, which leaves earlier. There I see Count Thun, who is once again on his way to see the Emperor at Ischl. Despite the rain, he has come in an open carriage and has walked straight out through the gate for local trains. The ticket collector, who does not recognize him, wants to take his ticket, but the Count brushes him aside with a small wave of his hand. After the Ischl train has left, I am told to leave the platform and return to the hot waiting room, but with some difficulty I obtain permission to stay. I pass the time watching people who use bribes to secure a compartment, and I resolve to insist on my rights, that is, to demand the same privilege. Meanwhile I am singing something to myself, which I later recognize as the aria from *The Marriage of Figaro*:

"If my lord Count would like to dance,
Would like to dance,
Let him but say so,
And I'll play him a tune."

(Another person might not have recognized the song.)

All afternoon I have been in an insolent, combative mood. I have spoken rudely to the waiter and the cab driver, though I hope without hurting their feelings. Now all sorts of bold and revolutionary thoughts come into my head, of the kind that suit Figaro's words and the comedy by Beaumarchais that I had seen at the Comédie Française. I think of the speech about great lords who have taken the trouble to be born; of the aristocratic prerogative that Count Almaviva wants to exercise over Susanna; of the jokes our spiteful opposition journalists make about Count Thun's name (*thun* means "to do" in German) by calling him Count Do-Nothing. I really do not envy him; he now has a difficult mission with the Emperor, while I am the real Count Do-Nothing, since I am going on vacation. Along with this come all sorts of cheerful plans for the holiday. A gentleman now arrives whom I know as a government representative at the medical examinations, who has earned the flattering nickname "the Government's bedfellow" for his activities in that capacity. By insisting on his official status, he obtains half of a first-class compartment, and I hear one guard say to another: "Where are we going to put the gentleman with the first-class half-compartment?" A fine bit of favoritism: I am paying for a full first-class compartment. I now get a whole compartment to myself, but not in a corridor coach, so there is no toilet available to me during the night. My complaints to the guard get nowhere, and I retaliate by suggesting that they at least cut a hole in the floor of the compartment for travelers who might need it. And in fact I wake at a quarter to three in the morning with an urge to urinate, after the following dream:

*Crowd of people; a student meeting. . . . A certain Count (Thun or Taaffe) is making a speech. Asked to say something about the Germans, he declares with a contemptuous air that their favorite flower is coltsfoot, and then puts something like a torn leaf, actually the crumpled skeleton of a leaf, into his buttonhole. I flare up, so I do flare up, but I am surprised at this attitude of mine.* Then, less distinctly: *It seems as though this were the great hall (the Aula); the exits are blocked, as if it were necessary to flee. I make my way through a series of handsomely furnished rooms, apparently government chambers, with furniture of a color between brown and violet, and at last I come to a corridor where a housekeeper, a fat elderly woman (Frauenzimmer), is sitting. I try to avoid speaking to her, but she evidently thinks I have a right to pass, because she asks whether she should accompany me with the lamp. I indicate to her, or tell her, that she is to stay standing on the stairs, and in this I seem to myself very clever, since I am avoiding being watched after all. I am now downstairs, and I find a narrow, steep path, which I follow.*

Again indistinctly. . . . *It is as though my second task were to get out of the city, as my first had been to get out of the house. I am riding in a one-horse cab and tell the driver to take me to a railway station. "I can't drive with you on the tracks themselves," I say, after he has objected that I have worn him out. Here it seems as though I had already driven with him along a route ordinarily traveled by rail. The stations are crowded; I consider whether to go to Krems or to Znaim, but I think that the court will be there, and I decide in favor of Graz or some such place. Now I am sitting in the railway coach, which is something like a streetcar, and in my buttonhole I have a long braided thing bearing violet-brown violets made of a stiff material, which attracts a great deal of attention.* Here the scene breaks off. *I am again in front of the railway station, but now I am with an elderly gentleman. I devise a scheme for remaining unrecognized, but I also see this plan already carried out. Thinking and experiencing are here, as it were, one and the same. He pretends to be blind, at least in one eye, and I hold a male urinal in front of him (which we had to buy, or did buy, in the city). So I am a sick-nurse and must hand him the urinal because he is blind. If the conductor sees us in this position, he must let us pass without drawing attention to us. At the same time, the posture of this man is visually observed.* Then I wake with an urge to urinate.

The whole dream gives the impression of a fantasy that carries the dreamer back to the revolutionary year 1848. The memory of that year had been revived by its anniversary in 1898, and also by a short excursion to the Wachau, where I had come to know Emmersdorf, a town I mistakenly took to be the resting place of the student leader Fischhof, to whom several features of the dream content may refer. The associations then lead me to England, to the house of my brother, who used jokingly to say "Fifty years ago" to his wife, after the title of a poem by Lord Tennyson, whereupon the children would correct him: "Fifteen years ago." This fantasy, however, which attaches itself subtly to the thoughts prompted by the sight of Count Thun, is like the façade of an Italian church, set in front of the building without being structurally connected to it. Unlike such façades, though, the fantasy is full of gaps and confusion, and the parts behind it break through in many places. The first situation of the dream is assembled from several scenes, into which I can separate it. The Count's arrogant bearing in the dream is copied from a scene at my secondary school, the Gymnasium, when I was fifteen. We had organized a conspiracy against an unpopular and ignorant teacher; its ringleader was a schoolmate who seems to have taken Henry VIII of England as his model. It fell to me to carry out the coup d'état, and a discussion of the importance of the Danube (*Donau*) for Austria (the Wachau!) was the occasion on which matters broke into open revolt. One of my fellow conspirators was our only aristocratic schoolmate, whom we called "the giraffe" because of his conspicuous height, and he stood exactly like the Count in the dream while being reprimanded by the tyrant of the school, the professor of German. The explanation of the favorite flower, and of putting into a buttonhole something that must again have been a flower, recalls the orchids I had brought to a lady friend that same day, as well as the rose of Jericho. Above all, it recalls the scene in Shakespeare's history plays that opens the civil wars of the Red and White Roses, a memory to which the mention of Henry VIII has opened the way. From roses it is not far to red and white carnations. Meanwhile two little rhymes, one German and one Spanish, slip into the analysis: "Roses, tulips, carnations, all flowers fade," and "*Isabelita, no llores, que se marchitan las flores*" ("Isabelita, do not weep, for the flowers wither"). The Spanish comes from *Figaro*. Here in Vienna, white carnations have become the emblem of the anti-Semites and red ones that of the Social Democrats. Behind this lies the memory of an anti-Semitic provocation during a railway journey through beautiful Saxony (Anglo-Saxon). The third scene contributing to the first situation of the dream belongs to my early student days. In the German students' club there was a discussion about the relation of philosophy to the sciences in general. A green youth, steeped in materialist doctrine, I pushed myself forward and defended a highly one-sided view. Thereupon a shrewd older fellow student, who has since shown his ability to lead men and organize the masses, and who moreover bears a name drawn from the animal kingdom, stood up and gave us a thorough dressing-down. He too, he said, had herded swine in his youth and had returned repentant to his father's house. I flared up (as in the dream), became very rude, and replied that since I now knew he had herded swine, I was not surprised at the tone of his remarks. (In the dream I am surprised at my German nationalist sentiment.) There was a great commotion, and demands came from all sides that I take back what I had said, but I stood firm. The man I had insulted was too sensible to follow the advice he was given to challenge me to a duel, and he let the matter drop.

The remaining elements of this scene of the dream have more remote origins. What does it mean that the Count proclaims the coltsfoot? Here I must consult my chain of associations. Coltsfoot (German *Huflattich*), lattice, lettuce, salad-dog: the dog in the manger, who begrudges others what he cannot eat himself. A good many terms of abuse can be discerned here: gir-*affe* (*Affe* being German for monkey or ape), pig, sow, dog. By a detour through a name I could even arrive at donkey, and so once more at contempt for an academic teacher. Furthermore, I translate coltsfoot, though I do not know how correctly, as *pisse-en-lit*, literally "piss-in-bed." I got this idea from Zola's *Germinal*, in which children are sent to gather salad greens of this kind. The dog, *chien* in French, has a name that sounds like the major excretory function (*chier*, as *pisser* stands for the minor one). Soon we shall have the indecent before us in all three of its categories, for the same *Germinal*, which has a great deal to do with the coming revolution, describes a very peculiar contest that depends on the production of gaseous excretions, called flatus. And now I must point out how long the way to this flatus has been in preparation. It begins with the flowers and proceeds by way of the Spanish rhyme about Isabelita to Ferdinand and Isabella, and then by way of Henry VIII to English history at the time of the Armada's expedition against England. After that victory, the English struck a medal bearing the inscription "*Afflavit et dissipati sunt*" ("He blew, and they were scattered"), for the storm had scattered the Spanish fleet. I had thought of using this phrase, half in jest, as the title of a chapter on "Therapeutics," should I ever have occasion to give a detailed account of my conception and treatment of hysteria.

Out of regard for the censor, I cannot give so detailed a solution of the second scene of the dream. At this point I put myself in the place of a certain eminent gentleman of that revolutionary period, who also had an adventure with an eagle, who is said to have suffered from incontinence of the bowels, and so on. I do not think I would be justified in slipping past the censor here, even though it was an aulic councillor, a court councillor (*aula*, *consiliarius aulicus*), who told me most of these stories. The series of rooms in the dream alludes to his Excellency's private railway car, into which I had a chance to glance for a moment. But, as so often in dreams, the rooms also signify a woman: *Frauenzimmer*, in which *Zimmer*, "room," is appended to *Frauen*, "women," to imply a touch of contempt. In the figure of the housekeeper I repay with poor thanks an intelligent elderly lady for the entertainment and the many good stories I have enjoyed at her house. . . . The detail of the lamp goes back to Grillparzer, who records a charming experience of a similar kind, which he later used in *Hero and Leander* (the waves of the sea and of love; the Armada and the storm).

I must likewise forgo a detailed analysis of the two remaining portions of the dream. I shall single out only those elements that lead to two childhood scenes, for whose sake alone I have taken up this dream. The reader will suspect that it is sexual material that forces me into this suppression, but he need not rest content with that explanation. Many things that must be kept secret from others are not kept secret from oneself, and here the issue is not considerations that lead me to hide the solution, but motives of the inner censor that conceal the real content of the dream from me. I may say, then, that the analysis reveals these three portions of the dream as impertinent boasting, the overflow of an absurd megalomania long since suppressed in my waking life. This megalomania nonetheless ventures to show itself in the manifest dream content through one or two projections (I seem clever to myself), and it makes the arrogant mood of the evening before the dream entirely intelligible. It is boasting in every department. Thus the mention of Graz refers to the phrase "What does Graz cost?", as though one could buy the whole city, which we like to use when we feel flush with money. Anyone who recalls Master Rabelais's unsurpassed account of *The Life and Deeds of Gargantua and His Son Pantagruel* will be able to supply the boastful content hinted at in the first portion of the dream. What follows belongs to the two promised childhood scenes. I had bought a new trunk for this journey, and its color, a brownish violet, appears several times in the dream: in the violet-brown violets of stiff material, next to a thing called a "girl-catcher," and in the furniture of the government chambers. That something new attracts people's attention is a well-known belief of children. Now, I have been told the following story from my childhood; I remember hearing the story rather than the event itself. I am told that at the age of two I still occasionally wet my bed, that I was often scolded for it, and that I consoled my father by promising to buy him a beautiful new red bed in N., the nearest large city. (Hence the detail inserted in the dream that we bought the urinal in the city, or had to buy it; one must keep one's promises. Note, too, the identification of the male urinal with the female trunk or box.) The whole megalomania of the child is contained in that promise. The significance of dreams about difficulty in urinating, as they occur in children, has already been considered in the interpretation of an earlier dream.

There was another domestic incident, from when I was seven or eight years old, that I remember very well. One evening before bed, I ignored the rules of discretion and relieved myself in my parents' bedroom, in their presence. In scolding me for this offense, my father remarked: "That boy will never amount to anything." The remark must have been a terrible blow to my ambition, because allusions to this scene return again and again in my dreams, and they are regularly coupled with lists of my accomplishments and successes, as though I wanted to say: "You see, I have amounted to something after all."

This childhood scene supplies the elements for the final image of the dream, in which, naturally, the roles are reversed for the sake of revenge. The elderly man, who is plainly my father (the blindness in one eye stands for the glaucoma he had on one side), is now urinating in front of me, just as I once urinated in front of him. Through the glaucoma I allude to cocaine, which helped my father through his operation, as though I had thereby kept my promise. I am also mocking him: because he is blind, I must hold the urinal for him, and I take pleasure in the allusions to my discoveries in the theory of hysteria, of which I am so proud.

The two childhood scenes of urinating are closely bound up with the desire for greatness, but their revival on the trip to Aussee was further encouraged by a chance circumstance: my compartment had no lavatory, and I had reason to expect some discomfort on the journey, which is exactly what happened in the morning. I woke with the sensation of a bodily need. One might be inclined to treat this sensation as the actual stimulus of the dream. I would rather take a different view, namely that the dream thoughts gave rise to the urge to urinate. It is quite unusual for me to be disturbed in sleep by any bodily need, at least at the hour I woke on this occasion, a quarter to four in the morning. To forestall a further objection, I should add that I have hardly ever felt the need to urinate after waking early on other journeys made in more comfortable conditions. In any case, I can leave this point undecided without damaging my argument.

Experience in dream analysis has also taught me that even when the interpretation of a dream at first seems complete, because its sources and the wish it fulfills are easy to demonstrate, important trains of thought always remain that lead from the dream back into earliest childhood. I have therefore been forced to ask whether this feature may be an essential condition of dreaming. If this thesis were generalized, every dream would contain, in its manifest content, a connection with what has been recently experienced, and, in its latent content, a connection with what was experienced longest ago. And in the analysis of hysteria I can actually show that these remote experiences have, in a real sense, remained recent up to the present day. But this conjecture still seems very difficult to prove, and I shall probably have to return to the part played by the earliest childhood experiences in another connection, in a later chapter.

Of the three peculiarities of dream memory considered at the outset, one, the preference for unimportant material in the dream content, has been satisfactorily explained by tracing it back to dream distortion. We have been able to establish the existence of the other two, the selection of recent material and of infantile material, but we have not been able to explain them by reference to the motive of the dream. We should keep these two characteristics in mind, since they have yet to be explained or assessed. A place will have to be found for them elsewhere, either in the psychology of the sleeping state or in the discussion of the structure of the psychic apparatus that we shall undertake later, once we have learned that dream interpretation allows us to observe the inner workings of that apparatus as though through a window.

At this point I may emphasize another result of the last few dream analyses. The dream often appears to have more than one meaning. Not only may several wish-fulfillments be united in it, as the examples show, but one meaning or one wish-fulfillment may also conceal another, until at the bottom one comes upon the fulfillment of a wish from the earliest period of childhood. Here, too, it may be asked whether the word "often" in this sentence should not more accurately be replaced by "regularly."

### (c) Somatic Sources of Dreams

If one tries to interest an educated layman in the problems of dreaming, and with that aim asks him where he thinks dreams come from, one generally finds that he believes himself already in secure possession of part of the answer. He thinks at once of the influence that disturbed or sluggish digestion ("dreams come from the stomach"), an awkward position of the body, and small incidents during sleep exert on the formation of dreams, and he does not seem to suspect that, even after all these factors have been taken into account, something still remains unexplained.

In the introductory chapter we discussed at length how large a role the scientific literature assigns to somatic sources of stimulation in the formation of dreams, so here we need only recall the results of that inquiry. We saw that three kinds of somatic stimuli are distinguished: objective sensory stimuli that come from external objects; inner states of excitation in the sense organs that have only a subjective basis; and bodily stimuli that originate inside the body. We also noticed that the authors tend to push the psychic sources of the dream into the background, or to ignore them altogether, in favor of these somatic sources.

In testing the claims made on behalf of these classes of somatic stimulation, we found the following. The significance of objective stimuli to the sense organs, whether chance stimuli occurring during sleep or stimuli that cannot be shut out of the sleeping mind, has been firmly established by numerous observations and confirmed by experiment. The part played by subjective sensory stimuli appears to be demonstrated by the reappearance in dreams of hypnagogic images, the sensory images that arise as one is falling asleep. And although the tracing of dream images and ideas, in the broadest sense, back to internal bodily stimulation cannot be demonstrated in every detail, it is supported by the well-known influence that a state of excitation in the digestive, urinary, and sexual organs exerts on the content of our dreams.

"Nerve stimulus" and "bodily stimulus," then, would be the somatic sources of the dream, and, according to several authors, its only sources of any kind.

But we have already encountered a number of doubts, which seem to call into question not so much the correctness of the somatic theory of stimulation as its sufficiency.

However confident all the proponents of this theory may have felt about the facts on which it rests, especially in the case of chance external nerve stimuli, which can be recognized in the content of the dream without any difficulty, none of them has been able to avoid conceding that the rich ideational content of dreams cannot be explained by external nerve stimuli alone. Miss Mary Whiton Calkins examined her own dreams and those of another person for six weeks with this question in mind, and found that an element of external sensory perception could be demonstrated in only 13.2 percent and 6.7 percent of them respectively. Only two cases in the whole collection could be traced to organic sensations. Here the statistics confirm what a quick glance at our own experience might have led us to suspect.

Repeated attempts have been made to set apart the "nerve-stimulus dream" from other forms of dream as a well-established subspecies. Spitta, for instance, divided dreams into nerve-stimulus dreams and association dreams. But this solution plainly remained unsatisfactory so long as no link could be shown between the somatic sources of dreams and their ideational content.

In addition to this first objection, that external sources of stimulation occur too seldom, a second objection arises: introducing sources of this kind does not adequately explain dreams. The proponents of the theory must account for two things. First, why is the external stimulus never recognized in the dream for what it really is, but regularly mistaken for something else, as in the alarm-clock dreams? And second, why does the mind's reaction to this misrecognized stimulus turn out so unpredictably and so variably? In answer to these questions, Strümpell tells us that because the mind turns away from the outer world during sleep, it is incapable of interpreting objective sensory stimuli correctly, and is forced instead to form illusions on the basis of vague prompts arriving from many directions. In his own words:

"As soon as a sensation, a complex of sensations, a feeling, or any psychic process whatever arises in the mind during sleep from an external or internal nerve stimulus and is perceived by the mind, this process calls up sensory images from the range of waking experience that the mind still retains; that is, it calls up earlier perceptions, either bare or accompanied by the psychic values belonging to them. It seems to gather around itself, as it were, a greater or smaller number of such images, and from these the impression arising from the nerve stimulus receives its psychic value. Here, as in ordinary speech about waking thought, we usually say that the mind interprets the impressions of nerve stimuli during sleep. The result of this interpretation is the so-called nerve-stimulus dream, that is, a dream whose composition is determined by the fact that a nerve stimulus produces its effect in psychic life according to the laws of reproduction."

Wundt's view agrees with this theory in all essentials. He says that the ideas in a dream are probably, for the most part, the result of sensory stimuli, especially those of general bodily sensation, and are therefore mostly fantastic illusions: probably memory images, only partly pure, that have been heightened into hallucinations. Strümpell found an apt simile for the relation between dream content and dream stimuli that follows from this theory. It is as though "the ten fingers of a person who knows nothing of music were to wander over the keyboard of an instrument." The implication is that the dream is not a psychic phenomenon arising from psychic motives, but the result of a physiological stimulus, which finds expression in psychic symptoms only because the apparatus affected by the stimulus is capable of no other form of expression. A similar assumption underlies, for example, the explanation of obsessive ideas that Meynert attempted with his famous simile of a dial whose individual figures stand out because they are carved in higher relief than the rest, so that certain ideas would press themselves forward simply by virtue of their physical prominence and not because of any meaning they carry.

However popular this theory of somatic dream stimuli may have become, and however attractive it may seem, its weak point is easy to show. Every somatic dream stimulus that provokes the psychic apparatus into interpreting it through the formation of illusions can give rise to an incalculable number of such attempts at interpretation, and can therefore be represented in the dream content by an extraordinary variety of different ideas. But the theory of Strümpell and Wundt cannot point to any motive that governs the relation between the external stimulus and the particular dream idea chosen to interpret it. It therefore cannot explain what Lipps, in his *Fundamental Facts of Mental Life*, calls the "peculiar choice" that the stimuli "often enough make in the course of their reproductive activity." Other objections can be raised against the basic assumption of the whole theory of illusions, the assumption that during sleep the mind is in no condition to recognize the true nature of objective sensory stimuli.
