The early physiologist Burdach demonstrates that the mind is perfectly able, even in sleep, to interpret correctly the sensory impressions that reach it and to respond in accordance with that correct interpretation. He shows this by pointing out that certain impressions that matter to a person can be exempted from the general neglect of sleep, as when a nurse sleeps through other sounds but wakes at the child's cry, and that one is more reliably awakened by one's own name than by some indifferent sound. All of this presupposes, of course, that the mind distinguishes among sensations even while asleep. From these observations Burdach concludes that what we must assume in the sleeping state is not an inability to interpret sensory stimuli but a lack of interest in them. The same arguments Burdach used in 1830 reappear unchanged in the work of Lipps in 1883, where they are turned against the theory of somatic stimuli. On this view the mind resembles the sleeper in the anecdote who, when asked, "Are you asleep?" answers "No," but who, when addressed again with the words "Then lend me ten florins," takes refuge in the excuse: "I'm asleep."

The inadequacy of the theory of somatic dream stimuli can also be shown in another way. Observation shows that external stimuli do not compel me to dream, even though these stimuli do appear in the dream as soon as, and if, I dream. When I receive a touch or a pressure while asleep, several reactions are open to me. I can ignore it, and discover only on waking that my leg has been uncovered or my arm has been lying under pressure; pathology offers a great many examples of powerful sensory and motor stimuli of various kinds that have no effect at all during sleep. Second, I can perceive the sensation in my sleep, feeling it through the sleep, as it were, which is what usually happens with painful stimuli, without weaving the pain into the fabric of a dream. Third, I can wake up because of the stimulus in order to get rid of it. Only as a fourth possible reaction may the nerve stimulus drive me to dream, and the other possibilities occur at least as often as dream formation does. This could not be the case unless the motive for dreaming lay somewhere outside the somatic sources of dreams.

Recognizing the shortcoming just described in explaining dreams through somatic stimuli, other authors, namely Scherner, later joined by the philosopher Volkelt, tried to define more precisely the psychic activities by which the many-colored images of the dream arise out of somatic stimuli. In doing so they moved the essential nature of dreams back into the province of the mind and of psychic activity. Scherner not only gave a poetic, admiring, glowing, and vivid description of the psychic peculiarities that unfold in the course of dream formation; he also believed he had guessed the principle by which the mind handles the stimuli at its disposal. According to Scherner, once fantasy has been freed from the fetters placed on it during the day and given free rein, the dream activity strives to represent symbolically the nature of the organ from which the stimulus comes. The result is a kind of dream-book, a guide to interpreting dreams, by means of which bodily sensations, the condition of the organs, and the nature of the stimuli can be inferred from the images of the dream. "Thus the image of a cat expresses an angry, discontented mood, and the image of a pale, smooth piece of pastry the nakedness of the body. The fantasy of the dream pictures the human body as a whole as a house, and each individual organ as a part of the house. In 'toothache dreams' a high vaulted entrance hall corresponds to the mouth, and a staircase to the descent of the throat into the digestive tract; in the 'headache dream' the ceiling of a room covered with loathsome, reptile-like spiders is chosen to stand for the top of the head," as Volkelt reports. "The dream uses several different symbols for the same organ. The breathing lungs, for instance, find their symbol in a stove filled with flames and a roaring draft, the heart in hollow chests and baskets, the bladder in round, bag-shaped objects or anything else that is hollow. It is especially important that at the end of the dream the stimulating organ or its function is represented without disguise, and usually on the dreamer's own body. Thus the toothache dream usually ends with the dreamer pulling a tooth out of his own mouth." This theory cannot be said to have found much favor among the authors. Above all, it seems extravagant, and no one has been inclined to find even the small measure of justification to which, in my opinion, it can lay claim. As can be seen, it amounts to a revival of the symbolic dream interpretation practiced by the ancients, except that the source from which interpretations are drawn is limited to the human body. The absence of any scientifically intelligible technique of interpretation must seriously restrict the usefulness of Scherner's theory. Arbitrariness in interpretation seems in no way ruled out, especially since a single stimulus can be expressed by several different representations in the dream content; indeed, Scherner's associate Volkelt already found himself unable to confirm the representation of the body as a house. A further objection is that here, once again, dream activity is credited to the mind as a useless and aimless activity, since on this theory the mind is content to spin fantasies about the stimulus that occupies it, without even remotely aiming at anything like a discharge of that stimulus.

But Scherner's theory of the symbolization of bodily stimuli in dreams suffers a heavy blow from yet another objection. These bodily stimuli are present at all times, and it is generally assumed that the mind is more open to them during sleep than when awake. It is therefore incomprehensible why the mind does not dream continuously all night long, and why it does not dream every night about all the organs. If one tries to evade this objection by stipulating that special stimuli must come from the eye, the ear, the teeth, or the intestines in order to arouse dream activity, one faces the difficulty of proving that this increase in stimulation is objectively present, which can be done in only a small number of cases. If the dream of flying symbolizes the rising and falling of the lungs, then, as Strümpell has already remarked, either this dream would be dreamed far more often, or it would have to be shown that breathing becomes more pronounced during the dream. A third possibility remains, the most probable of all: that from time to time special motives are at work that direct attention to the visceral sensations, which are present in everyone at all times. But this possibility takes us beyond the scope of Scherner's theory.

The value of Scherner's and Volkelt's discussions lies in their drawing attention to a number of features of dream content that need explaining and that seem to promise new knowledge. It is quite true that dreams contain symbolizations of the bodily organs and their functions: that water in a dream often signifies a need to urinate, that the male genital organ is often represented by a staff standing upright or by a pillar, and so on. In dreams that show a very lively field of vision and brilliant colors, in contrast to the dimness of other dreams, one can hardly reject the interpretation that they are "dreams of visual stimulation," any more than one can dispute that illusions contribute to dreams full of noise and a confusion of voices. Consider a dream like Scherner's, in which two rows of handsome fair-haired boys stand facing each other on a bridge, attack each other, and then return to their places, until at last the dreamer himself sits down on the bridge and pulls a long tooth out of his jaw; or a similar one of Volkelt's, in which two rows of drawers play a part and which again ends with the extraction of a tooth. Dream formations of this kind, which the authors report in great numbers, prevent us from discarding Scherner's theory as an idle invention without first trying to find its kernel of truth. We now face the task of giving the supposed symbolization of the dental stimulus an explanation of a different kind.

Throughout this discussion of the theory of the somatic sources of dreams, I have held back the argument that follows from our own dream analyses. If we have succeeded in proving, by a method other authors have not applied to the study of dreams, that the dream is a psychic act with a value of its own, that a wish supplies the motive for its formation, and that the experiences of the previous day furnish the immediate material for its content, then any other theory of dreams that neglects so important a method of investigation, and consequently makes the dream appear a useless and puzzling psychic reaction to somatic stimuli, can be dismissed without special comment. Otherwise there would have to be two entirely different kinds of dreams, which is highly improbable, one of which has come under our observation alone, while the other alone has been observed by the earlier authorities on dreams. What remains is to find a place within our own theory of dreams for the facts that are cited in support of the prevailing theory of somatic dream stimuli.

We have already taken the first step in this direction by setting up the thesis that the dream activity is compelled to work all the dream stimuli that are present at the same time into a unified whole. We have seen that when two or more experiences capable of making an impression are left over from the previous day, the wishes arising from them are united in a single dream; and similarly, that an impression of psychic value and the indifferent experiences of the previous day are combined in the dream material, provided that connecting ideas are available between them. The dream thus appears to be a reaction to everything that is simultaneously present as actual in the sleeping mind. So far as we have analyzed the dream material up to this point, we have found it to be a collection of psychic remnants and memory traces, which, because of the dream's evident preference for recent and infantile material, we were obliged to credit with a quality of present actuality, though we could not then say what that quality consisted in. It is now not difficult to predict what will happen when new material, in the form of sensations, is added to these actualities of memory. These stimuli likewise gain importance for the dream because they are actual, present at the moment of sleep, and they combine with the other psychic actualities to make up the material from which the dream is formed. Put differently, the stimuli that arise during sleep are worked up into the fulfilment of a wish, whose other components are the familiar remnants of daily experience. This union, however, is not inevitable; we have seen that the sleeping mind may adopt more than one attitude toward bodily stimuli. Wherever the union does take place, it has simply proved possible to find, for the dream content, the kind of representational material that can give expression to both classes of dream sources, the somatic as well as the psychic. Adding somatic material to the psychic sources of the dream does not change the dream's essential nature. It remains the fulfilment of a wish, however its expression may be shaped by the material that happens to be present.

I am glad to make room here for a number of peculiarities that cast the significance of external stimuli for the dream in a different light. I imagine that a combination of individual, physiological, and accidental factors, conditioned by the circumstances of the moment, determines how a person will respond in any particular case of strong objective stimulation during sleep. The depth of sleep, whether habitual or accidental, taken together with the intensity of the stimulus, will in one case allow the stimulus to be suppressed so that it does not disturb sleep; in another it will force an awakening; in a third it will support the effort to overcome the stimulus by weaving it into the fabric of the dream. Given how many such combinations are possible, external objective stimuli will find expression in one person's dreams more often than in another's. In my own case, since I sleep extremely well and stubbornly resist every kind of disturbance during sleep, external sources of irritation very rarely find their way into my dreams, while psychic motives evidently set me dreaming with great ease. In fact I have recorded only a single dream in which an objective, painful source of stimulation can be demonstrated, and it will be highly instructive to see what effect the external stimulus had in this very dream.

*I am riding on a grey horse, at first timidly and awkwardly, as though I were only leaning against something. I meet a colleague, P., who is also on horseback and is wearing a heavy woollen suit; he draws my attention to something (probably to the fact that my riding position is bad). Now I become more and more skilful on the horse, which is a most intelligent animal; I sit comfortably and notice that I already feel quite at home in the saddle. For a saddle I have a kind of padding that completely fills the space between the horse's neck and its rump. Riding this way, I pass with difficulty between two lumber wagons. After riding some distance up the street, I turn around and want to dismount, first in front of a small open chapel that stands close to the street. Then I actually dismount in front of a chapel standing near the first one. The hotel is on the same street; I could let the horse go there by itself, but I prefer to lead it. It seems as though I would be ashamed to arrive there on horseback. In front of the hotel stands a hall boy, who shows me a card of mine that has been found and makes fun of me because of it. On the card is written, underlined twice, "Eat nothing," followed by a second, indistinct sentence, something like "Do not work." At the same time I have a hazy sense that I am in a strange city where I do no work.*

It will not be obvious at first that this dream arose under the influence, or rather the compulsion, of a painful stimulus. On the previous day I had been suffering from boils, which made every movement a torture. One of them had finally grown to the size of an apple at the base of the scrotum and caused me the most unbearable pain with every step. A feverish lethargy, a loss of appetite, and the hard work I had nonetheless kept up throughout the day had combined with the pain to put me thoroughly out of temper. I was not really in a condition to carry out my duties as a physician, and given the nature and location of the ailment, one might have expected me to attempt almost anything other than riding, for which I was particularly unfit. Yet it is exactly this activity that the dream plunges me into, and it is the most emphatic denial of the suffering that could possibly be imagined. To begin with, I do not know how to ride. I do not ordinarily dream of riding, and I have sat on a horse only once in my life, without a saddle, and did not feel comfortable then. But in this dream I ride as though I had no boil on the perineum. Why? Precisely because I do not want one. Judging from its description, my saddle is the poultice that had allowed me to fall asleep. Presumably, being so well cared for, I felt nothing of my pain during the first few hours of sleep. Then the painful sensations made themselves felt and tried to wake me, whereupon the dream came and said soothingly: "Keep on sleeping; you won't wake up anyway! You have no boil at all, for you are riding a horse, and with a boil where yours is, riding would be impossible!" And the dream succeeded. The pain was stifled, and I slept on.

But the dream was not content to "suggest away" the boil by clinging stubbornly to an idea incompatible with the ailment, a strategy in which it behaved like the hallucinatory madness of the mother who has lost her child, or of the merchant whose fortune has been wiped out by losses. Beyond this, the dream used the details of the denied sensation, and of the image brought in to displace it, as a means of linking the material otherwise present in my mind to the dream situation, and of giving that material representation. I am riding a grey horse: the horse's colour corresponds exactly to the pepper-and-salt suit my colleague P. was wearing when I last met him in the country. I have been told that highly seasoned food causes boils; in any case, as an explanation of their origin, it is preferable to sugar, which is what ordinarily comes to mind in connection with them. My friend P. has been pleased to "ride the high horse" with me ever since he replaced me in the treatment of a woman patient with whom I had performed great feats. In the dream I first sit on the horse sideways, like a circus rider; in reality the patient led me wherever she pleased, like the horse in the old anecdote about the Sunday rider, the inexperienced weekend horseman whose mount carries him wherever it chooses. In this way the horse came to stand symbolically for a woman patient, and in the dream it is accordingly most intelligent. "I feel quite at home up here" refers to the position I held in this patient's household until my colleague P. took my place. "I thought you were firmly seated in the saddle there," one of my few well-wishers among the eminent physicians of this city recently remarked to me about that same household. It was indeed a feat to practise psychotherapy for ten hours a day while in such pain. But I know that I cannot keep up my especially demanding work for long without complete physical health, and the dream is full of gloomy allusions to the situation that would then follow. The card is the kind that neurasthenic patients carry and present to their doctors, setting out their ailments and the rules they have been given: no work and no food. Interpreting further, I find that the dream work has managed to travel from the wish situation of riding back to very early childhood scenes of quarrelling between me and my nephew, who now lives in England and who is, moreover, a year older than I. The dream has also drawn on elements from my journeys to Italy; the street in the dream is assembled from impressions of Verona and Siena. A still more thorough interpretation leads to sexual dream thoughts, and I recall what significance allusions to that beautiful country held in the dreams of a woman patient who had never been to Italy. The German phrase *gen Italien*, "toward Italy," sounds almost exactly like *Genitalien*, "genitals." At the same time there are references to the house in which I was physician before my friend P., and to the place where the boil is located.

Among the dreams mentioned in the previous chapter, several could serve as examples of how so-called nerve stimuli are worked over. The dream of drinking in deep draughts is one of these. In it the somatic excitation appears to be the only source of the dream, and the wish arising from the sensation, thirst, the only motive for dreaming. Something similar holds for the other simple dreams, wherever the somatic excitation by itself is capable of forming a wish. The dream of the sick woman who throws the cooling apparatus off her cheek at night shows a peculiar way of responding to painful stimuli with a wish fulfilment: the patient seems to have succeeded, for the moment, in making herself insensible to pain by attributing her pains to a stranger. My dream of the three Parcae, the Fates, is plainly a hunger dream, but it has found a way to trace the need for food back to the child's longing for its mother's breast, and to use this harmless desire as a cloak for a more serious one that may not express itself so openly. In the dream about Count Thun we saw how an incidental bodily need was brought into connection with the strongest, and also the most strongly suppressed, emotions of psychic life. And when the First Consul, in the case reported by Garnier, works the sound of an exploding bomb into a dream of battle before it wakes him, the purpose for which psychic activity generally concerns itself with sensations arising during sleep is revealed with extraordinary clarity. A young lawyer, deeply absorbed in his first major bankruptcy case, lies down to sleep the following afternoon and behaves exactly like the great Napoleon. He dreams of a certain G. Reich in Hussiatyn, a man he knows through the bankruptcy proceedings. But Hussiatyn, whose name echoes the German *husten*, "to cough," keeps forcing itself on his attention until he is obliged to wake, and he hears his wife, who is suffering from bronchial catarrh, coughing violently.

Let us compare the dream of Napoleon I, who, incidentally, was an excellent sleeper, with that of the sleepy student whose landlady woke him with a reminder that he had to go to the hospital. He promptly dreamed himself into a hospital bed and slept on, explaining his motive as follows: "If I'm already in the hospital, I won't have to get up to go there." This is plainly a dream of convenience. The sleeper openly admits to himself why he is dreaming, and in doing so he gives away one of the secrets of dreaming in general. In a certain sense all dreams are dreams of convenience: they serve to prolong sleep rather than end it. The dream is the guardian of sleep, not its disturber. We shall justify this view elsewhere with respect to the psychic factors that bring about awakening; here, however, we can already demonstrate that it applies to the influence of objective external stimuli. Either the mind ignores the causes of sensations altogether, if it can do so despite their intensity and despite a meaning it understands perfectly well; or it uses the dream to deny these stimuli; or, third, if it is forced to acknowledge the stimulus, it looks for an interpretation that will present the actual sensation as one element of a situation that is both desired and compatible with sleep. The actual sensation is woven into the dream in order to strip it of its reality. Napoleon may go on sleeping; it is only a dream memory of the thunder of the cannon at Arcole that is trying to disturb him.

The wish to sleep, which has suspended the conscious ego and which, together with the dream censor, contributes its share to the dream, must therefore always be reckoned among the motives of dream formation, and every successful dream is a fulfilment of this wish. How this general, constantly present, and unvarying wish to sleep relates to the other wishes, now one and now another of which finds fulfilment, will be explained later. In the wish to sleep we have found a factor that can make good the gap in the theory of Strümpell and Wundt, and account for the perverse and capricious way in which the external stimulus is interpreted. The correct interpretation, of which the sleeping mind is entirely capable, would imply an active interest and would require that sleep come to an end. Of all the possible interpretations, therefore, only those are admitted that are acceptable to the absolute censorship exercised by the wish to sleep. The situation resembles the lovers' exchange in *Romeo and Juliet*: it is the nightingale and not the lark, for if it is the lark, the night of love is over. From among the interpretations of the stimulus available at the moment, the one chosen is the one that can form the best connection with the wishes lying in wait in the mind. Everything is thus strictly determined, and nothing is left to chance. The misinterpretation is not an illusion but, if one likes, an excuse. Here again, however, we must acknowledge a process that departs from normal psychic procedure, just as in the case where the dream censor brings about substitution by means of displacement.

If external nerve stimuli and internal bodily stimuli are intense enough to compel the mind's attention, they constitute, provided they lead to dreaming and not to waking, a fixed point in the formation of the dream, a nucleus in the dream material for which a suitable wish fulfilment is then sought, much as, in the case described above, connecting ideas are sought between two dream stimuli. To this extent it is true of a number of dreams that the somatic element determines their content. In this extreme case a wish that is not, strictly speaking, currently active is aroused for the purpose of forming the dream. Yet the dream can do nothing except represent a wish as fulfilled in a situation; it is faced, so to speak, with the task of finding which wish can be represented and fulfilled by means of the situation now present. Even if this present material is painful or disagreeable, it is not useless for forming dreams. The psychic life has at its disposal even wishes whose fulfilment produces pain rather than pleasure. This sounds contradictory, but it becomes intelligible once we take into account the existence of two psychic agencies and the censorship that stands between them.

As we have heard, there are in psychic life repressed wishes that belong to the first system and whose fulfilment the second system opposes. Such wishes exist, and we do not mean this historically, in the sense that such wishes once existed and were later destroyed. The theory of repression, which is essential to the study of the psychoneuroses, holds that these repressed wishes continue to exist alongside an inhibition that weighs them down. Language has hit on the truth when it speaks of the "suppression" of such impulses. The psychic machinery for bringing these wishes to realisation remains intact and ready for use. But if such a suppressed wish should happen to be fulfilled, the defeated inhibition of the second system, the system capable of becoming conscious, expresses itself as a painful feeling. To conclude this discussion: if disagreeable sensations arising from somatic sources are present during sleep, the dream work takes advantage of this constellation to represent the fulfilment of an otherwise suppressed wish, with the censorship maintained to a greater or lesser degree.

This state of affairs makes a number of anxiety dreams possible, while another series of dream formations that seem to tell against the wish theory reveals a different mechanism. Anxiety in dreams may be psychoneurotic in nature, or it may arise from psychosexual excitation, in which case the anxiety corresponds to a repressed libido. Then this anxiety, like the whole anxiety dream, has the significance of a neurotic symptom, and we stand at the boundary where the wish-fulfilling tendency of dreams breaks down. In other anxiety dreams, however, the feeling of anxiety has a somatic source, as in people with lung or heart conditions who occasionally have difficulty breathing. The anxiety is then used to help strongly suppressed wishes achieve fulfilment in the form of a dream, wishes that, had they been dreamed from psychic motives, would have released the same fear. These two apparently conflicting cases are not hard to reconcile. Of two closely connected psychic formations, an emotional tendency and an ideational content, whichever is actually present supports the other in the dream. Sometimes anxiety of somatic origin supports the suppressed ideational content; at other times the ideational content, freed from suppression and driven forward by sexual emotion, assists the discharge of anxiety. In the first case one may say that an emotion of somatic origin receives a psychic interpretation. In the second, everything is psychic in origin, but the suppressed content is easily replaced by a somatic interpretation suited to anxiety. The difficulties in understanding all this have little to do with the dream itself; they arise because these questions touch on the problems of how anxiety develops and of repression.

The general sum of bodily feeling must certainly be counted among the dominant internal stimuli of dreams. It cannot supply the dream content, but it compels the dream thoughts to make a selection from the material available for representation in the dream content. It does so by placing within easy reach the part of the material that suits its own character, while holding back the rest. Moreover, this general feeling, carried over from the day, is probably connected with the psychic remnants that are significant for the dream.

If the somatic sources of excitation that arise during sleep, the sensations of sleep, are not unusually intense, they play a part in dream formation that is, in my judgment, similar to that of impressions from the day that have remained recent but are indifferent. That is, they are drawn into the dream if they lend themselves to combination with the ideational content of the psychic dream source, and otherwise not. They are treated as cheap, ever-available material, used whenever it is needed, rather than as a precious material that dictates how it must be used. The situation resembles that of a patron of the arts who brings an artist a rare stone, a piece of onyx, to be made into a work of art. The stone's size, its colour, and its veining help decide what head or what scene will be carved from it; but where marble or sandstone is plentiful and uniform, the artist simply follows the idea taking shape in his own mind. Only in this way, it seems to me, can we explain why dream content arising from bodily excitations of no unusual intensity does not appear in every dream and on every night.

An example, which brings us back to the interpretation of dreams, may best illustrate what I mean. One day I was trying to understand the meaning of the sensations, so often dreamed and so closely allied to anxiety, of being held back, of being unable to move from the spot, of being unable to finish something, and so on. That night I had the following dream: *I am very incompletely dressed, and I go from an apartment on the ground floor up a flight of stairs to an upper story. As I do so I take the steps three at a time, and I am pleased to find that I can climb them so quickly. Suddenly I see a servant girl coming down the stairs, toward me. I am ashamed and try to hurry away, and now the sensation of being held back appears: I am glued to the steps and cannot move from the spot.*

Analysis: The situation in the dream is taken from everyday reality. In a house in Vienna I have two apartments, connected only by an outside staircase. My consulting rooms and study are on a raised ground floor, and my living quarters are one story above. When I finish my work downstairs late at night, I go up the stairs to my bedroom. On the evening before the dream I had in fact made this short trip in somewhat disordered dress; I had taken off my collar, tie, and cuffs. In the dream this has turned into a more advanced state of undress, which, as usual, remains vague. Taking the stairs several at a time is my habitual way of climbing them. It is also the fulfilment of a wish recognised within the dream, for the ease of the feat has reassured me about the condition of my heart. Moreover, the way I climb the stairs makes an effective contrast with the sensation of being held back in the second half of the dream. It shows me, though no proof was needed, that the dream has no difficulty in representing physical actions as fully and completely carried out. One need only think of flying in dreams.

But the stairs I climb are not those of my own house. At first I do not recognise them; only the person coming toward me reveals the place they are meant to signify. This woman is the maid of the elderly lady I visit twice a day to give injections, and the stairs, too, closely resemble the ones I must climb there twice daily.

How do this staircase and this woman come into my dream? The shame of not being fully dressed is unquestionably sexual in character, yet the servant I dream of is older than I am, sullen, and not in the least attractive. These questions call up precisely the following circumstances. When I make my morning visit to this house, I am usually seized with an urge to clear my throat, and what I cough up lands on the stairs. There is no spittoon on either floor, and I take the view that the stairs ought to be kept clean not at my expense but by the provision of a spittoon. The housekeeper, likewise an elderly and sullen person, with an instinct for cleanliness, takes a different view of the matter. She lies in wait to see whether I take the liberty in question, and once she has caught me at it, I hear her growl distinctly. For days afterward she withholds her customary greeting when we meet. On the day before the dream, the housekeeper's position had been reinforced by the servant girl. I had just finished my usual hurried visit to the patient when the servant confronted me in the anteroom and remarked: "You might as well have wiped your shoes today, Doctor, before you came into the room. The red carpet is all dirty again from your feet." That is the whole claim the staircase and the servant girl can make to a place in my dream.

There is an intimate connection between my flying up the stairs and my spitting on them. Pharyngitis and heart disease are both said to be punishments for the vice of smoking, and on account of that vice I naturally enjoy no great reputation for tidiness with the housekeeper in either house. The dream fuses the two houses into a single image.

I must postpone further interpretation of this dream until I can account for the origin of the typical dream of being incompletely dressed. As a preliminary result of the dream just cited, I note only that the dream sensation of inhibited movement is always aroused at a point where some particular connection requires it. It cannot be caused by a peculiar condition of my motor faculties during sleep, for a moment earlier I had seen myself hurrying up the steps with ease, as if to confirm this very point.

### (d) Typical Dreams

In general, we cannot interpret another person's dream unless he is willing to supply the unconscious thoughts that lie behind its content, and this seriously limits the practical use of our method of dream interpretation. Usually each individual fashions his dream world with great freedom and according to his own peculiarities, which makes it unintelligible to others. In contrast, there are a certain number of dreams that almost everyone has dreamed in the same way, and which we customarily assume to have the same meaning for every dreamer. These typical dreams hold a particular interest because they probably arise from the same sources in everyone, and are therefore especially well suited to inform us about the sources of dreams.

Typical dreams deserve the most exhaustive investigation. Here, however, I shall examine only a few examples of the type in some detail, and for this purpose I shall select first the so-called embarrassment dream of nakedness, and then the dream of the death of loved relatives.

The dream of being naked or scantily clothed in the presence of strangers sometimes occurs with the further feature that one feels no shame about it at all. But the dream of nakedness deserves our interest only when shame and embarrassment are felt, when one wants to flee or hide, and when one experiences the strange inhibition of being unable to move from the spot and powerless to change the disagreeable situation. Only in this form is the dream typical; otherwise its core content may be drawn into all sorts of relations or replaced by individual embellishments. Its essence is a disagreeable feeling akin to shame, together with the wish to hide one's nakedness, chiefly by moving away, without being able to do so. I believe that most of my readers will at some point have found themselves in this situation in a dream.

The nature and manner of the undress are usually vague. The dreamer typically reports, "I was in my shirt," but this is rarely a clear image. In most cases the lack of clothing is so indefinite that the report expresses it as a set of alternatives: "I was in my chemise or in my petticoat." As a rule, the deficiency in dress is not serious enough to justify the shame attached to it. For someone who has served in the army, nakedness is often replaced by some way of wearing the uniform that breaks regulations: "I am on the street without my saber and I see officers coming," or "I am without my necktie," or "I am wearing checked civilian trousers," and so on.

The people before whom one feels ashamed are almost always strangers whose faces remain undefined. In the typical dream, one is never reproached, or even noticed, on account of the clothing that causes one such embarrassment. On the contrary, the people wear an air of indifference, or, as I had occasion to observe in one particularly clear dream, they look stiffly solemn. This deserves some thought.

The dreamer's shamed embarrassment and the spectators' indifference form a contradiction of a kind that often occurs in dreams. It would better suit the dreamer's feelings if the strangers stared at him in astonishment and laughed, or grew indignant. I believe, however, that this unpleasant feature has been eliminated by the tendency toward wish-fulfillment, while the embarrassment, retained for some reason or other, has been left standing, and so the two parts fail to agree. We have interesting evidence that the dream, its appearance partly distorted by the tendency toward wish-fulfillment, has not been properly understood. It has become the basis of a fairy tale familiar to all of us in Andersen's version, and it has recently received poetic treatment from L. Fulda in *The Talisman*.

In Andersen's tale, two impostors weave a costly garment for the Emperor which, they claim, will be visible only to the good and true. The Emperor goes out wearing this invisible garment, and since the fabric acts as a kind of touchstone, a test that reveals a person's true worth, the people are all frightened into behaving as though they did not notice his nakedness.

This is precisely the situation in our dream. It takes no great boldness to suppose that the unintelligible dream content prompted the invention of a state of undress in which the remembered situation becomes meaningful. That situation has then been stripped of its original meaning and put to other purposes. But we shall see that this kind of misunderstanding of dream content often arises from the conscious activity of the second psychic system, and must be recognized as a factor in the final shaping of the dream. We shall see, moreover, that similar misunderstandings, likewise occurring within one and the same psychic personality, play a leading part in the development of obsessions and phobias. We can also explain the source from which the material for this transformation is drawn. The impostor is the dream, the Emperor is the dreamer himself, and the moralizing tendency betrays a dim awareness that the latent dream content concerns forbidden wishes that have fallen victim to repression. The context in which such dreams appear during my analyses of neurotics leaves no room to doubt that the dream rests on a memory from earliest childhood. Only in childhood was there a time when we were seen in scanty clothing by our relatives as well as by unfamiliar nurses, servant girls, and visitors, and at that time we were not ashamed of our nakedness.

Among children who are a little older, one can observe that being undressed has a kind of intoxicating effect on them rather than making them ashamed. They laugh, leap about, and slap their bodies; the mother, or whoever is present, forbids this, saying: "Shame on you, you mustn't do that." Children often display exhibitionist cravings. One can hardly walk through a village in our part of the country without meeting some two- or three-year-old who lifts up his or her shirt before the passing traveler, perhaps in his honor. One of my patients has preserved in conscious memory a scene from his eighth year: he had just undressed before going to bed and was about to dance into his little sister's room in his undershirt when the servant stopped him. In the childhood histories of neurotics, undressing in front of children of the opposite sex plays a large part. In paranoia, the desire to be watched while dressing and undressing can be traced directly to such experiences. And among those who remain perverse there is a class who have intensified this childish impulse into a compulsion: the exhibitionists.

This period of childhood, when the sense of shame is absent, appears to our later recollection as a Paradise, and Paradise itself is nothing but a composite fantasy drawn from the childhood of the individual. That is also why human beings in Paradise are naked and unashamed until the moment when shame and fear are awakened; then comes the expulsion, and with it sexual life and cultural development begin. The dream can carry us back into this Paradise every night. We have already ventured the conjecture that impressions from earliest childhood, from the prehistoric period up to about the end of the fourth year, crave reproduction in and of themselves, independently of everything else and perhaps without regard to their content, and that their repetition is the fulfillment of a wish. Dreams of nakedness, then, are exhibition dreams.

The nucleus of the exhibition dream consists of two elements. The first is one's own person, seen not as a child but as one is in the present. The second is the scanty clothing, which emerges only obscurely, whether because it has been buried beneath so many later memories of being in a state of undress or because of the censor.

Next come the people before whom one feels ashamed. I know of no instance in which the actual spectators of those infantile exhibitions reappear in the dream, for the dream is hardly ever a simple recollection. Strangely enough, the persons who were the objects of our sexual interest in childhood are left out of all the reproductions found in dreams, in hysteria, and in obsessional neurosis. Paranoia alone restores the spectators to their places, and is fanatically convinced of their presence even though they remain invisible. What the dream puts in their place, the "many strange people" who take no notice of the spectacle before them, is precisely the wish-opposite of that single, intimate person for whom the exposure was intended. "Many strange people," moreover, frequently appear in dreams in other suitable contexts as well; as a wish-opposite, they always signify "a secret." One can see how even the restoration of the original state of affairs in paranoia is subject to this reversal. One is no longer alone. One is certainly being watched, but the watchers are "many strange, curiously indefinite people."

Repression also has its place in the exhibition dream. The disagreeable feeling in the dream is the reaction of the second psychic agency to the fact that the exhibition scene it has rejected has nevertheless managed to secure representation. The only way to avoid that feeling would be not to revive the scene at all.

We shall return later to the sensation of being inhibited. It is admirably suited to represent, in the dream, the conflict of the will, the act of saying no. According to our unconscious purpose, the exhibition is to continue; according to the demands of the censor, it is to be stopped.

The relation of our typical dreams to fairy tales and other poetic material is neither sporadic nor accidental. Now and then a poet's keen insight has analytically recognized the process of transformation, of which the poet is usually the instrument, and has followed it backward to its source in the dream. A friend has drawn my attention to the following passage in G. Keller's *Der grüne Heinrich* (*Green Henry*):

"I do not wish, dear Lee, that you should ever learn from experience the peculiar, piquant truth contained in the situation of Odysseus when he appears before Nausicaa and her companions, naked and covered with mud. Would you like to know what it means? Let us look at the incident closely. If you are ever separated from your home and from everything dear to you, and wander in a foreign country; when you have seen much and experienced much, when you have cares and sorrows, and are perhaps even wretched and forsaken, then some night you will inevitably dream that you are approaching your home. You will see it shining and gleaming in the loveliest colors; charming, delicate, and graceful figures will come out to meet you; and suddenly you will discover that you are going about in rags, naked and covered with dust. A nameless feeling of shame and fear seizes you; you try to cover yourself and hide, and you wake bathed in sweat. As long as there are human beings, this will be the dream of the care-laden man battered by fortune, and so Homer took his situation from the deepest depths of humanity's eternal nature."

This deep and eternal nature of humanity, which the poet usually counts on touching in his listeners, is made up of those stirrings of the psyche that are rooted in childhood, in the period that later becomes prehistoric. Suppressed and forbidden childhood wishes break through under cover of the homeless man's wishes, which are unobjectionable and capable of becoming conscious, and for this reason the dream given objective form in the legend of Nausicaa regularly takes the shape of an anxiety dream.

My own dream mentioned earlier, of hurrying up the stairs, which soon turns into being glued to the steps, is likewise an exhibition dream, since it displays the essential components of one. It must therefore be traceable to childhood experiences, and knowledge of these should tell us how far the servant girl's behavior toward me, her reproach that I had soiled the carpet, helped secure her the position she occupies in the dream. I can now supply the desired explanation. In psychoanalysis one learns to interpret closeness in time as a connection in substance. Two thoughts that follow each other immediately, though apparently unconnected, belong to a unity that can be inferred, just as an *a* and a *t* written side by side are to be pronounced as a single syllable, *at*. The same holds for the relation of dreams to one another. The staircase dream I have cited is taken from a series of dreams whose other members I know, having interpreted them, and a dream included in such a series must belong to the same context. Now, the other dreams in the series rest on the memory of a nurse who looked after me from some point while I was still being breastfed until I was two and a half, and of whom a hazy recollection has remained in my consciousness. According to what my mother recently told me, she was old and ugly, but very intelligent and thorough. According to the inferences I can draw from my dreams, she did not always treat me kindly, and spoke harshly to me when I showed too little aptitude for being trained in cleanliness. By trying to carry on this educational work, then, the servant girl acquires a claim to be treated in my dream as an incarnation of that prehistoric old woman. We may assume that the child gave his love to this governess despite her harsh treatment of him.

Another series of dreams that may be called typical are those in which a dear relative, such as a parent, brother or sister, or child, has died. Two classes of these dreams must be distinguished at once: those in which the dreamer remains untouched by sorrow while dreaming, and those in which he feels profound grief at the death and even expresses it in his sleep with passionate tears.

We may set aside dreams of the first group; they have no claim to be counted as typical. When analyzed, they turn out to mean something other than what they contain, and to be designed to conceal some other wish. Such is the case with the dream, discussed earlier, of the aunt who sees her sister's only son lying on a bier before her. This does not mean that she wishes her little nephew dead. As we have learned, it merely conceals a wish to see a beloved person again after a long separation, the same person she had last seen, after a similarly long interval, at the funeral of another nephew. This wish, which is the dream's real content, gives no cause for sorrow, and so no sorrow is felt in the dream. This case shows that the emotion contained in a dream belongs not to its manifest content but to its latent content, and that the emotional content has escaped the distortion that has befallen the content of its images and ideas.

It is a different matter with dreams in which the death of a beloved relative is imagined and sorrowful emotion is felt. These mean what their content says: the wish that the person in question may die. And since I can expect the feelings of all my readers, and of everyone who has dreamed something similar, to rebel against this interpretation, I must try to present my proof on the broadest possible basis.

We have already seen one example showing that the wishes represented as fulfilled in a dream are not always present wishes. They may also be dead, discarded, buried, and repressed wishes, to which we must nonetheless ascribe a kind of continued existence, since they reappear in the dream. They are not dead in the sense that people die. Rather, they resemble the shades of the dead in the *Odyssey*, which awaken to a certain kind of life as soon as they have drunk blood. In the dream, discussed earlier, of the dead child lying in a box, we were dealing with a wish that had been current fifteen years before and that the dreamer had frankly admitted ever since. It is perhaps not unimportant for the theory of dreams if I add that even this dream rests on a memory from earliest childhood. When the dreamer was a small child, though exactly when cannot be determined, she had heard that during the pregnancy of which she was the fruit, her mother had fallen into a deep depression and had passionately wished for the death of her child before its birth. Now grown up and pregnant herself, the dreamer follows her mother's example.

If someone dreams, with expressions of grief, that his father or mother, brother or sister, has died, I shall not use the dream as proof that he wishes them dead now. The theory of dreams does not require that much; it is content to conclude that the dreamer once wished them dead, at some point in childhood. I fear, however, that this limitation will do little to calm the objectors. They may dispute the possibility that they ever had such thoughts just as vigorously as they insist that they harbor no such wishes now. I must therefore reconstruct a portion of the submerged psychology of childhood from the evidence the present still provides.

Let us first consider the relation of children to their brothers and sisters. I do not know why we assume it must be a loving one, since instances of hostility between adult siblings force themselves on everyone's experience, and we so often know that the estrangement began in childhood or has always existed. But many grown people who today are tenderly attached to their brothers and sisters and stand by them lived with them in childhood in almost unbroken hostility. The older child mistreated the younger, slandered it, and took away its toys. The younger was consumed with helpless rage against the elder, envied and feared it, or directed its first stirrings of freedom and its first sense of injustice against its oppressor. The parents say the children do not get along, and cannot find the reason. It is not hard to see that the character even of a well-behaved child is not what we would wish to find in an adult. The child is absolutely egoistic; it feels its needs intensely and strives ruthlessly to satisfy them, especially against its competitors, other children, and first of all its brothers and sisters. We do not call the child wicked for this; we call it naughty. It is not held responsible for its misdeeds, either in our judgment or in the eyes of the criminal law. And rightly so, for we may expect that within this very period of life we call childhood, altruistic impulses and morality will awaken in the little egoist, and that, in Meynert's words, a secondary ego will overlay and restrain the primary one. Morality, to be sure, does not develop in all areas at once, and the length of the amoral period of childhood varies from one individual to another. Where this moral development fails to appear, we like to speak of "degeneration," though these are plainly cases of arrested development. Where the primary character has already been covered over by later development, an attack of hysteria can at least partly uncover it again. The resemblance between the so-called hysterical character and that of a naughty child is strikingly evident. Obsessional neurosis, by contrast, corresponds to a super-morality, imposed as a heightened check on the primary character as it begins to reassert itself.

Many people, then, who love their brothers and sisters and would feel bereaved by their death, carry in their unconscious hostile wishes against them from earlier times, wishes that can be realized in the dream. It is especially interesting to watch little children up to the age of three in their attitude toward their siblings. Until now the child has been the only one; now he is told that the stork has brought a new baby. The child looks the newcomer over and then delivers his verdict firmly: "The stork had better take it back again."

I hold in all seriousness that the child knows enough to reckon the disadvantage it can expect from the newcomer. I know of a lady, who today gets along very well with a sister four years younger, that she greeted the news of her little sister's arrival with the words: "But I shan't give her my red cap, anyway." If the child arrives at this realization only later, its hostility will be awakened at that point. I know of a case in which a girl not yet three tried to strangle an infant in its cradle because she suspected that its continued presence boded her no good. Children at this age are capable of envy in all its intensity and distinctness. Or perhaps the little brother or sister really has soon disappeared; the child has again drawn the entire affection of the household back to itself, and then the stork brings a new child. Is it unnatural, then, for the favorite to wish that this new rival might share the fate of the earlier one, so that he can be treated as well as he was in the interval? Under normal circumstances, of course, this attitude toward the younger infant is simply a function of the difference in age. After a certain time, a girl's maternal instincts will be awakened by the helpless newborn.

Feelings of hostility toward brothers and sisters must occur during childhood far more often than the dull observation of adults ever registers.

With my own children, who were born in quick succession, I missed the chance to make such observations. I am now making up for it through my little nephew, whose undisputed reign was disrupted after fifteen months by the arrival of a female rival. I am told that the young man behaves very chivalrously toward his little sister, that he kisses her hand and pets her. Yet I have satisfied myself that even before his second birthday he was using his new command of language to criticize this person who seems so unnecessary to him. Whenever the conversation turns to her, he chimes in and cries angrily, "Too 'ittle, too 'ittle." In the last few months, since the baby has outgrown this unflattering criticism through her splendid development, he has found another way to justify his insistence that she does not deserve so much attention. At every suitable opportunity he reminds us, "She hasn't any teeth." All of us also remember the eldest daughter of another of my sisters. At six years old, she spent an hour and a half going from one aunt to the next, seeking reassurance with the same question: "Lucy can't understand that yet, can she?" Lucy was her rival, two and a half years younger.

In every one of my female patients, without fail, I have found this dream of the death of brothers and sisters, pointing to an intensified hostility. I have met with only one exception, and it could easily be reinterpreted as a confirmation of the rule. Once, during a session, I was explaining this state of affairs to a lady because it seemed to bear on the symptoms we were discussing. To my astonishment, she replied that she had never had such dreams. She did, however, recall another dream that supposedly had nothing to do with the matter. She had first dreamed it at the age of four, when she was the youngest child, and had dreamed it repeatedly since. "A great many children, all of them the dreamer's brothers and sisters and her male and female cousins, were romping about in a meadow. Suddenly they all grew wings, flew up, and were gone." She had no idea what the dream meant, but we will have little difficulty recognizing it as a dream of the death of all her brothers and sisters, in its original form and only slightly affected by the censor. I venture to offer the following interpretation. One child out of a large number had died; in this case, the children of two brothers were being raised together as brothers and sisters. Is it not likely that our dreamer, then not yet four years old, asked some wise grown-up, "What happens to children when they die?" The answer was probably, "They grow wings and become angels." By this explanation, all the brothers, sisters, and cousins in the dream now have wings like angels, and, most important, they fly away. Our little angel-maker is left alone: imagine it, the only one remaining out of such a crowd! The detail of the children romping in a meadow points fairly unmistakably to butterflies, as though the child had been guided by the same association that led the ancients to picture Psyche, the soul, with the wings of a butterfly.

Someone may now object that, while children's hostile impulses toward their brothers and sisters may readily be granted, it is hard to see how a childish disposition could reach such a pitch of wickedness as to wish death on a rival or a stronger playmate, as though every offense could be atoned for only by capital punishment. Anyone who argues this way forgets that the child's idea of "being dead" shares little more than the words with our own. The child knows nothing of the horrors of decay, of shivering in the cold grave, of the terror of the infinite Nothing, which the grown-up, as all the myths of the Great Beyond attest, finds so hard to endure in imagination. The fear of death is foreign to the child. That is why a child plays with the dreadful word and threatens another child, "If you do that again you'll die, the way Francis died," at which the poor mother shudders, perhaps because she cannot forget that the great majority of mortals never live past childhood. It is still possible for a child of eight, coming home from a natural history museum, to say to its mother, "Mamma, I love you so much. If you ever die, I'm going to have you stuffed and set up here in the room so I can always, always see you!" So little does the childish conception of death resemble our own.

For a child who has been spared the sight of the suffering that comes before death, being dead means the same thing as "being gone," no longer bothering those who remain. The child does not distinguish the manner or means by which this absence comes about, whether through travel, estrangement, or death. If, during a child's prehistoric years, a nurse has been dismissed and the child's mother has died shortly afterward, the two experiences, as analysis reveals, merge in his memory. Many a mother has discovered to her sorrow how little children miss those who are away. Returning home after a summer journey of several weeks, she asks about them and is told, "The children didn't ask for their mother once." And if she really does depart for that "undiscovered country from whose bourn no traveller returns," as Hamlet calls death, the children at first seem to have forgotten her, and only later begin to remember their dead mother.

If, then, a child has reasons for wishing another child absent, nothing holds it back from dressing that wish in the form of the other child's death. And the emotional reaction to the death-wish dream proves that, for all the differences in content, the wish in the child is somehow the same as it is in adults.

If the child's death-wish toward its brothers and sisters can be explained by childish egotism, which leads it to see them as competitors, how are we to account for the same wish directed at the parents? They bestow love on the child and satisfy its needs, and for precisely these egotistical reasons the child ought to want them preserved.

We are helped in resolving this difficulty by the observation that dreams of a parent's death mostly concern the parent who shares the dreamer's sex: a man usually dreams of his father's death, a woman of her mother's. I cannot claim that this happens invariably, but the pattern prevails so plainly that it must be explained by some factor that operates universally. To put the matter boldly, it is as though a sexual preference becomes active at an early age, as though the boy regards his father as a rival in love and the girl takes the same attitude toward her mother, a rival whose removal can only be to his or her advantage.

Before rejecting this idea as monstrous, let the reader consider the actual relations between parents and children. What the demands of culture and piety require of this relationship must be distinguished from what daily observation shows to be the case. More than one source of hostile feeling lies hidden in the relations between parents and children, and the conditions under which wishes that cannot pass the censor may be stirred into action are supplied in abundance. Let us consider first the relation between father and son. I believe the sanctity we have attached to the commandment in the Decalogue dulls our perception of reality. Perhaps we hardly dare to notice that most of humanity fails to obey the fifth commandment, to honor one's father and mother. In the lowest strata of society as well as the highest, reverence for parents habitually gives way to other interests. The dim reports that have reached us through myth and legend from the primeval ages of human society give us an unpleasant picture of the father's power and the ruthlessness with which it was wielded. Kronos devours his children, as the wild boar devours the sow's litter; Zeus castrates his father and takes his place as ruler. The more despotically the father ruled in the ancient family, the more the son must have stood in the position of an enemy, and the greater his impatience, as appointed successor, to take command himself after his father's death. Even in our own middle-class families, the father tends to nourish the seed of hatred that naturally belongs to the paternal relationship by denying his son control over his own destiny, or the means to exercise it. A physician often has occasion to notice that a son's grief at the loss of his father cannot suppress his satisfaction at the freedom he has finally won. Every father clings frantically to whatever remains in present-day society of the sadly outdated *potestas patris*, the absolute authority that Roman law granted the head of the family. And every writer who, like Ibsen, places the ancient conflict between father and son at the center of his work can be sure of his effect. Conflict between mother and daughter arises when the daughter grows up and finds her mother a guardian over her while she longs for sexual freedom, and when, on the other side, the mother is warned by her daughter's budding beauty that the time has come to give up her own sexual claims.

All these conditions are well known and open to anyone's inspection. But they do not explain the dreams of a parent's death found in people for whom reverence toward their parents has long since become inviolable. Moreover, the preceding discussion has prepared us to expect that the death-wish toward parents must be explained by reference to earliest childhood.

In the case of psychoneurotics, the analyses carried out with them confirm this conjecture with a certainty that leaves no room for doubt. They show that the child's sexual wishes, insofar as they deserve that name in their embryonic state, awaken very early, and that the girl's first affections are directed toward her father and the boy's first childish cravings toward his mother. The father thus becomes a troublesome rival for the boy, as the mother does for the girl, and we have already seen with brothers and sisters how little it takes for such a feeling to lead the child to the death-wish. As a rule, sexual preference also shows itself early in the parents. It is a natural tendency for the father to indulge his little daughter and for the mother to side with her sons, although both work earnestly at raising the children when the spell of sex does not cloud their judgment. The child is keenly aware of any partiality and resists whichever parent rebuffs it. For the child, finding love in a grown-up means not only the satisfaction of a particular craving but also that its will is to be indulged in other respects. So when the child makes a choice between its parents that corresponds to their own, it obeys its own sexual impulse and at the same time reinforces the feeling that comes from the parents.

Most signs of these infantile inclinations go unnoticed, though some can be observed even after the first years of childhood. An eight-year-old girl of my acquaintance, whenever her mother is called away from the table, seizes the opportunity to proclaim herself her successor: "Now I'll be Mamma. Charles, would you like some more vegetables? Do have some, I beg you," and so on. A particularly gifted and lively girl, not yet four, in whom this piece of child psychology is unusually transparent, says outright, "Now Mother can go away, and then Father has to marry me and I'll be his wife." Nor does this wish by any means rule out the possibility that the child also loves its mother tenderly. If a little boy is allowed to sleep at his mother's side whenever his father goes on a journey, and must return to the nursery and to someone he likes far less once his father comes home, the wish may easily arise that his father would stay away forever, so that he could keep his place next to his dear, beautiful mamma. And the father's death is plainly one way to achieve this, for the child's experience has taught him that "dead" people, like Grandpa, are always away; they never come back.

Although observations of small children lend themselves to this interpretation without any forcing, they do not carry the full conviction that the psychoanalysis of adult neurotics presses upon the physician. In those analyses, the dreams in question are reported with preliminary remarks of such a kind that interpreting them as wish-dreams becomes unavoidable. One day I find a lady sad and in tears. She says, "I don't want to see my relatives anymore; they must be horrified by me." Then, almost without transition, she says she remembers a dream, though of course she does not know what it means. She dreamed it four years earlier, and it runs as follows: *A fox or a lynx is walking on the roof; then something falls down, or she falls down, and after that her mother is carried out of the house dead, at which the dreamer weeps bitterly.* No sooner had I told her that this dream must signify a childhood wish to see her mother dead, and that this dream was why she believed her relatives must be horrified by her, than she supplied material that explained it. "Lynx-eye" was an insult a street urchin had once hurled at her when she was very small, and when she was three, a brick had fallen on her mother's head, making her bleed badly.

I once had the opportunity to make a thorough study of a young girl who passed through several distinct mental states. In the frenzied excitement with which her illness began, she showed an intense aversion to her mother, striking and scolding her whenever she came near the bed, while remaining loving and obedient toward a much older sister. This was followed by a lucid but somewhat apathetic state, with badly disturbed sleep. It was during this phase that I began treating her and analyzing her dreams. A great many of them dealt, in more or less obscure ways, with her mother's death. In one she attended the funeral of an old woman; in another she saw her sisters sitting at the table dressed in mourning. There could be no doubt about what the dreams meant. As her recovery progressed, hysterical phobias appeared, the most tormenting of which was the idea that something had happened to her mother. Wherever she was, she constantly had to hurry home to reassure herself that her mother was still alive. Taken together with my other experiences, this case was highly instructive. It displayed, as though in translations into several languages, the different ways in which the psychic apparatus responds to the same stimulating idea. In the state of excitement, which I understand as the overpowering of the second psychic agency, the unconscious hostility toward the mother became strong enough to drive action. Then, once calm returned, the turmoil had been suppressed, and the censor had regained control, this hostility could reach only the realm of dreams, where it fulfilled the wish that the mother might die. And as the normal condition grew stronger still, the hostility produced an excessive concern for the mother as a hysterical counter-reaction and a form of defense. In light of these considerations, it is no longer puzzling why hysterical girls are so often extravagantly attached to their mothers.

On another occasion I gained a deep insight into the unconscious mental life of a young man whose compulsion neurosis had made life nearly unbearable. He could not go out on the street, because he was tormented by the obsession that he would kill everyone he met. He spent his days assembling evidence for an alibi in case he should be charged with any murder that might have taken place in the city. It hardly needs saying that this man was as moral as he was highly cultivated. The analysis, which incidentally led to a cure, revealed that these distressing compulsive ideas rested on murderous impulses toward his rather overly strict father. To his great surprise, these impulses had found conscious expression when he was seven years old, though of course they had originated much earlier in childhood. After his father's painful illness and death, when the young man was thirty-one, the obsessive self-reproach appeared, transferred onto strangers in the form of the phobia I have described. Anyone capable of wishing to push his own father off a mountaintop into an abyss can certainly not be trusted to spare the lives of people less closely bound to him. He does well to lock himself in his room.

In my experience, which is now extensive, parents play a leading part in the childhood psychology of everyone who later becomes neurotic. Falling in love with one parent and hating the other are among the essential elements of that fateful store of psychic impulses which forms during childhood and which matters so greatly for the symptoms of the later neurosis. But I do not believe that psychoneurotics are sharply set apart from normal people here, as though they were able to create something entirely new and peculiar to themselves. It is far more likely, as occasional observation of normal children also shows, that in their loving or hostile wishes toward their parents, psychoneurotics merely display in exaggerated form feelings that are present, less distinctly and less intensely, in the minds of most children. Antiquity has given us legendary material that confirms this, and the profound and universal power of these legends can be explained only by granting that this assumption about childhood psychology applies just as universally.

I am referring to the legend of King Oedipus and the drama of the same name by Sophocles. Oedipus, son of Laius, king of Thebes, and of Jocasta, is abandoned as a nursing infant, because an oracle has told his father that the son not yet born will be his murderer. The child is rescued and grows up as a king's son at a foreign court, until, uncertain of his origins, he too consults the oracle and is warned to avoid his homeland, for he is destined to murder his father and marry his mother. On the road leading away from what he believes is his home, he meets King Laius and kills him in a sudden quarrel. He then arrives at the gates of Thebes, where he solves the riddle of the Sphinx who bars the way. In gratitude the Thebans make him king and give him Jocasta's hand in marriage. He reigns in peace and honor for a long time and fathers two sons and two daughters with the woman he does not know is his mother, until at last a plague breaks out and the Thebans consult the oracle once more. Here Sophocles' tragedy begins. The messengers bring back the answer that the plague will end as soon as Laius's murderer is driven from the land. But where is he hiding?

"Where are they to be found? How shall we trace the perpetrators of so old a crime, where no conjecture leads to discovery?"

The action of the play consists of nothing but a revelation, gradually completed and artfully delayed, much like the work of a psychoanalysis: the revelation that Oedipus himself is the murderer of Laius, and the son of the murdered man and of Jocasta. Shattered by the atrocities he has unknowingly committed, Oedipus blinds himself and leaves his homeland. The oracle has been fulfilled.

*Oedipus Tyrannus* is a so-called tragedy of fate. Its tragic effect is said to lie in the opposition between the mighty will of the gods and the futile resistance of the human beings threatened with destruction. Resignation to the divine will and acknowledgment of one's own helplessness are supposed to be the lesson the deeply moved spectator takes from the play. Modern authors have accordingly tried to produce a similar tragic effect by building the same opposition into stories of their own invention. But audiences have sat unmoved while a curse or an oracle was fulfilled on blameless people despite all their struggles, and the later tragedies of fate have all failed to make an impression.

If *Oedipus Tyrannus* can move modern audiences no less than it moved the Greeks of Sophocles' day, the explanation cannot simply be that the effect of Greek tragedy rests on the opposition between fate and human will. It must be sought in the particular nature of the material through which that opposition is portrayed. There must be a voice within us ready to acknowledge the compelling power of fate in *Oedipus*, while we rightly dismiss the situations in Grillparzer's *Die Ahnfrau* (*The Ancestress*) and other later tragedies as arbitrary inventions. And there must be a corresponding element in the story of King Oedipus that answers to this inner voice. His fate moves us only because it might have been our own, because the oracle laid the same curse on us before our birth as it laid on him. Perhaps it is the lot of all of us to direct our first sexual impulses toward our mothers and our first hatred and violent wishes toward our fathers; our dreams convince us that it is. King Oedipus, who struck down his father Laius and married his mother Jocasta, is nothing other than the fulfilled wish of our childhood. But we have been luckier than he: unless we have become psychoneurotics, we have since managed to withdraw our sexual impulses from our mothers and to forget our jealousy of our fathers. We recoil from the man in whom this primitive wish has been fulfilled with the full force of the repression these wishes have undergone within us. By his analysis, which exposes the guilt of Oedipus, the poet compels us to recognize our own inner selves, where these impulses, though suppressed, are still present. The contrast with which the chorus leaves us—

"... Behold! this Oedipus, who unraveled the famous riddle and who was a man of eminent virtue; a man who trusted neither in popular favor nor in the good fortune of his fellow citizens; see what a storm of adversity has overtaken him at last!"

This warning is addressed to us and to our pride, to us who since childhood have grown so wise and so powerful in our own estimation. Like Oedipus, we live in ignorance of the wishes that offend morality, wishes that nature has forced upon us; and once they are revealed, we would gladly turn our eyes away from every scene of our childhood.

The text of Sophocles' tragedy itself contains an unmistakable hint that the Oedipus legend springs from extremely ancient dream material. That material is the painful disturbance of the child's relationship to its parents by the first stirrings of sexuality. Jocasta tries to comfort Oedipus, who does not yet know the truth but has grown uneasy because of the oracle. She mentions the dream that so many people dream, though she attaches no significance to it:

"Many men before now have dreamed that they shared their mother's bed. But he passes through life most easily who counts such things as trifles."

The dream of having sexual intercourse with one's mother came to many people then, as it does today, and they recount it with indignation and astonishment. It is, understandably, the key to the tragedy and the counterpart to the dream of the father's death. The story of Oedipus is the imagination's response to these two typical dreams. Just as an adult experiences such a dream with feelings of resistance, the legend must contain terror and self-punishment. The further form the legend takes is the work of a secondary elaboration that misunderstands its material and tries to bend it to theological purposes, as we saw earlier with the dream material of exhibitionism. The attempt to reconcile divine omnipotence with human responsibility must, of course, fail with this material, as it fails with every other.

I must not leave the typical dream of the death of loved relatives without saying something more about its significance for the theory of dreams in general. These dreams show us a highly unusual case: the dream thought created by the repressed wish escapes the censor entirely and passes into the dream unaltered. Some special conditions must be present to make such an outcome possible, and I find two factors that favor these dreams. First, there is no wish we believe to be further from us. We are convinced such a wish "would never occur to us even in a dream," and so the dream censor is unprepared for this monstrosity, just as the legal code of Solon, the lawgiver of ancient Athens, could establish no punishment for the murder of a father. Second, in this case the repressed and unsuspected wish is especially often met by a fragment of the day's experience in the form of worry about the life of the loved person. This worry cannot be registered in the dream except by making use of the wish that has the same content, and the wish, in turn, can hide behind the worry awakened during the day.
