Some may prefer to think the whole matter simpler, holding that we merely continue at night, in our dreams, whatever has occupied us during the day. If so, the dream of the death of loved ones is cut off from any connection with the explanation of dreams, and a problem that can easily be solved is needlessly left standing.

It is also instructive to trace how these dreams relate to anxiety dreams. In the dream of the death of loved persons, the repressed wish has found a way to evade the censor and the distortion the censor imposes. The unavoidable accompaniment in this case is that painful feelings are experienced in the dream. Thus the anxiety dream arises only when the censor is wholly or partly overpowered. Conversely, the censor is more easily overpowered when anxiety has already been supplied by bodily sources. This makes plain the purpose for which the censor performs its office and practices dream distortion: it does so to prevent the development of anxiety or other forms of painful emotion.

I spoke earlier of the egotism of the child's mind, and I may now return to the subject to suggest that dreams preserve this trait and thereby reveal their connection with childhood. Every dream is thoroughly egotistical; in every dream the beloved self appears, even if in disguise. The wishes fulfilled in dreams are invariably the wishes of this self, and when interest in another person seems to have caused a dream, the appearance is deceptive. I will analyze several examples that seem to contradict this claim.

I. A boy not yet four years old reports the following: *He saw a large platter, garnished, with a big piece of roast meat on it, and all of a sudden the meat was eaten up, not cut into pieces but eaten up. He did not see the person who ate it.*

Who might this mysterious stranger be, whose lavish meal the little boy dreams about? The previous day's experiences must supply the answer. For several days, on the doctor's orders, the boy had been living on a diet of milk. On the evening before the dream he had misbehaved, and as punishment he was sent to bed without supper. He had already gone through one such hunger cure and had borne it very bravely. He knew he would get nothing to eat, yet he did not dare say a word to show that he was hungry. Upbringing was beginning to have its effect on him, and this is visible even in the dream, which shows the first signs of dream distortion. There is no doubt that he himself is the person whose wishes are directed toward this abundant meal, and a meal of roast meat at that. But because he knows it is forbidden to him, he does not dare sit down to it himself, as children ordinarily do in their dreams (recall my little Anna's dream about strawberries). The eater remains anonymous.

II. I once dreamed that I saw in a bookshop's display a new volume in the Book-Lovers' Collection, a series I regularly buy, which includes monographs on art, on world history, on famous artistic centers, and so on. *The new series was called* Famous Orators *(or* Orations*), and the first volume bore the name of Dr. Lecher.*

In the course of analysis it seems unlikely that the fame of Dr. Lecher, the long-winded orator of the German Opposition, should occupy my thoughts while I dream. The fact is that a few days earlier I had taken on several new patients for psychological treatment and was now obliged to talk for ten to twelve hours a day. I myself am the long-winded orator.

III. On another occasion I dreamed that a university teacher I know said: *My son, the Myopic.* A dialogue of short speeches and replies followed. Then came a third part of the dream in which I and my sons appear. As far as the latent dream content is concerned, father, son, and Professor M. are merely lay figures, the jointed wooden mannequins that painters pose in place of living models, and they stand in for me and my eldest son. I will return to this dream later because of another peculiarity.

IV. The following dream offers an example of truly base egotistical feelings concealed behind affectionate concern:

*My friend Otto looks ill; his face is brown and his eyes bulge.*

Otto is my family physician, and I owe him a debt I can never hope to repay, for he has watched over my children's health for years. He has treated them successfully whenever they fell ill, and he has also given them presents on every occasion that offered him an excuse. He paid us a visit on the day of the dream, and my wife remarked that he looked tired and worn out. That night came my dream, which gives him several symptoms of Basedow's disease, a disorder of the thyroid gland. Anyone who disregarded my rules of dream interpretation would take the dream to mean that I am worried about my friend's health and that this worry finds expression in the dream. That would contradict not only the claim that the dream is a wish-fulfillment but also the claim that it is open only to egotistical impulses. But let whoever interprets the dream this way explain to me why I should fear that Otto has Basedow's disease, a diagnosis for which his appearance offers not the slightest justification.

My analysis, by contrast, yields the following material, drawn from an incident six years ago. A small party of us, including Professor R., was driving in pitch darkness through the forest of N., several hours from our country house. The coachman, who was not entirely sober, overturned us, carriage and all, down an embankment, and only by luck did we all escape unhurt. We were forced to spend the night at the nearest inn, where news of our accident aroused great sympathy. A gentleman who showed unmistakable signs of Basedow's disease, though only a brownish color of the face and bulging eyes with no goiter, placed himself entirely at our service and asked what he could do for us. Professor R. replied in his decisive way: "Nothing, except lend me a nightshirt." To which our generous friend answered, "I'm sorry, but I can't do that," and walked off.

Continuing the analysis, it occurs to me that Basedow is the name not only of a physician but also of a famous educator. (Now that I am awake, I am not entirely sure of this.) My friend Otto is the person I have asked to take charge of my children's physical education, particularly during puberty (hence the nightshirt), should anything happen to me. By showing Otto in the dream with the symptoms of our generous benefactor, I apparently mean to say: "If anything happens to me, my children can expect as little from him as we could expect that night from Baron L., despite all his well-meant offers." The egotistical turn of the dream should now be clear.

But where is the wish-fulfillment? It does not lie in revenge on my friend Otto, whose fate seems to be ill treatment in my dreams, but in the following circumstance. In representing Otto in the dream as Baron L., I have at the same time identified myself with someone else, namely Professor R., for I have asked something of Otto just as R. asked something of Baron L. on the occasion I described. And that is the point. Professor R., somewhat as I have done, has made his way independently, outside the established academic schools, and only in later years received the title he had long since earned. So once again I am wishing to be a professor! The very phrase "in later years" is a wish-fulfillment, for it means I will live long enough to guide my boy through puberty myself.

In the first edition of this book I gave only a brief account of the other forms of typical dreams, because I lacked enough good material. My experience has since grown, and it now allows me to divide these dreams into two broad classes. The first class consists of dreams that really do have the same meaning every time. The second consists of dreams that must be given widely different interpretations despite having the same or similar content. Among typical dreams of the first kind, I will examine closely the examination dream and the so-called dream of dental irritation.

Everyone who has earned his diploma by passing the final examination at the end of secondary school complains of the relentlessness with which he is pursued by the anxiety dream that he will fail, that he must repeat his studies, and so on. For the holder of a university degree, this typical dream gives way to another, in which he must sit the examination for his doctorate. In his sleep he protests in vain that he has been practicing for years, that he is already a university lecturer or the head of a law firm. These are the indelible memories of the punishments we suffered as children for misdeeds we had committed. They were revived in us on that *dies irae, dies illa*, the "day of wrath, that dread day," of the severe examination at the two critical turning points in our studies. The "examination phobia" of neurotics is likewise reinforced by this childish fear. Once we have stopped being schoolboys, it is no longer our parents and guardians, as at first, or our teachers, as later, who see to our punishment; the inexorable chain of cause and effect in life has taken over our further education. Now we dream of the school-leaving examination or of the doctoral examination whenever we fear that some outcome will punish us for having left something undone or for having failed to accomplish something as we should. In short, we dream of them whenever we feel the weight of responsibility. And who has not lost heart before these tests, even if he was among the righteous?

I owe the real explanation of examination dreams to a remark by a knowledgeable colleague, who once stated in a scientific discussion that in his experience the examination dream occurs only to people who passed the examination, never to those who failed it. As is increasingly confirmed, the anxiety dream of the examination occurs when the dreamer faces some responsible undertaking the next day, with the possibility of disgrace. It has therefore probably chosen an occasion from the past when great anxiety proved unjustified and was refuted by the outcome. This would be a striking example of the waking mind misunderstanding the content of a dream. We take the objection raised in the dream as an indignant protest: "But I'm already a doctor," and so on. In reality it would be a consolation offered by the dream, amounting to this: "Don't be afraid of tomorrow. Think of how frightened you were before your final examination, and nothing came of it. You are a doctor this very minute." The fear that we attribute to the dream, however, comes from the residues of the day's experience.

The tests of this explanation that I have been able to make on myself and on others, though not numerous enough, have been entirely successful. I failed, for instance, my doctoral examination in forensic medicine, yet that subject has never once troubled me in my dreams. By contrast, I have often been examined in my dreams in botany, zoology, or chemistry, subjects in which I sat the examinations with well-founded anxiety but escaped punishment through the mercy of fortune or of the examiner. In my dreams of the school-leaving examination, I am regularly examined in history. I passed that subject brilliantly at the time, but only, I must admit, because my good-natured professor, the one-eyed benefactor of another dream, did not overlook the fact that on the list of questions I had crossed out the second of three, as a sign that he should not insist on it. One of my patients withdrew before his final school examinations and made them up later, but he failed the officer's examination and never became an officer. He tells me that he dreams of the first examination often enough but never of the second.

The colleague I mentioned, Dr. Stekel of Vienna, points to the double meaning of the word *Matura*, which names the school-leaving examination but also suggests "mature" or "ripe." He claims to have observed that examination dreams occur very often when a sexual test lies ahead the following day, in which case the disgrace the dreamer fears would be a display of weak potency. A German colleague objects to this, apparently with good reason, on the grounds that in Germany this examination is called the *Abiturium*, a word that lacks any such double meaning.

Dreams of missing a train deserve to be placed beside examination dreams because they leave a similar emotional impression, and their explanation confirms the kinship. They are dreams of consolation, directed against another fear felt in the dream: the fear of dying. "Departing" is one of the most common and most readily available symbols of death. The dream thus says, consolingly, "Calm yourself; you are not going to die (to depart)," just as the examination dream soothes us by saying, "Don't be afraid; nothing will happen to you this time either." What makes both kinds of dream hard to understand is that the feeling of anxiety is attached directly to the expression of consolation. Stekel treats the symbolism of death at length in his recently published book *Die Sprache des Traumes* (*The Language of Dreams*).

For a long time the meaning of "dreams of dental irritation," which I have had to analyze often enough in my patients, escaped me, because, to my great astonishment, their interpretation was blocked by resistances of altogether unusual strength.

Overwhelming evidence finally convinced me that, in men, the driving force behind these dreams is nothing other than the craving to masturbate that dates from puberty. I shall analyze two such dreams, one of which is also a "dream of flight." Both come from the same person, a young man with a strong homosexual disposition that he has, however, repressed in his waking life.

*He is watching a performance of* Fidelio *from the orchestra stalls of the opera house, seated next to L., a man whose personality he finds congenial and whose friendship he would like to win. Suddenly he flies diagonally clear across the stalls; then he puts his hand in his mouth and pulls out two of his teeth.*

He himself describes the flight by saying it was as if he had been "thrown" into the air. Because the opera was *Fidelio*, he recalls the poet's words:

"He who has won a charming wife——"

Yet winning a charming wife is not among the dreamer's wishes. Two other lines from the same poem would fit him better:

"He who has made the lucky (great) throw,
To be a friend of a friend...."

In the German, a stroke of great good fortune is literally a "great throw," and the dream contains exactly this lucky throw. It is not, however, simply the fulfillment of a wish. It also conceals the painful reflection that in his pursuit of friendship he has often had the misfortune to be "thrown down," together with the fear that the same fate may befall him with the young man beside whom he has enjoyed the performance of *Fidelio*. This is followed by a confession that deeply shames this refined dreamer: once, after being rejected in this way by a friend, his burning desire passed over into sexual excitement, and he masturbated twice in succession.

The second dream runs as follows: *Two university professors whom he knows are treating him in my place. One of them does something to his penis, and he fears an operation. The other thrusts an iron bar at his mouth, so that he loses two teeth. He is bound with four silk cloths.*

The sexual meaning of this dream can hardly be doubted. The silk cloths amount to an identification with a homosexual man of his acquaintance. The dreamer has never had intercourse with a woman, and has never actually sought sexual relations with men either; he imagines sexual intercourse on the model of the masturbation he was once taught during puberty.

I believe that the frequent variations on the typical dream of dental irritation, such as the one in which another person pulls the tooth from the dreamer's mouth, can be understood through the same explanation. It may nevertheless be hard to see how "dental irritation" could come to carry this meaning. Here I would point to a very common displacement from below to above. This displacement works in the service of sexual repression: through it, all sorts of sensations and intentions that arise in hysteria, and that ought to be played out in the genitals, can be carried out instead on less objectionable parts of the body. It is another instance of the same displacement when, in the symbolism of unconscious thought, the face stands in for the genitals. The resemblance of the buttocks to the cheeks assists this, as does the usage of language, which calls the inner folds of the female genitals "lips," since they resemble the lips that surround the opening of the mouth. The nose is compared to the penis in countless allusions, and in both regions the presence of hair completes the likeness. Only one feature of the anatomy, the teeth, lies entirely beyond any such comparison, and it is precisely this combination of likeness and unlikeness that makes the teeth suitable for representation under the pressure of sexual repression.

I do not claim that the interpretation of the dream of dental irritation as a dream of masturbation, whose correctness I cannot doubt, has been cleared of all obscurity. I carry the explanation as far as I can and must leave the rest unsolved. But I should also point to a further connection revealed by an idiom. In our country there is a vulgar expression for the act of masturbation: "to pull one out," or "to pull one down." I cannot say where these colloquialisms come from or what symbolism underlies them, but the teeth would fit very well with the first of the two.

Dreams of flying or floating, of falling, of swimming, and the like make up the second group of typical dreams. What do they mean? No general answer can be given. As we shall see, they mean something different in each case; only the sensory material they contain always comes from the same source.

The material gathered in psychoanalysis forces us to conclude that these dreams repeat impressions from childhood, and specifically that they refer to the games of motion that hold such an extraordinary attraction for children. What uncle has never made a child fly by running across the room with it in his outstretched arms, or played at falling with it by rocking it on his knee and then suddenly straightening his leg, or lifted it high in the air and then pretended to let go? Children shout with delight at this and tirelessly demand more, especially when a little fright and dizziness are part of the game. In later years they repeat the experience in dreams, but in the dream they leave out the hands that held them, so that they now float and fall freely. Every small child's fondness for games like rocking and seesawing is well known, and when children see acrobatic feats at the circus, the memory of that rocking is revived. In some boys the hysterical attack consists simply of reproducing such feats, which they perform with great skill. Not infrequently these games of motion, harmless as they are in themselves, arouse sexual sensations. To use a word current among us that covers all these matters, it is the "Hetzen," the wild romping and chasing of childhood, that dreams of flying, falling, dizziness, and the like repeat, and the pleasurable sensations of that play have now been turned into fear. But as every mother knows, children's wild play has often enough ended in quarrels and tears.

I therefore have good reason to reject the explanation that dreams of flying and falling are produced by the state of our skin sensations during sleep, by the sensations of the lungs' movement, and so on. I find that these very sensations have been reproduced from the memory the dream draws upon, and that they therefore belong to the dream's content, not to its sources.

This material, uniform in character and origin and consisting of sensations of motion, is then put to use in representing the most varied dream thoughts. Dreams of flying, which are for the most part marked by delight, call for the most widely different interpretations: quite individual ones for some people, and even interpretations of a typical kind for others. One of my patients used to dream very often that she was suspended above the street at a certain height, without touching the ground. She was very short, and she shrank from every kind of contamination that comes with contact among human beings. Her dream of floating fulfilled both of her wishes, by lifting her feet off the ground and by letting her head rise into the upper air. For other women the dream of flying expressed a longing: "If only I were a little bird." Still others become angels at night because no one calls them angels by day. The close association between flying and the idea of a bird makes it understandable that in men the dream of flying usually has a meaning of coarse sensuality. Nor shall we be surprised to hear that this or that dreamer is always very proud of his ability to fly.

Dr. Paul Federn of Vienna has put forward the striking theory that a great many flying dreams are erection dreams, since the remarkable phenomenon of erection, which occupies the human imagination so constantly, must impress upon it a strong sense of gravity being suspended (compare the winged phalluses of the ancients).

Dreams of falling are most often marked by fear. When women have them, their interpretation presents no difficulty, because women always accept the symbolic sense of falling, which is a roundabout way of describing yielding to an erotic temptation. Nor have we yet exhausted the childhood sources of the dream of falling. Nearly all children have fallen at some time and then been picked up and petted; if they fell out of bed at night, their nurse picked them up and took them into her own bed.

People who often dream of swimming, of cleaving through the waves with great enjoyment, and so on, have usually been bedwetters, and in the dream they repeat a pleasure they long ago learned to give up. We shall soon see, from one example or another, what kinds of representation dreams of swimming readily lend themselves to.

The interpretation of dreams about fire bears out a nursery prohibition that forbids children to play with matches so that they will not wet the bed at night. These dreams, too, rest on the memory of childhood bedwetting. In my *Fragment of an Analysis of a Case of Hysteria* (1905), I gave the complete analysis and synthesis of such a fire dream in connection with the dreamer's childhood history, and showed which emotions of her later years this childhood material had been used to represent.

A considerable number of other "typical" dreams could be cited, if by that term we mean the frequent recurrence of the same manifest content among different dreamers. Examples include dreams of passing through narrow alleys or walking through a long suite of rooms; dreams of the burglar at night, against whom nervous people take precautions before going to sleep; and dreams of being chased by wild animals, such as bulls or horses, or of being threatened with knives, daggers, and lances. The last two are characteristic of the manifest dream content of people suffering from anxiety. A study devoted specifically to this material would be well worth undertaking. In its place I have two remarks to offer, though they do not apply exclusively to typical dreams.

I. The more one works at solving dreams, the more readily one must acknowledge that most of the dreams of adults deal with sexual material and give expression to erotic wishes. Only someone who actually analyzes dreams, who works forward from their manifest content to the latent dream thoughts, can form a judgment on this question. Someone who is content merely to record the manifest content, as Näcke does in his writings on sexual dreams, cannot. We should recognize at once that this fact is not surprising, and that it agrees entirely with the basic assumptions of dream interpretation. No other impulse has had to undergo as much suppression since childhood as the sexual impulse in its many components, and from no other impulse have so many intense unconscious wishes survived, wishes that now act during sleep to produce dreams. In interpreting dreams, the importance of sexual complexes must never be forgotten; nor, of course, must it be exaggerated to the point of treating them as the only factor.

Careful interpretation shows that many dreams should even be read bisexually, in that they yield an irrefutable secondary interpretation in which they fulfill homosexual feelings, that is, feelings that are common to the dreamer's normal sexual activity. But the claim of W. Stekel and Alfred Adler that all dreams are to be interpreted bisexually seems to me a generalization as unprovable as it is improbable, and I would not wish to support it. Above all, I would not know how to account for the evident fact that many dreams satisfy needs other than erotic ones, even in the widest sense of that word: dreams of hunger, of thirst, of convenience, and so on. Similar assertions, that "behind every dream one finds the death sentence" (Stekel) and that every dream shows "a continuation from the feminine to the masculine line" (Adler), likewise seem to me to go far beyond what is permissible in the interpretation of dreams.

We have already stated elsewhere that conspicuously innocent dreams invariably embody coarse erotic wishes, and we could confirm this with many fresh examples. But many dreams that seem indifferent, and that no one would suspect of any special meaning, can be traced back after analysis to unmistakably sexual wishes, often of an unexpected kind. Who, for example, would suspect a sexual wish in the following dream before its interpretation had been worked out? The dreamer reports: *Between two stately palaces stands a little house, set back somewhat, whose doors are closed. My wife leads me a short way along the street to the little house and pushes the door open, and then I slip quickly and easily into the interior of a courtyard that slopes steeply upward.*

Anyone experienced in translating dreams will of course see at once that forcing one's way into narrow spaces and opening locked doors are among the commonest sexual symbols, and will readily find in this dream a representation of attempted intercourse from behind, between the two stately buttocks of the female body. The narrow, sloping passage is of course the vagina. The help attributed to the dreamer's wife must be interpreted to mean that in reality only consideration for his wife holds him back from such an attempt. Further inquiry revealed that on the previous day a young woman had joined the dreamer's household who had pleased him and who had given him the impression that she would not be altogether opposed to an advance of this kind. The little house between the two palaces comes from a memory of the Hradschin, the castle district of Prague, and so points once again to the young woman, who is a native of that city.

When I stress to my patients how frequent the Oedipus dream is, the dream of having sexual intercourse with one's mother, they answer, "I can't remember any such dream." Immediately afterward, however, the memory surfaces of some other disguised and indifferent dream that the patient has dreamed repeatedly, and analysis shows it to have this same content, which is to say that it is another Oedipus dream. I can assure the reader that veiled dreams of sexual intercourse with the mother are far more common than open ones.

There are dreams of scenery and places in which the dreamer always lays emphasis on the assurance, "I have been here before." In such cases the place is always the mother's genitals; there is indeed no other place of which one can assert with such certainty that one "has been there before."

A great many dreams, often full of fear, that involve passing through narrow spaces or being in water are based on fantasies about life in the womb, about the stay inside the mother's body, and about the act of birth. The following is the dream of a young man who, in fantasy, had already used his opportunity while still an embryo to spy on an act of intercourse between his parents.

*He is in a deep shaft with a window in it, as in the Semmering railway tunnel. At first he sees only empty countryside through this window; then he composes a picture into it, which appears at once and fills the empty space. The picture shows a field being thoroughly worked over by a harrow, and the delightful air, the accompanying idea of hard work, and the bluish-black clods of earth make a pleasant impression. He then goes on and sees an elementary school opened... and he is surprised that so much attention is paid in it to the sexual feelings of the child, which makes him think of me.*

*At her summer resort on the ... Lake, she throws herself into the dark water at a spot where the pale moon is reflected in it.*

Dreams of this kind are birth dreams. They are interpreted by reversing the fact reported in the manifest content: instead of "throwing oneself into the water," read "coming out of the water," that is, "being born." The place from which one is born can be identified if one recalls the vulgar sense of the French *la lune*, "the moon," which is slang for the backside. The pale moon thus becomes the white "bottom," the nursery *Popo*, which the child soon takes to be the place it came from. What, then, could it mean that the patient wishes to be born at her summer resort? I asked her this, and she answered without hesitation: "Hasn't the treatment made me feel as though I'd been born again?" The dream thus becomes an invitation to continue the treatment at the summer resort, that is, to visit her there. It perhaps also contains a very shy allusion to the wish to become a mother herself.

I take another birth dream, along with its interpretation, from the work of Ernest Jones. "She stood at the seashore watching a small boy, who seemed to be hers, wading into the water. He went on until the water covered him, and she could see only his head bobbing up and down near the surface. The scene then changed to the crowded lobby of a hotel. Her husband left her, and she 'entered into conversation with' a stranger." Analysis revealed that the second half of the dream represented running away from her husband and entering into intimate relations with a third person, behind whom Mr. X.'s brother, mentioned in an earlier dream, was plainly indicated. The first part of the dream was a fairly obvious birth fantasy. In dreams, as in mythology, the delivery of a child from the waters of the womb is commonly represented, through distortion, as the child's entry into water; the births of Adonis, Osiris, Moses, and Bacchus are well-known examples among many others. The bobbing of the head up and down in the water at once reminded the patient of the sensation of quickening, the first movements of the child, that she had felt during her only pregnancy. Thinking of the boy going into the water set off a reverie in which she saw herself taking him out of the water, carrying him into the nursery, washing and dressing him, and installing him in her household.

The second half of the dream, therefore, represents thoughts about the elopement, which belonged to the first half of the underlying latent content, while the first half of the dream corresponded to the second half of the latent content, the birth fantasy. Beyond this reversal of order, further inversions took place within each half of the dream. In the first half, the child entered the water and then his head bobbed; in the underlying dream thoughts, the quickening came first and only then did the child leave the water, which is a double inversion. In the second half of the dream, her husband left her; in the dream thoughts, she left her husband.

Abraham reports another birth dream, from a young woman awaiting her first delivery. From a spot in the floor of the house, an underground canal leads directly into the water (the birth passage, the amniotic fluid). She lifts a trapdoor in the floor, and at once a creature appears, dressed in brownish fur and looking almost like a seal. This creature turns into the dreamer's younger brother, toward whom she has always stood in a motherly relation.

Dreams of rescue are connected with birth dreams. When a woman dreams of saving someone, especially of saving someone from water, the act is equivalent to giving birth. When the dreamer is a man, however, this meaning is modified.

Robbers, nighttime burglars, and ghosts, which we fear before going to bed and which sometimes even disturb our sleep, all spring from one and the same childhood memory. They are the nocturnal visitors who woke the child to set it on the chamber pot so that it would not wet the bed, or who lifted the covers to see exactly where the child was keeping its hands while it slept. In analyzing several of these anxiety dreams, I have been able to draw out a precise recollection of the nighttime visitor. The robbers were always the father. The ghosts more probably corresponded to female figures in white nightgowns.

II. Once one has become familiar with the abundant use of symbolism to represent sexual material in dreams, one naturally asks whether many of these symbols might not appear once and for all with a fixed meaning, like the signs in shorthand. One is then tempted to compile a new dream book on the cipher method. On this point it should be noted that this symbolism does not belong to the dream in particular. It belongs to unconscious thinking, especially that of the common people, and it is found in more complete form in a nation's folklore, myths, legends, and figures of speech, in its proverbs and its current jokes, than in its dreams.

The dream makes use of this symbolism to give its latent thoughts a disguised representation. Among the symbols employed in this way there are, of course, many that regularly or almost regularly mean the same thing. But one must keep in mind the curious plasticity of psychic material. Now and then a symbol in the dream content has to be interpreted not symbolically but in its literal sense. At other times the dreamer, owing to some particular set of memories, may claim the right to use anything whatever as a sexual symbol, even something not ordinarily used that way. Nor are even the most frequently used sexual symbols unambiguous every time.

With these limitations and reservations in mind, I may point out the following. The emperor and empress, or the king and queen, in most cases really represent the dreamer's parents, and the dreamer is the prince or princess. All elongated objects, such as sticks, tree trunks, and umbrellas (the umbrella because of the way it is stretched open, which might be compared to an erection), and all long, sharp weapons, such as knives, daggers, and pikes, are meant to represent the male member. A frequent but not very intelligible symbol for the same thing is the nail file, perhaps on account of the rubbing and scraping. Small cases, boxes, caskets, cupboards, and stoves correspond to the female organ. The poet Uhland employed the symbolism of lock and key very gracefully in his song about Count Eberstein in order to make a common bawdy joke. A dream of walking through a row of rooms is a brothel or harem dream. Staircases, ladders, and flights of steps, or climbing on them, whether upward or downward, are symbolic representations of the sexual act. Smooth walls that one climbs over, and the façades of houses down which one lowers oneself, often in great anxiety, correspond to the upright human body, and in the dream they probably repeat memories of small children clambering up their parents or nurses. "Smooth" walls are men. In anxiety dreams one is often holding fast to some projection of a house. Tables, set tables, and boards are women, perhaps by a kind of contrast that does away with the contours of the body. Since "bed and board" (*mensa et thorus*) constitute marriage, the board is often put for the bed in dreams, and, as far as practicable, the complex of sexual ideas is transposed onto the complex of eating.

Among articles of clothing, a woman's hat can frequently be interpreted with certainty as the male genital. In men's dreams the necktie often appears as a symbol for the penis. This is not only because neckties hang down long and are characteristic of men, but also because one can choose them at will, a freedom that nature denies in the case of the original the symbol stands for. Men who use this symbol in their dreams are very extravagant with neckties and own regular collections of them. All complicated machines and apparatus in dreams are very probably genitals, and in describing them dream symbolism proves itself as tireless as wit. Likewise, many landscapes in dreams, especially those with bridges or wooded mountains, can readily be recognized as descriptions of the genitals. Finally, wherever one encounters incomprehensible coined words, one may suspect combinations of components that carry a sexual meaning. Children, too, often signify the genitals in dreams, since men and women are in the habit of fondly calling their genital organ their "little one." A very recent symbol of the male genital is the flying machine, whose use is justified by its connection with flying and occasionally by its shape. To play with a little child, or to beat a little one, is often the dream's representation of masturbation.

Stekel gives a number of other symbols, some of them not sufficiently verified, and illustrates them with examples. According to him, right and left in dreams are to be understood in an ethical sense. "The right-hand way always signifies the road to righteousness, the left the road to crime. Thus the left may signify homosexuality, incest, and perversion, while the right signifies marriage, relations with a prostitute, and so on. The meaning is always determined by the individual moral standpoint of the dreamer." Relatives in dreams generally play the part of genitals. Stekel interprets the inability to catch up with a carriage as regret at being unable to bridge a difference in age. The luggage one travels with is the burden of sin that weighs one down. Stekel also assigns a fixed symbolic meaning to numbers, which appear frequently in dreams, but these interpretations seem neither sufficiently verified nor generally valid, although in individual cases the interpretation can usually be recognized as probable. In a recently published book by W. Stekel, *Die Sprache des Traumes* (*The Language of the Dream*), which I was unable to make use of, there is a list of the most common sexual symbols intended to prove that all sexual symbols can be used bisexually. He writes: "Is there a symbol which (if the fantasy in any way permits it) may not be used simultaneously in both the masculine and the feminine sense?" The clause in parentheses, to be sure, removes much of the absoluteness of this assertion, for the fantasy does not at all permit it. I do not think it superfluous, however, to state that in my experience Stekel's general claim must give way to the recognition of a greater variety. Besides those symbols that stand just as often for the male as for the female genitals, there are others that predominantly or almost exclusively designate one of the sexes, and still others for which only the male or only the female meaning is known. The imagination does not, in fact, permit long, rigid objects and weapons to be used as symbols of the female genitals, or hollow objects such as chests, boxes, and pouches to be used as symbols of the male genitals.

It is true that the tendency of the dream and of unconscious fantasy to use sexual symbols bisexually betrays an archaic trait, for in childhood the difference between the genitals is unknown, and the same genitals are attributed to both sexes.

These very incomplete suggestions may be enough to encourage others to make a more careful collection.

I shall now add a few examples of how such symbolism is applied in dreams. They will show how impossible it becomes to interpret a dream without taking dream symbolism into account, and how insistently that symbolism forces itself upon us in many cases.

1. The hat as a symbol of the man, or of the male genital. This is a fragment from the dream of a young woman who suffered from agoraphobia owing to a fear of temptation.

"I am walking in the street in summer, wearing a straw hat of peculiar shape. Its middle piece is bent upward and its side pieces hang downward" (here the description faltered) "in such a way that one hangs lower than the other. I am cheerful and in a confident mood, and as I pass a group of young officers I think to myself: None of you can have any designs on me."

Since she could produce no associations to the hat, I said to her: "The hat is really a male genital, with its raised middle piece and its two side pieces hanging down." I deliberately refrained from interpreting the detail that the two side pieces hung down unequally, although it is precisely such individual particulars that lead the way to an interpretation. I went on to say that if she only had a man with so virile a genital, she would not need to fear the officers; that is, she would want nothing from them, since it is chiefly her fantasies of temptation that keep her from going out unprotected and unaccompanied. I had already been able to give her this last explanation of her fear several times on the basis of other material.

The way the dreamer behaved after this interpretation is quite remarkable. She withdrew her description of the hat and claimed that she had never said the two side pieces hung downward. I was, however, too sure of what I had heard to let myself be misled, and I held to it. She was silent for a while, and then found the courage to ask why one of her husband's testicles hung lower than the other, and whether this was so in all men. With that, the peculiar detail of the hat was explained, and she accepted the whole interpretation. The hat symbol was familiar to me long before the patient told me this dream. From other, less transparent cases, I believe that the hat may also be taken as a female genital.

2. The little one as the genital, and being run over as a symbol of sexual intercourse. This is another dream of the same agoraphobic patient.

"Her mother sends her little daughter away, so that the child must go alone. She rides with her mother to the railway and sees her little one walking straight along the tracks, so that she cannot avoid being run over. She hears the bones crack." (At this she feels discomfort but no real horror.) "She then looks out of the carriage window to see whether the parts can be seen behind. She then reproaches her mother for having let the little one go out alone."

Analysis. It is no easy matter to give a complete interpretation of this dream. It forms part of a cycle of dreams and can be fully understood only in connection with the others, for it is difficult to isolate enough of the necessary material to prove the symbolism. The patient first finds that the railway journey is to be interpreted historically, as an allusion to her departure from a sanatorium for nervous diseases, with whose superintendent she had, naturally, been in love. Her mother took her away from this place, and the physician came to the railway station and handed her a bouquet of flowers as she left. She felt uncomfortable because her mother witnessed this tribute. Here, therefore, the mother appears as a disturber of her love affairs, which was the part this strict woman had actually played during her daughter's girlhood.

Her next thought concerned the sentence: "She then looks to see whether the parts can be seen behind." Taking the dream's surface at face value, one would naturally think of the parts of the little daughter who had been run over and crushed. Her thought, however, turns in an entirely different direction. She recalls that she once saw her father naked from behind in the bathroom. She then begins to talk about the difference between the sexes and asserts that in a man the genitals can be seen from behind, but in a woman they cannot. In this connection she now offers the interpretation herself: the little one is the genital, and her little one (she has a four-year-old daughter) is her own genital. She reproaches her mother for wanting her to live as though she had no genital, and she recognizes this reproach in the dream's opening sentence, in which the mother sends her little one away so that it must go alone. In her fantasy, going alone in the street means having no man and no sexual relations (*coire*, to go together), and this she does not like. By all her accounts, she really did suffer as a girl from her mother's jealousy, because she showed a preference for her father.

Stekel has noted "the little one" as a symbol for the male or the female genitals, and in this he can point to a very widespread usage of language.

The deeper interpretation of this dream depends on another dream from the same night, in which the dreamer identifies herself with her brother. She had been a tomboy and was always being told that she should have been born a boy. This identification with her brother shows with particular clarity that "the little one" signifies the genital. The mother threatened him (that is, her) with castration, which could only be understood as a punishment for playing with the parts. The identification therefore shows that she herself had masturbated as a child, though she now retained this fact only in a memory concerning her brother. According to the evidence of this second dream, she must have acquired at that time an early knowledge of the male genital, which she later lost. The second dream also points to the infantile sexual theory that girls come from boys through castration. When I told her of this childish belief, she at once confirmed it with an anecdote in which a boy asks a girl, "Was it cut off?" and the girl answers, "No, it's always been like that."

The sending away of the little one, the genital, in the first dream therefore also refers to the threatened castration. Finally, she blames her mother for her not having been born a boy.

That being run over symbolizes sexual intercourse would not be evident from this dream if we were not certain of it from many other sources.

3. The genital represented by buildings, stairways, and shafts. This is the dream of a young man inhibited by a father complex.

"He is taking a walk with his father in a place that is surely the Prater, Vienna's great public park, for the Rotunda, the large domed exhibition hall, can be seen. In front of it stands a small annex to which a captive balloon is tethered, though the balloon seems quite collapsed. His father asks him what all this is for. He is surprised at the question but explains it to his father. They come into a courtyard in which a large sheet of tin is lying. His father wants to tear off a big piece of it, but first looks around to see whether anyone is watching. He tells his father that all he has to do is speak to the watchman, and then he can take as much as he wants without any further difficulty. From this courtyard a stairway leads down into a shaft, whose walls are softly upholstered, something like a leather wallet. At the end of this shaft there is a longer platform, and then a new shaft begins...."

Analysis. This dream comes from a type of patient that is unfavorable from a therapeutic point of view. Such patients go along with the analysis without offering any resistance whatever up to a certain point, but from that point on they remain almost inaccessible. He very nearly analyzed this dream himself. "The Rotunda," he said, "is my genital, and the captive balloon in front of it is my penis, about whose weakness I have worried." We must, however, interpret in greater detail. The Rotunda is the buttocks, which the child regularly associates with the genital, and the smaller annex in front is the scrotum. In the dream his father asks him what all this is for, that is, he asks about the purpose and arrangement of the genitals. It is quite evident that this situation should be reversed and that the son should be the one asking. Since no such questioning by the father ever took place in reality, we must understand the dream thought as a wish, or take it conditionally, as follows: "If only I had asked my father for sexual enlightenment." We shall soon find the continuation of this thought in another place.

The courtyard in which the sheet of tin lies spread out is not, in the first instance, to be understood symbolically; it comes from his father's place of business. For reasons of discretion I have substituted tin for another material in which the father deals, without otherwise changing anything in the wording of the dream. The dreamer had entered his father's business and had taken a violent dislike to the questionable practices on which its profits chiefly depend. Hence the continuation of the dream thought above ("If only I had asked him") would be: "He would have cheated me just as he cheats his customers." For the tearing off, which represents commercial dishonesty, the dreamer himself supplies a second explanation, namely masturbation. This meaning is not only entirely familiar to us; it also fits very well with the fact that the secrecy of masturbation is expressed by its opposite ("Why, one can do it quite openly"). It agrees entirely with our expectations, moreover, that the masturbatory activity is once again shifted onto the father, just as the questioning was in the first scene of the dream. He at once interprets the shaft as the vagina, pointing to the soft upholstery of its walls.

That intercourse in the vagina should be described as a going *down*, rather than in the usual way as a going *up*, is something I have also found to hold true in other cases.

The dreamer himself supplies a biographical explanation for the details that at the end of the first shaft there is a longer platform, and then a new shaft. For some time he had had sexual relations with women, but had then given them up because of inhibitions, and he now hopes the treatment will allow him to take them up again. Toward the end, however, the dream grows indistinct, and to the experienced interpreter it becomes evident that in the second scene the influence of another subject has begun to assert itself. In this scene his father's business and its dishonest practices come to signify the first vagina, represented as a shaft, so that one might suspect a reference to the mother.

4. The male genital symbolized by persons, and the female by a landscape.

(The dream of a working-class woman whose husband is a policeman, reported by B. Dattner.)

... Then someone broke into the house, and she anxiously called for a policeman. But he went, by mutual agreement, with two tramps into a church, which was reached by a great many steps. Behind the church there was a mountain, and on top of it a dense forest. The policeman wore a helmet, a gorget, and a cloak. The two vagrants, who went along with the policeman quite peaceably, had sack-like aprons tied around their loins. A road led from the church to the mountain. On either side it was overgrown with grass and brushwood, which grew thicker and thicker as the road climbed toward the summit, where it spread out into a real forest.

5. A stairway dream.

(Reported and interpreted by Otto Rank.)

For the following transparent dream of nocturnal emission, I am indebted to the same colleague who supplied the dental-stimulus dream reported earlier.

"I am running down the staircase of an apartment house after a little girl whom I want to punish because she has done something to me. At the bottom of the stairs someone held the child for me. (A grown woman?) I seize hold of her, but I do not know whether I have struck her, for I suddenly find myself in the middle of the staircase, where I have intercourse with the child (in the air, as it were). It is not really intercourse; I only rub my genital against her external genital, and as I do so I see it very distinctly, as distinctly as I see her head, which is lying to one side. During the sexual act I see, hanging to my left and above me (also as if in the air), two small pictures, landscapes, showing a house on a green. On the smaller one my surname stood where the painter's signature should have been; it seemed to be meant as a birthday present for me. A small sign hung in front of the pictures, announcing that cheaper pictures could also be had. Then I see myself, very indistinctly, lying in bed, just as I had seen myself at the foot of the stairs, and I am awakened by a sensation of wetness caused by the emission."

Interpretation. On the evening of the dream day, the dreamer had been in a bookshop, where, while he waited, he looked at some pictures on display whose subjects resembled those of the dream pictures. He stepped closer to one small picture that particularly appealed to him in order to see the artist's name, which, however, turned out to be entirely unknown to him.

Later that same evening, in company, he heard about a Bohemian servant girl who boasted that her illegitimate child "was made on the stairs." The dreamer asked for the details of this unusual event and learned that the girl had gone with her lover to her parents' home, where there was no opportunity for sexual relations, and that the aroused man had performed the act on the staircase. Playing on the sly saying about wine adulterers, who are said to grow their wine not in the vineyard but in the cellar, the dreamer remarked, "The child really grew on the cellar steps."

These experiences of the day, which are quite prominent in the dream content, the dreamer readily recalled. But he just as readily recalled an old fragment of childhood memory that the dream had also put to use. The apartment house with the staircase was the house in which he had spent most of his childhood, and in which he had first become acquainted with sexual questions. In this house, among other things, he used to slide down the banister astride, and this aroused him sexually. In the dream, too, he comes down the stairs very quickly, so quickly that, as he distinctly insisted, he hardly touched the individual steps but rather "flew" or "slid down," as we used to say. When this childhood experience is taken into account, the opening of the dream appears to represent the element of sexual excitement. In the same house and in the residence next door, the dreamer used to play rough, combative games with the neighborhood children, in which he gratified himself just as he does in the dream.

If one recalls Freud's finding, from his investigation of sexual symbolism, that in dreams stairs or the climbing of stairs almost invariably symbolizes intercourse, the dream becomes clear. Both its driving force and its effect, as the emission shows, are purely libidinal. Sexual excitement was aroused during sleep, represented in the dream by the rapid running or sliding down the stairs, and the sadistic strand within it, rooted in the combative play of childhood, is indicated by the pursuit and overpowering of the child. The libidinal excitement intensifies and presses toward sexual action, represented in the dream by seizing the child and carrying her to the middle of the staircase. Up to this point the dream would be one of pure sexual symbolism, and would remain obscure to the inexperienced interpreter. But this symbolic gratification, which would have guaranteed undisturbed sleep, was not enough for so powerful a libidinal excitement. The excitement leads to orgasm, and with that the whole stairway symbolism is unmasked as a substitute for intercourse. Freud emphasizes the rhythmic character of both activities as one of the reasons the stairway lends itself to sexual symbolism, and this dream seems especially to confirm the point, for the dreamer expressly stated that the rhythm of a sexual act was the most pronounced feature of the entire dream.

One further remark concerns the two pictures. Apart from their literal meaning, they also carry the value of *Weibsbilder*, a German word that literally means "woman-pictures" but in everyday speech simply means "women." This is shown at once by the fact that the dream presents a large picture and a small one, just as its content presents a large (grown) girl and a little one. That cheaper pictures could also be had points to the prostitution complex, while the dreamer's surname on the small picture, and the thought that it was meant for his birthday, point to the parental complex: to be born on the stairway means to be conceived in intercourse.

The indistinct final scene, in which the dreamer sees himself lying in bed on the landing and feeling wet, seems to reach back into childhood even beyond infantile masturbation, and plainly has its prototype in similarly pleasurable episodes of bed-wetting.

6. A modified stair dream.

One of my patients, a man with severe nervous symptoms, was living in sexual abstinence; his fantasy was fixed on his mother, and he repeatedly dreamed of climbing stairs in her company. I once remarked to him that moderate masturbation would do him less harm than enforced abstinence. This suggestion provoked the following dream:

"His piano teacher reproaches him for neglecting his playing, and for not practicing the *Études* of Moscheles and Clementi's *Gradus ad Parnassum*." In connection with this he remarked that the *Gradus*, whose title means "steps to Parnassus," is simply a stairway, and that the piano itself is a stairway too, since it has a scale.

It is fair to say that there is no series of associations that cannot be adapted to represent sexual facts.

I conclude with the dream of a chemist, a young man who had been trying to give up his habit of masturbation by replacing it with intercourse with women.

Preliminary statement. On the day before the dream he had instructed a student in Grignard's reaction, in which magnesium is dissolved in absolutely pure ether with iodine acting as a catalyst. Two days earlier there had been an explosion during the same reaction, and the person conducting it had burned his hand.

Dream I. He is supposed to prepare phenylmagnesium bromide. He sees the apparatus with particular clarity, but he has put himself in place of the magnesium. He is now in a curious swaying posture. He keeps repeating to himself, "This is the right thing, it is working, my feet are beginning to dissolve and my knees are getting soft." Then he reaches down and feels for his feet, and meanwhile (he does not know how) he takes his legs out of the crucible, and again says to himself, "That cannot be.... Yes, it must be so, it has been done correctly." Then he half wakes and repeats the dream to himself, because he wants to tell it to me. He is distinctly afraid of having the dream analyzed. In this half-sleeping state he is greatly agitated, and keeps repeating, "Phenyl, phenyl."

II. He is in ...ing with his whole family, at half past eleven. He is supposed to be at the Schottentor for a rendezvous with a certain lady, but he does not wake up until half past eleven. He says to himself, "It's too late now; by the time you get there it will be half past twelve." The next moment he sees the whole family gathered around the table, his mother and the servant girl with the soup tureen standing out with particular clarity. Then he says to himself, "Well, if we're already eating, I certainly can't get away."

Analysis. He is sure that even the first dream contains a reference to the lady he is to meet at the rendezvous, for he dreamed it the night before the expected meeting. The student he had been instructing is a particularly disagreeable fellow. He had said to the chemist, "That isn't right," because the magnesium was still unaffected, and the chemist had answered as though he did not care in the least: "It certainly isn't right." The dreamer himself must be this student; he is as indifferent toward his analysis as the student is toward his synthesis. The "he" in the dream who carries out the operation, however, is me. How disagreeable he must seem to me with his indifference toward the result!

Moreover, he is the material on which the analysis (or synthesis) is performed, for what is at stake is the success of the treatment. The legs in the dream recall an impression from the previous evening. At a dancing lesson he had met a lady whom he wished to conquer, and he pressed her to him so tightly that at one point she cried out. When he stopped pressing against her legs, he felt her answering pressure, firm against his lower thighs up to just above the knees, the very spot mentioned in the dream. In this situation, then, the woman is the magnesium in the retort, which is at last beginning to work. He is feminine toward me, as he is masculine toward the woman. If it works with the woman, the treatment will work too. Feeling and becoming aware of himself in the region of his knees refers to masturbation and corresponds to his fatigue of the day before.... The rendezvous had in fact been set for half past eleven. His wish to oversleep and remain with his usual sexual objects, that is, with masturbation, corresponds to his resistance.

On the repetition of the name *phenyl*, he offers the following thoughts. All these radicals ending in *-yl* have always pleased him; they are very convenient to use: benzyl, acetyl, and so on. That, however, explained nothing. But when I proposed the radical *Schlemihl*, the German and Yiddish word for a hapless, ill-starred bungler, he laughed heartily and told me that during the summer he had read a book by Prévost containing a chapter titled "Les exclus de l'amour" ("Those Shut Out from Love"). Its descriptions had made him think of the schlemihls, and he added, "That is my case." He would once again have played the schlemihl if he had missed the rendezvous.

## VI The Dream-Work

Every earlier attempt to solve the problems of the dream has worked directly from the manifest dream content, the dream as it is retained in memory. These attempts either tried to draw an interpretation of the dream from that content or, when they gave up on interpretation, based their judgment of the dream on whatever evidence the content supplied. We alone have new data at our disposal. For us, a new body of psychic material stands between the dream content and the results of our investigation: the latent dream content, or dream thoughts, which our method brings to light. We arrive at the solution of a dream from these latent thoughts, not from the manifest content. This also confronts us with a problem that has never before existed. We must examine and trace the relations between the latent dream thoughts and the manifest dream content, and the processes by which the one has grown into the other.

We regard the dream thoughts and the dream content as two renderings of the same meaning in two different languages. More precisely, the dream content appears to us as a translation of the dream thoughts into another mode of expression, whose signs and rules of composition we must learn by comparing the original with the translation. The dream thoughts are intelligible to us the moment we have uncovered them. The dream content, by contrast, is written in a kind of picture-script, and its signs must be translated one by one into the language of the dream thoughts.

It would be a mistake, of course, to read these signs according to their value as pictures rather than their meaning as signs. Suppose I have before me a picture-puzzle, a rebus: a house with a boat on its roof, then a running figure whose head has been struck off by an apostrophe to show that a letter is to be dropped, and so on. As a critic, I might be tempted to call this composition and its parts nonsense. A boat does not belong on the roof of a house, and a man without a head cannot run. The man is also larger than the house, and if the whole is meant to depict a scene from nature, the scattered letters of the alphabet have no place in it, since letters do not occur in nature. I can judge the puzzle correctly only if I raise no such objections to the whole or its parts and instead take pains to replace each picture with the syllable or word it can stand for through some kind of reference. The words brought together in this way are no longer meaningless; they may form a phrase of great beauty and sense. The dream is a picture-puzzle of exactly this kind, and our predecessors in dream interpretation made the mistake of judging the rebus as an artistic composition. Judged that way, it appears nonsensical and worthless.

### (a) The Condensation Work

The first thing an investigator notices when comparing the dream content with the dream thoughts is that an enormous work of condensation has taken place. Next to the range and abundance of the dream thoughts, the dream is terse, meager, and laconic. Written down, a dream may fill half a page, while the analysis that contains its dream thoughts needs six, eight, or twelve times as much space. The ratio varies from dream to dream, but as far as I have been able to observe, its essential meaning never changes. As a rule, the extent of the compression is underestimated, because the dream thoughts that have been brought to light are taken for the complete material, whereas further interpretation may reveal new thoughts concealed behind the dream. We have already noted that one can never be certain of having interpreted a dream completely. Even when a solution seems satisfying and flawless, it always remains possible that the same dream expresses a further meaning. Strictly speaking, then, the amount of condensation cannot be determined.

An objection that seems quite plausible at first might be raised against the claim that the disproportion between dream content and dream thoughts justifies the conclusion that psychic material is heavily condensed in the formation of dreams. We so often have the impression of having dreamed a great deal during the night and then forgotten most of it. On this view, the dream we remember on waking would be only a remnant of the whole dream-work, and if we could recall that work completely, it might well match the dream thoughts in extent. This is partly true. There is no mistaking the observation that a dream is reproduced most accurately when one tries to recall it immediately on waking, and that the memory of it grows more and more defective as the day wears on toward evening. On the other hand, the impression that we have dreamed a good deal more than we can reproduce often rests on an illusion, whose cause will be explained later. Moreover, the possibility of forgetting does not affect the case for condensation in dream activity, since that case is proved by the groups of ideas belonging to the very parts of the dream that have remained in memory. If a large part of the dream really has been lost to memory, we have probably lost access to a new series of dream thoughts. It is entirely unjustified to expect that the lost portions of the dream relate only to the thoughts we already know from analyzing the portions that survive.

Because analysis yields so many ideas for each individual element of the dream content, many readers will chiefly doubt whether it is legitimate to count everything that comes to mind afterward, during analysis, as part of the dream thoughts. Can we really assume that all these thoughts were active during sleep and took part in forming the dream? Is it not more likely that some connections of thought develop in the course of analysis that played no part in forming the dream? I can meet this doubt only conditionally. It is true that particular connections of thought first arise during analysis. But one can always be sure that such new connections have been made only between thoughts already linked in the dream thoughts by other means. The new connections are, so to speak, corollaries or short circuits, made possible by the existence of other, more fundamental links. It must be granted that the great number of trains of thought revealed by analysis were already active in forming the dream. For when one has worked through a chain of thoughts that seems to have no bearing on the dream's formation, one suddenly comes upon a thought that is represented in the dream and indispensable to its interpretation, yet cannot be reached except through that very chain. The reader may turn here to the dream of the botanical monograph, which is plainly the product of an astonishing feat of condensation, even though I have not given its complete analysis.

How, then, are we to picture the psychic condition during sleep that precedes dreaming? Do all the dream thoughts exist side by side, or do they occur one after another? Or are several trains of thought built up simultaneously from different centers, meeting later on? In my opinion, it is not yet necessary to form a concrete picture of the psychic state in which dreams are formed. Only let us not forget that we are dealing with unconscious thought, and that the process may well differ from the one we observe in ourselves when we reflect deliberately and consciously.

That dream formation rests on a process of condensation, however, is beyond doubt. How is this condensation brought about?

When we consider that only a small fraction of the dream thoughts we discover are represented in the dream by any of its ideational elements, we might conclude that condensation works by omission. On this view, the dream is not a faithful translation or a point-by-point projection of the dream thoughts, but a very incomplete and defective reproduction of them. As we shall soon see, this view is quite inadequate. But let us take it as a starting point for now and ask: if only a few elements of the dream thoughts make their way into the dream content, what conditions determine which ones are chosen?

To shed light on this question, let us look at the elements of the dream content that must have met the conditions we are seeking. A dream formed under especially strong condensation will be the most suitable material for this inquiry. I select the dream of the botanical monograph, cited earlier.

Dream content: I have written a monograph on a certain plant (the identity of which remains obscure). The book lies before me, and I am just turning over a folded colored plate. Bound into every copy is a dried specimen of the plant, as though taken from a herbarium.

The most prominent element of this dream is the botanical monograph. It comes from impressions received on the day of the dream: I had actually seen a monograph on the genus "cyclamen" in a bookshop window. The genus itself is missing from the dream content, in which only the monograph and its connection with botany remain. The "botanical monograph" immediately reveals its relation to the work on cocaine I had once written. From cocaine, connections of thought lead on the one hand to a *Festschrift*, a commemorative volume of essays, and on the other to my friend the eye specialist Dr. Koenigstein, who had a share in putting cocaine to practical use. With the figure of Dr. Koenigstein is also linked the memory of an interrupted conversation I had with him the previous evening, and of my many thoughts about payment for medical services among colleagues. This conversation is the true stimulus of the dream. The monograph on cyclamen is likewise a recent impression, but an indifferent one. As I soon see, the "botanical monograph" of the dream turns out to be a common middle term between the two experiences of the day. It was taken over unchanged from the indifferent impression and bound to the psychologically significant experience through a wealth of associations.

Not only the combined idea "botanical monograph," but each of its separate elements, "botanical" and "monograph," leads deeper and deeper into the tangled web of the dream thoughts. To "botanical" belong memories of Professor Gartner (in German, *Gärtner* means gardener), of his blooming wife, of my patient whose name is Flora, and of a lady about whom I told the story of the forgotten flowers. Gartner, in turn, is connected with the laboratory and with the conversation with Koenigstein, and the mention of the two women patients belongs to that same conversation. A chain of thoughts, one end of which is the title of the hastily glimpsed monograph, leads in the other direction from the lady with the flowers to my wife's favorite flowers. Beyond this, "botanical" recalls not only an episode from my years at the Gymnasium, the classical secondary school, but also an examination I took at the university. A new subject, my hobbies, which came up in the same conversation, is linked to the chain of thoughts proceeding from the forgotten flowers through what I jokingly call my favorite flower, the artichoke. Behind "artichoke" lies, on the one hand, a memory of Italy, and on the other a childhood scene in which my relationship with books, since grown so intimate, first began. "Botanical," then, is a true nucleus, the point in the dream where many trains of thought converge, and I can assure the reader that these trains of thought were rightly and fairly brought into relation with one another in the conversation I have mentioned. We find ourselves here in a factory of thought, where, as in the "Weaver's Masterpiece":

"One tread moves thousands of threads,
The little shuttles fly back and forth,
The threads flow on unseen,
One stroke ties thousands of knots."

"Monograph" in the dream, for its part, bears on two subjects: the one-sidedness of my studies and the costliness of my hobbies.

This first investigation suggests that the elements "botanical" and "monograph" were admitted into the dream content because they could show the most extensive connections with the dream thoughts. They form nuclei where a great many dream thoughts converge, and they carry multiple meanings for the dream's interpretation. The fact underlying this explanation can be stated in another form: every element of the dream content turns out to be *over-determined*, which is to say that it is represented many times over in the dream thoughts.

We shall learn more by testing the remaining parts of the dream to see where they occur in the dream thoughts. The colored plate, as the earlier analysis showed, refers to a new subject, the criticism my work received from colleagues, as well as to a subject already represented in the dream, my hobbies, and also to a childhood memory in which I tear apart a book with colored plates. The dried specimen of the plant relates to an experience at the Gymnasium that centered on, and gave special emphasis to, the herbarium.

I can now see what kind of relation exists between dream content and dream thoughts. Not only are the elements of the dream determined many times over in the dream thoughts; each individual dream thought is also represented in the dream by several elements. The path of association leads from one element of the dream to a number of dream thoughts, and from one dream thought to several elements of the dream. Dream formation therefore does not proceed by having a single dream thought, or a group of them, supply the dream content with an abridged representative of itself, and then having another dream thought supply another abridged representative, much as members of a legislature are elected one by one by separate constituencies. Instead, the whole mass of dream thoughts undergoes a kind of working-over, in the course of which the elements that receive the strongest and broadest support stand out in relief. This is perhaps comparable to election by *scrutin de liste*, the French system in which voters cast their ballots for an entire slate of candidates rather than for a single representative of their own district. Whatever dream I take apart in this way, I always find the same basic principle confirmed: the dream elements are built from the entire mass of the dream thoughts, and each of them, in relation to the dream thoughts, proves to be determined many times over.

It is certainly not out of place to demonstrate this relation between dream content and dream thoughts with a fresh example, one distinguished by an especially artful interweaving of mutual relations. The dream belongs to a patient I am treating for claustrophobia, the fear of enclosed spaces. It will soon become clear why I feel obliged to give this exceptionally intellectual piece of dream activity the following title:

II. "A Beautiful Dream"

The dreamer is riding with a large company to X Street, where there is a modest roadside inn (which is not actually the case). A play is being performed in its rooms. He is first a spectator, then an actor. Finally the company is told to change their clothes so that they can return to the city. Some of the people are assigned rooms on the ground floor, others rooms on the floor above. Then a quarrel breaks out. Those upstairs are angry because those below have not yet finished, so they cannot come down. His brother is upstairs, he himself is below, and he is angry at his brother because of the crowding. (This part is obscure.) Besides, it was settled on their arrival who would be upstairs and who below. Then he walks alone up the slope along which X Street runs toward the city, and he walks with such difficulty and strain that he cannot move from the spot. An elderly gentleman joins him and grumbles about the King of Italy. Finally, toward the top of the slope, walking becomes much easier.

The difficulty in walking was so vivid that for some time after waking the dreamer was unsure whether it had been a dream or reality.

Judged by its manifest content, this dream hardly deserves praise. Contrary to the usual rules, I shall begin with the part the dreamer described as the most distinct.

The difficulty dreamed of, and probably actually felt during the dream, was a labored climb accompanied by shortness of breath. This was one of the symptoms the patient had in fact shown years earlier, and together with other symptoms it had been attributed at the time to tuberculosis, which he was probably simulating hysterically. We already know this sensation of being hindered, so characteristic of dreams, from the exhibition dreams, and here again we find it put to use as a ready-made material for representing anything at all. The part of the dream content in which the climb is hard at first and becomes easier near the top of the hill made me think, as I listened, of the well-known and masterly opening of Alphonse Daudet's *Sappho*. There a young man carries the girl he loves up a staircase. At first she is as light as a feather, but the higher he climbs, the more heavily she weighs on his arms. The scene symbolizes the course of events through which Daudet means to warn young men against squandering serious affection on girls of humble birth or questionable past. I knew that my patient had recently had a love affair with an actress and had broken it off, but I did not expect the interpretation that had occurred to me to prove correct. Moreover, the situation in *Sappho* was the reverse of the one in the dream.
