In the dream the climb was hard at first and easy later on, whereas in the novel the symbolism works only if what seemed easy at first turns out in the end to be a heavy burden. To my astonishment, the patient remarked that the interpretation closely matched the plot of a play he had seen at the theater the evening before. The play was called *Round about Vienna*, and it followed the career of a girl who is respectable at first but later drifts into the demi-monde, the shadowy world of kept women and courtesans. She has affairs with men in high places and so "climbs," but in the end she "goes down" faster and faster. This play had reminded him of another, called *From Step to Step*, whose advertisement showed a staircase of several steps.

To continue the interpretation: the actress with whom he had had his most recent, and complicated, affair had lived on X Street. There is no inn on that street. However, while he was spending part of the summer in Vienna on the lady's account, he had put up at a small hotel nearby; the German word is *abgestiegen*, meaning "stopped at," but literally "stepped down." As he was leaving the hotel, he said to the cab driver, "At least I didn't pick up any vermin," which, incidentally, is one of his phobias. The driver replied, "How could anyone stay there! It isn't a hotel at all, it's really nothing but a roadside inn!"

The roadside inn immediately calls a quotation to the dreamer's mind:

"Of that marvellous host
I was once a guest."

But the host in Uhland's poem is an apple tree. A second quotation now carries the train of thought further:

Faust (dancing with the young witch):

"A lovely dream once came to me;
I then beheld an apple tree,
And there two fairest apples shone:
They lured me so, I climbed thereon."

The Fair One:

"Apples have been desired by you,
Since first in Paradise they grew;
And I am moved with joy to know
That such within my garden grow."

(Translated by Bayard Taylor.)

There is not the slightest doubt about what the apple tree and the apples mean. A beautiful bosom ranked high among the charms with which the actress had bewitched our dreamer.

The connections uncovered by the analysis gave us every reason to suppose that the dream reached back to an impression from childhood. In this case it must refer to the patient's nurse; the patient is now a man of nearly fifty. For a child, the nurse's bosom is in truth a roadside inn. The nurse, like Daudet's Sappho, appears as an allusion to the mistress he had abandoned.

The patient's elder brother also appears in the dream content. He is upstairs, and the dreamer himself is below. This again is an inversion, for the brother, as I happen to know, has lost his social standing, while my patient has kept his. In reporting the dream, the dreamer avoided saying outright that his brother was upstairs and he himself below. That would have been too frank, since a person is said to be "down and out" when he has lost his fortune and position. The fact that something is shown inverted at this point in the dream must have a meaning. The inversion must apply instead to some other relation between the dream thoughts and the dream content, and there is a clue to how it should be taken. It plainly applies to the end of the dream, where the circumstances of the climb are the reverse of those in *Sappho*. It is now easy to see which inversion is meant. In *Sappho*, the man carries the woman with whom he has a sexual relationship. In the dream thoughts, conversely, a woman carries a man, and since this can happen only in childhood, the reference is once again to the nurse carrying the heavy child. The final part of the dream thus manages to represent Sappho and the nurse in a single allusion.

Just as the poet did not choose the name Sappho without reference to the sexual customs associated with her island of Lesbos, so the elements of the dream in which people act above and below point to sexual fantasies that occupy the dreamer, and which, as repressed cravings, are not unconnected with his neurosis. Dream interpretation by itself does not show that these are fantasies rather than memories of actual events. It only supplies us with a set of thoughts and leaves us to judge their value as realities. Real and imagined events at first appear here as equally valid, and not only here but also in the creation of psychic structures more important than dreams. A large company, as we already know, signifies a secret. The brother is nothing other than a stand-in, drawn back into the childhood scene by "fancying backwards," for all the later rivals for the woman's favor. By way of an experience indifferent in itself, the episode of the gentleman grumbling about the King of Italy again refers to the intrusion of people of low rank into aristocratic society. It is as though the warning Daudet gives to young men were to be supplemented by a similar warning addressed to the infant at the breast.

To provide a third example for studying condensation in dream formation, I will cite the partial analysis of a dream from an elderly woman who is undergoing psychoanalytic treatment. In keeping with the severe anxiety from which she suffered, her dreams contained an abundance of sexual thought material, and discovering it both astonished and frightened her. Because I cannot carry the interpretation to completion, the material seems to fall apart into several groups with no apparent connection.

III. Content of the dream: *She remembers that she has two June bugs in a box, which she must set at liberty, for otherwise they will suffocate. She opens the box, and the bugs are quite exhausted; one of them flies out of the window, but the other is crushed on the casement while she is shutting the window, as someone or other asks her to do* (expressions of disgust).

Analysis: Her husband is away traveling, and her fourteen-year-old daughter is sleeping in the bed next to hers. In the evening the girl points out that a moth has fallen into her glass of water, but she neglects to take it out, and in the morning she feels sorry for the poor little creature. A story she had read that evening told of boys throwing a cat into boiling water and described the animal's twitching. These are the occasions for the dream, and both are indifferent in themselves. She is further preoccupied with the subject of cruelty to animals. Years before, while the family was spending the summer at a certain place, her daughter had been very cruel to animals. The girl started a butterfly collection and asked her mother for arsenic to kill the butterflies. Once a moth flew about the room for a long time with a pin through its body; on another occasion she found that some moths kept to observe their metamorphosis had starved to death. When she was still very young, the same child used to pull the wings off beetles and butterflies. Now she would shrink in horror from such cruelty, for she has grown very kind.

This contrast occupies the patient's mind. It recalls another contrast, the one between appearance and disposition that George Eliot describes in *Adam Bede*. There a beautiful but vain and quite stupid girl is set beside a plain but high-minded one, and the aristocrat who seduces the little goose is set against the working man who feels like an aristocrat and behaves like one. It is impossible to judge character by appearance. Who could tell from her looks that she is tormented by sensual desires?

In the same year the girl started her butterfly collection, the region where they were staying was plagued by June bugs. The children wreaked havoc among the bugs and crushed them cruelly. At that time she saw a person who tore the wings off June bugs and ate them. She herself had been born in June and had also married in June. Three days after the wedding she wrote a letter home describing how happy she was. But she was by no means happy.

On the evening before the dream she had rummaged through her old letters and read several of them, comic and serious, aloud to her family. Among them was an extremely ridiculous letter from a piano teacher who had courted her when she was a girl, as well as one from an aristocratic admirer.

She blames herself because a bad book by Maupassant had fallen into the hands of one of her daughters. The arsenic her little girl asked for recalls the arsenic pills that restored the vigor of youth to the Duc de Mora in Daudet's *Le Nabab*. "Set at liberty" recalls a passage from *The Magic Flute*:

"I cannot compel you to love,
But I will not give you your liberty."

"June bugs" suggests Katie's words:

"I love you like a little beetle."

And in between comes the line from *Tannhäuser*: "For you are wrought with evil passion."

She lives in fear and anxiety about her absent husband. The dread that something may happen to him on his journey finds expression in numerous daytime fantasies. A short while earlier, during the analysis, she had come upon a complaint about his "senility" in her unconscious thoughts. The wish this dream conceals can perhaps best be guessed if I mention that several days before the dream she was suddenly astounded, in the middle of her work, by a command she found herself addressing to her husband: "Go hang yourself." It turned out that a few hours earlier she had read somewhere that hanging induces a vigorous erection. It was the wish for an erection that had broken free of repression in this terrifying, veiled form. "Go hang yourself" amounts to saying: "Get an erection, at any cost." Dr. Jenkins's arsenic pills in *Le Nabab* belong in this context, for the patient knew that the strongest aphrodisiac, cantharides, is prepared by crushing beetles, the so-called Spanish flies. The most important part of the dream content carries this meaning.

Opening and shutting the window is the subject of a standing quarrel with her husband. She likes to sleep with plenty of fresh air, and he does not. Exhaustion is the chief complaint she has these days.

In all three of the dreams just cited, I have marked with italics the phrases in which an element of the dream recurs in the dream thoughts, so as to make the manifold references of that element plain. Since the analysis of none of these dreams has been carried to completion, however, it is well worth examining a dream with a fully detailed analysis in order to demonstrate the manifold determination of its content. For this purpose I choose the dream of Irma's injection. This example will show without much effort that the work of condensation has used more than one means in forming the dream.

The chief figure in the dream content is my patient Irma, who appears with the features she has in waking life and who therefore, in the first instance, represents herself. But her posture as I examine her at the window is taken from the memory of another person, the woman for whom, as the dream thoughts show, I would like to exchange my patient. Insofar as Irma shows a diphtheritic membrane, which recalls my anxiety about my eldest daughter, she comes to represent that child of mine, and behind her is concealed the patient who died of poisoning and who is linked to my daughter by sharing her name. As the dream proceeds, the significance of Irma's personality changes, though her image as seen in the dream does not; she becomes one of the children we examine in the public clinics for children's diseases, where my friends reveal the difference in their mental abilities. This transfer was evidently brought about through the idea of my infant daughter. Through her reluctance to open her mouth, the same Irma is turned into an allusion to another woman I once examined, and beyond that to my wife, in the same connection. Furthermore, in the diseased changes I discover in her throat, I have gathered allusions to a great many other people.

None of the people I encounter as I follow the associations suggested by "Irma" appear in person in the dream. They are concealed behind the dream figure "Irma," who thus develops into a collective image, endowed, as one might expect, with contradictory features. Irma comes to represent these other people, who are discarded in the work of condensation, because I make happen to her everything that recalls them, detail for detail.

I can also construct a collective person for the purposes of condensation in another way, by uniting the actual features of two or more people in a single dream image. This is how Dr. M. in my dream was constructed. He bears the name of Dr. M. and speaks and acts as Dr. M. does, but his physical characteristics and his illness belong to another person, my eldest brother. A single feature, his paleness, is doubly determined, because both men share it. Dr. R. in my dream about my uncle is a similar composite. But there the dream image is produced in yet another way. I have not combined features peculiar to one man with features peculiar to the other, thereby trimming away certain traits from the remembered image of each. Instead I have adopted the method Francis Galton used to produce family portraits: he exposed photographs of several family members one on top of another on the same plate, so that the features they share stand out in heightened relief, while those that do not coincide cancel one another out and fade into obscurity. In the dream of my uncle, the blond beard stands out as an emphasized feature from a face that belongs to two people and is therefore blurred. The beard further alludes to my father and to me, an allusion made possible by its reference to growing gray.

The construction of collective and composite persons is one of the chief resources of dream condensation. There will soon be occasion to discuss it in another connection.

The notion "dysentery" in the dream about the injection is likewise determined in several ways: on the one hand by its similarity in sound to "diphtheria," the kind of resemblance that produces slips of speech, and on the other by its reference to the patient I sent to the Orient, whose hysteria had been misdiagnosed.

The mention of "propyls" in the dream also proves to be an instructive case of condensation. The dream thoughts contained not "propyls" but "amyls." One might suppose that a simple displacement had occurred in forming the dream. That is indeed the case, but the displacement furthers the aims of condensation, as the following supplementary analysis shows. If I dwell for a moment on the word "propyls," its similarity to "propylaeum," the monumental gateway, suggests itself. But a Propylaeum is found not only in Athens but also in Munich. The year before, I had visited a seriously ill friend in Munich, and the reference to him becomes unmistakable through "trimethylamine," which follows closely on "propyls" in the dream.

I pass over the striking fact that here, as elsewhere in dream analysis, associations of the most widely differing value are used to establish connections between thoughts as though they were equivalent. Instead I give in to the temptation to picture the process by which "amyls" in the dream thoughts is replaced by "propyls" in the dream content as though it could be traced out in concrete form.

On one side is the chain of ideas about my friend Otto, who does not understand me, who thinks I am in the wrong, and who gives me the liqueur that smells of amyl. On the other side, connected to the first by contrast, is the chain of ideas about my friend William, who understands me, who would always think I was in the right, and to whom I owe so much valuable information about the chemistry of the sexual processes.

The features of the "Otto" associations that should particularly attract my attention are determined by the recent events that gave rise to the dream; "amyls" is among these elements, which are destined to enter the dream content. The "William" group of associations is distinctly enlivened by the contrast with Otto, and those of its elements that correspond to the ones already aroused in the "Otto" group are thrown into relief. Throughout this dream I keep referring to a person who provokes my displeasure and to another whom I can set against that person at will, and I summon the friend against the enemy, feature for feature. Thus "amyls" in the Otto group calls up memories in the other group that belong to chemistry, and "trimethylamine," which receives support from several directions, finds its way into the dream content. "Amyls," too, might have entered the dream content unchanged, but it yields to the influence of the "William" associations, because the whole range of memories covered by the name "William" is searched for an element capable of supplying "amyls" with a double determination. The association "propyls" lies close to "amyls," and Munich with its Propylaeum comes from the "William" series to meet it. The two groups are united in "propyls–Propylaeum." This intermediate element enters the dream content as a kind of compromise. A common middle term permitting manifold determination has been created here. It thus becomes perfectly clear that manifold determination must ease an element's entry into the dream content. For the sake of forming this middle term, attention has been displaced, without any regard for meaning, from what is really intended to something lying close to it among the associations.

The study of the injection dream has now given us some insight into the process of condensation in dream formation. We have been able to recognize several details of the condensing process: the selection of elements that recur in the dream content more than once, the formation of new unities such as collective persons and composite images, and the construction of a common middle term. The purpose condensation fulfills and the means by which it is accomplished will be investigated when we come to study the psychic processes of dream formation as a whole. For the present, let us be content to establish dream condensation as an important relation between the dream thoughts and the dream content.

The condensing activity of dreams becomes most tangible when it takes words and names as its material. Dreams often treat words as things, and words therefore undergo the same combinations, displacements, and substitutions, and so also condensations, as ideas of things. The results are comic and bizarre verbal coinages. On one occasion a colleague had sent me one of his essays, in which, in my judgment, he had overestimated the value of a recent physiological discovery and had expressed himself in extravagant terms. The following night I dreamed a sentence that obviously referred to this paper: "That is in truly norekdal style." Resolving this coinage gave me trouble at first, although it was unquestionably formed as a parody of superlatives such as "colossal" and "pyramidal." But it was not easy to say where it came from. At last the monster fell apart into two names, Nora and Ekdal, from two well-known plays by Ibsen. I had earlier read a newspaper essay on Ibsen by the same author whose latest work I was thus criticizing in the dream.

II. One of my female patients dreams that *a man with a light beard and a peculiar glittering eye is pointing to a signboard attached to a tree, which reads: uclamparia—wet.*

Analysis: The man looked rather authoritative, and his peculiar glittering eye at once recalled the basilica of St. Paul's near Rome, where she had seen the mosaic portraits of all the popes who have reigned so far. One of the early popes had a golden eye; this was in fact an optical illusion, to which the guides usually draw attention. Further associations showed that the man's general appearance corresponded to her own clergyman (the pope), the shape of the light beard recalled her doctor (myself), and his stature recalled her father. All these people stand in the same relation to her: each guides and directs the course of her life. On further questioning, the golden eye recalled gold, and gold recalled money, namely the rather expensive psychoanalytic treatment, which worries her a great deal. Gold also recalls the gold cure for alcoholism, and so Mr. D., whom she would have married had it not been for his clinging to the disgusting habit of drink. She does not object to someone taking an occasional drink; she herself sometimes drinks beer and liqueurs. This brings her back again to her visit to St. Paul's Outside the Walls and its surroundings. She remembers that at the neighboring monastery of the Three Fountains she drank a eucalyptus liqueur made by the Trappist monks who live there. She then relates how the monks transformed this malarial, swampy region into a dry and healthy neighborhood by planting many eucalyptus trees. The word "uclamparia" then resolves into "eucalyptus" and "malaria," and "wet" refers to the former swampy character of the place. "Wet" also suggests "dry." Dry is in fact the name of the man she would have married but for his overindulgence in alcohol. The unusual name Dry is of Germanic origin (*drei* means "three") and so alludes to the Abbey of the Three (*drei*) Fountains mentioned above. In speaking of Mr. Dry's habit, she used the strong expression, "He could drink a fountain." Mr. Dry himself jokes about his habit by saying, "You know I must drink, because I am always dry," punning on his name. The eucalyptus also refers to her neurosis, which was at first diagnosed as malaria. She went to Italy because her attacks of anxiety, accompanied by marked trembling and shivering, were thought to be malarial in origin. She bought some eucalyptus oil from the monks and maintains that it did her much good.

The condensation *uclamparia—wet* is therefore the point of junction for the dream as well as for the neurosis.

III. In a rather long and wild dream of my own, whose main subject is apparently a sea voyage, the next port of call is named Hearsing and the one after that Fliess. Fliess is the name of my friend who lives in B., and who has often been the destination of my travels. Hearsing, however, is assembled from the names of places in the vicinity of Vienna, which so often end in "-ing": Hietzing, Liesing, Mödling. The old name of Mödling, Medelitz, suggests *meae deliciae*, "my delight," and so my own name, since *Freude* is German for "joy." To these is added the English "hearsay," which points to slander and establishes the link with the indifferent stimulus of the previous day: a poem in the humorous weekly *Fliegende Blätter* about a slanderous dwarf named "Saidhe Hashesaid." Joining the final syllable "-ing" to the name Fliess yields "Vlissingen," a real port on the sea route my brother passes when he comes from England to visit us. But the English name for Vlissingen is Flushing, which means blushing and recalls erythrophobia, the fear of blushing, a condition I treat. It also reminds me of a recent publication on this neurosis by Bekhterev, which had given me cause for anger.

IV. On another occasion I had a dream consisting of two parts. The first was the vividly remembered word "Autodidasker." The second faithfully reproduced a brief and harmless fantasy I had developed a few days earlier, to the effect that when I next saw Professor N., I must tell him: "The patient about whose condition I last consulted you really is suffering from a neurosis, just as you suspected." The coinage "Autodidasker" must therefore satisfy two requirements: it must contain or represent a compressed meaning, and that meaning must have a valid connection with my intention, carried over from waking life, of giving Professor N. his due credit.

"Autodidasker" separates easily into "author" (German *Autor*), "autodidact," and Lasker, with whom the name Lassalle is associated. The first of these words leads to the occasion of the dream, which this time is significant. I had brought my wife several volumes by a well-known author, J. J. David, a friend of my brother's who, as I have learned, comes from the same town I do. One evening she spoke to me about the deep impression made on her by the touching sadness of a story in one of David's novels about a talented but dissolute man, and our conversation turned to the signs of talent we see in our own children. Under the influence of what she had just read, my wife voiced a concern about our children, and I comforted her by remarking that such dangers are precisely the ones education can avert. During the night my train of thought went further, took up my wife's concern, and linked all sorts of other things to it. An opinion on marriage that the writer had once expressed to my brother showed my thoughts a side path that might lead to representation in the dream. This path led to Breslau, where a woman who was a very good friend of ours had married. In Breslau I found Lasker and Lassalle, two examples that gave shape to our concern about being ruined by a woman, and that allowed me to represent both forms of this harmful influence at once. "*Cherchez la femme*," "look for the woman," the phrase in which these thoughts can be summed up, brings me, when taken in another sense, to my brother, who is still unmarried and whose name is Alexander. Now I see that "Alex," as we shorten the name, sounds almost like an inversion of "Lasker," and that this factor must have helped send my thoughts on their detour by way of Breslau.

But this play with names and syllables carries yet another meaning. It represents my wish that my brother may have a happy family life, in the following way. In the novel of artistic life *L'Œuvre*, the author, as is well known, included an incidental account of himself and his own domestic happiness, in which he appears under the name Sandoz. He probably arrived at this name by the following route. Zola, inverted, as children so love to do with names, gives "Aloz." But that was still too transparent for him, so he replaced the syllable "Al," which also begins the name Alexander, with the third syllable of that same name, "sand," and thus "Sandoz" came about. My "Autodidasker" originated in a similar way.

My fantasy of telling Professor N. that the patient we had both seen was suffering from a neurosis entered the dream in the following way. Shortly before the close of my working year, I received a patient whose case defeated my powers of diagnosis. A serious organic disease, perhaps some change in the spine, had to be assumed but could not be proved. It would have been tempting to diagnose a neurosis, which would have ended all difficulties, had the patient not so energetically denied the sexual history without which I am unwilling to accept a neurosis. In my embarrassment I called for help on the physician I respect above all others, as many people do, and to whose authority I defer most completely. He listened to my doubts, told me he thought them justified, and then said: "Keep observing the man; it is probably a neurosis." Since I know he does not share my views on the causes of the neuroses, I held back my disagreement, but I did not hide my skepticism. A few days later I told the patient that I did not know what to do with him and advised him to see someone else. At that, to my great astonishment, he began to beg my pardon for having lied to me, saying he had been deeply ashamed, and he now revealed to me exactly that piece of sexual etiology I had been expecting, and which I considered necessary before I could assume that a neurosis was present. This came as a relief, but also as a humiliation, for I had to admit that my consultant, who had not been troubled by the absence of any supporting case history, had observed correctly. I resolved to tell him so the next time I saw him, and to say that he had been right and I had been wrong.

That is exactly what I do in the dream. But what wish could possibly be fulfilled by my admitting that I was wrong? Being wrong is precisely my wish: I wish to be wrong in my apprehensions. More exactly, I wish that my wife, whose fears I have taken over in the dream thoughts, may turn out to be mistaken. The subject on which this question of being right or wrong turns in the dream lies not far from what truly concerns the dream thoughts. It is the same pair of alternatives, organic or functional damage caused by a woman, or more properly by sexual life, which takes the form of either tabetic paralysis, the late paralysis brought on by syphilis, or a neurosis. And it is with this same pair of alternatives that the manner of Lassalle's ruin is more or less loosely connected.

In this tightly knit dream, which nonetheless becomes quite transparent under careful analysis, Professor N. plays a part for several reasons. He appears partly because of this analogy and partly because of my wish to be the one in the wrong. He appears also because of the associated references to Breslau and to the family of our friend who is married there. But he appears above all because of a small incident connected with our consultation. Having dealt with our medical problem by offering the suggestion I have described, he turned his attention to personal matters. "How many children do you have now?" "Six." A gesture of respect and reflection. "Girls or boys?" "Three of each. They are my pride and my treasure." "Well, the girls present no difficulty, but the boys give trouble later on, in their upbringing." I replied that so far they had been very manageable. Naturally this second diagnosis, concerning the future of my boys, pleased me no more than his earlier one, that my patient had only a neurosis. These two impressions, then, are bound together by contiguity, by having been received one after the other. When I take the story of the neurosis into the dream, I am substituting it for the conversation about education, which proves to be even more closely connected with the dream thoughts because it bears so intimately on the worries my wife later expressed. Thus even my fear that N. may prove right in his remarks about the difficulty of raising boys finds its way into the dream content, concealed behind the representation of my wish to be wrong in such apprehensions. One and the same fantasy, without alteration, represents both of the conflicting alternatives.

The verbal constructions of dreams closely resemble those known to occur in paranoia, which are also found in hysteria and in obsessional ideas. The linguistic habits of children, who at certain stages actually treat words as objects and invent new languages and artificial grammars, are here the common source for both the dream and the psychoneuroses.

When speeches occur in a dream and are expressly distinguished from mere thoughts, it is an invariable rule that the dream speech derives from a remembered speech in the dream material. Either the wording has been preserved intact, or it has been slightly altered in the course of expression. Frequently the dream speech is pieced together from several remembered speeches, the wording staying the same while the meaning may have shifted so as to carry two or more senses. Not infrequently the dream speech is merely an allusion to the occasion on which the remembered speech was made.

### (b) The Work of Displacement

While we were collecting examples of dream condensation, another kind of relation, no less significant, must have caught our attention. We have seen that the elements which force themselves forward in the dream content as its essential components by no means play the same part in the dream thoughts. The converse of this thesis is also true: what is clearly essential in the dream thoughts need not be represented in the dream at all. The dream is, so to speak, eccentric in the literal sense of being off-center. Its contents are grouped around elements other than those that form the center of the dream thoughts.

In the dream about the botanical monograph, for example, the central point of the dream content is apparently the element "botanical." The dream thoughts, however, are concerned with the complications and conflicts that arise when colleagues render one another services and so place themselves under mutual obligation, and then with the reproach that I am in the habit of sacrificing too much to my hobbies. The element "botanical" would find no place at all in this nucleus of the dream thoughts if it were not loosely connected to it by an antithesis, for botany was never among my favorite studies. In my patient's Sappho dream, the climbing up and down, the being upstairs and downstairs, is made the central point. The dream, however, is concerned with the danger of sexual relations with persons of low station, so that only one of the elements of the dream thoughts seems to have been carried over into the dream content, and that one elaborated out of all proportion. Similarly, in the dream about the June bugs, whose subject is the relation between sexuality and cruelty, the factor of cruelty does reappear. But it appears in a different connection and without any mention of the sexual. It has been torn from its context and transformed into something strange. Again, in the dream about my uncle, the blond beard that seems to be its central point appears to have no rational connection with the wishes for greatness that we recognized as the nucleus of the dream thoughts. It is only to be expected that such dreams should give an impression of displacement. In complete contrast to these examples, the dream of Irma's injection shows that individual elements can claim the same place in the formation of the dream that they occupy in the dream thoughts.

Our first response to these new and entirely variable relations between the dream thoughts and the dream content is likely to be astonishment. When, in some psychic process of ordinary life, one idea has been singled out from among several others and has acquired particular vividness in consciousness, we usually take this as proof that the victorious idea possesses an especially high degree of psychic value, a certain degree of interest. We now discover that the value of the individual elements in the dream thoughts is not preserved in the formation of the dream, or is not taken into account. There is no doubt about which elements of the dream thoughts are of the highest value, since our judgment tells us at once. Yet in the formation of the dream, the elements emphasized with intense interest may be treated as though they were of little worth, while other elements, which were certainly of little worth in the dream thoughts, are put in their place.

At first we are given the impression that the psychic intensity of the individual ideas plays no part at all in the selection the dream makes, and that only the greater or lesser number of their determinations matters. One might be inclined to think that what gets into the dream is not what is important in the dream thoughts but what occurs in them several times over. This assumption, however, does little to advance our understanding of dream formation. For it is impossible, at the outset, to believe that the two factors of multiple determination and intrinsic value do not push in the same direction when they influence the dream's selection. The most important ideas in the dream thoughts are probably also the ones that recur most often, since the individual dream thoughts radiate from them as from central points. And still the dream may reject elements that are both strongly emphasized and multiply supported, while taking into its content elements that possess only the second of these properties.

This difficulty may be resolved by considering another impression gained in our investigation of the multiple determination of the dream content. Perhaps many a reader has already passed judgment on that investigation by saying that the multiple determination of dream elements is no significant discovery, because it is self-evident. In analysis one starts from the dream elements and records every notion connected with them. It is no wonder, then, that these elements should turn up with particular frequency in the body of thought obtained in this way. I cannot accept the validity of this objection, but I shall say something myself that sounds much like it. Among the thoughts that analysis brings to light, many can be found that lie far from the central idea of the dream and stand out from the rest as artificial insertions made for a definite purpose. That purpose is easily discovered. These are precisely the thoughts that establish a connection, often a forced and far-fetched one, between the dream content and the dream thoughts. If these elements were weeded out, the dream content would often lack not only over-determination but even sufficient determination by the dream thoughts. We are thus led to conclude that multiple determination, which decides the dream's selection, is perhaps not always a primary factor in dream formation. It is often the secondary manifestation of a psychic power still unknown to us. Nevertheless, multiple determination must still govern the entry of individual elements into the dream, for we can observe that it is established with considerable effort in cases where it does not arise from the dream material unaided.

It is now a short step to the assumption that dream activity gives expression to a psychic force which, on the one hand, strips elements of high psychic value of their intensity and, on the other, creates new values out of elements of small value by way of over-determination. These new values then make their way into the dream content. If this is how the process works, then in the formation of the dream there has occurred a transference and displacement of the psychic intensities of the individual elements, and the textual difference between the dream and the thought content is its result. The process we are assuming here is nothing less than the essential part of dream activity, and it deserves the name of dream displacement. Dream displacement and dream condensation are the two craftsmen to whom the shaping of the dream may chiefly be attributed.

I think we also have an easy task in identifying the psychic force that makes itself felt in dream displacement. The result of displacement is that the dream content no longer resembles the core of the dream thoughts at all, and that the dream reproduces only a distorted form of the dream wish in the unconscious. But we are already acquainted with dream distortion. We have traced it back to the censorship that one psychic agency exercises over another within mental life. Dream displacement is one of the chief means of achieving this distortion. The old legal maxim applies: *Is fecit, cui profuit*, "he did it who profited by it." We may assume that dream displacement is brought about by the influence of this censor, the endopsychic repulsion.

How the factors of displacement, condensation, and over-determination interact in the formation of the dream, and which of them is dominant and which subordinate, are questions reserved for later investigation. For the present we may state a second condition that elements must satisfy in order to get into the dream: they must be withdrawn from the censorship exercised by resistance. From now on we shall treat dream displacement as an unquestionable fact in the interpretation of dreams.

### (c) Means of Representation in the Dream

In the course of this investigation we shall come upon two further conditions that exert an unquestionable influence on the selection of material for the dream. They operate alongside the two factors we have already found at work in transforming the latent dream material into the manifest content, namely condensation and displacement. Even at the risk of seeming to halt our progress, I should like to glance at the processes by which the interpretation of dreams is accomplished. I do not deny that the best way to make them clear, and to show that they are reliable enough to withstand attack, would be to take a single dream as a model. I would develop its interpretation as I did in Chapter II with the dream of "Irma's Injection," then assemble the dream thoughts I had uncovered and reconstruct the formation of the dream from them. In this way I would supplement the analysis of dreams with a synthesis of them. I have done this with several examples for my own instruction. But I cannot undertake it here, because I am prevented by considerations concerning the psychic material such a demonstration would require, considerations that every right-minded person must approve. In the analysis of dreams these considerations pose less difficulty, since an analysis may be incomplete and still retain its value even if it leads only a short way into the labyrinth of the dream's thoughts. A synthesis, by contrast, could not be convincing unless it were complete. I could offer a complete synthesis only of the dreams of persons unknown to the reading public. Since, however, only neurotic patients provide me with the means of doing this, this part of the account of dreams must be postponed until I can carry the psychological explanation of the neuroses far enough, in another place, to show their connection with the subject under consideration.

From my attempts to construct dreams synthetically out of the dream thoughts, I know that the material obtained through interpretation varies in value. One part of it consists of the essential dream thoughts. These would completely replace the dream, and would in themselves be sufficient to replace it if there were no censorship. The other part may be grouped under the term "collaterals." Taken as a whole, they represent the means by which the real wish arising from the dream thoughts is transformed into the dream wish. A first group of these collaterals consists of allusions to the actual dream thoughts. Considered schematically, they correspond to displacements from the essential to the nonessential. A second group comprises the thoughts that link these nonessential elements, which have become significant through displacement, with one another, and that extend from them into the dream content. Finally, a third group contains the ideas and connections of thought that, in the work of interpretation, lead us from the dream content to the intermediate collaterals. Not all of these need to have taken part in the formation of the dream.

At this point we are interested only in the essential dream thoughts. These usually prove to be a complex of thoughts and memories of the most elaborate construction, possessing all the properties of the thought processes we know from waking life. Not infrequently they are trains of thought that proceed from more than one center but are not without points of connection. Almost invariably a chain of thought stands beside its contradictory counterpart, linked to it by associations of contrast.

The individual parts of this complicated structure naturally stand in the most varied logical relations to one another. They form foreground and background, digressions and illustrations, conditions, chains of argument, and objections. The whole mass of these dream thoughts is then subjected to the pressure of the dream activity, in which the parts are turned about, broken up, and pushed together, much like ice floes in a drift. A question then arises: what becomes of the logical ties that until now gave the structure its form? How does the dream represent "if," "because," "as though," "although," "either–or," and all the other conjunctions without which we cannot understand a phrase or a sentence?

Our first answer must be that the dream has no means at its disposal for representing these logical relations among the dream thoughts. In most cases it disregards all such conjunctions and works over only the objective content of the dream thoughts. It is left to the interpretation of the dream to restore the coherence that the dream activity has destroyed.

If the dream lacks the ability to express these relations, the psychic material from which the dream is made must be responsible. The visual arts are limited in the same way. Painting and sculpture are restricted in comparison with poetry, which can make use of speech, and here too the reason for the limitation lies in the material each art works with as it strives to express something. Before painting came to understand the laws of expression that bound it, it tried to escape this disadvantage. In old paintings, small labels were hung from the mouths of the figures, bearing the words the artist despaired of expressing in the picture itself.

Perhaps someone will object to the claim that the dream dispenses with the representation of logical relations. There are dreams in which the most complicated intellectual operations take place, in which proofs are offered and refuted, and puns and comparisons are made, just as in waking thought. But here too appearances deceive. If the interpretation of such dreams is pursued, it turns out that all of this is dream material and not the representation of intellectual activity within the dream. What the apparent thinking of the dream reproduces is the content of the dream thoughts, not the relations among them, and it is in establishing such relations that thinking consists. I shall give examples of this. But the thesis most easily established is that all speeches occurring in a dream, and expressly marked as such, are unchanged or only slightly modified copies of speeches likewise found among the memories in the dream material. Often the speech is merely an allusion to an event contained in the dream thoughts, while the meaning of the dream is something else entirely.

I shall not deny, however, that a critical thought activity also takes part in the formation of the dream, one that does more than merely repeat material from the dream thoughts. I shall have to explain the influence of this factor at the close of this discussion. It will then become clear that this thought activity is called forth not by the dream thoughts but by the dream itself, after the dream is, in a certain sense, already finished.

For the present, then, we shall consider it settled that the logical relations among the dream thoughts receive no particular representation in the dream. Where a contradiction appears in the dream, for instance, it is either a contradiction directed against the dream itself or one derived from the content of one of the dream thoughts. A contradiction in the dream corresponds to a contradiction among the dream thoughts only in a highly indirect way.

But painting eventually succeeded in conveying, by means other than the dangling label, at least the intention behind the figures' speech: their tenderness, their menace, their air of warning, and the like. In the same way, the dream has found it possible to take account of a few of the logical relations among its dream thoughts by suitably modifying its own peculiar method of representation. Experience shows that different dreams go to different lengths in this respect. One dream disregards the logical coherence of its material entirely, while another tries to indicate it as fully as possible. In doing so, the dream departs more or less widely from the material it is meant to work over. The dream takes a similarly varying attitude toward the temporal coherence of the dream thoughts, when such coherence has been established in the unconscious, as in the dream of Irma's injection.

But by what means is the dream activity able to indicate these relations in the dream material, which are so difficult to represent? I shall try to enumerate them one by one.

In the first place, the dream acknowledges the connection that undeniably exists among all the parts of the dream thoughts by combining this material into a single composition, as a situation or an event. It reproduces logical connection in the form of simultaneity. Here it acts somewhat like the painter who gathers all the philosophers or all the poets into a single picture of the School of Athens or of Parnassus. They were never all present together in any hall or on any mountaintop, yet from the standpoint of reflective thought they do form a unity.

The dream carries out this method of representation down to the details. Whenever it shows two elements close together, it vouches for an especially intimate connection between the corresponding elements in the dream thoughts. It works as our system of writing does. When *t* and *o* are written together as *to*, the two letters are to be pronounced as a single syllable. When *t* is followed by *o* after a space, the space shows that *t* is the last letter of one word and *o* the first letter of the next. Accordingly, dream combinations are not made from arbitrary and wholly incongruous elements of the dream material, but from elements that also stand in a fairly intimate relation to one another in the dream thoughts.

To represent causal relations, the dream has two methods, which are essentially reducible to one. The more frequent method applies when the dream thoughts run along the lines of "Because this was so, such and such must happen." It consists in presenting the premise as an introductory dream and attaching the conclusion to it in the form of the main dream. If my interpretation is correct, the sequence may also be reversed. The more fully worked-out part of the dream always corresponds to the conclusion.

A female patient, whose dream I shall give in full later, once provided me with a neat example of this kind of representation of causal relation. Her dream consisted of a short prologue followed by a very elaborate but well-organized dream composition, which might be titled "A Flower of Speech." The prologue runs as follows: She goes to the two maids in the kitchen and scolds them for taking so long to prepare

“a little bite of food.” She also sees a great many coarse dishes in the kitchen, turned upside down so that the water can drain off them, and stacked in a heap. The two maids go to fetch water and must, as it were, step into a river that reaches right up to the house or into the yard.

Then follows the main dream, which begins: She is descending from a height, climbing over balustrades of a curious design, and she is glad that her dress does not catch on anything, and so on. The introductory dream refers to the house of the lady’s parents. She has probably often heard her mother say the words that are spoken in the kitchen. The piles of unwashed dishes come from a modest earthenware shop that occupied the same building. The second part of this dream alludes to the dreamer’s father, who always had a great deal to do with servant girls, and who later contracted a fatal illness during a flood; the house stood near the bank of a river. The thought concealed behind the introductory dream, then, runs something like this: “Because I was born in this house, in such narrow and unlovely circumstances…” The main dream takes up the same thought and presents it in a form altered by the tendency toward wish-fulfillment: “I am of exalted origin.” Properly stated, then, the whole thought reads: “Because I was born in such low circumstances, my career has gone thus and so.”

As far as I can see, dividing a dream into two unequal portions does not always signify a causal relation between the thoughts of the two portions. It often seems as though the same material were being presented in the two dreams from different points of view. Or it seems as though the two dreams had arisen from two separate centers in the dream material, with overlapping contents, so that what forms the center of one dream serves in the other merely as an allusion, and the reverse. But in a certain number of cases, a division into a shorter preliminary dream and a longer main dream really does signify a causal relation between the two portions. The other method of representing causal relation is used with less abundant material, and it consists in the transformation of one image in the dream, whether a person or a thing, into another. A causal relation is asserted only when we actually witness this transformation taking place within the dream, not when we merely notice that one thing has taken the place of another. I said that both methods of representing causal relation come down to the same thing. In both, causation is represented by succession: in the one case by the sequence of the dreams, in the other by the immediate transformation of one image into another. In the great majority of cases, of course, causal relation is not expressed at all, but is lost in the sequence of elements that is unavoidable in the dream process.

The dream is altogether unable to express the alternative “either/or.” It habitually takes both members of the alternative into a single context, as though each had an equal claim. A classic example is the dream of Irma’s injection. Its latent thoughts plainly mean: I am not to blame for the persistence of Irma’s pains; the fault lies either with her resistance to accepting my solution, or with the unfavorable sexual conditions under which she lives, which I am powerless to change, or else her pains are not hysterical at all but organic. The dream, however, fulfills all of these possibilities, though they very nearly exclude one another, and it is quite ready to draw from the dream-wish a fourth solution of the same kind. It was only after interpreting the dream that I inserted the “either/or” into the sequence of the dream thoughts.

When a dreamer, in telling a dream, finds occasion to use “either/or” (“It was either a garden or a living room,” and so on), what occurs in the dream thoughts is not really an alternative but an “and,” a simple addition. When we use “either/or,” we are usually describing a certain indistinctness in some element of the dream, an indistinctness that can still be cleared up. The rule of interpretation for such cases is this: the separate members of the alternative are to be treated as equals and joined by “and.” For example, after waiting a long time in vain for the address of a friend who was living in Italy, I dreamed that I received a telegram giving me this address. On the strip of telegraph paper I saw printed in blue the following: the first word was blurred, perhaps “via,” or “villa,” or possibly “Casa”; the second was distinctly “Sezerno.” This second word, which sounds like an Italian name and reminds me of our discussions of etymology, also expresses my annoyance that my friend had kept his place of residence secret from me for so long. Each member of the threefold suggestion for the first word proves, in the course of analysis, to be a self-sufficient and equally well-justified starting point in the chain of ideas.

On the night before my father’s funeral, I dreamed of a printed placard, a card or poster, something perhaps like the signs in railway waiting rooms that announce a prohibition against smoking. It read either:

*It is requested to shut the eyes*

or

*It is requested to shut an eye*

which I am in the habit of writing in a single combined form: *It is requested to shut the / an eye(s).*

Each of the two variants has its own particular meaning and leads the interpretation down its own particular path. I had arranged the simplest possible funeral, for I knew what the deceased had thought about such matters. Other members of the family, however, did not approve of such puritanical simplicity; they thought we would be shamed before the mourners. Hence one of the wordings in the dream asks for the “shutting of one eye,” that is, for people to be indulgent and look the other way. Here the meaning of the blurring that we describe with an “either/or” is particularly easy to see. The dream-work has failed to construct a single wording that would be unified and yet ambiguous enough for the dream thoughts. As a result, the two main trains of thought are already kept apart even in the dream content.

In a few cases, the division of a dream into two equal parts expresses the alternative that the dream finds so difficult to represent.

The dream’s attitude toward the category of antithesis and contradiction is most striking. This category is simply ignored; the word “No” seems not to exist for the dream. The dream shows a particular preference for reducing opposites to a unity or representing them as one and the same thing. It also takes the liberty of representing any element whatever by its desired opposite, so that, for any element that has an opposite, it is impossible at first to tell whether it should be taken negatively or positively in the dream thoughts. In one of the dreams just mentioned, whose introductory portion we have already interpreted (“because my origins are such”), the dreamer descends over a balustrade holding a blossoming branch in her hands. This image suggests to her the angel in paintings of the Annunciation, who carries a lily stem in his hand (her own name is Mary), and also the girls in white robes who walk in the procession on Corpus Christi Day, when the streets are decorated with green boughs. The blossoming branch in the dream is therefore quite certainly an allusion to sexual innocence. But the branch is thickly covered with red blossoms, each resembling a camellia. By the end of her walk, the dream continues, the blossoms have already fallen away considerably; then come unmistakable allusions to menstruation. Yet this same branch, carried like a lily and as if by an innocent girl, is also an allusion to Camille, the heroine of *La Dame aux Camélias*, who, as is well known, always wore a white camellia, but a red one during her menstrual periods. The same blossoming branch (“the flower of maidenhood” in Goethe’s songs about the miller’s daughter) represents at once sexual innocence and its opposite. And the same dream that expresses the dreamer’s joy at having passed through life unsullied also hints in several places, as in the falling of the blossoms, at the opposite train of thought: that she had been guilty of various sins against sexual purity, namely in her childhood. In analyzing the dream we can clearly distinguish the two trains of thought, of which the comforting one seems superficial and the reproachful one deeper. The two are diametrically opposed, and their similar but contrasting elements have been represented by identical dream elements.

The mechanism of dream formation is favorable in the highest degree to only one of the logical relations. This is the relation of similarity, correspondence, contiguity, the “just as,” which the dream can represent as it can no other, and by the most varied means. The correspondences occurring in the dream, the cases of “just as,” are the chief supports on which dreams are built, and no small part of the dream-work consists in creating new correspondences of this kind wherever the ones already at hand are barred from the dream by the censorship of resistance. The tendency toward condensation shown by the dream-work assists in representing the relation of similarity.

Similarity, agreement, and common ground are generally expressed in the dream by fusion into a unity, which is either already present in the dream material or newly created. The first case may be called identification, the second composition. Identification is used when the dream is concerned with persons, composition when things are being unified; but composites are also made out of persons. Places are often treated as persons.

Identification consists in giving representation in the dream content to only one of several persons who are linked by some common feature, while the second person, or the others, seem to be suppressed so far as the dream is concerned. This single representative person enters into all the relations and situations belonging either to himself or to the persons he stands for. In composition involving persons, by contrast, the dream image already contains features that are characteristic of each of the persons concerned but not common to them, so that a new unity, a composite person, results from the union of these features. The composition itself can be achieved in various ways. The dream figure may bear the name of one of the persons it refers to, in which case we know, in a manner quite like knowledge in waking life, that this or that person is meant, while the visual features belong to someone else. Or the dream image itself may be made up of visual features that in reality belong partly to one person and partly to the other. Instead of visual features, the part played by the second person may also be represented by the mannerisms usually attributed to him, the words he usually speaks, or the situations in which he is usually imagined. With this last method of characterization, the sharp distinction between identification and composition of persons begins to disappear. It may also happen that the formation of such a mixed personality fails. The action of the dream is then attributed to one person, and the other, as a rule the more important one, is introduced as an inactive and indifferent onlooker. As Stekel has observed, the dreamer will report something like: “My mother was there too.”

The common feature that justifies the union of the two persons, that is, the feature that occasions it, may either be represented in the dream or be absent from it. As a rule, the identification or composition of persons serves precisely to spare the dream from representing this common feature. Instead of repeating, “A is hostile toward me, and so is B,” I form a composite person out of A and B in the dream, or I imagine A performing some unaccustomed action that is characteristic of B. The dream figure obtained in this way appears in some new connection, and the fact that it signifies both A and B entitles me to insert what the two have in common, their hostility toward me, at the proper place in the interpretation. In this way I often achieve a quite extraordinary degree of condensation in the dream content. I can spare myself the direct representation of very complicated relations belonging to one person if I can find a second person who has an equal claim to some of those relations. It is also obvious how far representation by identification can circumvent the resisting censorship, which subjects the dream-work to such harsh conditions. What offends the censorship may lie in the very ideas that are connected in the dream material with one particular person. I then find a second person who is likewise related to the objectionable material, but only to part of it. Contact at the one point that offends the censorship now entitles me to form a composite person, who is characterized on both sides by indifferent features. This person, the product of composition or identification, is unobjectionable to the censorship and is therefore fit to be admitted into the dream content. Through the application of dream condensation, I have satisfied the demands of the dream censorship.

When a dream represents a common feature of two persons, this is usually a hint to look for another, concealed common feature whose representation the censorship has made impossible. A displacement of the common feature has taken place here, partly in order to make representation easier. From the fact that the composite person appears to me with an indifferent common feature, I must infer that another common feature, by no means indifferent, exists in the dream thoughts.

According to what has been said, the identification or composition of persons serves various purposes in the dream: first, to represent a feature common to the two persons; second, to represent a displaced common feature; and third, to express a community of features that is merely wished for. Since the wish for a community between two persons often coincides with the wish to exchange one for the other, this relation too is expressed in the dream through identification. In the dream of Irma’s injection, I wish to exchange this patient for another; that is, I wish the other woman were my patient, as Irma has been. The dream takes account of this wish by showing me a person who is called Irma but who is examined in a position in which I have had occasion to see only the other woman. In the dream about my uncle, this substitution becomes the center of the dream: I identify myself with the minister by judging and treating my colleague as shabbily as he does.

It has been my experience, and I have found no exception to it, that every dream deals with the dreamer’s own person. Dreams are absolutely egotistical. Where my ego does not appear in the dream content, and only a stranger does, I may safely assume that my ego is concealed behind that person by means of identification, and I am entitled to insert my ego in that place. On other occasions, when my ego does appear in the dream, the situation in which it is placed tells me that another person is hiding behind it. In that case the dream is meant to notify me that, in the interpretation, I must transfer to myself something connected with this other person, namely the hidden common feature. There are also dreams in which my ego appears together with other persons who, once the identification is resolved, likewise turn out to be my ego. Through these identifications I am instructed to unite in my ego certain ideas whose acceptance the censorship has opposed. I may also give my ego multiple representation in a single dream, sometimes directly and sometimes through identification with strangers. An extraordinary amount of thought material can be condensed by means of a few such identifications.

Resolving the identification of places designated by their own names is even less difficult than resolving that of persons, because here the disturbing influence of the ego, which is all-powerful in the dream, is absent. In one of my dreams about Rome, the place in which I find myself is called Rome; yet I am surprised at the large number of German placards on a street corner. The placards are a wish-fulfillment that immediately suggests Prague. The wish itself probably dates from a period in my youth when I was filled with a German nationalist spirit that is suppressed today. At the time of the dream I was looking forward to meeting a friend in Prague. The identification of Rome and Prague is thus explained by a desired common feature: I would rather meet my friend in Rome than in Prague; for the purposes of this meeting, I should like to exchange Prague for Rome.

The capacity to create composites is one of the chief causes of the fantastic character so common in dreams, since it introduces into the dream elements that could never have been objects of perception. The psychic process at work in forming composites is evidently the same one we use in waking life when we conceive or fashion a centaur or a dragon. The only difference is that in the fantastic creations of waking life, the deciding factor is the impression the new creation is meant to make, while the composite in the dream is determined by an influence independent of the form of the image: the common feature in the dream thoughts. Dream composition can be carried out in a great many ways. In the most artless method, the properties of one thing are represented, and this representation is accompanied by the knowledge that they also belong to another object. A more careful technique unites the features of the one object with those of the other in a new image, making skillful use of resemblances that actually exist between the two. Depending on the subject matter and the wit at work in the composition, the new creation may turn out wholly absurd or merely fantastically ingenious. If the objects to be condensed into a unity are too incongruous, the dream-work contents itself with creating a composite that has a relatively distinct core, to which less distinct modifications are attached. Here the fusion into a single image has, as it were, failed; the two representations overlap and give rise to something like a contest between visual images. Similar effects might be obtained in a drawing if one tried to construct a concept out of individual perceptual images.

Dreams naturally abound in such composites. I have given several examples in the dreams already analyzed, and I shall add more. In the dream described earlier, which tells the career of my patient “in flowery language,” the dreamer carries a blossoming branch in her hand, which, as we have seen, signifies at once innocence and sexual transgression. Moreover, the way the blossoms are clustered recalls cherry blossoms; the blossoms themselves, taken one by one, are camellias; and the whole thing also gives the impression of an exotic plant. The dream thoughts reveal the common feature among the elements of this composite. The blossoming branch is made up of allusions to gifts by which she was induced, or was supposed to be induced, to show herself agreeable: cherries in her childhood, and a spray of camellias in later years. The exotic feature is an allusion to a much-traveled naturalist who tried to win her favor by giving her a drawing of a flower. Another female patient creates an intermediate element out of the bathing huts at a seaside resort, the outdoor privies of the countryside, and the garrets of our city apartment houses. Human nakedness and exposure are common to the first two elements, and from their connection with the third we may infer that the garret, too, was once the scene of exposure, in her childhood. A male dreamer creates a composite place out of two locations where “treatment” is given: my consulting room and the public hall where he first met his wife. Another female patient, after her elder brother has promised to treat her to caviar, dreams that his legs are thickly covered with black caviar grains. Two elements have been united here with the caviar grains to form a new idea, the idea of “what she has inherited from her brother”: “contagion” in the moral sense, and the memory of a skin rash in childhood that made her legs look as though studded with red dots instead of black ones. In this dream, parts of the human body are treated as objects, as is usually the case in dreams. In one of the dreams reported by Ferenczi, there appeared a composite made up of the person of a physician and a horse, with a nightshirt spread over it. Analysis revealed the common feature of these three components once the nightshirt had been recognized as an allusion to the dreamer’s father in a scene from her childhood. In each of the three cases, the object had been a target of her sexual curiosity. As a child she had often been taken by her nurse to the army stud farm, where she had ample opportunity to satisfy a curiosity that was at that time still uninhibited.

I have already asserted that the dream has no means of expressing the relations of contradiction, contrast, and negation. I am now about to contradict this assertion for the first time. Some of the cases that may be grouped under the word “contrast” are represented, as we have seen, simply by identification, that is, when an exchange or substitution can be connected with the contrast. We have given repeated examples of this. Another group of contrasts in the dream thoughts, which perhaps falls under the heading “turned into its opposite,” is represented in the dream in a remarkable manner that may almost be called witty. The “inversion” does not itself enter the dream content. Instead, it reveals its presence there by the fact that some part of the dream content, already formed and available for other reasons, is inverted, as it were, after the fact. This process is easier to illustrate than to describe. In the fine “Up and Down” dream, the representation of climbing is an inversion of a prototype in the dream thoughts, namely the opening scene of Daudet’s *Sappho*. In the dream, the climbing is difficult at first and easy later on, whereas in the novel’s scene it is easy at first and grows steadily harder. Likewise, “above” and “below” are inverted in the dream with reference to the dreamer’s brother. This points to a relation of opposition or contrast between two parts of the subject matter of the dream thoughts, and we have found that relation in the fact that, in the dreamer’s childhood fantasy, he is carried by his nurse, while in the novel, by contrast, it is the hero who carries his beloved. My dream about Goethe's attack on Mr. M. contains an inversion of the same kind, and it must be set right before the dream can be interpreted. In the dream, Goethe attacks a young man, Mr. M.; in reality, according to the dream-thoughts, an eminent man who is my friend had been attacked by an unknown young author. In the dream I reckon time from the date of Goethe's death; in reality the reckoning was made from the year in which the paralytic was born. The thought that determines the dream material turns out to be an objection to treating Goethe as a lunatic. "The other way around," says the dream: "if you cannot understand the book, it is you who are dull-witted, not the author." All of these dreams of inversion seem, moreover, to allude to the contemptuous phrase "to turn one's back on someone," which in German is *einem die Kehrseite zeigen*, literally "to show someone one's reverse side." The inversion involving the dreamer's brother in the Sappho dream belongs here as well. It is also striking how often inversion becomes necessary in dreams inspired by repressed homosexual feelings.

Inversion, or transformation into the opposite, is one of the dream-work's favorite methods of representation, and one of the most adaptable. Its first function is to fulfill a wish with respect to some particular element of the dream-thoughts. "If only it were the other way around!" is often the best expression of the ego's relation to a disagreeable memory. But inversion becomes extraordinarily useful to the censor, because it distorts the material represented to a degree that all but paralyzes our understanding of the dream. For this reason, whenever a dream stubbornly refuses to yield its meaning, it is always permissible to try inverting particular portions of its manifest content, and not infrequently everything then becomes clear.

Besides this inversion of subject matter, inversion in time must not be overlooked. A common device of dream distortion is to present the final outcome of an event, or the conclusion of an argument, at the beginning of the dream, and to supply the premises of the conclusion or the causes of the effect at its end. Anyone who has not taken this technical device into account stands helpless before the problem of dream interpretation.

In some cases, indeed, we can arrive at the sense of a dream only by subjecting its content to several inversions in different directions. In the dream of a young patient suffering from an obsessional neurosis, for example, the memory of an infantile death-wish against a feared father lay hidden behind the following words: *His father scolds him because he comes home so late.* But both the context of the psychoanalytic treatment and the dreamer's own associations show that the sentence must read: He is angry at his father, and his father always comes home too early, that is, too soon. He would have preferred that his father not come home at all, which amounts to the wish that his father should die. As a little boy, the dreamer had committed a sexual aggression against another person while his father was away, and he had been threatened with punishment in the words: "Just wait until your father comes home."

If we want to trace the relations between dream content and dream-thoughts further, the best course is to take the dream itself as our starting point and to ask: what do certain formal characteristics of dream representation signify with respect to the dream-thoughts?

Chief among the formal characteristics that must catch our attention are the variations in distinctness among individual parts of a dream, or among whole dreams compared with one another. The intensity of individual dream images varies across a whole scale. At one end lies a sharpness of depiction that we are inclined to rate higher than that of reality, though without justification. At the other lies an exasperating indistinctness that is declared to be characteristic of dreams, because it cannot quite be compared with any degree of indistinctness we ever perceive in real objects. We usually describe the impression an indistinct dream object leaves on us as "fleeting," while we think of the more distinct images as holding steady for a longer span of perception. We must now ask what conditions in the dream material produce these differences in vividness among the parts of the dream content.

Certain expectations will inevitably arise here, and they must be answered. Because real sensations during sleep can become part of the dream material, it will probably be assumed that these sensations, or the dream elements derived from them, stand out by a peculiar intensity, or, conversely, that whatever is especially vivid in a dream can probably be traced to such real sensations. My experience has never confirmed this. It is not true that the elements of a dream derived from impressions received during sleep, from nervous excitations, are distinguished by their vividness from elements based on memories. The factor of reality counts for nothing in determining the intensity of dream images.

One might further expect that the sensory intensity, or vividness, of individual dream images bears some relation to the psychic intensity of the corresponding elements in the dream-thoughts. In the dream-thoughts, intensity is identical with psychic value: the most intense elements are in fact the most significant ones, and they form the center of the dream. We know, however, that these are precisely the elements the censor usually keeps out of the dream content. Still, it might be possible that the elements standing nearest to them and representing them would show a higher degree of intensity, without for that reason becoming the center of the dream's representation. This expectation, too, is destroyed when we compare the dream with its material. The intensity of the elements in the one has nothing to do with the intensity of the elements in the other; between the dream material and the dream there takes place a complete "transvaluation of all psychic values." The very element that is transient and hazy, pushed into the background by more forceful images, is often the one and only element in which we can trace any direct derivative of the subject that wholly dominated the dream-thoughts.

The intensity of dream elements turns out to be determined in a different way, by two factors independent of each other. It is easy to see from the start that the elements through which the wish-fulfillment is expressed are represented most distinctly. Analysis also teaches us, however, that the greatest number of trains of thought proceed from the most vivid elements of the dream, and that the most vivid elements are at the same time the most fully determined. The meaning does not change if we restate this empirical finding as follows: the greatest intensity is shown by those dream elements whose formation required the most extensive work of condensation. We may therefore expect that this condition and the one imposed by the wish-fulfillment can be expressed in a single formula.
