I want to guard against confusing the problem I have just been considering, namely the causes of greater or lesser intensity or distinctness in individual dream elements, with another problem that concerns the varying distinctness of whole dreams or sections of dreams. In the first case, the opposite of distinctness is blurredness; in the second, it is confusion. Admittedly, the intensities rise and fall together on the two scales. A part of the dream that seems clear to us usually contains vivid elements, while an obscure dream is made up of less intense ones. But the problem posed by the scale running from the apparently clear to the indistinct or confused is far more complicated than the one posed by variations in the vividness of individual elements, and for reasons I will give later I shall set it aside here. In isolated cases we are astonished to find that the impression of clarity or obscurity a dream produces has no bearing at all on its structure, and that it arises instead from the dream material as one of its components. I remember, for instance, a dream that seemed so well constructed, so flawless and clear, that while I was still half asleep I resolved to recognize a new class of dreams: those that had escaped the mechanisms of condensation and displacement and might therefore be called "fantasies during sleep." Closer examination showed that this rare dream had the same gaps and flaws in its construction as any other, and for that reason I abandoned the category of dream fantasies. Reduced to its simplest terms, the content of the dream was that I was explaining to a friend a difficult and long-sought theory of bisexuality, and the wish-fulfilling power of the dream was responsible for making this theory, which incidentally was never actually stated in the dream, appear so clear and flawless. What I had taken for a judgment on the finished dream was thus part of the dream content, and the essential part. The dream-work had, so to speak, extended its operations into waking thought, and had presented to me in the form of a judgment the portion of the dream material it had failed to reproduce exactly. I once encountered the exact opposite in a female patient. At first she was entirely unwilling to tell a dream that the analysis required, "because it was so obscure and confused." After repeatedly denying that her own description was accurate, she declared that several people had appeared in the dream, herself, her husband, and her father, and that it seemed as though she did not know whether her husband was her father, or who her father was anyway, or something of the kind. When this dream was considered alongside the ideas that occurred to her during the session, it proved beyond doubt to concern the story of a servant girl who had to confess that she was expecting a child and who now faced doubts as to "who the father really was." In this case, too, the obscurity of the dream is a part of the material that prompted it. A portion of that material was represented through the form of the dream. The form of the dream, or of dreaming itself, is used with astonishing frequency to represent the concealed content.

Comments on the dream and seemingly harmless remarks about it often serve, in the subtlest way, to conceal a part of what was dreamed, though they usually betray it as well. When a dreamer says, for example, "Here the dream is vague," the analysis may yield a childhood memory of listening to someone cleaning himself after defecating. Another example deserves to be recorded in detail. A young man has a very distinct dream that recalls fantasies from his childhood, fantasies that have remained conscious to him. He was staying at a summer hotel one evening; he mistook his room number and walked into a room where an elderly lady and her two daughters were undressing for bed. He continues: "Then there are some gaps in the dream; then something is missing; and at the end there was a man in the room who wanted to throw me out, and I had to wrestle with him." He tried in vain to recall the content and purpose of the boyhood fantasy to which the dream evidently alludes. We finally realize that the content we were looking for had already been supplied in his remarks about the indistinct part of the dream. The "gaps" were the genital openings of the women preparing for bed, and "here something is missing" described the chief characteristic of the female genitals. In those early years he had burned with curiosity to see a female genital, and he was still inclined to hold on to the infantile sexual theory that attributes a male organ to women.

All the dreams of a single night belong, in their content, to the same whole. Their division into several parts, their grouping, and their number are all full of meaning and may be taken as information coming from the latent dream content. In interpreting dreams that consist of several principal sections, or dreams belonging to the same night, one must not overlook the possibility that these separate, successive dreams express the same feelings in different material. Of such parallel dreams, the one that comes first is usually the most distorted and the most bashful, while the one that follows is bolder and more distinct.

Pharaoh's dream in the Bible of the ears of grain and the cattle, which Joseph interpreted, was of this kind. Josephus reports it in his *Antiquities of the Jews* in greater detail than the Bible does. After relating the first dream, the king said: "When I had seen this vision I awaked out of my sleep, and being in disorder, and considering with myself what this appearance should be, I fell asleep again, and saw another dream much more wonderful than the first, which did still more affright and disturb me." After hearing the dream, Joseph said: "This dream, O King, although seen under two forms, signifies one and the same issue of things."

In his *Contribution to the Psychology of Rumor*, Jung relates how a schoolgirl's veiled erotic dream was understood by her friends without any interpretation and then continued by them with variations. Commenting on the reports of this dream, he observes "that the last of a long series of dream pictures contained precisely the same thought whose representation had been attempted in the first picture of the series. The censor pushed the complex out of the way as long as possible, through constantly renewed symbolic concealments, displacements, deviations into the harmless, and so on."

Scherner was well acquainted with these peculiarities of dream distortion, and at the end of his theory of organic stimulation he describes them as a special law: "But finally, in all nerve stimuli that issue in symbolic dream formations, the fantasy observes the general law of representing at the beginning of the dream only the remotest and freest allusions to the stimulating object; toward the end, however, when its power of representation is exhausted, it presents the stimulus, or the organ concerned, or its function, in undisguised form, and in this way the dream names its organic motive and comes to its end."

Otto Rank has furnished a new confirmation of Scherner's law in his work *A Self-Interpreting Dream*. The dream he reports, a girl's, consisted of two dreams separated in time during the same night, the second of which ended in a nocturnal emission. This emission dream could be interpreted in every detail, even setting aside many of the ideas the dreamer contributed, and the abundant connections between the two dream contents showed that the first dream expressed in bashful language the same thing as the second. The latter, the emission dream, thus made possible a full explanation of the former. From this example Rank draws, with complete justice, conclusions about the significance of emission dreams in general.

In my experience, however, it is only in rare cases that one is in a position to read clarity or confusion in a dream as certainty or doubt in the dream material. Later I shall try to identify the factor in dream formation on whose influence this scale of qualities essentially depends.

In some dreams that stay with a particular situation and setting for a while, there occur interruptions described in words like these: "But then it seemed as though it were at the same time another place, and there such and such a thing happened." What interrupts the main course of the dream in this way, a course that may later resume, turns out to be a subordinate idea, a thought interpolated into the dream material. A conditional relation in the dream-thoughts is represented in the dream by simultaneity. German makes the link plain in the near-identity of *wenn* and *wann*, words for "if" and "when."

What does the sensation of inhibited movement signify, the sensation that occurs so often in dreams and is so closely allied to anxiety? One wants to move and cannot stir from the spot; one wants to accomplish something and meets one obstacle after another. The train is about to leave and one cannot reach it; one's hand is raised to avenge an insult and its strength gives way. We have already met this sensation in dreams of exposure, but have made no serious attempt to interpret it. It is convenient but inadequate to answer that there is motor paralysis during sleep, which makes itself felt through this sensation. We may ask: "Why, then, do we not dream continually of such inhibited movements?" And we are justified in supposing that this sensation, which can appear at any moment in sleep, serves some purpose of representation, and is called forth by a need in the dream material for this kind of representation.

The failure to accomplish something does not always appear in the dream as a sensation; it may also appear simply as part of the dream content. I believe a case of this sort is especially well suited to show us what this feature of dreams means. I shall give an abridged account of a dream in which I seem to be accused of dishonesty. *The setting is a mixture of a private sanatorium and several other buildings. A footman appears and summons me to an examination. I know in the dream that something has gone missing, and that the examination is taking place because I am suspected of having taken the lost article.* Analysis shows that "examination" is to be understood in two senses, and also means a medical examination. *Conscious of my innocence, and of the fact that I have been called in as a consultant, I calmly follow the footman. At the door we are met by another footman, who points at me and says, "Is that the man you've brought? Why, he is a respectable person." Then, without any footman, I enter a great hall in which machines are standing, and which reminds me of an Inferno with its hellish instruments of punishment. On one apparatus I see a colleague strapped down, who has every reason to take notice of me, but he pays me no attention. Then I am given to understand that I may now go. Then I cannot find my hat, and cannot go after all.*

The wish the dream fulfills is obviously that I should be recognized as an honest man and allowed to go; all sorts of material contradicting this idea must therefore be present in the dream-thoughts. That I may go is the sign of my acquittal. If, then, the dream supplies at its close an event that prevents me from going, we may readily conclude that the suppressed material of the contradiction is asserting itself in this feature. My being unable to find my hat therefore means: "You are not an honest man after all." Failure to accomplish something in a dream is the expression of a contradiction, a "No," and my earlier statement that dreams cannot express negation must be revised accordingly.

In other dreams, where the failure to accomplish something appears not only as a situation but also as a sensation, the same contradiction is expressed more emphatically, in the form of a volition opposed by a counter-volition. The sensation of inhibited movement thus represents a conflict of will. We shall learn later that this very motor paralysis is one of the fundamental conditions of the psychic process in dreaming. The impulse transmitted to the motor pathways is nothing other than the will, and the fact that we are certain to find this impulse inhibited in sleep makes the whole process extraordinarily well suited to representing a volition together with the "No" that opposes it. My explanation of anxiety makes it easy to understand why the sensation of thwarted will is so closely allied to anxiety, and why the two are so often linked in dreams. Anxiety is a libidinal impulse that issues from the unconscious and is inhibited by the preconscious. When a sensation of inhibition in a dream is accompanied by anxiety, therefore, there must also be present a volition that was once capable of arousing libido; there must be a sexual impulse.

I shall discuss elsewhere what significance and what psychic force should be ascribed to such expressions of judgment as "After all, it's only a dream," which frequently surface in dreams. For the present I will say only that they serve to depreciate the value of what is being dreamed. A related problem, the meaning of the fact that some content is occasionally labeled within the dream itself as "dreamed," the riddle of the "dream within a dream," has been solved along similar lines by W. Stekel through the analysis of several convincing examples. The part of the dream that is "dreamed" is once again to be depreciated in value and robbed of its reality. What the dreamer goes on dreaming after waking from the dream within the dream is what the dream-wish wants to put in the place of the extinguished reality. It may therefore be assumed that the "dreamed" part contains the representation of reality, the real memory, while the continuing dream contains the representation of what the dreamer wishes. To include a given content in a "dream within a dream" is therefore equivalent to wishing that what has just been designated a dream had never happened. The dream-work uses dreaming itself as a means of deflection.

### (d) Regard for Presentability

Until now we have been trying to determine how the dream represents the relations among the dream-thoughts, but several times we have extended our inquiry to the further question of what alterations the dream material undergoes for the purposes of dream formation. We now know that the dream material, after being stripped of most of its relations, is subjected to compression, while displacements of intensity among its elements force a psychic revaluation of that material. The displacements we have considered proved to be substitutions of one idea for another, the substitute being connected with the original in some way through associations. These displacements were put to the service of condensation, since in this way a common intermediate element could take the place of two elements in the formation of the dream. We have not yet mentioned any other kind of displacement.

But the analyses show that a second kind exists, and that it shows itself as a change in the verbal expression given to the thought in question. In both cases displacement follows a chain of associations, but the process takes place in different psychic spheres. In the first case, one element is substituted for another; in the second, an element exchanges its verbal expression for a different one.

This second kind of displacement is of great theoretical interest, and it is also especially well suited to explain the fantastic absurdity in which the dream disguises itself. As a rule, the displacement exchanges a colorless, abstract expression in the dream-thought for one that is visual and concrete. The advantage of this substitution, and therefore its purpose, is plain. Whatever is visual can be represented in the dream and worked into situations, whereas an abstract expression would confront the dream with the kind of difficulty an illustrated newspaper would face if asked to render a political editorial entirely in pictures. Nor is the possibility of representation the only gain. The change can also serve the interests of condensation and of the censor. Once an abstract and unwieldy dream-thought has been recast in figurative language, it becomes easier to establish the identities and cross-references between this new expression and the rest of the dream material. The dream depends on these connections and invents them whenever they are lacking. Concrete terms lend themselves to this better because, in every language, their long development has made them richer in associations than conceptual ones. It is reasonable to suppose that much of the intermediate work in dream formation, the work that reduces the separate dream-thoughts to the tersest and simplest possible expression, proceeds in this way: by finding a suitable paraphrase for each individual thought. A thought whose expression has already been settled on other grounds will then exert a sorting and selecting influence on the means available for expressing another thought, and it may do so continually throughout the process, much as happens in the work of a poet. When a rhyming poem is being composed, the second line of a rhyming pair is bound by two conditions: it must express the right meaning, and it must express it in a way that secures the rhyme. The best poems are probably those in which the poet's search for a rhyme is unconscious, and in which the two thoughts have influenced each other's choice of words from the start, so that only a slight adjustment is needed to make them rhyme.

In some cases the change of expression serves dream condensation more directly, by allowing the dream to invent a verbal construction that is ambiguous and can therefore express more than one dream-thought at once. In this way the whole range of wordplay is placed at the disposal of the dream-work. The part that words play in forming dreams should not surprise us. Because a word is a junction point for a number of ideas, it carries a kind of built-in ambiguity, and the neuroses, such as obsessions and phobias, exploit the opportunities words offer for condensation and disguise just as readily as the dream does. It is easy to show that the dream's disguise also profits from this displacement of expression. A single ambiguous word set in place of two meanings naturally confuses us, and a figurative expression used instead of the plain everyday one defeats our understanding. This is all the more so because the dream never tells us whether its elements are to be taken literally or figuratively, or whether they refer to the dream material directly or only by way of some intervening figure of speech. I have already cited several representations in dreams that are held together by nothing but ambiguity: "her mouth opens without difficulty" in the dream of Irma's injection, and "I cannot go yet" in the dream reported most recently. I shall now cite a dream whose analysis depends more heavily on the figurative expression of abstract thought. Once again, the difference between this kind of interpretation and interpretation by symbolism can be sharply drawn. In symbolic interpretation of dreams, the key to the symbolism is chosen arbitrarily by the interpreter. In our cases of verbal disguise, by contrast, all the keys are common knowledge and are drawn from established habits of speech. If the right idea occurs to us at the right moment, dreams of this kind can be solved wholly or in part without any statement from the dreamer at all.

A lady, a friend of mine, has the following dream: *She is at the opera. It is a Wagner performance that has gone on until 7:45 in the morning. In the orchestra stalls and the pit there are tables, where people are eating and drinking. Her cousin and his young wife, just back from their honeymoon, sit beside her at one of these tables, and next to them sits a member of the aristocracy. The idea about him is that the young wife has brought him back from her wedding trip, quite openly, just as she might bring back a hat from her travels. In the middle of the stalls stands a high tower, topped by a platform enclosed by an iron railing. Up there stands the conductor, who has the features of Hans Richter. He keeps running back and forth behind the railing, sweating terribly, and from this position he conducts the orchestra, which is arranged around the base of the tower. She herself sits in a box with a woman friend (someone I know). Her youngest sister tries to hand her a large piece of coal up from the stalls, with the idea that she had not known it would last so long and that by now she must be terribly cold.* (It was somewhat as if the boxes had to be heated during the long performance.)

The dream is senseless enough, although its situation is well developed: the tower in the middle of the stalls from which the conductor leads the orchestra, and above all the coal that her sister hands up to her. I deliberately asked for no analysis of this dream. Knowing something of the dreamer's personal circumstances, I was able to interpret parts of it on my own. I knew that she had once had warm feelings for a musician whose career had been cut short by insanity. I therefore decided to take the tower in the stalls verbally. It then became clear that the man she wished to see in Hans Richter's place towered above all the other members of the orchestra. The tower must therefore be described as a composite image formed by juxtaposition. With its pedestal it represents the man's greatness, but with its railing at the top, behind which he runs about like a prisoner or a caged animal (an allusion to the unfortunate man's name), it represents his later fate. "Lunatic tower" is perhaps the phrase in which both thoughts might have met.

Having discovered the dream's method of representation, we may try the same key on its second apparent absurdity, the coal her sister hands her. "Coal" must mean "secret love":

> "No coal, no fire so hotly glows
> As the secret love which no one knows."

She and her friend remain seated, while her younger sister, who still has prospects of marriage, hands the coal up to her "because she did not know it would last so long." The dream does not say what would last so long. In retelling it we would supply "the performance," but in the dream we must take the sentence as it stands, recognize it as ambiguous, and add "until she marries." The interpretation "secret love" is then confirmed by the cousin who sits with his wife in the stalls, and by the open love affair attributed to her. The contrasts between secret love and open love, between the dreamer's fire and the young wife's coldness, dominate the dream. And here, once again, a person "in a high position" appears as a middle term linking the aristocrat and the musician who had once been entitled to high hopes.

This discussion has finally brought to light a third factor, whose share in transforming the dream-thoughts into the dream-content should not be regarded as trivial. It is the regard for presentability (in German, *Darstellbarkeit*) in the particular psychic material the dream uses: fitness for representation, chiefly through visual images. Among the various subsidiary ideas attached to the essential dream-thoughts, the dream prefers the one that allows visual representation. The dream-work does not hesitate to recast a rigid thought promptly into another verbal form, even a less usual one, so long as that form makes dramatization possible and so relieves the psychological strain of constricted thinking. Pouring the content of a thought into a new mold in this way can also serve the work of condensation, establishing connections with another thought that would not otherwise exist. That other thought may itself have changed its original expression beforehand in order to meet these connections halfway.

Given the part that puns, quotations, songs, and proverbs play in the mental life of educated people, we would fully expect disguises of this sort to be used with extraordinary frequency. For a few kinds of material, a universally applicable dream symbolism has been established on the basis of commonly known allusions and equivalents. Much of this symbolism, moreover, the dream shares with the psychoneuroses, and with legends and popular customs.

Indeed, on closer inspection we must recognize that in using this method of substitution the dream is generally doing nothing original. To reach its goal, which in this case is the possibility of dramatization without interference from the censor, it simply follows paths already laid down in unconscious thought. It favors those transformations of the suppressed material that can also become conscious in the form of wit and allusion, and with which all the fantasies of neurotics are filled. Here, all at once, we come to understand Scherner's method of dream interpretation, whose essential truth I have defended elsewhere. The fancy's preoccupation with one's own body is by no means peculiar to the dream or characteristic of it alone. My analyses have shown me that it occurs regularly in the unconscious thought of neurotics, and that it goes back to sexual curiosity, which in the adolescent boy or girl is directed toward the genitals of the opposite sex, or even of the same sex. But, as Scherner and Volkelt very aptly point out, the house is not the only group of ideas used to symbolize the body, whether in the dream or in the unconscious fantasies of neurosis. I do know some patients who have held steadily to an architectural symbolism for the body and the genitals (sexual interest certainly extends far beyond the external genital organs). For them, posts and pillars signify legs, as in the Song of Songs; every gate suggests a bodily opening, a "hole"; every water main suggests the urinary apparatus; and so on. But the groups of associations drawn from plant life and from the kitchen are chosen just as eagerly to conceal sexual images. In the case of plants, ordinary language, the product of fanciful comparisons reaching back to the most ancient times, has prepared the way abundantly: the "vineyard" of the Lord, the "seed," the "garden" of the maiden in the Song of Songs. The ugliest as well as the most intimate details of sexual life may be dreamed of in seemingly harmless allusions to cooking, and the symptoms of hysteria become practically unintelligible if we forget that sexual symbolism can hide behind the most commonplace and inconspicuous things, which make its best hiding place. That some neurotic children cannot bear the sight of blood or raw meat, that they vomit at the sight of eggs and noodles, and that the fear of snakes, natural to human beings, becomes monstrously exaggerated in neurotics: all of this has a definite sexual meaning. Wherever the neurosis uses a disguise of this sort, it walks the paths once trodden by all of humanity in the early ages of civilization, paths whose existence is still attested today by habits of speech, superstitions, and customs.

Here I insert the flower dream of a woman patient that I promised earlier, in which I have italicized everything that is to be interpreted sexually. For the dreamer, this lovely dream seemed to lose all its charm once it had been interpreted.

(a) Preliminary dream: *She goes into the kitchen to the two maids and scolds them for taking so long to prepare "a little bite of food." She also sees a great many coarse dishes standing in the kitchen, turned upside down so that the water can drain off them, and piled in a heap.* Later addition: *The two maids go to fetch water and have to step, as it were, into a river that comes up into the house or into the yard.*

(b) Main dream: *She is climbing down from a high place, over railings or fences of a curious construction, joined together into large squares and made up of a mass of little squares. It is really not meant for climbing; she is worried about finding a place to put her foot, and she is glad that her dress does not catch anywhere and that she stays so respectable as she goes. She is also carrying a large bough in her hand, really the branch of a tree, thickly covered with red blossoms; it has many branches and spreads out. Connected with it is the idea of cherry blossoms, but they look like camellias in full bloom, which of course do not grow on trees. As she climbs down she first has one, then suddenly two, and later only one again. By the time she reaches the bottom, the lower blossoms have already largely fallen off. Now that she is at the bottom, she sees a porter who is combing (as she would like to put it) just such a tree, that is, plucking thick tufts of hair from it, which hang from it like moss. Other workmen have cut off such boughs in a garden and thrown them into the street, where they lie about, so that many people take some. But she asks whether that is right, whether anyone may take one. In the garden stands a young man, someone she knows who is not a member of her family, and she goes up to him to ask how such boughs could be transplanted into her own garden. He embraces her; she resists and asks what he means by it, whether it is permissible to embrace her like that. He says there is nothing wrong in it, that it is allowed. He then offers to go with her into the other garden to show her how the transplanting is done, and he says something to her that she does not quite understand: "Besides, three meters" (later she says square meters) "or three fathoms of ground are missing." It seems as though the man wanted something from her in return for his kindness, as though he meant to compensate himself in her garden, as though he wanted to get around some law or other and gain some advantage from it without doing her any harm. She does not know whether he actually shows her anything.*

I must mention one more series of associations that frequently conceals sexual meaning both in dreams and in the neuroses: the series connected with changing one's residence. "To move house" is readily replaced by "to remove," an ambiguous expression that can also refer to clothing. If the dream also contains a "lift," or elevator, one may think of the verb "to lift," and hence of lifting up one's clothing.

I naturally have an abundance of such material, but reporting it would take us too far into the discussion of neurotic conditions. Everything points to the same conclusion: we need not assume any special symbolizing activity of the mind in the formation of dreams. On the contrary, the dream makes use of symbolizations already present, ready-made, in unconscious thought, because these better satisfy the requirements of dream formation, both through their fitness for dramatization and, above all, through their freedom from the censor.

### (e) Examples—Arithmetic and Speech in the Dream

Before assigning the fourth of the factors governing dream formation to its proper place, I shall cite several examples from my collection of dreams. Their purpose is partly to illustrate how the three factors already known to us work together, and partly to supply proof for assertions made so far without demonstration, or to draw irrefutable conclusions from them. In the account of the dream-work given above, I found it very difficult to support my conclusions with examples. An example for a particular thesis is convincing only when considered within a full dream interpretation. Torn from its context, it loses its significance; yet a dream interpretation, even a far from exhaustive one, soon grows so long that it obscures the thread of the argument it was meant to illustrate. This technical reason may excuse me for now mixing together all sorts of things that have nothing in common except their bearing on the preceding chapter.

We shall first consider a few examples of very peculiar or unusual methods of representation in dreams. A lady dreams the following: *A servant girl is standing on a ladder as though to clean the windows, and she has with her a chimpanzee and a gorilla cat (later corrected to angora cat). She throws the animals at the dreamer; the chimpanzee snuggles up to her, and she finds this disgusting.* This dream has achieved its purpose by the simplest possible means: it has taken a figure of speech literally and represented it according to the meaning of its words. "Ape," like animal names in general, is a term of abuse, and the situation in the dream means nothing more than "hurling insults." The same collection will soon supply further examples of this simple device.

Another dream proceeds in a very similar way: *A woman with a child whose skull is conspicuously deformed; the dreamer has heard that the child came to be this way because of its position in the mother's womb. The doctor says the skull could be given a better shape by compression, but that this would harm the brain. She thinks that because it is a boy, he will not suffer so much from the deformity.* This dream contains a plastic, three-dimensional representation of the concept "childhood impressions," which the dreamer had heard about in the course of explanations concerning her treatment.

In the following example the dream-work takes a different route. The dream contains a memory of an outing to the Hilmteich, a lake near Graz: *There is a terrible storm outside; a wretched hotel; water is dripping from the walls, and the beds are damp.* (The last part of the content is expressed less directly than I have put it.) The dream signifies "superfluous." The abstract idea in the dream-thoughts is first made ambiguous by a certain straining of language: it has perhaps been replaced by "overflowing," or by "fluid" and "super-fluid," and then represented by an accumulation of similar impressions. Water inside, water outside, water in the beds in the form of damp: everything fluid and "super" fluid. That the dream pays much less attention to the spelling of words than to their sound need not surprise us when we recall that rhyme enjoys the same liberties.

Language has at its disposal a great many words that were originally meant in a pictorial and concrete sense but are now used in a faded, abstract one, and in other cases this has made it very easy for the dream to represent its thoughts. The dream need only restore to such words their full meaning, or trace their development a short way back. For example, a man dreams that a friend, struggling to get out of a very tight place, calls on him for help. The analysis shows that the tight place is a hole, and that the dream is symbolically using the very words he had said to his friend: "Be careful, or you'll get yourself into a hole." Another dreamer climbs a mountain from which he has an extraordinarily broad view. He is identifying himself with his brother, who edits a "review" concerned with relations with the Far East.

Collecting such methods of representation and arranging them according to the principles on which they rest would be a separate undertaking. Some of these representations are quite witty, and give the impression that no one would ever have guessed them had the dreamer not reported them himself.

1. A man dreams that he is asked for a name, which he cannot recall. He himself explains that this means: "It doesn't occur to me in the dream."

2. A woman patient tells of a dream in which all the people involved were especially big. "That means," she adds, "that it must be about an episode from my early childhood, because at that time all grown-ups naturally seemed immensely big to me."

In other dreams, the move back into childhood is expressed differently, by translating time into space. The people and scenes in question appear as though at a great distance, at the end of a long road, or as though seen through the wrong end of a pair of opera glasses.

3. A man who in waking life tends toward abstract and indefinite expressions, but who is otherwise well endowed with wit, dreams, in a certain context, that he is at a railway station as a train is coming in. But then the station platform moves toward the train, which stands still: an absurd reversal of the real state of affairs. This detail, again, is nothing more than a signal reminding us that something else in the dream should be turned around. The analysis of the same dream brings back the memory of a picture book in which men were shown standing on their heads and walking on their hands.

4. On another occasion the same dreamer reports a short dream that almost recalls the technique of a rebus, a puzzle in which words are spelled out by pictures. *His uncle gives him a kiss in an automobile.* He immediately adds the interpretation, which I would never have found: it means *autoerotism*. This could have been made as a joke in waking life.

The dream-work often manages to represent very awkward material, such as proper names, by forcing into use extremely far-fetched references. In one of my dreams the elder Brücke has given me a task. I prepare a specimen, and skim something from it that looks like crumpled tinfoil. (I will return to this later.) The word corresponding to this image, which was not easy to find, is "stanniol," the old term for tinfoil, and I now realize that what I have in mind is the name of the author Stannius, which appeared on a treatise on the nervous system of fishes that I regarded with awe in my youth. The first scientific task my teacher ever gave me did in fact concern the nervous system of a fish, the Ammocoetes, the larval form of the lamprey. That name, obviously, could never have been rendered in a picture puzzle, the kind of rebus in which words are spelled out through images.

I should not leave out a dream with a curious content, which is remarkable also as a child's dream and is very easily explained by analysis. A lady relates: "I remember that as a child I dreamed over and over that the dear Lord had a pointed paper hat on his head. At table they often made me wear just such a hat, so that I could not look at the other children's plates and see how much of a particular dish each of them had been given. Since I have learned that God is omniscient, the dream means that I know everything in spite of the hat they make me wear."

The nature of the dream-work, and the way it handles its material, the dream thoughts, can be shown very instructively through the numbers and calculations that occur in dreams. Superstition, moreover, attaches special significance to numbers in dreams. I shall therefore give a few more examples of this kind from my own collection.

I. The following comes from the dream of a lady shortly before the end of her treatment:

*She wants to pay for something or other; her daughter takes 3 florins and 65 kreuzer from her purse; but the mother says: "What are you doing? It only costs 21 kreuzer."*

This fragment was immediately intelligible to me, without further explanation, from what I knew of the dreamer's circumstances. The lady was a foreigner who had placed her daughter in a school in Vienna, and she could continue her treatment with me only as long as her daughter remained in the city. In three weeks the daughter's school year would end, and with it the treatment. On the day before the dream, the head of the school had urged her to consider letting the child stay on for another year. She had evidently carried this suggestion further and concluded that, in that case, she could also continue her treatment for one more year. This is what the dream refers to, for a year equals 365 days, and the three weeks remaining before the close of the school year and of the treatment equal 21 days (though the hours of treatment are not that many). The numbers that referred to time in the dream thoughts are given money values in the dream, and not without a deeper meaning, since "time is money." In the Austrian currency of the day, a florin was worth 100 kreuzer, so 365 kreuzer are exactly 3 florins and 65 kreuzer. The smallness of the sums appearing in the dream is a self-evident wish-fulfillment: the wish has reduced the cost of both the treatment and the year's schooling.

II. The numbers in another dream involve more complicated relations. A young woman, though one who has already been married for several years, learns that an acquaintance of about her own age, Elsie L., has just become engaged. She then dreams:

*She is sitting in the theater with her husband, and one side of the orchestra stalls is entirely unoccupied. Her husband tells her that Elsie L. and her fiancé had also wanted to go, but had only been able to get poor seats, three for 1 florin and 50 kreuzer, and of course they could not take those. She thinks they did not lose much by it.*

Where do the 1 florin and 50 kreuzer come from? From an event of the previous day that is genuinely trivial. The dreamer's sister-in-law had received 150 florins as a present from her husband and had promptly got rid of them by buying some jewelry. Note that 150 florins is a hundred times 1 florin and 50 kreuzer. And where does the 3 attached to the theater seats come from? There is only one association for it: the bride is exactly that many months, three, younger than the dreamer. The solution of the dream comes from asking about the detail of one side of the orchestra remaining empty. This is an undisguised allusion to a small incident that had given her husband good reason to tease her. She had decided to go to the theater one week and had taken care to buy tickets several days in advance, paying the extra fee charged for advance booking. When they arrived, they found one side of the house nearly empty; she had certainly had no need to hurry.

I shall now put the dream thoughts in place of the dream: "It really was nonsense to marry so early; there was no need for me to be in such a hurry. From Elsie L.'s case I can see that I would have got a husband just the same, and one a hundred times better (husband, sweetheart, treasure), if I had only waited (the antithesis to her sister-in-law's haste). I could have bought three such men with the money (the dowry!)."

Our attention is drawn to the fact that the numbers in this dream have changed their meanings and relations far more than in the previous example. The transforming and distorting activity of the dream has been greater here, and we interpret this to mean that these dream thoughts had to overcome a particularly great amount of inner psychic resistance before they could be represented. Nor should we overlook that the dream contains an absurd element: two people taking three seats. We anticipate our later discussion of absurdity in dreams when we observe that this absurd detail of the dream content is meant to represent the most strongly emphasized element of the dream thoughts: "It was nonsense to marry so early." The number 3, which belongs to a quite subordinate relation between the two women being compared (their three months' difference in age), has thus been skillfully employed to produce the nonsense the dream required. And the reduction of the actual 150 florins to 1 florin and 50 kreuzer corresponds to the disdain for her husband contained in the dreamer's suppressed thoughts.

III. Another example displays the arithmetical powers of the dream, which have brought dreams into such disrepute. A man dreams:

*He is sitting at the home of the B——s (a family he knew in earlier years) and says: "It was nonsense of you not to let me marry Amy." Then he asks the girl: "How old are you?" She answers: "I was born in 1882." "Ah, then you are 28 years old."*

Since the dream took place in 1898, this is obviously poor arithmetic, and if there were no other way of explaining it, the dreamer's inability to calculate might be compared to that of a patient suffering from general paralysis, the brain disease whose sufferers are notorious for failing at the simplest sums. My patient, however, was one of those men who think constantly about every woman they see. For several months, the person who regularly followed him in my office was a young lady whom he used to meet, about whom he frequently asked, and toward whom he was very eager to be polite. It was this lady whose age he estimated at 28. So much for the result of the apparent calculation. But 1882 was the year in which he had married. He had been unable to resist striking up conversations with the two women he met at my house, two girls who were by no means young and who took turns opening the door for him; and since he did not find them very responsive, he had explained it to himself by supposing that they probably regarded him as an elderly, "settled" gentleman.

IV. For another number dream with its interpretation, one distinguished by its obvious determination, or rather over-determination, I am indebted to B. Dattner:

My landlord, a policeman in the municipal service, dreamed that he was standing at his post in the street, which was the realization of a wish. The inspector then came up to him, wearing on his gorget, the metal plate at the collar of his uniform, the numbers 22 and 62, or 26; at any rate there were many twos on it. When the dreamer recounted the dream, he immediately split the number 2262 into parts, which indicates that the components have separate meanings. It occurred to him that the day before, while on duty, he and his colleagues had been discussing their length of service. The occasion had been an inspector who had been pensioned at 62. The dreamer had completed only 22 years of service and still needed 2 years and 2 months to qualify for a pension of 90 percent. The dream first shows him the fulfillment of a long-cherished wish, the rank of inspector. The superior with 2262 on his collar is himself; he takes care to do his duty on the street, which is another favored wish; he has served his 2 years and 2 months and can now retire from the service on full pension, like the 62-year-old inspector.

If we keep these examples in mind, along with similar ones still to come, we may say that the dream activity does not calculate at all, whether correctly or incorrectly. It merely joins together, in the form of a calculation, numbers that occur in the dream thoughts and that can serve as allusions to material incapable of being represented directly. It thus uses numbers as material for expressing its purposes in exactly the same way that it uses names and speeches, which are presentations of words.

For the dream activity cannot compose a new speech. However many speeches and replies may occur in dreams, whether sensible or absurd in themselves, analysis always shows that the dream has merely taken from the dream thoughts fragments of speeches that were actually delivered or heard, and has treated them with complete arbitrariness. It has not only torn them from their context and mutilated them, taking up one piece and discarding another, but has also joined them together in new ways, so that a speech which seems coherent in the dream breaks apart into three or four sections in the course of analysis. In this new use of the words, the dream has often set aside the meaning they had in the dream thoughts and drawn an entirely new meaning from them. On closer inspection, the more distinct and compact components of a dream speech can be distinguished from others that serve as connectives and have probably been supplied afterward, much as we fill in omitted letters and syllables when we read. A dream speech therefore has the structure of breccia, the kind of rock in which larger fragments of different materials are held together by a solidified cementing mass.

Strictly speaking, this description holds only for those speeches in the dream that have something of the sensory character of speech and are experienced as "speeches." The others, which have not been felt as though heard or spoken, and which carry no accompanying auditory or motor emphasis in the dream, are simply thoughts of the kind that occur in our waking mental activity, and they pass unchanged into many dreams. Our reading also appears to furnish an abundant and not easily traceable source of material for speeches, though this material is of an indifferent nature. Everything, however, that appears conspicuously in the dream as a speech can be traced to real speeches that the dreamer himself has made or heard.

We have already met examples explaining such dream speeches in the analyses of dreams cited for other purposes. Here is one example in place of many, all of which lead to the same conclusion.

*A large courtyard in which corpses are being cremated. The dreamer says: "I'm leaving, I can't look at this." (Not a distinct speech.) Then he meets two butcher boys and asks: "Well, did it taste good?" One of them answers: "No, it wasn't good." As though it had been human flesh.*

The harmless occasion for this dream is as follows. After having supper with his wife, the dreamer pays a visit to his neighbor, a worthy but by no means appetizing woman. The hospitable old lady is just finishing her evening meal and presses him to taste it (in place of the word "presses," men jokingly use a compound word with a sexual meaning). He declines, saying he has no appetite. "Go on, you can manage a little more," or something of the kind. So the dreamer is forced to taste and praise what is offered: "But that's good!" When he is alone again with his wife, he grumbles about the neighbor's insistence and about the quality of the food he has tasted. "I can't stand the sight of it," a phrase that does not appear as an actual speech even in the dream, is a thought referring to the physical charms of the lady who offered him the food, and it would be translated to mean that he does not want to look at her.

More instructive will be the analysis of another dream, which I cite here for the sake of the very distinct speech that forms its nucleus, though I shall explain it fully only when we come to consider emotions in dreams. I dream very distinctly:

*I have gone to Bruecke's laboratory at night, and on hearing a soft knock at the door, I open it to the late Professor Fleischl, who enters with several strangers, says a few words, and sits down at his table.*

Then follows a second dream:

*My friend Fl. has come to Vienna in July without attracting much attention; I meet him on the street in conversation with my late friend P., and I go somewhere or other with the two of them. They sit down facing each other as though at a small table, while I sit at its narrow end, facing them. Fl. speaks of his sister and says: "In three-quarters of an hour she was dead," and then something like: "That is the threshold." Since P. does not understand him, Fl. turns to me and asks how much I have told P. about his affairs. At this, seized by strange emotions, I want to tell Fl. that P. (cannot possibly know anything, because he) is not alive. But, noticing the mistake myself, I say: "Non vixit." Then I look at P. searchingly, and under my gaze he grows pale and blurred, his eyes a sickly blue, and at last he dissolves. I rejoice greatly at this; I now understand that Ernst Fleischl, too, was only an apparition, a revenant, and I find it entirely possible for such a person to exist only as long as one wishes it, and to be made to vanish by another person's wish.*

This beautiful dream combines so many of the problematic features of dream content that I should like, "by my life," to give a complete solution to them all. There is the criticism exercised within the dream itself, in that I notice my own mistake of having said "Non vixit," "he did not live," instead of "Non vivit," "he is not alive." There is the unconstrained dealing with dead persons whom the dream itself declares to be dead. There is the absurdity of my inference and the intense satisfaction it gives me. But in reality I am incapable of doing what I do in the dream, namely, sacrificing such dear persons to my ambition. With every disclosure of the true meaning of the dream, which I know well, I should have been put to shame. I am therefore content to select a few of the dream's elements for interpretation, some here and others later on.

The scene in which I annihilate P. with a glance forms the center of the dream. His eyes turn strange and eerily blue, and then he dissolves. This scene is an unmistakable copy of one I actually experienced. I was a demonstrator at the Physiological Institute, with duties beginning in the early morning hours, and Bruecke learned that I had several times arrived late at the student laboratory. So one morning he came punctually for the opening of the class and waited for me. What he said to me was brief and to the point, but the words did not matter at all. What overwhelmed me were the terrible blue eyes with which he looked at me and before which I melted away, just as P. does in the dream, for P. has exchanged roles with him, much to my relief. Anyone who remembers the eyes of the great master, which remained wonderfully beautiful into old age, and who has ever seen him angry, can easily imagine the emotions of the young offender on that occasion.

For a long time, however, I could not account for the "Non vixit" with which I pronounce sentence in the dream, until I remembered that these two words had such great distinctness in the dream not because they were heard or spoken, but because they were seen. Then I knew at once where they came from. On the pedestal of the statue of Emperor Joseph in the Hofburg in Vienna, one may read the following beautiful words:

*Saluti patriae vixit*
*non diu sed totus.*

("For the welfare of his country he lived, not long, but wholly.")

From this inscription I had taken something that suited the one hostile train of thought among the dream thoughts, and that was now meant to say: "That fellow counts for nothing; he is not even alive." I now also recalled that I had the dream a few days after the unveiling of the memorial to Fleischl in the arcades of the university. On that occasion I had once again seen Brücke's statue, and I must have thought with regret, unconsciously, that my highly gifted friend P., with his great devotion to science, had forfeited by his premature death his rightful claim to a statue in those halls. So in the dream I erected this memorial to him. My friend P.'s first name is Joseph.

By the rules of dream interpretation, I would still not be justified in replacing *non vivit* ("he is not alive"), which is what I need, with *non vixit* ("he did not live"), which the memory of the Joseph monument has placed at my disposal. Something now draws my attention to the fact that in this dream scene two trains of thought about my friend P. converge, one hostile and the other friendly. The first lies on the surface and the second is concealed, yet both are expressed in the same words: *non vixit*. Because my friend P. has served science well, I raise a statue to him; but because he is guilty of an evil wish, which is expressed at the end of the dream, I annihilate him. I have constructed here a sentence with a peculiar resonance, and some model must have influenced me. But where might I find a similar antithesis, a parallel of this kind between two opposing attitudes toward the same person, each claiming to be fully valid and each trying not to trespass on the other? Such a parallel occurs in only one place, but there it leaves a deep impression on the reader. It is the speech in which Brutus justifies himself in Shakespeare's *Julius Caesar*: "As Caesar loved me, I weep for him; as he was fortunate, I rejoice at it; as he was valiant, I honour him; but, as he was ambitious, I slew him." Is this not the same sentence structure, and the same contrast of thought, that I have uncovered in the dream thought? In the dream, then, I am playing Brutus. If only I could find in the dream thoughts one more trace confirming this surprising sidelong connection! The following detail may be such a trace: *my friend comes to Vienna in July*. Nothing in reality supports this detail. As far as I know, my friend has never been in Vienna in July. But the month of July is named after Julius Caesar, and so it might well supply the needed allusion to the intermediate thought that I am playing the part of Brutus.

Oddly enough, I once really did play Brutus. When I was a boy of fourteen, I performed the scene between Brutus and Caesar from Schiller's poems before an audience of children. My partner was my nephew, who was a year older than I and had come to us from England. He too was a *revenant*, a ghost returning from the past, for in him I recognized the playmate of my earliest childhood. Until the end of my third year we had been inseparable. We had loved each other and fought with each other, and, as I have already suggested, this childhood relationship has continually shaped my later feelings toward people my own age. My nephew John has since found many incarnations, each of which has revived now one aspect, now another, of this character, which is so indelibly fixed in my unconscious memory. At times he must have treated me very badly, and I must have stood up bravely to my tyrant, for in later years I was often told of the brief speech with which I defended myself when my father, who was John's grandfather, took me to task: "I hit him because he hit me." This childhood scene must be what causes *non vivit* to branch off into *non vixit*. In the language of later childhood, hitting is called *wichsen*, a word whose sound echoes *vixit*. Literally it means to smear with shoe polish, and from that it comes to mean to tan someone's hide, to thrash. The dream-work does not hesitate to exploit connections of this kind. My hostility toward my friend P. has little basis in reality. He was far superior to me, and he might therefore have been a new edition of my childhood playmate. This hostility can surely be traced to my complicated relationship with John in our infancy. I shall, however, return to this dream later.

### (f) Absurd Dreams—Intellectual Performances in the Dream

In interpreting dreams so far, we have come upon absurdity in the dream content so often that we can no longer put off investigating its cause and meaning. We recall, of course, that the absurdity of dreams has given the opponents of dream research their chief argument for regarding the dream as nothing more than the meaningless product of a diminished and fragmentary mental activity.

I begin with examples in which the absurdity of the dream content is merely apparent and vanishes as soon as the dream is examined more closely. There are a few dreams that concern the dreamer's dead father, and at first one is inclined to think this is a matter of chance.

I. Here is the dream of a patient who had lost his father six years earlier:

*A terrible accident has befallen his father. He was traveling on the night train when it derailed. The seats were driven together, and his head was crushed from side to side. The dreamer sees him lying in bed with a wound above his left eyebrow, running vertically. The dreamer is surprised that his father has met with a misfortune, since he is already dead, as the dreamer adds when telling the dream. His father's eyes are so clear.*

By the standards prevailing among critics of dreams, this content would have to be explained as follows. At first, while the dreamer pictures his father's accident, he has forgotten that his father has been in his grave for years. As the dream goes on, this memory comes to life and makes him surprised at his own dream even while he is still dreaming it. Analysis, however, shows that such explanations are entirely futile. The dreamer had commissioned an artist to make a bust of his father and had inspected it two days before the dream. It is this bust that seems to him to have met with an accident. The sculptor had never seen the father and was working from photographs supplied to him. On the very day before the dream, the devoted son had sent an old family servant to the studio to see whether he would reach the same verdict on the marble head, namely that it had turned out too narrow from side to side, from temple to temple.

Then comes the mass of memories that helped to form this dream. Whenever business worries or family troubles harassed him, the dreamer's father had a habit of pressing his temples with both hands, as if trying to compress a head that seemed to be growing too large for him. When the dreamer was four years old, he was present when a pistol went off by accident and blackened his father's eyes (*his eyes are so clear*). During his life, whenever the father was thoughtful or sad, a deep wrinkle appeared at the spot where the dream shows the wound. In the dream the wrinkle is replaced by a wound, and this points to the dream's second source. The dreamer had taken a photograph of his little daughter. The plate slipped from his hand, and when he picked it up it showed a crack that ran like a vertical furrow across the forehead and reached as far as the curve of the eye socket. He could not shake off his superstitious forebodings at the time, for on the day before his mother's death a photographic plate bearing her likeness had cracked as he was handling it.

The absurdity of the dream is therefore merely the result of a carelessness in verbal expression that does not bother to distinguish the bust and the photograph from the original. We are all used to saying of a picture, "Don't you think Father has come out well?" Of course, the appearance of absurdity in this dream could easily have been avoided. If one were permitted to judge from a single case, one might be tempted to say that this semblance of absurdity is admitted, or even desired.

II. Here is another, very similar example from my own dreams. I lost my father in 1896.

*After his death my father has been politically active among the Magyars and has united them into a political body. Along with this I see a small, indistinct picture: a crowd of people, as in the Reichstag, and a person standing on one or two benches, with others around him. I remember that on his deathbed he looked very much like Garibaldi, and I am glad that this promise has really come true.*

This is certainly absurd enough. I dreamed it at the time when parliamentary obstruction had brought Hungary into a state of lawlessness. The deliberate stalling of business in parliament had halted the work of government, and the Hungarians were going through the crisis from which Koloman Széll rescued them. The scene in the dream consists of very small pictures, and this trivial circumstance helps to explain the element. Our thoughts are ordinarily represented visually in pictures that strike us as life-size. My dream picture, however, reproduces a woodcut printed in the text of an illustrated history of Austria. It shows Maria Theresa at the Diet of Pressburg, in the famous scene of "*Moriamur pro rege nostro*" ("Let us die for our king"). In the dream my father, like Maria Theresa, stands surrounded by the crowd. But he stands on one or two benches, and so he resembles a judge on the bench. (*He has united them*: here the link is the phrase "We shall need no judge.") Those of us who stood around my father's deathbed actually did notice that he looked very much like Garibaldi. He had a rise in temperature after death, and his cheeks glowed redder and redder. Here we involuntarily continue the lines: "And behind him, in shadowy radiance, lay that which subdues us all—the common."

This elevation of our thoughts prepares us to deal with that very "common" thing. The rise in temperature after death corresponds to the words "*after his death*" in the dream content. The most agonizing of his sufferings had been a complete paralysis of the intestines, an obstruction, which set in during his last weeks. All sorts of disrespectful thoughts are attached to this. A man my own age had lost his father while still at the Gymnasium, and I had been deeply moved at the time and offered him my friendship. He once told me mockingly about the distress of a female relative whose father had died in the street and been carried home. When the body was undressed, it turned out that the bowels had emptied at the moment of death or soon after. The dead man's daughter was profoundly unhappy that this ugly detail should stain her memory of her father. We have now reached the wish embodied in this dream. Who would not wish to stand pure and great before his children after death? And what has become of the dream's absurdity? It appeared only because the dream faithfully represented a perfectly acceptable figure of speech, one in which we are used to overlooking whatever absurdity exists between its parts. Here too we cannot deny that the semblance of absurdity is wanted and has been deliberately produced.

III. In the next example I can catch the dream-work in the act of deliberately manufacturing an absurdity for which the subject matter gives no occasion at all. It comes from the dream I had after meeting Count Thun before my vacation trip. *I am riding in a one-horse carriage and tell the driver to take me to a railway station. "Of course I cannot drive with you on the railway line itself," I say, after the driver has raised an objection, as though I had worn him out. At the same time it seems as though I had already driven with him a distance that one usually covers by train.* Analysis gives the following explanation for this confused and senseless story.

During the day I had hired a one-horse carriage to take me to an out-of-the-way street in Dornbach. The driver did not know the way and simply kept driving on, as such good people will, until I noticed and showed him the way, not sparing him a few mocking remarks. A line of thought led from this driver to the aristocratic personage I was to meet later. For the present I will remark only that what strikes us middle-class plebeians about the aristocracy is their fondness for taking the driver's seat. Does not Count Thun steer the Austrian coach of state? The next sentence of the dream refers to my brother, whom I identify with the driver of the one-horse carriage. This year I had refused to take the trip through Italy with him (*"Of course I cannot drive with you on the railway line itself"*). This refusal was a kind of punishment for his habitual complaint that I usually wore him out on these trips, which enters the dream unchanged, by rushing him from place to place and making him see too many fine things in a single day. That evening my brother had gone with me to the station, but shortly before we arrived he had jumped out at the state railway division of the Western Station in order to catch a train to Purkersdorf. I remarked that he could stay with me a little longer, since he did not travel to Purkersdorf on the state railway but on the Western Railway. That is why in the dream I rode in the carriage a distance that one usually covers by train. In reality it was just the opposite. I told my brother, "The distance you would ride on the state railway, you could ride in my company on the Western Railway." The whole confusion of the dream is thus produced by my putting the word "carriage" in place of "state railway." This substitution does good work, admittedly, in bringing the driver and my brother together. I then find in the dream a piece of nonsense that my explanation hardly seems to clear up, and that almost contradicts my earlier remark (*"Of course I cannot drive with you on the railway line itself"*). But since I have no reason whatever to confuse the state railway with the one-horse carriage, I must have deliberately shaped the whole puzzling story in the dream in this way.

But with what intention? We shall now learn what the absurdity in a dream signifies, and what motives admitted or created it. In the present case the mystery is solved as follows. In the dream I needed something absurd and incomprehensible in connection with "driving" (*Fahren*), because the dream thoughts contained a certain judgment that required representation. One evening, at the home of the hospitable and clever lady who appears in another scene of the same dream as the "hostess," I heard two riddles that I could not solve. The rest of the company already knew the answers, and so I cut a rather ludicrous figure as I tried and failed to find them. Both were plays on words. The first turned on *Vorfahren*, which literally means "to drive up in front" but also means "forefathers" or "ancestors." The second turned on *Nachkommen*, which literally means "to come after" or "to comply" but also means "offspring." They ran as follows:

*The coachman does it*
*At the master's behest;*
*Everyone has it,*
*In the grave does it rest.*
(Ancestry.)

It was confusing to find that half of the second riddle was identical with the first:

*The coachman does it*
*At the master's behest;*
*Not everyone has it,*
*In the cradle does it rest.*
(Offspring.)

I had seen Count Thun drive up (*vorfahren*) in such a high and mighty fashion, and I had slipped into the mood of Beaumarchais's Figaro, who finds the only merit of aristocratic gentlemen in their having taken the trouble to be born (*Nachkommen*, to become offspring). For these reasons the two riddles became intermediate thoughts for the dream-work. Aristocrats are easily confused with coachmen, and in our country coachmen used to be called "brothers-in-law," so the work of condensation could bring my brother into the same representation. But the dream thought at work in the background was this: *It is nonsense to be proud of one's ancestors* (*Vorfahren*). *I would rather be an ancestor* (*Vorfahr*) *myself*. For the sake of this judgment, "It is nonsense," the dream contains nonsense. We can now also solve the last riddle in this obscure passage of the dream, namely that I have *already driven before* (*vorher gefahren*, *vorgefahren*) with the coachman.

A dream therefore becomes absurd when the judgment "That is nonsense" occurs among the elements of the dream thoughts, and in general when scorn and criticism are the motives of one of the unconscious trains of thought. Absurdity thus becomes one of the means by which the dream-work expresses contradiction. It also expresses contradiction by reversing a relation in the material between the dream thoughts and the dream content, and by making use of the sensation of being unable to move. But absurdity in a dream is not to be translated simply as "no." It is meant rather to reproduce the mood of the dream thoughts, which combines mockery and ridicule with contradiction. Only for this purpose does the dream-work produce anything ridiculous. Here again it turns a part of the latent content into a manifest form.

We have in fact already met a convincing example of the meaning of an absurd dream. This is the dream, interpreted without analysis, of the Wagner performance that lasts until 7:45 in the morning, with the orchestra conducted from a tower, and so on. It evidently means to say: *It is a crazy world and an insane society. The one who deserves something does not get it, and the one who cares nothing for it has it.* With this the dreamer means to compare her fate with her cousin's. Dreams about a dead father were the first to give us examples of absurdity, and this is by no means an accident. In them the conditions for creating absurd dreams are grouped together in a typical way. The father's authority provoked the child's criticism at an early age, and his strict demands led the child to watch especially closely for every weakness of the father's, as an excuse for its own failings. But the piety that surrounds the father's personality in our thoughts, especially after his death, strengthens the censorship that keeps this criticism from becoming conscious.

IV. Here is another absurd dream about a dead father:

*I receive a notice from the town council of my native city about the costs of a stay in the hospital in the year 1851, made necessary by an attack I suffered. I make fun of the matter, for in the first place I was not yet alive in 1851, and in the second place my father, to whom the notice might refer, is already dead. I go to him in the adjoining room, where he is lying on a bed, and tell him about it. To my astonishment he recalls that in that year, 1851, he was once drunk and had to be locked up, or confined. It was when he was working for the firm of T——. "So you drank too?" I ask. "You married soon afterward?" I calculate that I was born in 1856, which seems to me to follow immediately.*

In light of the preceding discussion, we shall read the insistence with which this dream parades its absurdities as a sure sign of an especially bitter and passionate dispute in the dream thoughts. It is all the more astonishing, then, that in this dream the dispute is carried on openly, and the father is named as the target of the satire. Such openness seems to contradict our assumption that a censor operates in the dream-work. We may explain it, however, by saying that the father here is only a figure placed in front of someone else. The real conflict is with another person, who appears in the dream through a single allusion. Usually a dream deals with rebellion against other people, and the father lies hidden behind them. Here the reverse is true. The father acts as a man of straw standing in for others, and so the dream dares to deal openly with a figure who is usually held sacred, because it knows for certain that he is not the one really meant.

We learn of this state of affairs by considering what occasioned the dream. It occurred after I had heard that an older colleague, whose judgment is considered infallible, had expressed disapproval and astonishment that one of my patients was then in his fifth year of psychoanalytic work with me. The opening sentences of the dream allude, under a thin disguise, to the fact that this colleague had for a time taken over duties that my father could no longer perform (expenses, hospital fees). When our friendly relations broke down, I was thrown into the same conflict of feelings that arises when father and son fall out, given the part the father plays and the functions he once fulfilled. The dream thoughts now bitterly resent the reproach that I am not making better progress, a reproach that extends from the treatment of this patient to other matters. Does this colleague know anyone who can get on faster? Does he not know that conditions of this kind are usually incurable and last a lifetime? What are four or five years compared with a whole life, especially when the treatment has made the patient's life so much easier?

The impression of absurdity in this dream arises largely because sentences from different parts of the dream thoughts are strung together without any reconciling transition. The sentence beginning *I go to him in the adjoining room* leaves the subject of the preceding sentences and faithfully reproduces the circumstances in which I told my father of my engagement. The dream is thus trying to remind me of the noble unselfishness the old man showed on that occasion, and to contrast it with the conduct of another, newer person. I now see that the dream is permitted to make fun of my father because the dream thoughts hold him up as an example to another man, in full recognition of his merits. It is in the nature of every censorship that it allows untruths to be told about forbidden things more readily than truths. The next sentence, in which my father remembers having once been drunk and locked up for it, likewise contains nothing that is actually true of my father. The person he covers here is no less important a figure than the great Meynert. I followed in his footsteps with deep veneration, and after a brief period of indulgence his attitude toward me turned into open hostility. The dream reminds me of his own statement that in his youth he had been addicted to chloroform and had had to enter a sanatorium for it. It also reminds me of a second experience with him, shortly before his death. I had carried on a bitter controversy with him in print about hysteria in men, whose existence he denied. When I visited him in his last illness and asked how he was, he dwelt on the details of his condition and he ended with the words: "You know, I have always been one of the prettiest cases of male hysteria." So, to my satisfaction and to my astonishment, he conceded the very thing he had resisted for so long and so stubbornly. But the fact that in this scene I can use my father to stand in for Meynert does not rest on the analogy that has been found between the two men. It rests instead on the slight but entirely adequate representation of a conditional sentence in the dream thoughts, which in full would read: "Of course, if I belonged to the second generation, if I were the son of a professor or a court councillor, I would have advanced more quickly." In the dream, accordingly, I turn my father into a court councillor and a professor. The most obvious and most irritating absurdity of the dream lies in its treatment of the date 1851, which seems to me scarcely distinguishable from 1856, as if a difference of five years meant nothing at all. Yet this is precisely the idea in the dream thoughts that demands expression. Four or five years: that is how long I enjoyed the support of the colleague mentioned at the outset. It is also how long I kept my fiancée waiting before I married her. And, by a coincidence the dream thoughts eagerly seize upon, it is also how long I am now keeping one of my best patients waiting for the completion of his cure. "What are five years?" the dream thoughts ask. "That is no time at all for me; it doesn't even count. I have time enough ahead of me, and just as what you refused to believe came true in the end, so I shall accomplish this too." Moreover, the number 51, once detached from the digits of the century, is determined in yet another way, and in the opposite sense, which is why it recurs in the dream. Fifty-one is an age at which a man seems especially exposed to danger. I have seen many of my colleagues die suddenly at that age, among them one who had been appointed to a professorship only a few days before, after waiting a long time for it.

V. Another absurd dream that plays with numbers runs as follows:

*One of my acquaintances, Mr. M., has been attacked in an essay by no less a figure than Goethe, and with justifiable vehemence, as we all agree. Mr. M. has naturally been crushed by this attack. He complains of it bitterly at a dinner party, but he says that his reverence for Goethe has not suffered from this personal experience. I try to find some explanation of the chronological relations, which seem improbable to me. Goethe died in 1832. Since his attack on M. must of course have taken place earlier, Mr. M. must have been a very young man at the time. It seems plausible to me that he was eighteen. But I do not know exactly what year it is at present, and so the whole calculation dissolves into obscurity. The attack, moreover, is contained in Goethe's well-known essay "Nature."*

We shall soon find a way to account for the nonsense of this dream. Mr. M., whom I had come to know at a dinner party, had recently asked me to examine his brother, who was showing signs of paralytic insanity, the progressive mental deterioration known as general paralysis.
