The suspicion proved correct. What made the visit painful was that the patient embarrassed his brother by bringing up the escapades of his youth when nothing in the conversation called for it. I had asked the patient to tell me the year of his birth, and had him perform several small calculations in order to bring out the weakness of his memory, tests he passed fairly well. I now see that in the dream I am behaving like a paralytic ("I do not know exactly what year it is at present"). Other material in the dream comes from another recent source. The editor of a medical journal, a friend of mine, had accepted for publication a very unfavorable, indeed a "crushing," review of the latest book by my friend Fl. of Berlin. The reviewer was very young and hardly competent to pass judgment. I felt I had the right to intervene, and took the editor to task. He sincerely regretted having accepted the review but would not promise to set matters right. I thereupon broke off relations with the journal, and in my letter of resignation expressed the hope that our personal friendship would not suffer from the incident. The third source of the dream is an account, still fresh in my memory at the time, that a female patient had given me of her brother's mental illness. He had fallen into a frenzy, crying "Nature, Nature!" The attending physicians believed the cry came from his reading of Goethe's beautiful essay and that it pointed to overwork in his study of natural philosophy. I thought rather of the sexual sense in which, in our part of the world, even less educated people use the word "nature," and the fact that the unfortunate man later mutilated his genitals seemed to show that I was not far wrong. He was eighteen years old when the frenzy struck.

If I add that my friend's book, the one so severely criticized ("One wonders whether the author is crazy or we are," another critic had remarked), deals with the chronological relations of life and traces the length of Goethe's life to a multiple of a number significant in biology, it will readily be granted that in the dream I am putting myself in my friend's place ("I try to find some explanation of the chronological relations"). But I behave like a paralytic, and the dream revels in absurdity. What this means, as the dream thoughts put it ironically, is: "Of course he is the fool, the lunatic, and you are the man of genius who knows better. But perhaps it is the other way around?" And this "other way around" is explicitly represented in the dream. Goethe has attacked the young man, which is absurd, whereas it is perfectly possible even today for a young fellow to attack the immortal Goethe; and I calculate from the year of Goethe's death, whereas I had the paralytic calculate from the year of his birth.

I have already promised, however, to show that every dream springs from egoistic motives. I must therefore account for the fact that in this dream I take up my friend's cause as my own and put myself in his place. My rational conviction in waking life would not be enough to make me do this. Now, the story of the eighteen-year-old patient and the various interpretations of his cry of "Nature" alludes to the way I have set myself against most physicians by asserting a sexual cause for the psychoneuroses. I may well say to myself: "The same kind of criticism your friend has met with, you will meet with too, and indeed have already met with to some extent." And so I may replace the "he" in the dream thoughts with "we": "Yes, you are right; we two are the fools." That it is my own cause at stake, *mea res agitur*, is clearly shown by the mention of Goethe's short and incomparably beautiful essay, for it was a public reading of that essay that led me to study natural science, at a time when I was still undecided about my future in the final year of the Gymnasium, the classical secondary school.

VI. I am also obliged to show that another dream, one in which my own ego does not appear, is egoistic. Earlier I mentioned a short dream in which Professor M. says, "My son, the myopic . . . ," and I stated that it was only a preliminary to another dream in which I play a part. Here is that main dream, omitted before, which challenges us to explain its absurd and unintelligible coinage of words.

*On account of some events or other in the city of Rome, it is necessary for the children to flee, and they do. The scene then shifts to a gate, a double gate in the antique style (the Porta Romana in Siena, as I realize while still dreaming). I am sitting on the edge of a well, very sad, almost in tears. A female figure, a nurse or a nun, brings out the two boys and hands them over to their father, who is not I. The elder is unmistakably my eldest son; I do not see the other's face. The woman who brings out the boy asks him for a parting kiss. She is marked by a red nose. The boy refuses her the kiss, but, holding out his hand to her in farewell, says "Auf Geseres," and to both of us (or to one of us) "Auf Ungeseres." I have the idea that the latter signifies an advantage.*

This dream is built on a tangle of thoughts stirred up by a play I had seen at the theater, *Das neue Ghetto* ("The New Ghetto"). The Jewish question, anxiety about the future of my children, to whom I cannot give a homeland of their own, and anxiety about raising them so that they may enjoy the rights of native citizens: all these can easily be recognized in the dream thoughts that accompany it.

"By the waters of Babylon we sat down and wept." Siena, like Rome, is famous for its beautiful fountains. In the dream I must find some substitute for Rome among places I know. Near the Porta Romana in Siena we had seen a large, brightly lit building, which turned out to be the Manicomio, the insane asylum. Shortly before the dream I had heard that a fellow Jew had been forced to resign a position at a state asylum, a post he had obtained only with great effort.

Our interest is caught by the phrase "Auf Geseres," where the situation sustained throughout the dream would lead us to expect "Auf Wiedersehen," that is, "Goodbye until we meet again," and by its entirely meaningless opposite, "Auf Ungeseres."

According to information I have received from Hebrew scholars, *Geseres* is a genuine Hebrew word, derived from the verb *goiser*, and is best rendered as "ordained sufferings" or "fated disaster." From the way it is used in Jewish colloquial speech, one might take it to mean "wailing and lamentation." *Ungeseres* is my own coinage, and it is the first word to attract my attention, though for the moment it baffles me. But the small remark at the end of the dream, that *Ungeseres* signifies an advantage over *Geseres*, opens the way to associations and to an explanation. The same relation holds for caviar: the unsalted kind is prized more highly than the salted. "Caviar to the general," meaning a delicacy too fine for common taste, and "noble passions": here lies hidden a joking allusion to a member of my household who, being younger than I, will, I hope, watch over my children's future. This also fits the fact that another member of my household, our worthy nurse, is clearly indicated by the nurse or nun of the dream. But a connecting link is still missing between the pair "salted" and "unsalted" and the pair *Geseres* and *Ungeseres*. That link is to be found in "soured" and "unsoured," that is, leavened and unleavened, whose German forms, *gesäuert* and *ungesäuert*, echo the words of the dream. In their flight, their exodus out of Egypt, the children of Israel had no time to let their bread rise, and in memory of this they eat unleavened bread to this day at Passover, the Jewish Easter. Here I can also find a place for a sudden recollection that came to me at this point in the analysis. I remembered how my friend from Berlin and I had strolled through Breslau, a city strange to us both, at the end of the Easter holidays. A little girl asked me the way to a certain street. I had to tell her I did not know it, and I remarked to my friend, "I hope that later in life the little one will show more discernment in choosing the people she lets guide her." Shortly afterward a sign caught my eye: "Dr. Herod, office hours . . ." I said to myself, "I hope this colleague doesn't happen to be a children's specialist." Meanwhile my friend had been setting out his views on the biological significance of bilateral symmetry, and had begun a sentence: "If we had only one eye in the middle of our foreheads, like the Cyclops . . ." This leads us to the professor's words in the preliminary dream, "My son, the myopic," and now I have been brought to the chief source of *Geseres*. Many years ago, when this son of Professor M., today an independent thinker, was still at his school desk, he contracted an eye disease which the doctor declared to be cause for concern. In his opinion, as long as it stayed in one eye it would not matter, but if it spread to the other eye it would be serious. The disease healed in the one eye without leaving any ill effects; soon afterward, however, its symptoms did in fact appear in the other. The boy's terrified mother at once summoned the physician to her secluded country retreat. But he now took a different view. "What sort of *Geseres* are you making of this?" he said to her impatiently. "If one side got well, the other side will get well too." And so it turned out.

And now for the connection between all this and myself and those dear to me. The school desk at which Professor M.'s son learned his first lessons has passed into the possession of my eldest son. It was given to his mother, into whose mouth I put the words of parting in the dream. One of the wishes that can be attached to this transfer is now easy to guess. The desk is designed to keep the child from becoming shortsighted and one-sided. Hence the myopia (and behind it the Cyclops) and the discussion of bilateral symmetry. The concern about one-sidedness has a double meaning: along with physical one-sidedness, it can refer to one-sidedness of intellectual development. Does it not seem as though the scene in the dream, for all its madness, were setting its denial against precisely this anxiety? After the child has said his word of farewell to one side, he calls out its opposite to the other, as though to restore the balance. He is acting, so to speak, in obedience to bilateral symmetry!

Thus the dream often carries its deepest meaning precisely where it seems most absurd. In every age, those who had something to say and could not say it without danger to themselves have gladly put on the fool's cap and bells. The listener for whom the forbidden words were meant was more likely to tolerate them if he could laugh at them and flatter himself that what displeased him was obviously absurd. The dream behaves exactly like the prince in the play who must feign madness, and so one may say of the dream what Hamlet says of himself, when he substitutes an obscure witticism for his real situation: "I am but mad north-north-west; when the wind is southerly I know a hawk from a handsaw."

My solution to the problem of absurdity in dreams, then, is this: the dream thoughts are never absurd, at least not those belonging to the dreams of sane people, and the dream-work produces absurd dreams, or dreams with individual absurd elements, whenever it has to represent, in its own mode of expression, the criticism, ridicule, and derision present in the dream thoughts. My next task is to show that the dream-work is brought about essentially by the cooperation of the three factors already mentioned, together with a fourth still to be named; that it accomplishes nothing less than a transposition of the dream thoughts, while observing the three conditions prescribed for it; and that the question of whether the mind works in dreams with all its faculties or with only some of them thereby loses its force and does not apply to the actual circumstances. But since there are plenty of dreams in which judgments are passed, criticisms made, and facts recognized, in which astonishment is expressed at some particular element, and in which arguments and explanations are attempted, I must meet the objections that might be drawn from such occurrences by citing selected examples.

My answer is as follows. Everything in a dream that appears to be an exercise of the critical faculty is to be regarded not as an intellectual achievement of the dream-work but as part of the material of the dream thoughts, from which it has passed, as a finished structure, into the manifest content of the dream. I can go further still. Even the judgments we pass on a dream as we remember it after waking, and the feelings its recollection arouses, belong in good part to the latent dream content and must be fitted into their proper place in the interpretation.

I. I have already given a striking example of this. A female patient does not want to relate her dream because it is too vague. She has seen a person in it and does not know whether it was her husband or her father. Then follows a second fragment in which a "manure can" appears, prompting the following memory. As a young housewife, she once jokingly announced, in the presence of a young relative who often visited the house, that her next concern would be to get a new manure can. The next morning one was delivered to her, but it was filled with lilies of the valley. This part of the dream served to represent the saying "Not grown on your own manure," a German idiom for something that is not of one's own making. When the analysis is completed, we find that the dream thoughts concern the lingering effects of a story she had heard in her youth, about a girl who had given birth to a child whose real father was uncertain. Here the dream's mode of representation spills over into waking thought, allowing one element of the dream thoughts to be represented by a judgment passed, in the waking state, on the dream as a whole.

II. A similar case. One of my patients has a dream that strikes him as interesting, for immediately on waking he says to himself, "I must tell the doctor about that." The dream is analyzed and reveals the clearest allusion to an affair in which he had become involved during the treatment, and about which he had resolved "to tell me nothing."

III. Here is a third example, from my own experience:

*I am going to the hospital with P. through a district in which there are houses and gardens. With this comes the idea that I have already seen this district several times in dreams. I do not know my way very well. P. shows me a route that leads around a corner to a restaurant (indoors, not a garden). There I ask for Mrs. Doni and am told that she lives at the back, in a small room, with three children. I go there, and on the way I meet an indistinct person with my two little girls, whom I take with me after I have stood with them for a while. Something like a reproach against my wife for having left them there.*

On waking I feel great satisfaction, which I attribute to the prospect of learning from the analysis what is meant by the idea "I have already dreamed of that." But the analysis teaches me nothing on that point. It shows me only that the satisfaction belongs to the latent dream content and not to my judgment of the dream. It is satisfaction at having had children in my marriage. P. is someone with whom I traveled the road of life for a certain stretch, but who has since far outstripped me socially and materially, and whose marriage, however, has remained childless. The two occasions for the dream, which furnish the proof of this, can be found through a complete analysis. The day before, I had read in the newspaper the death notice of a Mrs. Dona A——y (from which I make "Doni"), who had died in childbirth. My wife told me that the dead woman had been attended by the same midwife who had attended her at the birth of our two youngest boys. The name Dona had caught my attention, since I had recently come across it for the first time in an English novel. The other occasion for the dream lies in its date: I dreamed it on the night before the birthday of my eldest boy, who, it appears, has a gift for poetry.

IV. The same satisfaction stayed with me after waking from the absurd dream in which my father, after his death, had played a political role among the Magyars. It is explained by the persistence of the feeling that accompanied the dream's last sentence: *"I remember that on his deathbed he looked so much like Garibaldi, and I am glad that it has really come true." (A forgotten continuation belongs here.)* I can now supply from the analysis what fills this gap. It is a reference to my second son, to whom I gave the first name of a great historical figure who attracted me powerfully in my boyhood, especially during my stay in England. After deciding to use this name should the expected child be a son, I had to wait a year, and I greeted him with it in great satisfaction the moment he was born. It is easy to see how a father's craving for greatness is transferred, in his thoughts, to his children, and it will readily be believed that this is one of the ways in which the suppression of that craving, which life makes necessary, is accomplished. The little fellow earned a place in the text of this dream because the same mishap, quite forgivable in a child or a dying man, of soiling his clothes had happened to him. Compare with this the allusion to "Stuhlrichter," literally "stool judge," meaning a presiding judge, but with *Stuhl* also carrying the sense of stool in the bodily sense, and the dream's wish: to stand before one's children great and pure.

V. I am now called on to find expressions of judgment that remain within the dream itself and are neither carried over into nor transferred to our waking thoughts, and it will be a great relief if I can find examples among dreams already cited for other purposes. The dream of Goethe attacking Mr. M. seems to contain a considerable number of acts of judgment. "I try to find some explanation of the chronological relations, which seem improbable to me." Does this not look like a critical impulse directed against the nonsensical idea that Goethe should have launched a literary attack on a young man of my acquaintance? "It seems plausible to me that he was eighteen years old." That sounds very much like the result of a dim-witted calculation, and "I do not know exactly what year it is" would be an instance of uncertainty or doubt within the dream.

But I know from the analysis that these acts of judgment, which seem to have been performed for the first time in the dream, admit of a different reading, in light of which they become indispensable to the interpretation while every absurdity disappears. With the sentence "I try to find some explanation of the chronological relations," I put myself in the place of my friend, who really is trying to explain the chronological relations of life. The sentence thereby loses its meaning as a judgment objecting to the nonsense of the sentences before it. The interjection "which seem improbable to me" belongs with the later "it seems plausible to me." In almost the same words I had answered the lady who told me the story of her brother's illness: "It seems improbable to me that the cry of 'Nature, Nature!' had anything to do with Goethe; it seems far more plausible that it had the sexual meaning you are familiar with." A judgment was certainly passed here, though not in the dream but in reality, on an occasion that the dream thoughts remember and make use of. The dream content appropriates this judgment just as it does any other fragment of the dream thoughts.

The number eighteen, to which the judgment in the dream is so senselessly attached, still preserves a trace of the context from which the real judgment was torn. Finally, "I am not certain what year it is" is intended for nothing else than to carry out my identification with the paralytic, during whose examination this very point had in fact been confirmed.

In resolving these apparent acts of judgment in dreams, it is worth recalling a rule of interpretation: any coherence the dream fabricates among its constituent parts should be disregarded as specious and inessential, and every element of the dream must be taken on its own and traced back to its source. The dream is a conglomerate, and for the purposes of investigation it has to be broken up into its elements. Other circumstances, however, show us that dreams also express a psychic force which establishes this apparent coherence, a force that subjects the material obtained by the dream activity to a secondary elaboration. What we encounter here are manifestations of this force, to which we shall later turn our attention as the fourth of the factors that take part in the formation of dreams.

VI. I shall select further examples of critical activity from dreams already cited. In the absurd dream about the communication from the town council, I ask the question: "You married soon after? I calculate that I was born in 1856, which seems to me to follow immediately." This takes on the full form of an inference. My father married shortly after his attack in 1851; I am the eldest son, born in 1856; everything agrees perfectly. We know that this inference was inserted by the wish-fulfillment, and that the sentence governing the dream thoughts runs as follows: four or five years is no time at all; it need not enter the calculation. Yet every part of this chain of inference can be traced to the dream thoughts in a different way, in both its content and its form. It is the patient whose endurance my colleague complains about who intends to marry immediately after his treatment ends. The way I deal with my father in the dream recalls an interrogation or examination, and with it the figure of a university instructor who used to take down a complete record of particulars when enrolling his class: "Born when?" 1856. "*Patre?*", meaning "Father's name?" The applicant would then give his father's first name with a Latin ending, and we students assumed that the Aulic Councillor, as he was titled by the imperial court, drew conclusions from the father's first name that the student's own name would not always have supplied. On this account, the drawing of inferences in the dream would be nothing more than a repetition of the drawing of inferences that appears as part of the subject matter of the dream thoughts. From this we learn something new. When an inference occurs in the dream content, it invariably comes from the dream thoughts. It may be contained in them as a piece of remembered material, or it may act as a logical link in a series of dream thoughts. In either case, an inference in the dream represents an inference in the dream thoughts.

The analysis of this dream should be carried further at this point. Connected with the Professor's interrogation is the memory of a register of university students, published in Latin in my day, and also the memory of my own course of study. The five years allotted to the study of medicine were, as usual, not enough for me. I went on working unconcernedly through the years that followed; among my acquaintances I was regarded as an idler, and there was doubt whether I would "get through." Then, all at once, I resolved to take my examinations, and I did get through, despite the delay. This furnishes a fresh confirmation of the dream thoughts, which I defiantly hold up to my critics: "Even if you refuse to believe it because I take my time, I shall reach a conclusion." The German word here, *Schluss*, means both an end and a logical conclusion, or inference. "It has often turned out that way."

In its opening portion this dream contains several sentences that can hardly be denied the character of an argument. Nor is this argument at all absurd; it could just as well belong to waking thought. In the dream I make fun of the town council's communication, because, first, I was not yet in the world in 1851, and second, my father, to whom it might refer, is already dead. Both points are not only correct in themselves but coincide exactly with the arguments I would use if I actually received such a communication. We know from our earlier analysis that this dream springs from deeply embittered and scornful dream thoughts. If we may further assume that the motive for censorship is a very strong one, we can understand why the dream activity has every reason to construct a flawless refutation of a baseless insinuation, modeled on a pattern contained in the dream thoughts. Analysis shows, however, that in this case the dream activity was not free to compose a copy of its own; it was obliged to use material from the dream thoughts for its purpose. Imagine an algebraic equation that contains, besides its figures, plus and minus signs and the signs for powers and roots, and imagine someone copying it without understanding it. Such a copyist would carry over the signs of operation along with the figures, failing to distinguish between the two kinds of symbol. The two arguments can be traced to the following material. It pains me to think that many of the assumptions on which I base my solution of the psychoneuroses will, once they become known, provoke skepticism and ridicule. I must maintain, for instance, that impressions from the second year of life, or even from the first, leave a lasting trace on the temperament of people who later fall ill, and that these impressions, though greatly distorted and exaggerated by memory, can furnish the original and fundamental basis of hysterical symptoms. Patients to whom I explain this at the proper moment habitually parody the explanation by declaring themselves willing to search for memories from a time when they were not yet alive. It would be entirely in keeping with my expectations if my disclosure of the unsuspected part played by the father in the earliest sexual impulses of female patients were to meet with a similar reception. And yet, by my well-founded conviction, both positions are correct. In support of this I recall certain cases in which the father died when the child was very young, and later events, otherwise inexplicable, proved that the child had unconsciously preserved memories of the persons who had passed so early out of its life. I know that both of my assertions rest on inferences whose validity will be attacked. When the dream activity takes the very material of these inferences, which I fear will be contested, and uses it to set up incontestable inferences, it is accomplishing a wish-fulfillment.

VII. In a dream that I have so far only touched on, astonishment at the subject about to be raised is plainly expressed at the very outset:

"The elder Brücke must have set me some task or other; strangely enough, it concerns the dissection of my own lower body, pelvis and legs, which I see before me as though in the dissecting room, though without feeling the absence of my body and without a trace of horror. Louise N. is standing nearby, doing her work beside me. The pelvis has been eviscerated; now its upper aspect is visible, now its lower, and the two views blend together. Thick, fleshy red lumps can be seen (which even in the dream make me think of hemorrhoids). There was also something lying over these that had to be carefully picked out, and it looked like crumpled tinfoil. Then I was once again in possession of my legs and made a journey through the city, but took a carriage because I was tired. To my astonishment the carriage drove into the doorway of a house, which opened and let it into a passage that bent sharply at its end and finally led on into the open air. At last I wandered through changing scenery with an Alpine guide who carried my things. For part of the way he carried me, out of consideration for my tired legs. The ground was muddy, and we went along the edge; people were sitting on the ground, a girl among them, like Indians or Gypsies. Before this I had made my own way across the slippery ground, constantly astonished that I could manage it so well after the dissection. At last we came to a small wooden house that ended in an open window. Here the guide set me down and laid two wooden boards, which stood ready, across the windowsill, so that the chasm that had to be crossed to reach the window might be bridged. Now I became truly frightened about my legs. Instead of the expected crossing, I saw two grown men lying on wooden benches along the walls of the hut, and something like two sleeping children beside them. It seemed as though it was not the boards but the children that were meant to make the crossing possible. I awoke with frightened thoughts."

Anyone who has formed a proper idea of how extensive dream condensation is will easily imagine how many pages a detailed analysis of this dream would fill. Fortunately for the present context, I shall take from it only the single instance of astonishment in the dream, which appears in the parenthetical remark "strangely enough." Let us consider the occasion of the dream. It was a visit from Louise N., the lady who assists with the work in the dream. She says, "Lend me something to read." I offer her *She*, by Rider Haggard. "A strange book, but full of hidden meaning," I try to explain to her; "the eternal feminine, the immortality of our emotions—" Here she interrupts me: "I already know that book. Haven't you something of your own?" "No, my own immortal works are still unwritten." "Well, when are you going to publish your so-called latest revelations, which you promised us would make good reading?" she asks, somewhat sarcastically. I now realize that she is speaking for someone else, and I fall silent. I think of the effort it costs me to publish even my work on dreams, in which I must surrender so much of my own intimate character. "The best that you know you cannot tell the children." The dissection of my own body, which I am ordered to carry out in the dream, is thus the self-analysis that the communication of my dreams requires. The elder Brücke quite properly finds a place here: in the first years of my scientific work I once neglected a discovery until his energetic commands compelled me to publish it. But the other trains of thought that start from my conversation with Louise N. go too deep to become conscious. They are diverted onto the related material that the mention of Rider Haggard's *She* awakened in me. The comment "strangely enough" belongs with this book and with another by the same author, *The Heart of the World*, and many elements of the dream are drawn from these two fantastic novels. The muddy ground over which the dreamer is carried, and the chasm that must be crossed by means of the boards brought along for the purpose, come from *She*; the Indians, the girl, and the wooden house come from *The Heart of the World*. In both novels a woman is the leader, and both concern perilous wanderings; *She* tells of an adventurous journey to an undiscovered country, a place scarcely ever trodden by human foot. According to a note I find in my record of the dream, the fatigue in my legs was a real sensation in those days. It was doubtless accompanied by a weary state of mind and the doubting question, "How much farther will my legs carry me?" The adventure in *She* ends with the woman leader meeting her death in the mysterious fire at the center of the earth, instead of winning immortality for herself and others. A fear of this kind has unmistakably arisen in the dream thoughts. The "wooden house," too, is surely the coffin, which is to say the grave. But the dream activity has achieved its masterpiece by representing this most unwelcome of all thoughts through a wish-fulfillment. I have, in fact, been in a grave once before, but it was an empty Etruscan tomb near Orvieto: a narrow chamber with two stone benches along the walls, on which the skeletons of two adults had been laid. The interior of the wooden house in the dream looks exactly like this, except that wood has taken the place of stone. The dream seems to say, "If you must lie in your grave so soon, let it be this Etruscan grave," and through this interpolation it transforms the saddest of expectations into one that is genuinely to be desired. As we shall learn, it is unfortunately only the idea accompanying an emotion that the dream can turn into its opposite, and not, as a rule, the emotion itself. So I wake with "frightened thoughts," even after the dream has been made to represent my idea that perhaps the children will achieve what has been denied to the father. This idea is a fresh allusion to the strange novel in which a person's identity is preserved through a series of generations spanning two thousand years.

VIII. In the course of another dream there is a similar expression of astonishment at what is experienced in it. This astonishment, however, is connected with a striking and skillfully contrived attempt at explanation, one that might well be called a stroke of genius, so that I would have to analyze the whole dream for its sake alone, even if the dream did not possess two other features of interest. I am traveling on the Southern Railway during the night between the eighteenth and nineteenth of July, and in my sleep I hear someone call out, "Hollthurn, ten minutes." I immediately think of Holothurians, the sea cucumbers, and of a natural history museum, and I think that this is a place where brave men vainly resisted the domination of their overlord. Yes, the Counter-Reformation in Austria! As though it were a place in Styria or the Tyrol. Now I distinctly see a little museum in which the remains or the possessions of these men are preserved. I would like to get off, but I hesitate. Women with fruit are standing on the platform; they crouch on the ground and, in that position, hold out their baskets invitingly. I hesitate, unsure whether we still have time, but we are still standing. I am suddenly in another compartment, in which the upholstery and seats are so narrow that one's back presses directly against the backrest. I am surprised at this, but I may have changed carriages while asleep. There are several people, among them an English brother and sister, and a row of books stands distinctly on a shelf on the wall. I see *The Wealth of Nations*, then *Matter and Motion* (by Maxwell); the books are thick and bound in brown linen. The man asks his sister about a book by Schiller, and whether she has forgotten it. The books seem at first to be mine, then seem to belong to the brother and sister. At this point I want to join the conversation in order to confirm and support what is being said—. I wake up sweating all over, because all the windows are shut. The train is stopping at Marburg.

While I was writing down the dream, a part of it came back to me that my memory had wanted to leave out. I say to the brother and sister about a certain work, "It is from . . ." but I correct myself: "It is by . . ." The man remarks to his sister, "He said it correctly."

The dream begins with the name of a station, which must have partly awakened me. For this name, which was Marburg, I substituted Hollthurn. That I heard Marburg when it was first called, or perhaps when it was called a second time, is proved by the mention of Schiller in the dream, since Schiller was born in Marburg, though not in the Marburg in Styria. On this occasion, although I was traveling first class, the circumstances were very disagreeable. The train was overcrowded. In my compartment I had come upon a gentleman and a lady who appeared to be people of rank, but who lacked the good breeding, or did not think it worth the trouble, to conceal their displeasure at my intrusion. My polite greeting went unanswered, and although the man and the woman sat side by side, with their backs to the direction of travel, the woman hastily claimed the seat opposite her, next to the window, by laying her umbrella on it. The door was immediately closed, and pointed remarks were exchanged about the opening of windows. I was probably recognized at once as someone hungry for fresh air. It was a hot night, and the air in the compartment, sealed on every side, was almost suffocating. My experience as a traveler leads me to believe that such inconsiderate and overbearing conduct marks people who have paid only part of their fare, or none of it. When the conductor came and I presented my dearly bought ticket, the lady called out ungraciously, almost threateningly, "My husband has a pass." She was a stately figure with sour features, of an age not far from that at which feminine beauty fades; the man never had a chance to say anything at all and sat there motionless. I tried to sleep. In the dream I take terrible revenge on my disagreeable traveling companions; no one would suspect what insults and humiliations lie concealed behind the disjointed fragments of the first half of the dream. Once this desire has been satisfied, the second wish, to exchange my compartment for another, makes itself felt. The dream changes scene so often, and without raising the slightest objection to such changes, that it would not have been at all remarkable if it had promptly replaced my traveling companions with more agreeable ones drawn from my memory. But this was one of the cases in which something or other objected to the change of scene and considered an explanation of it necessary. How did I suddenly come to be in another compartment? I certainly could not remember changing carriages. So there was only one explanation: I must have left the carriage while asleep. This is a rare occurrence, but the experience of the neuropathologist furnishes examples of it. We know of people who undertake railway journeys in a twilight state of clouded consciousness without betraying their abnormal condition by any sign, until at some station along the way they fully recover consciousness and are surprised at the gap in their memory. And so, while still dreaming, I declare my own case to be one of *automatisme ambulatoire*.

Analysis allows another solution. The attempt at explanation, which so astonishes me if I am to attribute it to the dream activity, is not original but is copied from the neurosis of one of my patients. I have already spoken elsewhere of a highly cultivated man, gentle in his conduct, who shortly after the death of his parents began to accuse himself of murderous inclinations and who suffered from the precautions he had to take to guard himself against them. At first, walking in the street became painful for him because of a compulsion to account for everyone he met and to know where each of them had disappeared to. If one of them suddenly slipped out of his pursuing gaze, he was left with a painful feeling and the thought that he might possibly have done away with the man. Among other things, this compulsive idea concealed a Cain fantasy, for "all men are brothers." Since the task was impossible to accomplish, he gave up taking walks and spent his life shut up within his four walls. But news of murders committed outside kept reaching his room through the newspapers, and his conscience, in the form of a doubt, kept accusing him of being the murderer. For a time the certainty that he had not left his home for weeks protected him against these accusations, until one day it dawned on him that he might have left his house in an unconscious condition and committed the murder without knowing anything about it. From then on he locked the front door, handed the key over to his old housekeeper, and strictly forbade her to give it to him even if he demanded it.

This, then, is the origin of the attempted explanation that I may have changed carriages in an unconscious condition. It has been carried over in finished form from the material of the dream thoughts into the dream, and it is plainly intended to identify me with this patient. My memory of him was awakened by an easy association. A few weeks earlier I had made my last night journey with this man. He was cured, and he was escorting me into the country to his relatives, who had sent for me. Since we had a compartment to ourselves, we left all the windows open through the night, and for as long as I stayed awake we had a delightful conversation. I knew that hostile impulses toward his father, dating from his childhood and bound up with sexual material, had been at the root of his illness. By identifying myself with him, I wanted to make an analogous confession to myself. The second scene of the dream in fact resolves itself into a wanton fantasy: that my two elderly traveling companions had behaved so rudely toward me because my arrival kept them from exchanging the caresses they had planned for the night. This fantasy, however, goes back to a scene in early childhood in which, probably driven by sexual curiosity, I intruded into my parents' bedroom and was ordered out of it by my father's emphatic command.

I consider it unnecessary to multiply examples further. All of them would confirm what we have learned from those already cited: that an act of judgment in the dream is nothing but the repetition of a prototype that it has in the dream thoughts. In most cases it is an inappropriate repetition, introduced in an unfitting context; occasionally, however, as in our last example, it is so artfully placed that it can give the impression of independent thought activity in the dream. At this point we might turn our attention to the psychic activity that, while it does not seem to take part regularly in the formation of dreams, strives, wherever it does take part, to fuse together in a consistent and intelligible way those dream elements that are incongruous because of their different origins. We think it best, however, to take up first the expressions of emotion that appear in the dream and to compare them with the emotions that analysis reveals to us in the dream thoughts.

### (g) The Affects in the Dream

A profound remark of Stricker's has drawn our attention to the fact that the expressions of emotion in the dream cannot be dismissed in the offhand way in which we are accustomed to shake off the dream itself once we have awakened. "If I am afraid of robbers in the dream, the robbers, to be sure, are imaginary, but the fear of them is real," and the same holds true if I feel glad in the dream. By the testimony of our feelings, an emotion experienced in the dream is in no way less valid than one of equal intensity experienced in waking life, and the dream presses its claim to be accepted as part of our real mental experience more forcefully on account of its emotional content than on account of its content of ideas. In waking life we cannot make this separation, because we have no way of assessing an emotion psychologically except in connection with the content of some idea. When an affect and an idea do not match, whether in kind or in intensity, our waking judgment is thrown into confusion.

It has always caused astonishment that in dreams the content of an idea does not bring with it the emotional effect we would expect it to produce in waking thought. Strümpell believed that ideas in the dream are stripped of their psychic value. Yet the dream also offers the opposite case, in which intense emotion is attached to content that seems to give no occasion for it. In a dream I may find myself in a horrible, dangerous, or disgusting situation and feel no fear or revulsion at all. At other times I am terrified by harmless things and delighted by childish ones.

This riddle of the dream disappears more suddenly and more completely than perhaps any other dream problem once we move from the manifest content to the latent content. We no longer need to explain it, because it no longer exists. Analysis shows that the content of ideas has undergone displacements and substitutions, while the affects have remained unchanged. It is no wonder, then, that an idea altered by the dream's distortion no longer fits the affect that has stayed intact. Nor is there any cause for wonder once analysis has restored the correct content to its original place.

In a psychic complex that has been subjected to the resisting censor, the affects are the unyielding element, and they alone can guide us toward filling in what is missing. This situation shows itself even more clearly in the psychoneuroses than in the dream. There the affect is always in the right, at least as far as its quality is concerned, although its intensity may be heightened by a displacement of neurotic attention. A hysteric may be surprised to find himself so frightened of a trifle, and a patient with obsessive ideas may be astonished to produce such painful self-reproach out of nothing at all. Both are mistaken in treating the content of the idea, the trifle or the nothing, as the essential thing, and both defend themselves in vain because they take that idea as the starting point of their thinking. Psychoanalysis shows them the right way by recognizing that the affect, on the contrary, is justified, and by searching for the idea that belongs to it, which has been suppressed and replaced by a substitute. The assumption here is that the release of an affect and the content of an idea do not form the inseparable organic unity we are accustomed to suppose. The two parts may instead be, so to speak, soldered together in such a way that analysis can detach them from each other. Dream interpretation shows that this is in fact the case.

I give first an example in which analysis explains the apparent absence of affect from an idea that ought to have forced an emotional response.

I. *The dreamer sees three lions in a desert, one of which is laughing, but she is not afraid of them. Then, however, she must have fled from them, for she is trying to climb a tree, but she finds that her cousin, who is a teacher of French, is already up in the tree, and so on.*

Analysis yields the following material for this dream. A sentence from the dreamer's English lesson had become the indifferent occasion for it: "The lion's greatest beauty is his mane." Her father wore a beard that framed his face like a mane. Her English teacher was named Miss Lyons. An acquaintance had sent her the ballads of Loewe, a name that in German means "lion." These, then, are the three lions, and why should she have been afraid of them? She had read a story in which a Black man who had incited his fellows to revolt is hunted with bloodhounds and climbs a tree to save himself. Then come fragments in a playful mood, such as the instructions for catching lions from the comic magazine *Die Fliegenden Blätter*: "Take a desert and strain it; the lions will remain behind." There is also a very amusing but not very proper anecdote about an official who is asked why he does not take more trouble to win the favor of his superior, and who answers that he has been trying to work his way in, but the man ahead of him is already up. The whole matter becomes intelligible once we learn that on the day of the dream the lady had received a visit from her husband's superior. He was very polite to her and kissed her hand, and she was not in the least afraid of him, even though he is a "big shot" (in German, *ein grosses Tier*, literally "a big animal") and plays the part of a "social lion" in the capital of her country. This lion is therefore like the lion in *A Midsummer Night's Dream*, who reveals himself to be only Snug the joiner in costume. Such is the stuff of all dream lions when the dreamer is not afraid.

II. As my second example, I cite the dream of the girl who saw her sister's little son lying dead in a coffin, and who, I may now add, felt no pain or grief at the sight. We know from the analysis why she did not. The dream merely concealed her wish to see the man she loved once again, and the affect has to be attuned to the wish, not to its disguise. There was no occasion for grief at all.

In some dreams the emotion at least remains attached to the idea that has replaced the one to which it really belongs. In others the breakup of the complex goes further. The affect appears to be entirely separated from its proper idea and finds a place somewhere else in the dream, where it fits into the new arrangement of the dream elements. This resembles what we have learned about acts of judgment in the dream. If the dream thoughts contain a significant inference, the dream contains one as well, but in the dream the inference may be shifted onto entirely different material. Not infrequently this shift follows the principle of antithesis.

I illustrate this last possibility with the following dream, which I have analyzed with the utmost thoroughness.

III. *A castle by the sea; later it lies not directly on the sea but on a narrow canal that leads to the sea. A certain Mr. P. is its governor. I stand with him in a large salon with three windows, in front of which rise projections of a wall, like the battlements of a fort. I belong to the garrison, perhaps as a volunteer naval officer. We fear the arrival of enemy warships, for we are at war. Mr. P. intends to leave; he gives me instructions on what must be done if the dreaded event occurs. His sick wife is in the threatened castle with her children. As soon as the bombardment begins, the large hall is to be cleared. He breathes heavily and tries to get away; I hold him back and ask him how I should send him news if necessary. He says something more, and then suddenly falls over dead. I have probably burdened him needlessly with my questions. After his death, which makes no further impression on me, I consider whether the widow should remain in the castle, whether I should report the death to the commander-in-chief, and whether I should take over command of the castle as next in rank. I now stand at the window and review the ships as they pass. They are merchant vessels that dart past on the dark water, several of them with more than one smokestack, others with bulging decks (very much like the railway stations in the preliminary dream, which I have not recounted). Then my brother is standing beside me, and we both look out the window at the canal. At the sight of one ship we are frightened and cry out: "Here comes the warship!" It turns out, however, that these are only the same ships I already know, returning. Now comes a little ship, oddly cut off so that it ends in the middle of its breadth; curious things like cups or salt cellars can be seen on its deck. We call out as if with one voice: "That is the breakfast ship."*

*The rapid motion of the ships, the deep blue of the water, the brown smoke from the funnels: all this together makes a highly tense and somber impression.*

The settings of this dream are assembled from several journeys to the Adriatic: Miramare, Duino, Venice, and Aquileia. A short but enjoyable Easter trip to Aquileia with my brother, a few weeks before the dream, was still fresh in my memory. The naval war between America and Spain also plays a part, along with the worry it caused me about my relatives living in America. Emotion appears at two points in this dream. At one point an emotion we would expect is missing, and the dream expressly emphasizes that the governor's death makes no impression on me. At another point, when I see the warships, I am frightened and experience all the sensations of fear while asleep. In this well-constructed dream the affects have been distributed so as to avoid any obvious contradiction. There is no reason for me to be frightened by the governor's death, and it is fitting that, as commander of the castle, I should be alarmed at the sight of a warship. Analysis shows, however, that Mr. P. is nothing but a substitute for my own ego, just as in the dream I am his substitute. I am the governor who suddenly dies. The dream thoughts concern the future of those dear to me after my premature death, and no other disagreeable thought is to be found among them. The fright attached to the sight of the warship must therefore be transferred from it to this disagreeable thought.

Conversely, analysis shows that the region of the dream thoughts from which the warship comes is filled with the most joyful memories. A year earlier, in Venice, on an enchantingly beautiful day, we stood at the windows of our room on the Riva degli Schiavoni and looked out over the blue lagoon, which was busier than usual. English ships were expected and were to be given a festive reception, and suddenly my wife called out, happy as a child: "Here come the English warships!" In the dream I am frightened by these very words; once again we see that speech in dreams originates in speech from waking life. I shall soon show that even the element "English" in this remark has not been lost to the dream work. On the way from the dream thoughts to the dream content, then, I convert joy into fright, and I need only hint that by means of this very transformation I give expression to part of the latent content. The example shows, however, that the dream work is free to detach the occasion for an affect from its context in the dream thoughts and to insert it anywhere it likes in the dream content.

I take the opportunity this example happens to offer to analyze more closely the "breakfast ship," whose appearance so nonsensically brings to an end a situation that had until then been rationally sustained. Looking more closely at this dream object, I am struck by the fact that it was black, and that, because it was cut off at its widest point, the truncated end closely resembled an object that had caught our interest in the museums of the Etruscan cities. This was a rectangular tray of black clay with two handles, on which stood things like coffee cups or teacups, very similar to a modern breakfast service. When we asked about it, we learned that it was the toilette set of an Etruscan lady, with little boxes for rouge and powder, and we joked to each other that it would not be a bad idea to bring something like it home to the lady of the house. The dream object therefore signifies a "black toilette," the German word *Toilette* also meaning "dress," and so a mourning dress, and it refers directly to a death. The other end of the dream object recalls the boat (in German, *Nachen*), a word that, as a philologist friend has told me, derives from the Greek root *νέκυς*, "corpse." In prehistoric times the dead were laid on such boats and left to the sea for burial. This circumstance explains the return of the ships in the dream:

"Quietly the old man on his rescued boat drifts into the harbor."

It is the homeward voyage after the shipwreck. The German word for shipwreck, *Schiffbruch*, means literally "ship-breaking," and the breakfast ship looks as though it had been broken off in the middle. But where does the name "breakfast" ship come from? Here the "English" comes in, left over from the warships. Breakfast is a breaking of the fast. The breaking belongs once more to the shipwreck, the *Schiffbruch*, and the fasting is connected with the mourning dress.

The only thing about this breakfast ship that the dream has newly created is its name. The thing itself existed in reality, and it recalls to me the merriest hours of my last journey. Because we distrusted the food in Aquileia, we brought provisions with us from Görz and bought a bottle of excellent Istrian wine in Aquileia. While the little mail steamer made its slow way through the Canale delle Mee and into the lonely stretch of lagoon toward Grado, we ate our breakfast on deck. We were the only passengers, and it tasted to us as few breakfasts ever have. This, then, was the "breakfast ship," and it is behind this very memory of great enjoyment that the dream hides the saddest thoughts about an unknown and ominous future.

The detachment of emotions from the groups of ideas that gave rise to them is the most striking thing that happens to them in the course of dream formation, but it is neither the only change they undergo on the way from the dream thoughts to the manifest dream nor even the most essential one. If we compare the affects in the dream thoughts with those in the dream, it becomes clear at once that wherever there is an emotion in the dream, it is also present in the dream thoughts, but the reverse is not true. In general, the dream is poorer in affect than the psychic material from which it was worked up. Once I have reconstructed the dream thoughts, I find that the most intense psychic impulses are regularly struggling in them for expression, usually in conflict with others sharply opposed to them. When I turn back to the dream, I often find it colorless and without any of the more intense strains of feeling. The dream work has brought down to the level of indifference not only the content of my thoughts but also their emotional tone. I might say that a suppression of affects has taken place. Take, for example, the dream of the botanical monograph. It answers to a passionate plea for my freedom to act as I am acting and to arrange my life as seems right to me and to me alone. The dream that results sounds indifferent: I have written a monograph, it lies before me, it is furnished with colored plates, and dried plants are bound into each copy. It has the stillness of a battlefield after the fighting, with no trace left of the tumult of battle.

Things may also turn out differently, and vivid expressions of affect may appear in the dream. But we shall first dwell on the undeniable fact that many dreams appear indifferent, while it is never possible to enter deeply into the dream thoughts without being deeply moved.

A complete theoretical explanation of this suppression of emotion in the course of the dream work cannot be given here; it would require a most careful investigation of the theory of the emotions and of the mechanism of repression. I shall make room for only two thoughts. For other reasons, I am compelled to conceive of the release of affect as a centrifugal process, one that sends its discharge outward from the nervous center but directed toward the interior of the body, analogous to the nervous impulses that set muscles in motion or glands to secrete. Just as the sending of motor impulses toward the outside world appears to be suspended in sleep, so the centrifugal arousal of emotion by unconscious thought may be made more difficult during sleep. The affective impulses stirred up while the dream thoughts are running their course would then themselves be weak excitations, and those that make their way into the dream would be no stronger. On this line of argument, the "suppression of affects" would not be a result of the dream work at all, but a result of the state of sleep. This may be so, but it cannot possibly be the whole story. We must also remember that all the more complex dreams have proved to be a compromise produced by a conflict of psychic forces. On the one hand, the thoughts that make up the wish must contend with the opposition of a censorship; on the other, we have often seen that even in unconscious thinking each train of thought is yoked to its contradictory opposite. Since all these trains of thought are capable of carrying emotion, we shall hardly go wrong, broadly speaking, if we regard the suppression of emotion as the result of the restraint that the opposing currents impose on one another and that the censor imposes on the tendencies it has suppressed. The restraint of affects would then be the second effect of the dream censorship, just as the distortion of the dream was the first.

I shall insert an example of a dream in which the indifferent emotional tone of the content can be explained by a contrast within the dream thoughts. I have the following short dream to relate, which every reader will find disgusting:

IV. *A small rise of ground, and on it something like an open-air latrine: a very long bench, at the end of which is a large toilet opening. The whole back edge is thickly covered with little heaps of excrement of every size and degree of freshness. A shrub behind the bench. I urinate on the bench; a long stream of urine rinses everything clean, the patches of excrement come off easily and fall into the opening. Yet it seems as though something remained at the end nevertheless.*

Why did I feel no disgust in this dream?

Because, as analysis shows, the most pleasant and gratifying thoughts took part in forming it. When I analyze it, I think at once of the Augean stables cleansed by Hercules. I am this Hercules. The rise of ground and the shrub belong to Aussee, where my children are now staying. I have discovered the infantile causes of the neuroses and have thereby protected my own children from falling ill. The bench, minus the opening of course, is a faithful copy of a piece of furniture given to me as a present by an affectionate woman patient, and it reminds me how my patients honor me. Even the museum of human excrement admits of a less disagreeable interpretation. However much it disgusts me, it is a souvenir of the beautiful land of Italy, where, as everyone knows, the latrines in the small towns are equipped in no other way. The stream of urine that washes everything clean is an unmistakable allusion to greatness. This is how Gulliver puts out the great fire in Lilliput, though in doing so he earns the displeasure of the tiniest of queens. This is also how Gargantua, the superman of Master Rabelais, takes his revenge on the Parisians, straddling Notre Dame and directing his stream of urine onto the city. Only the evening before, I had been leafing through Garnier's illustrations to Rabelais before going to bed. And, strangely enough, here is further proof that I am the superman: the platform of Notre Dame was my favorite spot in Paris. Every free afternoon I used to climb the towers of the church and clamber about among the monsters and devil masks there. The fact that all the excrement vanishes so quickly before the stream corresponds to the motto *Afflavit et dissipati sunt*, "He blew, and they were scattered," which I intend someday to use as the title of a chapter on the treatment of hysteria.

Now for the occasion of the dream. It had been a hot summer afternoon. That evening I had given a lecture on the relation between hysteria and the perversions, and everything I had to say displeased me thoroughly and seemed to me worthless. I was tired, took no pleasure in my difficult work, and longed to get away from this rummaging in human filth, to see my children and then the beauties of Italy. In this mood I went from the lecture hall to a café to find some modest refreshment in the open air, for I had lost my appetite. But one of my listeners came with me. He asked permission to sit with me while I drank my coffee and swallowed my roll, and he began to flatter me. He told me how much he had learned from me, that he now saw everything with different eyes, that I had cleansed the Augean stables of the theory of the neuroses of its errors and prejudices; in short, that I was a very great man. My mood was ill-suited to his hymn of praise. I struggled against disgust and went home early to escape him. Before going to sleep I leafed through Rabelais and read a short story by C. F. Meyer called *Die Leiden eines Knaben* (*The Sufferings of a Boy*).

The dream was drawn from these materials, and Meyer's story added the memory of childhood scenes (compare the last scene of the dream about Count Thun). The mood of the day, marked by disgust and annoyance, carries over into the dream to the extent that it is allowed to supply nearly all the material of the dream content. But during the night the opposite mood of vigorous and even exaggerated self-assertion was awakened and dispelled the earlier one. The dream had to take a form that could express both self-depreciation and exaggerated self-assertion in the same material. This compromise produced an ambiguous dream content, and also an indifferent emotional tone, because the opposing feelings held each other in check.

According to the theory of wish fulfillment, this dream could not have occurred had the suppressed but pleasurable train of thought concerning my own aggrandizement not been coupled with the opposing thoughts of disgust. For disagreeable things are not meant to be represented in the dream; painful thoughts from the day can force their way into the dream only if they lend a disguise to the wish fulfillment.

The dream work can dispose of the affects in the dream thoughts in yet another way, besides admitting them or reducing them to zero: it can turn them into their opposites. We have already met the rule of interpretation that any element of the dream may be interpreted by its opposite as well as by itself. One can never tell at the outset which of the two to set down; only the context can decide. Some suspicion of this state of affairs has evidently found its way into popular awareness, for dream books very often interpret dreams according to the principle of contraries. Such reversal into the opposite is made possible by the close chaining of associations, which in our thinking links the idea of a thing with the idea of its opposite. Like every other displacement, it furthers the aims of the censor, but it is also frequently the work of wish fulfillment, since wish fulfillment consists precisely in replacing an unwelcome thing with its opposite. The emotions of the dream thoughts can appear in the dream transformed into their opposites just as readily as its ideas can, and this inversion of feeling is probably, as a rule, the work of the dream censor. In social life, too, the suppression and inversion of emotion are useful, above all for the purposes of dissimulation, as the analogy we have been drawing for the dream censor has already shown. If I am speaking with someone to whom I owe consideration, and I must tell him something unpleasant, it is almost more important to hide the expression of my feeling from him than to soften the wording of my thoughts. If I address him in polite words while my looks or gestures convey hatred and disdain, the effect on him will be little different from what it would have been had I recklessly flung my contempt in his face. Above all, then, the censor bids me suppress my emotions. And if I have mastered the art of dissimulation, I can hypocritically display the opposite emotion, smiling when I would like to be angry and feigning affection when I would like to destroy.

We already know an excellent example of this kind of inversion carried out for the dream censor's purposes. In the dream about my uncle's beard, I feel great affection for my friend R. at the very moment that the dream thoughts are abusing him as a simpleton, and indeed because they are doing so. It was from this example of inverted emotion that we drew our first proof that the censor exists. Nor do we need to suppose that the dream-work conjures up such a counter-emotion out of nothing. It usually finds one lying ready in the material of the dream thoughts, and it simply intensifies it with the psychic force of the resisting impulse until the emotion becomes strong enough to be enlisted in forming the dream. In the dream of my uncle just mentioned, the affectionate counter-emotion probably arose from an infantile source, as the continuation of the dream would suggest. Owing to the peculiar nature of my childhood experiences, the relation between uncle and nephew has become the source of all my friendships and all my hatreds, as the analysis of that dream has already shown.

There is a class of dreams that deserves to be called "hypocritical," and it puts the theory of wish-fulfilment to a severe test. My attention was drawn to them when Dr. M. Hilferding brought up for discussion in the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society a dream recorded by the Austrian writer Peter Rosegger, which I reproduce below.

In the eleventh volume of his *Waldheimat*, in the story *Fremd gemacht*, Rosegger writes as follows:

"I have generally enjoyed sound and healthy sleep, yet I have lost the rest of many a night. Through all the long years of my modest existence as a student and man of letters, I dragged behind me the shadow of a genuine tailor's life, like a ghost I could not shake off. I cannot say that I dwelt on my past often or vividly during the day. A young man setting out to storm heaven and earth, newly emerged from the skin of the Philistine, has other things to think about. Nor, as a dashing young fellow, did I give any thought to my dreams at night. Only later, when I had fallen into the habit of reflecting on everything, or when the Philistine within me began to assert himself again, did it strike me that whenever I dreamed, I was always the journeyman tailor, always working long hours in my master's shop without any pay. As I sat there sewing and pressing, I knew perfectly well that I no longer belonged there, and that as a citizen of a town I had other business to attend to. But I was forever on holiday, forever going out into the country, and it was then that I would sit beside my master and help him. I often felt miserable about it and regretted the loss of time I might have spent on better and more useful things. If something failed to come out to the right measure or cut, I had to put up with a scolding from the master. Often, as I sat with my back bent in the dingy shop, I resolved to give notice that I was quitting. Once I actually did so, but the master paid no attention, and the next time I was sitting beside him again, sewing.

"How happy I was when I woke after such wearisome hours! I would then resolve that if this dream came intruding again, I would throw it off with all my strength and cry aloud: 'It is only an illusion. I am in bed, and I want to sleep.' And the next night I would be sitting in the tailor's shop again.

"So the years went by with dismal regularity. Once, while the master and I were working at Alpelhofer's, the house of the peasant where I had begun my apprenticeship, he was particularly dissatisfied with my work. 'I should like to know where in the world your thoughts are!' he cried, and gave me a dark look. I thought the most sensible thing would be to stand up, explain to him that I was only there as a favor, and walk out. But I did not do it. I even submitted when the master took on an apprentice and ordered me to make room for him on the bench. I moved into the corner and went on sewing. That same day another tailor was hired, a bigoted man, a Czech who had worked for us nineteen years earlier and had then fallen into the lake on his way home from the tavern. When he tried to sit down, there was no room for him. I looked at the master questioningly, and he said to me: 'You have no talent for tailoring. You may go. You are free.' My fright at this was so overwhelming that I woke up.

"The gray of morning was glimmering through the clear window of my beloved home. I was surrounded by works of art. In the handsome bookcase stood the eternal Homer, the gigantic Dante, the incomparable Shakespeare, the glorious Goethe, all of them shining and immortal. From the next room came the bright little voices of the children, waking up and chattering with their mother. I felt as though I had found once more that idyllically sweet, peaceful, poetic, and spiritual life which I have so often and so deeply imagined as the contemplative happiness of humankind. And yet I was annoyed that I had not given my master notice first, instead of letting him dismiss me.

"And how remarkable it is: after the night on which the master 'dismissed' me, I had peace. I no longer dreamed of my tailoring, of that experience which lay in the distant past, which in its simplicity was truly a happy one, and which nevertheless cast a long shadow over the later years of my life."

In this series of dreams by a poet who had been a journeyman tailor in his youth, it is hard to recognize the dominance of wish-fulfilment. Everything delightful took place in waking life, while the dream seemed to drag along behind it the ghostly shadow of an unhappy existence long since forgotten. My own dreams of a similar kind have put me in a position to offer some explanation of such dreams. As a young doctor I worked for a long time in the chemical institute without being able to accomplish anything in that exacting science, and for that reason I never think, when awake, about this fruitless episode of my life, of which I am genuinely ashamed. Yet I have a recurring dream in which I am working in the laboratory, carrying out analyses and having various experiences there. Like examination dreams, these dreams are disagreeable, and they are never very distinct. While I was analyzing one of them, my attention was caught by the word "analysis," and it gave me the key to understanding them all. For I had since become an "analyst." I now perform analyses that are highly praised, though they are psychoanalyses. I then understood that whenever I grew proud of these waking analyses and wanted to boast of how much I had achieved with them, the dream would hold up before me at night those other, unsuccessful analyses of which I had no reason to be proud. These are the punishment dreams of the upstart, like those of the tailor who became a celebrated poet.

But how can the dream place itself at the service of self-criticism in its conflict with the pride of the parvenu, and take as its content a sensible warning rather than the fulfilment of a forbidden wish? I have already said that answering this question involves many difficulties. We may conclude that the foundation of the dream was first laid by a fantasy of overweening ambition, but that only the suppression and humbling of that fantasy reached the dream content in its place. We should also remember that the psychic life contains masochistic tendencies to which such an inversion might be attributed. A more thorough investigation of the individual dreams, however, reveals yet another element. In an indistinct, subordinate part of one of my laboratory dreams, I was exactly the age that placed me in the gloomiest and least successful year of my professional career. I still had no position and no means of support, and then suddenly I discovered that I had my choice among many women I might marry! So I was young again, and what is more, she was young again: the woman who has shared all these hard years with me. In this way one of the wishes that continually gnaw at the heart of an aging man was revealed as the unconscious instigator of the dream. The struggle raging in other psychic strata between vanity and self-criticism certainly determined the dream's content, but it was the more deeply rooted wish for youth that alone made the dream possible. Even awake, one may say to oneself: "Things are very pleasant now, and times were once very hard; but they were pleasant even then, for you were still so young."

When we consider dreams reported by a poet, we may often assume that he has left out of his account those details which struck him as disturbing and which he considered unimportant. His dreams therefore present us with a riddle that could easily be solved if we had an exact reproduction of the dream content.

Otto Rank has pointed out to me that a very similar upstart's dream is told in Grimm's fairy tale of the brave little tailor, "Seven at One Blow." The tailor, who has become a hero and married the king's daughter, dreams one night, as he lies beside the princess, his wife, about his old trade. Growing suspicious, she orders armed guards to stand by the following night, listen to what the dreamer says in his sleep, and put him to death. But the little tailor is warned in time and knows enough to correct his dream.

The whole complex of processes, of suspension, subtraction, and inversion, by which the emotions of the dream thoughts finally become the emotions of the dream, can be observed well in a suitable synthesis of dreams that have been completely analyzed. I shall now consider a few instances of emotional excitement in dreams that illustrate some of the cases discussed above.

In the dream about the odd task that old Brücke sets me, of dissecting and preparing my own pelvis, the horror appropriate to such a task is absent from the dream itself. This absence is a wish-fulfilment in several senses. The dissection signifies self-analysis, which I am carrying out, so to speak, by publishing my book on dreams, and which has been so disagreeable to me that I have already put off printing the finished manuscript for more than a year. The wish now stirs that I might disregard this feeling of reluctance, and that is why I feel no horror in the dream. The German word for horror, *Grauen*, also means "to grow gray," and in that second sense too I should like to escape it. I am going gray quickly, and the gray in my hair warns me as well that I must not hold back any longer. For, as we know, the thought finds expression at the end of the dream that I might have to leave it to my children to reach the goal of the difficult journey.

In the two dreams that shift the expression of satisfaction to the moments immediately after waking, the satisfaction in the first case is motivated by the expectation that I am now about to learn what is meant by "I have already dreamed of this," and it refers in reality to the birth of my first child. In the second case it is motivated by the conviction that "what has been announced by a sign" is now about to happen, and this satisfaction is the same one I felt at the arrival of my second son. Here the same emotions that governed the dream thoughts have remained in the dream. But the process is probably not this simple in every dream. If we examine the two analyses a little more closely, we see that this satisfaction, which does not fall victim to the censor, receives a reinforcement from a source that does have reason to fear the censor. The emotion drawn from that second source would certainly provoke opposition if it did not disguise itself in a similar, freely admitted feeling of satisfaction, if it did not, so to speak, slip in behind it.

Unfortunately, I cannot demonstrate this in the dream specimens themselves, but an example from another sphere will make my meaning clear. I construct the following case. Suppose there is someone close to me whom I hate so much that a strong feeling arises in me that I would be glad if something were to befall him. But the moral side of my nature does not give way to this feeling. I do not dare express the ill-wish, and when something happens to him that he has not deserved, I suppress my satisfaction and force myself to think and speak words of regret. Everyone has found himself in such a position. Now suppose that the hated person brings a well-deserved misfortune upon himself through some fault of his own. Now I may give free rein to my satisfaction that he has met with just punishment, and I voice an opinion on the matter that agrees with the opinion of many other, impartial people. Yet I notice that my satisfaction is more intense than theirs, because it has received an addition from another source: from my hatred, which until now the inner censor had prevented from releasing any emotion, but which under the changed circumstances is no longer held back.

This case is broadly typical of society, wherever people who have aroused antipathy, or who belong to an unpopular minority, incur some guilt.
