Their punishment does not correspond to their offense; it corresponds to their offense plus all the ill will that has been directed against them and has until then found no outlet. Those who inflict the punishment are undoubtedly committing an injustice, but they are kept from realizing it by the satisfaction that arises when a long-standing suppression within them is released. In such cases the emotion is justified in its quality but not in its quantity, and self-criticism, once satisfied on the first point, is only too ready to neglect examining the second. Once you have opened the doors, more people get through than you originally meant to let in.

This mechanism explains, insofar as it can be explained psychologically at all, a striking feature of the neurotic character: that a stimulus capable of arousing emotion produces a response that is qualitatively justified but quantitatively excessive. The excess comes from sources of emotion that have remained unconscious and have until now been suppressed. These sources can establish an associative connection with the actual stimulus, and so find release for their emotion through the outlet that the unobjectionable and acknowledged source has opened. We are thus reminded that the relation between the suppressed and the suppressing psychic agencies is not always one of mutual restraint. The cases in which the two agencies cooperate and strengthen each other to produce a pathological emotion deserve just as much attention.

I ask the reader to apply these hints about the psychic mechanism to the understanding of emotional expression in dreams. A satisfaction that appears in a dream, and that can readily be traced to its proper place in the dream thoughts, is not always fully explained by that connection alone. As a rule, one must look for a second source in the dream thoughts, a source on which the censor's pressure bears, and which under that pressure would have produced not satisfaction but the opposite feeling. The presence of the first source, however, enables this second source to free its own satisfaction from suppression and add it to the satisfaction arising from the first. The emotions in a dream therefore appear to be formed by the confluence of several tributaries, and to be overdetermined with respect to the material of the dream thoughts. Sources of affect capable of supplying the same emotion join together in the dream-work to produce it.

Some insight into these tangled relations can be gained by analyzing the remarkable dream that centers on the words "Non vixit," Latin for "he did not live." In this dream, emotional expressions of different kinds are compressed together at two points in the manifest content. Hostile and painful feelings overlap at the point where I annihilate my adversary and friend with those two words; in the dream itself I am "seized by strange emotions." At the end of the dream I am greatly pleased, and quite ready to believe in a possibility I recognize as absurd when awake: that there are *revenants*, ghosts of the dead who return, and that they can be disposed of by a mere wish.

I have not yet mentioned what occasioned this dream. It is essential, and it goes a long way toward explaining the dream. I had received word from my friend in Berlin, whom I have called F., that he was about to undergo an operation, and that relatives of his living in Vienna would keep me informed of his condition. The first reports after the operation were not reassuring and made me anxious. I would have liked most of all to go to him myself, but at the time I was suffering from a painful illness that made every movement torture. From the dream thoughts I learn that I feared for my dear friend's life. I knew that his only sister, whom I had never met, had died young after the briefest of illnesses. (In the dream F. speaks of his sister and says: "In three-quarters of an hour she was dead.") I must have imagined that his own constitution was not much sturdier, and that I would soon be traveling to him, despite my health, in response to far worse news, and that I would arrive too late, for which I would reproach myself forever.

This reproach of arriving too late has become the central point of the dream, but it has been represented in a scene in which the revered teacher of my student years, Brücke, reproaches me for the same fault with a terrible look from his blue eyes. The reason for this displacement of the scene will soon be clear: the dream cannot reproduce the situation in the form in which I actually experienced it. It does leave the blue eyes to the other man, but it gives me the role of the annihilator, an inversion that is plainly the work of wish-fulfilment. My concern for my friend's life, my self-reproach for not having gone to him, my shame (he had come to see me in Vienna several times), my wish to consider myself excused by my illness: all this makes up a storm of feeling that is distinctly felt in sleep and that raged through every region of the dream thoughts.

But there was another circumstance surrounding the dream that had quite the opposite effect. Along with the unfavorable news in the first days after the operation, I received an instruction not to speak to anyone about the whole matter. This hurt my feelings, since it betrayed an unnecessary distrust of my discretion. I knew, of course, that the request did not come from my friend, and that it was due to clumsiness or excessive caution on the part of the messenger. Still, the concealed reproach pained me because it was not altogether unjustified. Only reproaches that "have something in them" have the power to wound, as everyone knows. Long before, in the case of two men who were friendly with each other and who were both willing to honor me with their friendship, I had quite needlessly repeated to one what the other had said about him. This incident, to be sure, had nothing to do with my friend F.'s affairs. Nor have I forgotten the reproaches I had to endure at the time. One of the two friends between whom I made trouble was Professor Fleischl; the other I may call Joseph, a name also borne by my friend and adversary P., who appears in the dream.

Two elements of the dream bear witness to the reproach that I am incapable of keeping anything to myself: first, the word "inconspicuously," and second, Fl.'s question as to how much of his affairs I had told P. But it is the admixture of these memories that transposes the reproach of arriving too late from the present back to the time when I was working in Brücke's laboratory. And by replacing the second person in the dream's annihilation scene with a Joseph, I manage to represent not only the first reproach, that I arrive too late, but also a second, more severely suppressed reproach, that I keep no secrets. The condensing and substituting work of this dream, and the motives behind it, are now plain.

My anger at the instruction not to say anything, originally quite trivial, receives reinforcement from sources flowing far beneath the surface, and so swells into a torrent of hostile feeling toward people who are in reality dear to me. The source of this reinforcement lies in childhood. I have already said that my friendships and my enmities with people of my own age go back to my childhood relations with my nephew, who was a year older than I. He had the upper hand in these relations, and I learned early how to defend myself. We lived together inseparably and loved each other, and at the same time, as the accounts of older people testify, we fought with each other and accused each other. In a certain sense all my friends are incarnations of this first figure, the one "which early appeared to my blurred sight," as Goethe puts it; they are all *revenants*. My nephew himself returned in my adolescence, and then we played Caesar and Brutus together. An intimate friend and a hated enemy have always been indispensable to my emotional life. I have always been able to create them anew, and not infrequently my childhood ideal has been so closely realized that friend and enemy coincided in the same person, though not, of course, at the same moment, nor in repeated alternation, as had been the case in my earliest childhood.

I do not wish to trace here the way in which a recent occasion for emotion may reach back, through connections like those I have just described, to one in childhood, so as to substitute that earlier occasion for itself and gain a heightened emotional effect. Such an investigation would belong to the psychology of the unconscious and would find its place in a psychological explanation of the neuroses. For the purposes of dream interpretation, let us assume that a childhood memory emerges, or is formed by the imagination, to roughly the following effect. Two children get into a fight over some object (what exactly, we shall leave undecided, although the memory, or the hint of a memory, has one quite definite object in mind—and each of them claims that he got to it first and therefore has the first right to it. They come to blows, since might makes right. The dream suggests that I must have known I was in the wrong, for I notice the error myself, but this time I am the stronger and hold the field. The defeated boy runs to my father, his grandfather, and accuses me, and I defend myself with words I know from my father's telling: "I hit him because he hit me." This recollection, or more probably this fantasy, forces itself on my attention during the analysis, though from what I now know I cannot say how. It becomes a junction point among the dream thoughts, gathering the emotional excitations at work in them as the basin of a fountain gathers the streams of water that flow into it. From this point the dream thoughts run along the following paths: "It serves you right that you had to give up your place to me. Why did you try to push me out of mine? I don't need you; I'll soon find someone else to play with," and so on. From here, in turn, paths open along which these thoughts pass back into the representation of the dream.

I once had occasion to reproach my late friend Joseph for just such an *ôte-toi que je m'y mette*, a French phrase meaning "get out of the way so that I can take your place." He had stood next after me in the line of promotion in Brücke's laboratory, but advancement there was very slow. Neither of the two assistants moved from his post, and youth grew impatient. My friend knew that his own span of life was limited, and he was bound by no tie of affection to his superior, who was seriously ill. The wish to see that superior removed therefore lent itself to an ugly interpretation: it might aim at something more than promotion. Some years earlier the same wish for freedom had naturally been even stronger in me. Wherever in the world there are ranks and promotions, the door is open to wishes that must be suppressed. Shakespeare's Prince Hal, even at his sick father's bedside, cannot resist the temptation to see how the crown fits. But the dream, as one can readily understand, punishes this ruthless wish not in me but in him.

"As he was ambitious, I slew him." Because he could not wait for the other man to make way for him, he himself has been put out of the way. I harbor these thoughts directly after attending the unveiling of the statue to that other man at the university. Part of the satisfaction I feel in the dream can therefore be read as: a just punishment; it served you right.

At this friend's funeral, a young man made a remark that seemed out of place: "The preacher talked as though the world couldn't go on without this one human being." In him, the resentment of a sincere man whose grief has been spoiled by exaggeration was beginning to stir. But the dream thoughts attach themselves to this remark: "No one is really irreplaceable. How many men have I already followed to the grave, yet I am still alive. I have outlived them all; the field is mine." Such a thought, arising at a moment when I fear that if I travel to see my friend I shall no longer find him among the living, can develop in only one further direction: I am glad to be outliving someone, glad that it is he who has died and not I, glad that I hold the field as I once did in that imagined childhood scene. This satisfaction, which springs from childhood sources, at the fact that the field is mine accounts for the greater part of the emotion that appears in the dream. I am glad to be the survivor, and I express the feeling with the naïve egotism of the husband who says to his wife, "If one of us dies, I shall move to Paris." To my mind it is so much a matter of course that I shall not be the one.

There is no denying that it takes considerable self-control to interpret one's own dreams and report them. One must be prepared to reveal oneself as the sole villain among all the noble souls with whom one shares the breath of life. So it seems to me entirely natural that revenants, the dead who return, exist only as long as one wants them, and that a wish can do away with them. This is what my friend Joseph was punished for. But the revenants are the successive incarnations of my childhood friend, and I am also satisfied that I have found a replacement for that person again and again. A substitute will no doubt soon be found even for the friend I am now about to lose. No one is irreplaceable.

But what has the dream censor been doing all this while? Why does it not raise the strongest objection to a train of thought marked by such brutal selfishness, and turn the satisfaction attached to it into deep revulsion? I think the reason is that other, unobjectionable trains of thought also end in satisfaction, and they cover the emotion arising from forbidden infantile sources with their own. In another layer of thought, I said to myself at that festive unveiling: "I have lost so many dear friends, some through death, some through the breaking off of friendship. Is it not a fine thing that I have found substitutes for them, that I have gained one who means more to me than the others could, and whom I shall keep from now on, at an age when new friendships are not easily made?" The satisfaction of having found this substitute for lost friends can pass into the dream without interference, but behind it the hostile satisfaction from the infantile source slips in as well. Childish affection no doubt helps to strengthen the justified affection of today, but childish hatred has also found its way into the representation.

Beyond this, the dream refers distinctly to yet another chain of thoughts that can express itself as satisfaction. My friend had recently had a little daughter, born after long waiting. I knew how deeply he had grieved for the sister he lost at an early age, and I wrote to him that he would transfer to this child the love he had felt for her. This little girl would at last make him forget his irreparable loss.

This chain, too, links up with the intermediate thoughts of the latent dream content, from which paths spread out in opposite directions: No one is irreplaceable. You see, nothing but revenants; everything one has lost comes back. The bonds of association between the contradictory elements of the dream thoughts are drawn still tighter by a chance circumstance. My friend's little daughter bears the same name as the girl who was my playmate in early youth, who was exactly my age and was the sister of my oldest friend and adversary. I heard the name "Pauline" with satisfaction, and to allude to this coincidence I replaced one Joseph in the dream with another Joseph, and did not overlook the similarity in sound between the names Fleischl and F. From here a train of thought runs to the naming of my own children. I insisted that their names should not be chosen by the fashion of the day but should honor the memory of people we had loved. Their names make the children revenants. And finally, is not having children the only path to immortality open to any of us?

I shall add only a few remarks about the emotions of the dream from another point of view. An emotional inclination, what we call a mood, may be the dominant element in the mind of a sleeping person and may produce a corresponding mood in the dream. This mood may come from the experiences and thoughts of the day, or it may have a bodily origin; in either case it will be accompanied by the chains of thought that correspond to it. In the first case the content of these ideas produces the emotional inclination directly; in the second, the ideas are called up afterward by a disposition of feeling that arises in the body. This difference has no effect on the formation of the dream. That formation is always bound by the restriction that it can represent only the fulfillment of a wish, and that it may lend its psychic driving force only to the wish. A mood actually present during sleep receives the same treatment as a sensation that actually rises to the surface during sleep: it is either ignored or reinterpreted so as to signify a wish fulfillment. Unpleasant moods during sleep become a driving force of the dream by stirring up energetic wishes, which the dream must then fulfill. The material to which these moods are attached is reworked until it becomes suitable for expressing the fulfilled wish. The more intense and dominant the element of unpleasant mood in the dream thoughts, the more surely will the most rigorously suppressed wish impulses seize the opportunity to gain representation. They find that the hardest part of the work needed to secure representation has already been done for them, since the distress, which they would otherwise have had to generate by their own effort, is already present. With this discussion we touch once again on the problem of anxiety dreams, which we may regard as marking the outer boundary of the dream-work's domain.

### (h) Secondary Elaboration

We may at last proceed to an account of the fourth of the factors that take part in forming the dream.

If we continue to examine the dream content in the manner already described, testing conspicuous features for their origin in the dream thoughts, we encounter elements that can be explained only by making an entirely new assumption. I have in mind cases in which the dreamer shows astonishment, anger, or resistance within the dream, and does so against a part of the dream content itself. Most of these exercises of the critical faculty in dreams are not actually directed against the dream content. They turn out to be pieces of dream material that have been taken over and put to suitable use, as I have shown with fitting examples. Some cases of this kind, however, cannot be disposed of in that way, because no counterpart for them can be found in the dream material. What, for instance, is the meaning of the criticism that occurs not infrequently in dreams: "Well, it's only a dream"? This is a genuine criticism of the dream, of the kind I might make while awake. Fairly often it is the prelude to waking; still more often it is preceded by a painful feeling that subsides once the certainty of dreaming has been established. The thought "But it's only a dream," occurring within the dream, has the same aim as the words placed in the mouth of the beautiful Helen in Offenbach's operetta: it seeks to make light of what has just happened and to secure indulgence for what is to come. Its purpose is to reassure, and so to speak lull to sleep, a certain agency that at that moment has every reason to stir and forbid the continuation of the dream, or of the scene. It is more pleasant to go on sleeping and put up with the dream, "since it's only a dream anyway." I imagine that the disparaging criticism "But it's only a dream" enters the dream at the moment when the censor, which has never been entirely asleep, realizes it has been taken by surprise by a dream it has already let through. It is too late to suppress the dream, and so the censor meets the anxiety or painful feeling that the dream has aroused with this remark. It is the psychic censor's *esprit d'escalier*, the "staircase wit" of a person who thinks of the right reply only after leaving the room.

This example gives us flawless proof that not everything in the dream comes from the dream thoughts, and that a psychic function indistinguishable from our waking thought can contribute to the dream content. The question now is whether this happens only in wholly exceptional cases, or whether the psychic agency that ordinarily acts only as censor takes a regular part in forming dreams.

We must decide for the second view without hesitation. It is beyond dispute that the censoring agency, whose influence we have so far recognized only in the limitations and omissions of the dream content, is also responsible for insertions and additions to that content. These insertions are often easy to recognize. They are reported hesitantly, prefaced by an "as if"; they are not especially vivid in themselves; and they are regularly placed at points where they can link two portions of the dream content or smooth the sequence between two sections of the dream. They hold in the memory less firmly than the genuine products of the dream material. If the dream is subject to forgetting, they are the first to drop away, and I am strongly inclined to believe that our frequent complaint that we have dreamed a great deal, forgotten most of it, and kept only fragments rests on the immediate loss of precisely these connecting thoughts. In a complete analysis these insertions often betray themselves by the fact that no material for them can be found in the dream thoughts. After careful examination, however, I must call this a rare case. Usually the inserted thoughts can be traced to an element in the dream thoughts that could not have earned a place in the dream either on its own merits or through overdetermination. The psychic function in dream formation that we are now considering resorts to original creation only in the most extreme cases; whenever possible, it makes use of whatever it can find in the dream material.

What distinguishes and reveals this part of the dream-work is its tendency. This function behaves much as the poet maliciously says the philosopher does: with its scraps and rags, it patches the gaps in the structure of the dream. The result of its effort is that the dream loses its appearance of absurdity and incoherence and approaches the pattern of an intelligible experience. But the effort is not always entirely successful. So there are dreams that, on superficial examination, may seem perfectly logical and correct. They start from a possible situation, carry it forward through consistent changes, and, though this is very rare, arrive at a not unnatural conclusion. These dreams have been subjected to the most thorough elaboration by a psychic function similar to our waking thought. They seem to have a meaning, but this meaning lies very far from the dream's real significance. When they are analyzed, one is convinced that the secondary elaboration has handled the material very freely and preserved its true relations as little as possible. These are the dreams that have, so to speak, already been interpreted before we subject them to waking interpretation. In other dreams this purposeful elaboration has succeeded only up to a point. Up to that point consistency seems to prevail; then the dream becomes nonsensical or confused, and perhaps at last rises a second time to an appearance of rationality. In still other dreams the elaboration has failed completely, and we find ourselves helpless before a senseless heap of fragmentary contents.

I do not wish to deny this fourth dream-shaping power the capacity to furnish the dream with new contributions of its own creation. It will soon seem familiar to us; indeed, it is the only one of the four with which we are already acquainted. But surely its influence, like that of the others, shows itself mainly in preferring and selecting psychic material already created in the dream thoughts. There is one case in which it is largely spared the work of building, as it were, a façade for the dream, because a structure of this kind is already present and complete in the material of the dream thoughts, waiting to be used. I am in the habit of calling this element of the dream thoughts a "fantasy," and I may avoid misunderstanding if I offer at once the daydream of waking life as an analogy. Psychiatrists have not yet fully recognized or investigated the part this element plays in our mental life, though M. Benedikt has, it seems to me, made a highly promising start. The significance of the daydream has not escaped the unerring insight of poets; Daudet's description of the daydreams of one of the minor characters in *Nabab* is universally known. The study of the psychoneuroses reveals the astonishing fact that these fantasies or daydreams are the immediate forerunners of hysterical symptoms, or at least of a great many of them. Hysterical symptoms depend directly not on memories themselves but on fantasies built on the basis of memories. Because conscious daytime fantasies occur so frequently, these formations come within the range of our knowledge. But just as there are conscious fantasies, there are a great many unconscious ones, which must remain unconscious because of their content and because they derive from repressed material. A closer look at the character of these daytime fantasies shows how justly they have been given the same name as the products of our nocturnal thinking: dreams. They share an essential part of their properties with night dreams, and examining them would in fact have offered the shortest and best route to understanding night dreams.

Like dreams, they are wish fulfillments. Like dreams, a good many of them rest on impressions from childhood experiences. Like dreams, their creations enjoy a certain indulgence from the censor. If we trace how they are formed, we see how the wish motive at work in producing them has taken the material from which they are built, mixed it together, rearranged it, and composed it into a new whole. They stand in the same relation to the childhood memories from which they derive as certain of Rome's curious palaces stand to the ancient ruins whose dressed stones and columns supplied the material for buildings in a modern style.

In the "secondary elaboration" of the dream content, which we have attributed to our fourth dream-making factor, we find once again the same activity that is allowed to express itself unhindered by other influences in the creation of daydreams. We may say without further preamble that this fourth factor tries to shape something like a daydream out of the material at hand. Where such a daydream has already been formed in connection with the dream thoughts, however, this factor of the dream-work will prefer to take hold of it and work it into the dream content. There are dreams that consist merely of the repetition of such a daytime fantasy, one that has perhaps remained unconscious, as in the boy's dream of riding in a war chariot with the heroes of the Trojan War. In my dream "Autodidasker," at least the second part is a faithful repetition of a daytime fantasy, harmless in itself, about my dealings with Professor N. More often, the fantasy supplied in this way forms only one part of the dream, or only one part of the fantasy makes its way into the dream content, and this follows from the complexity of the conditions the dream must satisfy as it comes into being. On the whole, the fantasy is treated like any other component of the latent material, yet it is often still recognizable in the dream as a unit. In my own dreams there are often passages that stand out by an impression different from that of the rest. They seem to me to be in a state of flux, to be more coherent and at the same time more fleeting than other parts of the same dream. I know that these are unconscious fantasies that have entered the dream through their associations, but I have never managed to pin one of them down. Beyond this, these fantasies, like all the other components of the dream thoughts, are jumbled together and condensed, one covered by another, and so on. There are all degrees, from the case in which they may make up the dream content, or at least the dream façade, without alteration, to the opposite case in which they are represented in the dream content by only one of their elements or by a remote allusion to such an element. The extent to which the fantasies can withstand the demands of the censor and the pressure toward condensation also decides, of course, their fate among the dream thoughts.

In choosing examples for dream analysis I have, wherever possible, avoided dreams in which unconscious fantasies play a fairly important part, because introducing this psychic element would have required an extended discussion of the psychology of unconscious thought. Even in my examples, however, I cannot leave the "fantasy" out entirely, since it often enters the dream whole and still more often visibly pervades it. I may mention one more dream, which seems to be made up of two distinct and opposed fantasies that overlap at certain points. The first is superficial, while the second becomes, as it were, the interpreter of the first.

The dream, the only one for which I have no careful notes, runs roughly as follows. The dreamer, an unmarried young man, is sitting in an inn, which he sees accurately. Several people come to fetch him, among them someone who wants to arrest him. He says to his companions at the table, "I'll pay later; I'm coming back." But they call to him with scornful laughter, "We know all about that; that's what everybody says." One guest calls after him, "There goes another one." He is then led into a narrow room, where he finds a woman with a child in her arms. One of his escorts says, "This is Mr. Müller." A police commissioner or some other official is leafing through a bundle of tickets or papers, repeating, "Müller, Müller, Müller." At last the commissioner asks him a question, which he answers with "Yes." He then looks at the woman and notices that she has grown a large beard.

The two components are easily separated here. The superficial one is the fantasy of being arrested, which seems to have been newly created by the dream-work. Behind it appears the fantasy of marriage, and this material, by contrast, has been only slightly changed by the dream activity. The features the two fantasies share stand out sharply, as in one of Galton's composite photographs, in which several faces are exposed one on top of another on the same plate so that their common features emerge clearly while individual differences blur. The bachelor's promise to return to his place at the regulars' table, the skepticism of his drinking companions, made worldly-wise by long experience, the call "There goes another one," meaning another one gone off to be married: all these features can just as easily bear the other interpretation. So can the affirmative answer given to the official. The leafing through the bundle of papers with the repetition of the name corresponds to a minor but well-known feature of wedding celebrations, the reading aloud of the congratulatory telegrams that have arrived at odd times and are, of course, all addressed to the same name. In the matter of the bride's appearance in this dream, the marriage fantasy has even prevailed over the arrest fantasy that conceals it. The fact that the bride ends up with a beard I can explain from a question I put to the dreamer, though I had no chance to carry out a full analysis. On the previous day he had been crossing the street with a friend who was just as hostile to marriage as he was, and he had pointed out a beautiful brunette coming toward them. His friend had remarked: "Yes, if only these women didn't grow beards like their fathers as they got older."

This dream does, of course, contain elements on which the distortion has done more thorough work. The remark "I will pay later," for instance, may refer to the father-in-law's conduct in the matter of the dowry, though this is uncertain. Plainly, all sorts of misgivings keep the dreamer from giving himself over with pleasure to the fantasy of marriage. One of these fears, that a man loses his freedom when he marries, has taken shape in the transformation of the wedding into a scene of arrest.

Let us return to the thesis that the dream-work prefers to use a fantasy that is already finished and at hand rather than create one afresh from the material of the dream thoughts. If we keep this fact in mind, we may be able to solve one of the most interesting riddles of the dream. I have already related the dream of Maury, who was struck on the back of the neck by a piece of wood and awoke in possession of a long dream, a complete romance set in the time of the French Revolution. The dream is reported as coherent and as fully explained by the disturbing stimulus alone, a stimulus whose arrival the sleeper could not have anticipated. Only one assumption then seems to remain: that the whole richly elaborated dream must have been composed, and must have run its course, in the brief interval between the moment the wood fell on Maury's cervical vertebrae and the moment the blow woke him. We would not feel justified in attributing such speed to waking thought, and so we are inclined to credit the dream-work with a remarkable acceleration of thinking as one of its characteristic traits.

This inference quickly became popular, but more recent writers, among them Le Lorrain and Egger, have raised emphatic objections to it. Some doubt whether Maury reported his dream accurately; others try to show that our waking minds can work quite as fast as anything we might concede without reservation to the dream-work. The debate raises fundamental questions, and I do not think settling them is my immediate concern. I must admit, however, that Egger's argument, for one, has not struck me as convincing against Maury's guillotine dream. I would propose the following explanation. Is it so very improbable that Maury's dream presents a fantasy that had been stored in his memory, fully finished, for years, and that was awakened, or better, alluded to, at the moment he became aware of the disturbing stimulus? The difficulty of composing so long a story, with all its details, in the exceedingly short time available to the dreamer then disappears, because the story was already composed. Had the wood struck Maury's neck while he was awake, there might have been time for the thought, "Why, that's like being guillotined." But because it struck him while he was asleep, the dream-work quickly seized on the incoming stimulus as an occasion to construct a wish-fulfillment, as though it were thinking (and this is meant entirely figuratively): "Here is a fine opportunity to realize the wishful fantasy I formed at such and such a time while I was reading."

That this dream romance is exactly the kind a young man would invent under the sway of powerful impressions seems to me beyond question. Who would not have been carried away, especially a Frenchman and a student of the history of civilization, by accounts of the Reign of Terror, when the aristocracy, men and women alike, the flower of the nation, showed that it was possible to die with a light heart and kept their quick wit and refinement of manner until the fatal summons came? How tempting to imagine oneself in the midst of it all, as one of the young men who takes leave of his lady by kissing her hand and then climbs the scaffold without fear! Or perhaps ambition is the ruling motive of the fantasy: the ambition to put oneself in the place of one of those powerful figures who, by sheer force of thought and fiery eloquence, governed the city in which the heart of mankind was then beating so convulsively; who, driven by conviction, sent thousands of human beings to their deaths and prepared the way for the transformation of Europe; and who, all the while, could not be sure of their own heads and might one day lay them beneath the blade of the guillotine, perhaps in the role of one of the Girondists or of the hero Danton. The detail that Maury remembered being "accompanied by an innumerable multitude" seems to show that his fantasy was an ambitious one of this kind.

Yet this fantasy, ready for so long, need not be lived through again in sleep. It is enough for it to be, so to speak, "touched off." What I mean is this. In Mozart's *Don Giovanni*, a band plays a few bars during the supper scene and Leporello remarks that the tune comes from *The Marriage of Figaro*. When something like that happens to me, when a few notes are struck and someone names the opera they come from, memories suddenly surge up within me, none of which I could bring back to consciousness a moment later. The characteristic phrase acts as an entry point through which an entire complex is set in motion all at once. There is no reason it should be different with unconscious thought. The waking stimulus activates the psychic entry point that opens onto the whole guillotine fantasy. That fantasy, however, is not reviewed in sleep; it is reviewed only afterward, in waking memory. On awakening, one recalls in detail the fantasy that the dream treated as a single whole. And there is, after all, no way of making sure that one has truly remembered anything one dreamed. The same explanation, that we are dealing with finished fantasies set in motion as wholes by the waking stimulus, may be applied to other dreams that arise from such a stimulus, for instance Napoleon's battle dream at the explosion of the bomb. I do not mean to claim that every dream produced by a waking stimulus admits of this explanation, or that the problem of the accelerated flow of ideas in dreams can be entirely solved in this way.

We must not neglect the relation between this secondary elaboration of the dream content and the other factors in the dream-work. Might the process run as follows? The factors that create the dream, namely the drive toward condensation, the need to evade the censor, and the regard for what the dream's psychic means can represent, first produce a provisional dream content, which is then modified until it satisfies the demands of a second agency. This is hardly likely. We must assume instead that the demands of this agency are built in from the very start as one of the conditions the dream must meet, and that this condition, like those of condensation, censorship, and presentability, acts simultaneously on the whole mass of material in the dream thoughts, steering and selecting from it. Of the four conditions governing the formation of dreams, however, the one we have recognized last appears to make the least binding demands on the dream.

There is strong reason to infer that this psychic function, which carries out the so-called secondary elaboration of the dream content, is identical with the work of our waking thought. Our waking, preconscious thought behaves toward any object of perception exactly as this function behaves toward the dream content. It is natural for waking thought to impose order on perceptual material, to construct relationships within it, and to bring it under the requirements of intelligible coherence. We even go too far in doing so: conjurers deceive us precisely by exploiting this intellectual habit. In our effort to assemble the sensory impressions presented to us into something comprehensible, we often commit the most bizarre errors and even distort the truth of the material before us. The proofs of this are too familiar to need lengthy discussion here. We overlook misprints on a page because our imagination supplies the correct words. The editor of a widely read French newspaper is said to have wagered that he could insert the words "from in front" or "from behind" into every sentence of a long article without any of his readers noticing. He won the bet.

Years ago a curious example of mistaken association caught my attention in a newspaper. A bomb thrown by an anarchist had exploded in the French Chamber of Deputies, and Dupuy had quelled the resulting panic by calmly announcing, "La séance continue," "The session continues." Afterward, the visitors in the gallery were asked to give their impressions of the attempted assassination. Among them were two men from the provinces. One said that he had heard a detonation immediately after a speech ended, but had assumed it was the custom in parliament to fire a shot whenever a speaker finished. The other, who had evidently already heard several speakers, had arrived at the same idea, with one variation: he supposed the shot was a mark of approval, reserved for an especially successful speech.

The psychic agency that approaches the dream content demanding that it be intelligible, that subjects it to a preliminary interpretation and in so doing completely misunderstands it, is therefore nothing other than our normal thinking. In our work of interpretation, the rule must be to treat the apparent coherence of the dream as being of suspect origin in every case, and, whether its elements are clear or confused, to follow the same regressive path back to the dream material.

We now learn what essentially determines the scale of quality in dreams, from confusion to clarity, which I mentioned earlier. Those parts of the dream on which the secondary elaboration has been able to work seem clear to us; those where its power has failed seem confused. And since the confused parts of a dream are often also the less vividly impressed ones, we may conclude that the secondary dream-work also contributes to the sensory intensity of the individual dream images.

If I were to look for something to compare with the final form of the dream as it emerges under the influence of normal thinking, nothing would suit better than the mysterious inscriptions with which the Munich comic weekly *Die Fliegenden Blätter* has long amused its readers. The reader is meant to believe that a given sentence conceals a Latin inscription, while the sentence itself, for the sake of contrast, is written in dialect and is as vulgar in meaning as possible. To produce this effect, the letters are pulled out of their groupings into syllables and rearranged. Here and there a genuine Latin word emerges; elsewhere we believe we see abbreviations of such words; and at still other points we let ourselves be carried past the senselessness of the scattered letters by what look like crumbled fragments or gaps in a weathered inscription. If we do not wish to fall for the joke, we must give up looking for an inscription, take the letters as we find them, and combine them into words of our own language, disregarding the arrangement presented to us.

I shall now attempt to sum up this extended discussion of the dream-work. We were faced with the question of whether the mind brings all its faculties into full play in forming dreams, or only a fragment of them, and that fragment restricted in its operation. Our investigation leads us to reject this way of framing the question entirely, as inadequate to the facts. But if we are to answer on the same ground on which the question was put to us, we must accept two conceptions that appear to be opposed and mutually exclusive. The psychic activity involved in forming a dream divides into two functions: producing the dream thoughts, and transforming them into the dream content. The dream thoughts are entirely correct and are formed with all the psychic effort of which we are capable. They belong to our thoughts that have not become conscious, the same thoughts from which our conscious thoughts also arise through a certain transposition. However much there may be about them that is worth knowing and mysterious, these problems have no particular bearing on the dream and no claim to be treated alongside the problems of dreams.

The second part of the activity, by contrast, which converts the unconscious thoughts into the dream content, is peculiar to dream life and characteristic of it. And this distinctive dream-work is much further removed from the pattern of waking thought than even the most determined detractors of mental activity in dreams have supposed. It is not, one might say, more careless, more inaccurate, more forgetful, or more incomplete than waking thought; it is something qualitatively different altogether, and therefore not comparable to it in any way. As a rule it does not think, calculate, or judge at all; it confines itself to transforming. It can be described exhaustively if we keep in mind the conditions its product must satisfy. That product, the dream, must at all costs be withdrawn from the censor, and to this end the dream-work employs the displacement of psychic intensities, carried as far as a transvaluation of all psychic values. Thoughts must be reproduced exclusively or predominantly in the material of visual and auditory memory traces, and this requirement imposes on the dream-work a regard for presentability, which it satisfies by supplying further displacements. Greater intensities must (probably) be produced than the dream thoughts have available on any given night, and this purpose is met by the extensive condensation carried out on the components of the dream thoughts. Little attention is paid to the logical relations within the thought material; these ultimately find a disguised representation in the formal peculiarities of the dream. The emotions attached to the dream thoughts undergo smaller changes than their ideational content. As a rule they are suppressed; where they survive, they are detached from the ideas and grouped together according to their similarity. Only one part of the dream-work, the revision, varying in extent, carried out by partially awakened conscious thought, corresponds at all to the conception that earlier writers have tried to extend to the entire activity of dream formation.

## VII The Psychology of the Dream Activities

Among the dreams that others have told me, there is one that deserves particular attention at this point. A female patient told it to me; she had heard it in turn at a lecture on dreams, and I do not know its original source. The dream evidently made a deep impression on her, for she went so far as to imitate it. She repeated its elements in a dream of her own, and by this borrowing she expressed her agreement with it on a certain point.

The essential facts of this illustrative dream are as follows. A father had watched for days and nights at the bedside of his sick child. After the child died, he went to rest in an adjoining room, but he left the door ajar so that he could look from his room into the next, where the body lay surrounded by burning candles. An old man had been left to keep watch, and he sat near the body murmuring prayers. After sleeping a few hours, the father dreamed that the child was standing beside his bed, clasping his arm and calling out reproachfully, "Father, don't you see that I am burning?" The father woke and noticed a bright light coming from the adjoining room. He rushed in and found that the old man had fallen asleep and that a candle had fallen over, burning the coverings and one arm of the beloved body.

The meaning of this moving dream is simple enough, and the explanation the lecturer gave, as my patient reported it, was correct. The bright light shining through the open door into the sleeper's eyes produced the same impression on him that it would have produced had he been awake: that a falling candle had started a fire near the body. It is quite possible that when he went to sleep he had feared the elderly watchman was not equal to his task.

We find nothing to change in this interpretation. We can add only that the content of the dream must be overdetermined, and that the child's words in the dream consisted of phrases it had actually spoken while alive, phrases connected in the father's mind with important events. Perhaps the complaint "I am burning" recalled the fever from which the child died, and the words "Father, don't you see?" recalled some emotionally charged occasion unknown to us.

Yet once we have recognized this dream as a meaningful event that can be fitted into the context of our mental life, it may seem surprising that a dream should have occurred at all in circumstances that called for immediate waking. We also notice that the dream does not lack a wish-fulfillment. The child behaves as if it were alive; it warns the father itself; it comes to his bed and clasps his arm, as it probably did on the occasion that gave rise to the first part of its speech in the dream. It was for the sake of this wish-fulfillment that the father slept a moment longer. The dream prevailed over conscious reflection because it could show the child alive once more. Had the father woken first and then drawn the conclusion that sent him into the next room, he would have shortened the child's life by that one moment.

The peculiar feature of this brief dream that claims our interest is plain enough. Until now we have been chiefly concerned to establish what the secret meaning of a dream consists of, how that meaning can be discovered, and what means the dream-work uses to conceal it. Our greatest interest, that is, has so far centered on the problems of interpretation. Now, however, we encounter a dream that is easily explained, whose sense lies in plain view; and we notice that despite this, the dream still preserves the essential features that so clearly distinguish our dreaming from our waking thought, and these features plainly demand an explanation of their own. Even after all the problems of interpretation have been cleared away, we can still feel how incomplete our psychology of the dream remains.

Before we enter this new territory, however, let us pause and consider whether we have overlooked something important on the way here. For it must be frankly admitted that we have so far been traveling the easy and comfortable stretch of our journey. Until now, unless I am mistaken, every path we have followed has led toward light, toward clarification, and toward full understanding. But from the moment we try to penetrate more deeply into the mental processes of the dream, every path leads into darkness. It is quite impossible to *explain* the dream as a psychic process, for to explain something means to trace it back to what is already known, and we do not yet possess any body of psychological knowledge under which we could place, as their fundamental explanation, the conclusions that may be drawn from our psychological study of dreams. On the contrary, we shall be compelled to construct a series of new assumptions about the structure of the psychic apparatus and the forces at work within it. We must take care not to carry these assumptions beyond the simplest chain of logical connections, or their value will dissolve into uncertainty. And even if we make no errors in our reasoning and take account of every logical possibility, we shall still run the risk of complete failure, because our basic data are probably incomplete. Nor will it be possible to arrive at an explanation of the construction and workings of the psychic instrument, or at least to establish one, even through the most careful investigation of the dream or of any other single mental activity. To that end it will instead be necessary to gather together whatever emerges as decisively constant from a comparative study of a whole series of psychic activities. The psychological conceptions we derive from analyzing the dream process will therefore have to wait, so to speak, at a junction, until they can be linked with the results of other investigations that may have reached the heart of the same problem from a different starting point.

### (a) Forgetting in Dreams

I propose, then, to turn first to a subject that has given rise to an objection we have not yet addressed, one that threatens to undermine the very foundations of our work in dream interpretation. It has been objected from more than one quarter that we do not really know the dream we wish to interpret, or, more precisely, that we have no assurance of knowing it as it actually occurred. What we remember of the dream, and what we subject to our methods of interpretation, has first of all been distorted by our treacherous memory, which seems peculiarly unsuited to retaining dreams and may have dropped precisely the most important part of their content. When we pay attention to our dreams, we often have reason to complain that we dreamed far more than we can remember, that we unfortunately know nothing beyond this one fragment, and that even the fragment seems strangely uncertain. Everything, moreover, suggests that our memory reproduces the dream not only in fragments but also inaccurately and falsely. Just as we may doubt whether the dream material was really as disconnected and confused as we remember it, so we may also doubt whether a dream was really as coherent as we recount it. We may wonder whether, in trying to reproduce it, we have filled the gaps, whether present in the dream or created by forgetting, with new material chosen at random; whether we have embellished it, rounded it off, and arranged it until any judgment of its real content becomes impossible. One author, Spitta, has in fact expressed the belief that everything orderly and coherent in a dream is first introduced during our attempt to recall it. We are thus in danger of having wrested from our hands the very object whose value we set out to determine.

So far, in our interpretations, we have disregarded these warnings. Indeed, we found the demand for interpretation to be no less pressing in the smallest, most trivial, and most uncertain elements of the dream content than in its distinct and definite parts. In the dream of Irma's injection we read, "I quickly called in Dr. M.," and we assumed that even this small addition would not have found its way into the dream unless it had a particular origin. This led us to the history of that unfortunate patient to whose bedside I had "quickly" called in my older colleague. In the apparently absurd dream that treated the difference between 51 and 56 as a *quantité négligeable*, a negligible quantity, the number 51 was mentioned several times. Instead of taking this as self-evident or unimportant, we inferred from it a second train of thought in the latent content of the dream, one that led to the number 51. Following this clue, we arrived at the fears that set fifty-one years as a limit to life, in the sharpest contrast to a dominant train of thought that boastfully acknowledged no limit to life at all. In the dream "Non Vixit" I found an insignificant interpolation that I had at first overlooked: "As P. does not understand him, Fl. asks me," and so on. When the interpretation came to a standstill, I returned to these words and found through them the way to the childhood fantasy that appeared in the dream thoughts as an intermediate point of connection. This came about by way of the poet's verses:

*Seldom have you understood me,*
*Seldom have I understood you,*
*But when we got into the mire,*
*We at once understood each other.*

Every analysis will furnish examples showing how indispensable the most insignificant features of a dream are to its analysis, and how the completion of the work is delayed when attention is not directed to them from the start. In the same way, we have respected every shade of verbal expression in the dream when interpreting it. When we were confronted with wording that was senseless or inadequate, betraying an unsuccessful effort to render the dream in proper form, we respected even these defects of expression. In short, what the authorities regarded as an arbitrary improvisation, hastily concocted to suit the occasion, we have treated as a sacred text. This contradiction calls for an explanation.

The explanation works in our favor, though without discrediting the authorities. From the standpoint of our newly acquired understanding of how dreams originate, the contradictions resolve into complete agreement. It is true that we distort the dream in attempting to reproduce it, and here we find another instance of what we have called the secondary elaboration of the dream by normal thought, a process often misunderstood. But this distortion is itself only one part of the elaboration to which the dream thoughts are regularly subjected under the influence of the dream censor. The authorities have here guessed at or observed the part of dream distortion that operates most visibly. To us this matters little, for we know that a more extensive and less readily understood work of distortion has already selected the dream from among the hidden thoughts as its object. The authorities err only in regarding the changes the dream undergoes while being recalled and put into words as arbitrary and impossible to resolve, and therefore as likely to mislead us in interpreting it. They underestimate how thoroughly determined mental life is. Nothing in this domain is arbitrary. It can be shown quite generally that a second train of thought immediately takes over the determination of whatever elements the first has left undetermined. Suppose, for example, that I wish to think of a number entirely at will. This is impossible. The number that occurs to me is definitely and necessarily determined by thoughts within me, thoughts that may be far removed from my momentary intention. The changes the dream undergoes when it is revised in the waking state are just as far from arbitrary. They remain associatively connected with the content whose place they take, and they show us the way to that content, which may itself be a substitute for something else.

When analyzing dreams with patients, I regularly use the following test of this assertion, and it has never failed. If the account of a dream seems difficult to understand at first, I ask the dreamer to repeat it. He rarely does so in the same words. The passages where the wording has changed I have come to recognize as the weak points in the dream's disguise. They are of the same use to me as the embroidered mark on Siegfried's garment was to Hagen in the old German legend, where the hero's wife sewed a small cross onto his clothing to mark the one spot where he could be wounded, and his enemy used it to strike him down. The analysis can begin at these points. My announcement that I intend to take special pains to solve the dream has put the narrator on his guard, and at once, driven by resistance, he protects the weak points of the dream's disguise by replacing the revealing expressions with more remote ones. In doing so he draws my attention to the expressions he has dropped. From the effort he makes to prevent the dream from being solved, I can also draw conclusions about the care with which the dream's garment was woven.

The authors are less justified, however, in attaching so much importance to the doubt that our judgment meets with in recounting a dream. This doubt does indeed reveal a lack of intellectual certainty, but our memory offers no guarantees at all, and yet we yield far more often than is objectively justified to the pressure to trust what it tells us. Doubt about whether the dream, or any particular detail of it, has been correctly reproduced is, once again, merely an offshoot of the dream censor, that is, of the resistance against the dream thoughts making their way into consciousness. This resistance has not entirely spent itself in producing displacements and substitutions, and so it clings, in the form of doubt, to whatever has been allowed to pass through. We can recognize this doubt all the more easily because it takes care not to attack the intense elements of the dream, only the weak and indistinct ones. We already know that a complete revaluation of all psychic values has taken place between the dream thoughts and the dream. Distortion was made possible only by this alteration of values; it regularly expresses itself in this way, and sometimes contents itself with nothing more. If doubt attaches to an indistinct element of the dream content, we may take the hint and recognize in that element a direct offshoot of one of the outlawed dream thoughts. The situation resembles that of one of the republics of antiquity or the Renaissance after a great revolution. The old noble and powerful ruling families have been banished; all the high offices are filled by newcomers; within the city itself only the very poor and powerless citizens, or the distant followers of the defeated party, are tolerated. Even they do not enjoy full rights of citizenship. They are watched with suspicion. In place of the suspicion in this comparison, we have, in our case, doubt. I therefore insist that in analyzing dreams one should free oneself entirely from the whole business of estimating reliability, and that whenever there is the slightest possibility that this or that occurred in the dream, it should be treated as a full certainty. Until one has resolved to set these considerations aside in tracing the dream elements, the analysis will remain at a standstill. The aversion toward the element in question shows its psychic effect in the person being analyzed in that the unwelcome idea calls up no thoughts in his mind. This effect is not, in fact, self-evident. It would be perfectly consistent for someone to say, "Whether this or that was in the dream I do not know, but the following thoughts occur to me in that connection." Yet he never puts it this way, and it is precisely this disruptive effect of doubt on the analysis that marks it as an offshoot and instrument of psychic resistance. Psychoanalysis is rightly suspicious. One of its rules states: whatever interferes with the continuation of the work is a resistance.

The forgetting of dreams, too, remains unfathomable so long as we leave the power of the psychic censor out of the explanation. The feeling of having dreamed a great deal during the night and retained only a little may, in a number of cases, have a different meaning. It may signify that the dream-work went on perceptibly throughout the night and left behind only this short dream. There is no doubt, however, that the dream is progressively forgotten after waking. One often forgets it despite painful efforts to remember. Yet I believe that just as people generally overestimate how much they forget, they also overestimate the gaps in their knowledge, judging them by the gaps that appear in the dream. Everything that forgetting has removed from the content of a dream can often be recovered through analysis. In a whole series of cases, at least, it is possible to discover from a single surviving fragment not the dream itself, which matters little, but all the thoughts behind it. This requires a greater expenditure of attention and self-control in the analysis, and that is all. At the same time, it suggests that the forgetting of dreams is not without hostile intent.

Analysis yields convincing proof that the forgetting of dreams is purposeful and serves the resistance, through the study of a preliminary stage of forgetting. It often happens that, in the middle of the work of interpretation, an omitted fragment of the dream suddenly comes to the surface. The part of the dream thus rescued from forgetting is always the most important. It lies on the shortest road to the solution of the dream, and for that very reason it was the part most objectionable to the resistance. Among the dream examples I collected for this treatise, there was one occasion on which I had to insert such a piece of dream content after the fact. It was a traveling dream in which I took revenge on a disagreeable female traveling companion; I left it almost entirely uninterpreted because parts of it were coarse and unpleasant. The omitted part ran: "I said about a book by Schiller, 'It is *from* . . .' but corrected myself, for I noticed the mistake myself, 'It is *by*.' Upon this the man remarked to his sister, 'Indeed, he said it correctly.'"

The self-correction that occurs in dreams, which some authors find so remarkable, does not deserve our consideration. I shall instead show, from my own memory, the model for the grammatical error in the dream. I was nineteen when I visited England for the first time and spent a day on the shore of the Irish Sea. I naturally amused myself by collecting the sea creatures left behind by the waves, and I was busy in particular with a starfish (the dream begins with the place name Hollthurn, which echoes *holothurian*, the sea cucumber) when a pretty little girl came up to me and asked, "Is it a starfish? Is it alive?" I answered, "Yes, *he* is alive," and then, ashamed of my mistake, repeated the sentence correctly. For the grammatical mistake I made then, the dream substitutes another, one quite common among Germans. *Das Buch ist von Schiller* should be translated not as "the book is *from*" but as "the book is *by*" Schiller. That the dream-work makes this substitution because the word *from*, through its sound, permits a remarkable condensation with the German adjective *fromm*, meaning pious or devout, no longer surprises us after everything we have learned about the aims of the dream-work and its reckless choice of means.

But what does this harmless memory of the seashore mean in relation to the dream? It illustrates, by a very innocent example, that I had used the wrong gender; that is, I had put "he," the word that denotes sex or the sexual, where it did not belong. This is surely one of the keys to the solution of the dream. Anyone who has heard how the book title *Matter and Motion* came about will readily be able to supply the missing parts. The reference is to Molière's *The Imaginary Invalid*, where a physician asks, "*La matière est-elle louable?*" ("Is the matter satisfactory?"), meaning the patient's stool, and where *motion* refers to a movement of the bowels.

Moreover, I can prove conclusively, by a demonstration before one's very eyes, that the forgetting of dreams is in large part the work of resistance. A patient tells me that he has dreamed, but that the dream has vanished without a trace, as if nothing had happened. We go on working, however. I come upon a resistance, which I make clear to the patient; by encouraging and urging him, I help him come to terms with some disagreeable thought; and as soon as I have succeeded, he exclaims, "Now I can remember what I dreamed." The same resistance that interfered with his work that day had also made him forget the dream. By overcoming the resistance, I brought the dream back into memory.

In the same way, a patient who reaches a certain point in the work may recall a dream he had three, four, or more days earlier, which had lain forgotten all that time.

Psychoanalytic experience has furnished still another proof that the forgetting of dreams depends more on resistance than on the gulf between the waking and sleeping states, as the authorities have believed. It often happens to me, as it does to other analysts and to patients in treatment, that we are woken from sleep by a dream, as we would put it, and immediately afterward, in full possession of our mental faculties, begin to interpret it. In such cases I have often not rested until I reached a full understanding of the dream, and yet it would happen that by morning I had forgotten the work of interpretation just as completely as the dream content itself, though I knew that I had dreamed and that I had interpreted the dream. The dream more often carried the results of the interpretation with it into oblivion than the mind succeeded in keeping the dream in memory. Yet between this work of interpretation and waking thought there is none of the psychic gap by which alone the authorities seek to explain the forgetting of dreams. Morton Prince objects to my explanation of dream-forgetting on the grounds that it is merely a special case of amnesia for dissociated states, and that because my theory cannot be reconciled with other types of amnesia, it is worthless for other purposes as well. He thereby leads the reader to suspect that in all his descriptions of such dissociated states he has never attempted to find a dynamic explanation for these phenomena. Had he done so, he would surely have discovered that repression, and the resistance it produces, "is quite as much the cause of this dissociation as of the amnesia for its psychic content."

That dreams are forgotten no more readily than other mental acts, and that they cling to memory just as firmly as other psychic activities, was demonstrated to me by an experiment I was able to carry out while preparing this manuscript. I had kept in my notes many dreams of my own that, for one reason or another, I had been able to analyze only imperfectly or not at all at the time. To obtain material illustrating my claims, I tried to analyze some of them one to two years later. I succeeded in every case without exception. Indeed, I may even say that the interpretation went more easily at this later date than when the dreams were recent. As a possible explanation, I would suggest that I had since overcome some of the resistances that had troubled me at the time of the dream. In these later interpretations I compared the dream thoughts I had uncovered earlier with those I uncovered now, which were usually more abundant, and I invariably found the earlier results contained, unaltered, within the later ones. My surprise soon faded, however, when I recalled that I had long been in the habit of interpreting dreams from years past that patients occasionally told me, treating them as though they had been dreamed the night before, with the same method and the same success. I shall report two examples of such delayed interpretation when I come to discuss anxiety dreams. When I first undertook this experiment, I had good reason to expect that the dream would behave in this respect like a neurotic symptom. When I treat a neurotic patient by psychoanalysis, a hysteric for instance, I must explain not only the symptoms that brought the patient to me but also the earliest symptoms of the illness, which have long since been forgotten. I find the older problem easier to solve than the more pressing one of the present. As early as 1895, in the *Studies on Hysteria* (*Studien über Hysterie*), I was able to report the explanation of a first hysterical attack of anxiety that a woman over forty had suffered in her fifteenth year.

I may now turn, less formally, to some further remarks on the interpretation of dreams. They may be of use to readers who wish to test my claims by analyzing their own dreams.

No one should expect the meaning of his dreams to come to him overnight without effort. Practice is required even to perceive endoptic phenomena, the visual sensations that arise within the eye itself, and other sensations that ordinarily escape our attention, although no psychic motive opposes this class of perceptions. It is considerably harder to gain command over "unwelcome ideas." Anyone who wishes to do so must satisfy the requirements laid down in this treatise. Following the rules given here, he must strive throughout the work to suppress in himself all criticism, all prejudice, and every emotional or intellectual bias. He should keep in mind the precept that the physiologist Claude Bernard gave to the experimenter in the laboratory: *"Travailler comme une bête,"* "work like a beast of burden." Bernard meant that one should be as persistent as an animal at its labor, and just as indifferent to the outcome. Whoever follows this advice will no longer find the task difficult. A dream cannot always be interpreted in a single sitting. After following a chain of thoughts, you often feel that your capacity for work is spent and that the dream will tell you nothing more that day. It is then best to break off and return to the work the next day. Another part of the dream content then claims your attention, and you find an opening into a new layer of the dream thoughts. We may call this the "fractional" interpretation of dreams.

It is extremely hard to persuade the beginner that his task is not finished even when he possesses a complete interpretation of the dream, one that is ingenious and coherent and that accounts for every element. Another interpretation of the same dream, superimposed on the first, may also be possible, and it may have escaped him. It is genuinely difficult to conceive of the abundant unconscious streams of thought that press for expression in our minds. It is just as difficult to credit the skill with which the dream-work, through its ambiguous mode of expression, kills seven flies with one blow, like the journeyman tailor in the fairy tale. The reader will constantly be tempted to accuse the author of squandering his ingenuity for nothing, but anyone with experience of his own will learn better.

Can every dream be interpreted? The answer is no. We must remember that the work of interpretation contends with the same psychic forces that were responsible for distorting the dream. Whether a person can master these inner resistances through intellectual interest, self-control, psychological knowledge, and practice in interpretation becomes a question of which forces prevail. Some progress is always possible. One can at least go far enough to become convinced that the dream is an ingenious construction, and usually far enough to gain some idea of its meaning. Very often a second dream confirms and extends the interpretation adopted for the first. An entire series of dreams stretching over weeks or months may rest on a common foundation and must therefore be interpreted together. In successive dreams one can often observe how one dream takes as its central point what appears only at the periphery of the next, or the reverse, so that the two complement each other in interpretation. I have already shown by examples that the various dreams of a single night are, as a rule, to be treated as a whole.

Even in the most thoroughly interpreted dreams, we must often leave one portion in darkness. During the interpretation we notice that it marks the beginning of a tangle of dream thoughts that cannot be unraveled and that has contributed nothing new to the dream content. This is the dream's keystone, the point at which it reaches up into the unknown. The dream thoughts we encounter in interpretation must, as a rule, remain without any conclusion. They spread out in every direction into the netlike tangle of our world of thought. The dream-wish rises from some denser point in this fabric, like a mushroom from its mycelium, the threadlike underground network from which it grows.

Let us now return to the facts of dream-forgetting, for we have neglected to draw an important conclusion from them. Waking life shows an unmistakable intention to forget the dream formed during the night, either whole and immediately on waking, or piece by piece over the course of the day. We recognize that the chief agent in this forgetting is the psychic resistance to the dream, the same resistance that already opposed the dream during the night. The question then arises: what did dream formation actually achieve against this resistance? Consider the most striking case, in which waking life disposes of the dream as though it had never happened. If we take into account the interplay of psychic forces, we are compelled to assert that the dream would never have come into being had the resistance ruled as firmly at night as it does by day. We conclude, therefore, that the resistance loses part of its force during the night. We know that it has not been extinguished, since we have demonstrated its share in dream formation through the distortion it produces. We are thus led to the possibility that the resistance weakens at night and that this weakening makes dream formation possible. We can then readily understand why the resistance, having regained its full strength on waking, immediately casts aside what it was forced to admit while it was in abeyance. Descriptive psychology teaches us that the chief condition of dream formation is the sleeping state of the mind. We may now add this further explanation: *The sleeping state makes dream formation possible by reducing the endopsychic censorship.*

We are certainly tempted to regard this as the only conclusion the facts of dream-forgetting permit, and to draw from it further deductions about the relative distribution of energy in sleep and waking. But we shall stop here for now. Once we have penetrated somewhat deeper into the psychology of the dream, we shall find that the origin of dream formation can be conceived differently. The resistance that prevents the dream thoughts from reaching consciousness may perhaps be evaded without itself being diminished. It is also plausible that the state of sleep makes both conditions favorable to dream formation possible at once, the weakening of the resistance as well as its evasion. But we shall pause here and take up this line of thought again later.

We must now consider another series of objections to our method of interpretation. In interpreting a dream, we drop all the purposive ideas that ordinarily direct our reflection, the guiding aims that we may call "end-presentations." We fix our attention on a single element of the dream and note whatever unwelcome thoughts occur to us in connection with it. We then take up the next component of the dream content and repeat the operation. Without caring where our thoughts lead, we let ourselves be carried along until we find ourselves rambling from one subject to another. Throughout, we cherish the confident hope that in the end, and without effort, we shall come upon the dream thoughts from which the dream arose. Against this the critic raises the following objection. It is nothing remarkable, he says, that one can arrive somewhere by starting from a single element of a dream, since every idea can be linked by association with something. What is remarkable is only that one should manage to strike the dream thoughts in the course of so aimless and arbitrary an excursion. Probably it is a self-deception. The investigator follows the chain of associations from one element until, for some reason, it appears to break off. He then takes up a second element, and it is only natural that the association, at first unlimited, should now narrow. He still has the earlier chain in mind, and so in his analysis he will more readily hit upon thoughts that share something with those of the first chain. He then imagines that he has found a thought representing a point of junction between two elements of the dream. He grants himself complete freedom in connecting thoughts, excluding only the transitions from one idea to another that occur in normal thinking. In the end, therefore, it is not hard for him to concoct something he calls the dream thought out of a series of "intermediate thoughts." These thoughts are otherwise unknown, so there is no guarantee for them, yet he passes them off as the psychic equivalent of the dream. All of this involves arbitrary procedure and an over-ingenious exploitation of coincidence. Anyone willing to go to this pointless trouble can work out any interpretation he likes for any dream whatever.
