If such objections are actually raised against us, we may point in our defense to the consistency of our interpretations and to the surprising connections with other dream elements that emerge as we follow up the individual ideas. We may also point to how improbable it is that anything covering and explaining the dream as completely as our interpretations do could have been obtained except by following psychic connections that already existed. We can also justify ourselves by noting that the method of dream analysis is identical with the method used to resolve hysterical symptoms. There the correctness of the method is attested by the emergence and disappearance of the symptoms; the reading of the text, so to speak, is confirmed by the illustrations set within it. But we have no reason to avoid the problem of how one can reach a predetermined goal by following a chain of thoughts spun out so arbitrarily and aimlessly. Although we cannot solve this problem, we can dispose of it entirely.

It is demonstrably false to say that we surrender ourselves to an aimless course of thought when, as in dream interpretation, we abandon reflection and allow unwelcome ideas to rise to the surface. It can be shown that we are able to renounce only those purposive ideas that are known to us. As soon as these cease, unknown purposive ideas come into play at once, or, to put it more precisely, unconscious ones, and these then determine the course of the unwelcome ideas. Thinking without any purposive idea cannot be brought about by any influence we can exert on our own mental life. Nor do I know of any state of mental derangement in which such thinking establishes itself. Psychiatrists have been far too quick, in this field, to abandon their belief in the coherence of psychic structure. I have established that an unregulated stream of thought, lacking any purposive idea, occurs no more in hysteria and paranoia than in the formation or resolution of dreams. Perhaps it does not appear at all in the endogenous mental disorders. Even the deliria of confusional states make sense, according to the ingenious theory of Leuret, and become incomprehensible to us only because of gaps. I have reached the same conviction wherever I have had occasion to observe them. Deliria are the work of a censorship that no longer troubles to conceal its operation. Rather than helping to rework the material into a form it would no longer object to, it ruthlessly strikes out whatever it does object to, so that what remains appears disconnected. This censorship behaves much like the Russian newspaper censor at the frontier, who lets the readers in his charge receive foreign periodicals only after he has blacked out objectionable passages with his pencil.

The free play of ideas, following any chain of association whatever, may perhaps appear in destructive organic lesions of the brain. But what passes for such free play in the psychoneuroses can always be explained as the effect of censorship on a train of thought that a concealed purposive idea has pushed into the foreground. It has been considered an unmistakable sign of association free of purposive ideas when the emerging ideas (or images) are linked by so-called superficial associations: by assonance, by verbal ambiguity, by causal connection without any inner relation of meaning. These are all the associations we permit ourselves in jokes and wordplay. This mark of distinction does hold for the chains of thought that lead us from the elements of the dream content to the collateral thoughts, and from these to the dream thoughts proper. Our dream analyses have furnished many surprising examples. No connection was too loose and no joke too objectionable to form a bridge from one thought to the next. But the right way to understand such tolerance is not far to seek. *Whenever one psychic element is linked to another by an objectionable or superficial association, there also exists a correct and deeper connection between the two, which has succumbed to the resistance of the censorship.*

The true explanation for the predominance of superficial associations is the pressure of the censorship, not the suppression of purposive ideas. Superficial associations take the place of deep ones in the representation whenever the censorship makes the normal paths of connection impassable. Imagine a mountainous region in which some general interruption of traffic, a flood perhaps, has made the long, broad highways impassable. Traffic would then have to be maintained over steep and inconvenient footpaths ordinarily used only by hunters.

Here we can distinguish two cases, though they are essentially one. In the first case, the censorship is directed only against the connection between two thoughts, which escape its opposition once they are detached from each other. The two thoughts then enter consciousness one after the other, and their connection stays hidden. In its place, a superficial connection between them occurs to us, one we would not otherwise have thought of. As a rule it attaches to some other facet of the complex of ideas than the one from which the suppressed but essential connection arises. In the second case, both thoughts fall under the censorship because of their content. Both then appear not in their true form but in a modified, substitute form. The two substitute thoughts are chosen so that a superficial association between them reproduces the essential relation that existed between the thoughts they have replaced. In both cases, then, the pressure of the censorship has displaced a normal and serious association with a superficial and apparently absurd one.

Because we know of this displacement, we do not hesitate to rely even on superficial associations in dream analysis.

The psychoanalysis of neurotics makes extensive use of two axioms. The first is that when the conscious purposive idea is abandoned, control over the train of ideas passes to concealed purposive ideas. The second is that superficial associations are merely substitutes, displaced from suppressed and deeper ones. Psychoanalysis in fact makes these two axioms the pillars of its technique. When I ask a patient to give up all reflection and tell me whatever comes into his mind, I hold firmly to the assumption that he will be unable to drop the purposive idea of the treatment. I consider myself justified in concluding that what he tells me, however harmless and arbitrary it may seem, is connected with his morbid condition. My own person is another purposive idea of which the patient has no inkling. A full appreciation and detailed proof of both these explanations therefore belong to a description of psychoanalytic technique as a method of therapy. We have here reached one of the neighboring subjects at which we intend to leave the topic of dream interpretation.

Of all the objections, only one is valid and still stands: we ought not to attribute every mental event in the work of interpretation to the nocturnal dream-work. When we interpret in the waking state, we build a road leading from the dream elements back to the dream thoughts. The dream-work traveled in the opposite direction, and it is not at all likely that these roads are equally passable both ways. On the contrary, it has been shown that during the day we cut new paths through fresh connections of thought, and these meet the intermediate thoughts and the dream thoughts at different points. We can see how fresh thought material from the day finds its place among the chains of interpretation. Probably, too, the added resistance that has accrued since the night compels us to make new and longer detours. But the number and form of the collateral thoughts we spin in this way during the day are of no psychological consequence, so long as they lead us to the dream thoughts we are seeking.

### (b) Regression

Now that we have defended ourselves against objections, or at least shown where our weapons of defense lie, we need no longer postpone the psychological investigations for which we have so long been preparing. Let us gather together the chief results of our inquiry so far. The dream is a psychic act of real consequence. Its driving force is always the fulfillment of a wish. It cannot be recognized as a wish, and it has many peculiarities and absurdities, because of the influence of the psychic censorship to which it was subjected while being formed. Besides the pressure to escape this censorship, the following factors played a part in its formation: a strong tendency to condense psychic material, a regard for dramatization in mental images, and, though not always, a regard for giving the dream a rational and intelligible exterior. Each of these propositions leads onward to psychological postulates and assumptions. We shall have to investigate the mutual relation between the wish motive and these four conditions, as well as the relations of the conditions to one another. And we shall have to place the dream in its connection with mental life as a whole.

At the beginning of this chapter we cited a dream to remind ourselves of the riddles that remain unsolved. Interpreting this dream of the burning child gave us no difficulty, although it was not given completely in our present sense. We asked why the father should have dreamed at all rather than waking up, and we recognized as the dream's sole motive the wish to represent the child as alive. That yet another wish played a part here we shall be able to show after later discussion. For the present, then, we may say that the thought process of sleep was transformed into a dream for the sake of wish-fulfillment.

If we reverse the wish-fulfillment, only one quality remains to distinguish the two kinds of psychic occurrence from each other. The dream thought might have run: "I see a glow coming from the room where the body lies. Perhaps a candle has fallen over, and the child is burning!" The dream reproduces the result of this reflection unchanged. But it represents that result as a situation taking place in the present, one perceptible to the senses like an experience of waking life. This is the most common and most striking psychological characteristic of the dream. A thought, usually the one wished for, is made objective in the dream and represented as a scene, or, as it seems to us, as something experienced.

But how are we to explain this characteristic peculiarity of the dream-work? Or, to put it more modestly, how are we to bring it into relation with the psychic processes?

On closer examination, it is clear that the dream's manifest form displays two pronounced characteristics that are almost independent of each other. One is representation as a present situation, with the "perhaps" omitted. The other is the transformation of the thought into visual images and speech.

In this particular dream, the change that shifts the expectation in the dream thoughts into the present is perhaps not especially striking. This probably accords with the special, or rather subordinate, role that wish-fulfillment plays in this dream. Let us take another dream, one in which the dream-wish does not separate itself in sleep from a continuation of waking thoughts: the dream of Irma's injection. Here the dream thought that reaches representation is in the optative, the grammatical mood of wishing: "If only Otto could be blamed for Irma's illness!" The dream suppresses the optative and replaces it with a simple present: "Yes, Otto is to blame for Irma's illness." This, then, is the first of the changes that even an undistorted dream makes to the dream thought. But we shall not dwell long on this first peculiarity. We can clarify it by referring to the conscious fantasy, the daydream, which treats its ideational content in the same way. Daudet's Monsieur Joyeuse wanders the streets of Paris without work while his daughter is led to believe that he has a position and is sitting in his office. He, too, dreams in the present tense of circumstances that might win him a patron and a job. The dream therefore employs the present tense in the same way, and with the same justification, as the daydream. The present is the tense in which a wish is represented as fulfilled.

The second quality, however, belongs to the dream alone and sets it apart from the daydream: its ideational content is not thought but transformed into perceptible images, which we believe in and seem to experience. We should add that not every dream shows this transformation of ideas into sensory images. Some dreams consist entirely of thoughts, and yet we cannot for that reason deny that they are genuine dreams. My dream "Autodidasker—the waking fantasy with Professor N." is of this kind; it contains scarcely more perceptible elements than if I had thought its content during the day. Moreover, every long dream contains elements that have not undergone the transformation into the perceptible, and that are simply thought or known, just as we habitually think or know things in waking life. We should also recall that this transformation of ideas into perceptible images is not confined to dreams. It occurs as well in hallucinations and visions, which may appear spontaneously in healthy people or as symptoms of the psychoneuroses. In short, the relation we are investigating here is by no means exclusive to the dream. Nevertheless, wherever this feature appears in a dream, it strikes us as the most remarkable thing about it, so much so that we cannot imagine dream life without it. Explaining it, however, requires a very detailed discussion.

Among all the remarks on the theory of dreams to be found in the authorities on the subject, there is one I want to single out as deserving attention. In the course of a discussion of dreams in his *Psychophysik*, the great G. T. Fechner expresses his belief that the scene of action of dreams is different from that of waking ideation. No other assumption allows us to grasp the special qualities of dream life.

The idea this places at our disposal is one of psychical locality. We shall set aside entirely the fact that the mental apparatus we are dealing with is also familiar to us as an anatomical specimen, and we shall carefully resist the temptation to determine this psychical locality in any anatomical sense. We shall remain on psychological ground, and we shall ask only that we picture the instrument that carries out our mental functions as something like a compound microscope, a photographic camera, or some similar apparatus. Psychical locality, then, corresponds to a point inside such an apparatus at which one of the preliminary stages of an image comes into being. In the microscope and the telescope, as is well known, such points are to some extent imaginary: they are regions where no tangible component of the apparatus is actually situated. I think it unnecessary to apologize for the imperfections of this or any similar figure. Such comparisons are meant only to help us make sense of the complexity of mental activity by breaking that activity apart and assigning each individual function to an individual component of the apparatus. As far as I know, no one has yet ventured to work out the composition of the mental instrument by dissecting it in this way. I see no harm in the attempt. I believe we may give free rein to our speculations, provided that we keep our judgment cool and do not mistake the scaffolding for the building. Since all we need for a first approach to any unknown subject is the help of provisional ideas, we shall prefer the crudest and most concrete hypothesis to any other.

We therefore picture the mental apparatus as a compound instrument, whose component parts we shall call agencies, or, for the sake of clarity, systems. We then anticipate that these systems may stand in a constant spatial relation to one another, like the various lens systems of a telescope, arranged one behind another. Strictly speaking, there is no need to assume that the psychical systems are actually arranged in space. It is enough for our purpose if a fixed order is established by the fact that, in certain mental processes, excitation passes through the systems in a definite temporal sequence. In other processes this sequence may be altered; we leave that possibility open. For brevity, we shall from now on refer to the component parts of the apparatus as "psi-systems."

The first thing that strikes us is that this apparatus of psi-systems has a direction. All our mental activity starts from stimuli, whether internal or external, and ends in innervations, the nerve impulses that set the muscles in motion. We therefore ascribe to the apparatus a sensory end and a motor end. At the sensory end lies a system that receives perceptions; at the motor end lies another that opens the gates to movement. The mental process generally runs its course from the perceptual end to the motor end. In its most general form, then, our diagram of the mental apparatus shows a row of systems stretched between a perceptual end, marked P, and a motor end, marked M, with the current of excitation flowing from the first to the second.

This, however, merely satisfies a requirement long familiar to us: that the mental apparatus must be built like a reflex apparatus. The reflex act remains the model for every psychical function.

We now have reason to introduce a first differentiation at the sensory end. The perceptions that reach us leave a trace in our mental apparatus, which we may call a "memory trace." The function relating to this memory trace we call memory. If we hold seriously to our resolve to attach psychical processes to systems, then the memory trace can consist only of lasting modifications in the elements of those systems. But, as has been pointed out elsewhere, obvious difficulties arise if one and the same system is supposed both to preserve faithfully the modifications of its elements and to remain fresh and receptive to new occasions for modification. Following the principle that guides our undertaking, we shall divide these two functions between two different systems. We assume that a first system at the front of the apparatus receives perceptual stimuli but retains nothing of them, which is to say that it has no memory, and that behind it lies a second system, which transforms the momentary excitations of the first into lasting traces. Our diagram would then show the perceptual system, P, followed by a series of memory systems, which we label Mem, Mem′, Mem″, and so on, with the motor end, M, lying beyond them.

We know that from the perceptions acting on the P-system we retain something besides their content, and something just as lasting. Our perceptions turn out to be linked with one another in memory, above all when they once occurred simultaneously. We call this the fact of association. Now it is clear that if the P-system has no memory whatever, it cannot preserve traces of associations either; the individual P-elements would be intolerably hampered in their function if a residue of some earlier connection made itself felt against a new perception. We must assume, on the contrary, that the memory system is the basis of association. The fact of association, then, consists in this: as a result of reduced resistance and the smoothing of pathways leading from one of the Mem-elements, excitation is transmitted to a second Mem-element rather than to a third.

On further investigation we find it necessary to assume not one but several such Mem-systems, in which the same excitation, transmitted by the P-elements, is fixed in a variety of ways. The first of these Mem-systems will in any case contain the record of association by simultaneity, while in those lying farther off the same excitatory material will be arranged according to other kinds of coincidence, so that these later systems might represent, for instance, relations of similarity and the like. It would of course be idle to try to put into words the psychical significance of such a system. Its character would lie in the closeness of its relations to particular elements of the raw memory material, or, if we wish to point toward a more fundamental theory, in the gradations of resistance to conduction toward those elements.

We may insert here a general observation that perhaps points to something of importance. The P-system, which has no capacity to retain modifications and therefore no memory, supplies our consciousness with the whole variety of sensory qualities. Our memories, by contrast, are unconscious in themselves, and those most deeply imprinted are no exception. They can be made conscious, but there is no doubt that they exert all their effects while in the unconscious state. What we call our character rests, to be sure, on the memory traces of our impressions, and indeed on those impressions that affected us most strongly: the impressions of our early youth, which almost never become conscious. But when memories do become conscious again, they show no sensory quality at all, or only a very slight one compared with perceptions. If it can be confirmed that memory and quality exclude each other where consciousness in the psi-systems is concerned, a most promising insight opens up into the conditions that govern the excitation of neurons.

What we have so far assumed about the structure of the mental apparatus at its sensory end follows independently of the dream and of the psychological explanations derived from it. The dream, however, provides evidence for our knowledge of another part of the apparatus. We have seen that it was impossible to explain dream formation without venturing to assume two psychical agencies, one of which subjects the activity of the other to a critique, with the result that this activity is excluded from consciousness.

We have seen that the criticizing agency stands in closer relation to consciousness than the agency it criticizes. The former stands between the latter and consciousness like a screen. We have also found essential reasons for identifying the criticizing agency with the one that directs our waking life and determines our voluntary, conscious actions. If, as our theory develops, we now replace these agencies with systems, then the criticizing system, for the reason just mentioned, must be placed at the motor end. We now enter both systems into our diagram and give them names that express their relation to consciousness. In this third version of the diagram, the sequence runs from the perceptual system, P, through the memory systems, to the unconscious, then to the preconscious, and finally to the motor end, M.

The last of the systems at the motor end we call the preconscious, to indicate that excitatory processes within it can reach consciousness without further delay, provided certain other conditions are met: for example, that they attain a certain intensity, that the function we must call attention is distributed in a certain way, and the like. This is also the system that holds the keys to voluntary movement. The system behind it we call the unconscious, because it has no access to consciousness except by way of the preconscious, and in passing through the preconscious its excitation must submit to certain modifications.

In which of these systems, then, do we locate the impulse that gives rise to a dream? For the sake of simplicity, let us say in the unconscious system. We shall find in later discussions, admittedly, that this is not quite correct, and that dream formation is compelled to link up with dream thoughts belonging to the preconscious system. But we shall also learn later, when we come to the dream wish, that the driving force of the dream is supplied by the unconscious, and on account of this latter factor we shall take the unconscious system as the starting point of dream formation. Like every other thought formation, this dream impulse will strive to continue on into the preconscious and from there to gain admission to consciousness.

Experience teaches us that during the day the path leading from the preconscious to consciousness is closed to the dream thoughts by the resistance of the censorship. At night the dream thoughts do gain admission to consciousness, but the question is how, and by virtue of what change. If they were admitted simply because the resistance standing guard on the boundary between the unconscious and the preconscious sinks at night, we should get dreams composed of the material of our ideas, lacking the hallucinatory character that interests us here.

The lowering of the censorship between the two systems, the unconscious and the preconscious, can account only for dreams like "Autodidasker," not for dreams like the one about the burning child, which we set before ourselves as a problem at the very outset of these investigations.

We can describe what happens in the hallucinatory dream in no other way than by saying that the excitation takes a backward course. Instead of moving toward the motor end of the apparatus, it moves toward the sensory end and finally reaches the perceptual system. If we call the direction in which psychical processes advance from the unconscious in waking life the progressive direction, we may then say that the dream has a regressive character.

This regression is certainly one of the most important features of the dream process, but we must not forget that it does not belong to the dream alone. Deliberate recollection and other processes of our normal thinking also involve a backward movement in the mental apparatus, from some complex act of ideation to the raw material of the memory traces that underlie it. In the waking state, however, this backward movement never goes beyond the memory images; it cannot produce the hallucinatory vividness of perceptual images. Why is it different in dreams? When we discussed the dream's work of condensation, we could not avoid assuming that the intensities attached to ideas are transferred wholesale from one idea to another by the dream-work. It is probably this alteration of the ordinary psychical process that makes it possible for the perceptual system to be charged to the point of full sensory vividness, in the direction opposite to that of thought.

I hope we are far from deceiving ourselves about the significance of this discussion. We have done nothing more than give a name to an inexplicable phenomenon. We call it regression when an idea in a dream is turned back into the perceptible image from which it once arose. But even this step needs justifying. Why give the phenomenon a name if the name teaches us nothing new? I believe, however, that the term "regression" earns its place insofar as it connects a fact already familiar to us with a diagram of the mental apparatus that has a direction. Here, for the first time, constructing such a diagram proves worth the trouble, because with its help another characteristic of dream formation becomes clear to us without further reflection. If we regard the dream as a process of regression within our hypothetical mental apparatus, we can readily understand the empirically established fact that the logical relations among the dream thoughts are either lost entirely in the dream-work or find expression only with difficulty. According to our diagram, these relations are contained not in the first Mem-systems but in those lying farther forward, and in the course of regression they must give up their expression in favor of perceptual images. In regression, the structure of the dream thoughts is broken down into its raw material.

But what change makes possible this regression, which cannot occur during the day? Here we must be content with conjecture. There must clearly be some alteration in the charges of energy belonging to the individual systems, making them more or less accessible to the discharge of excitation; but in any apparatus of this kind, the same effect on the course of excitation could be produced by more than one sort of change. This naturally brings to mind the state of sleep and the many shifts of energy it produces at the sensory end of the apparatus. During the day a continuous current flows from the perceptual psi-system toward motility; at night this current ceases and no longer prevents excitation from flowing in the opposite direction. This would seem to be the "isolation from the external world" that, according to the theory of some authors, is supposed to explain the psychological character of dreams. In explaining the regression of dreams, however, we shall also have to take into account the other regressions that arise in pathological waking states. In those cases, the explanation just given plainly leaves us stranded, for there regression occurs despite an uninterrupted sensory current flowing in the progressive direction.

The hallucinations of hysteria and paranoia, as well as the visions of mentally normal people, I can explain as genuine regressions, that is, as thoughts transformed into images; and only those thoughts undergo this transformation that are intimately connected with suppressed or unconscious memories. As an example, I shall cite one of my youngest hysterical patients, a twelve-year-old boy who was kept from falling asleep by terrifying "green faces with red eyes." The source of this apparition was the suppressed, though once conscious, memory of another boy whom he had often seen over a period of four years, and who had set him a cautionary example of many childish bad habits, among them masturbation, which had now become the subject of the patient's own self-reproach. His mother had remarked at the time that the ill-mannered boy had a greenish complexion and red eyes, meaning eyes with red rims. Hence the terrible vision, which constantly reminded the patient of his mother's warning that such boys go mad, cannot make progress at school, and are doomed to an early death. Part of this prediction came true in the young patient's case: he could not keep up with his high school studies, and, as an examination of his involuntary fantasies revealed, he lived in great dread of the rest of the prophecy. After a brief period of successful treatment, however, his sleep was restored, his fears vanished, and he finished his school year with an excellent record.

I may add here the interpretation of a vision that a forty-year-old hysterical woman told me she had experienced in her normal life. On opening her eyes one morning, she saw in the room her brother, whom she knew to be confined in an insane asylum. Her little son lay asleep beside her. Fearing that the child would be frightened at the sight of his uncle and fall into convulsions, she pulled the sheet over him, whereupon the phantom vanished. This vision is a recasting of one of her childhood memories, which, though conscious, is intimately bound up with all the unconscious material in her mind. Her nursemaid had told her that her mother, who died young, when the patient was only a year and a half old, had suffered from epileptic or hysterical convulsions dating back to a fright caused by her brother, the patient's uncle, who had appeared to her disguised as a ghost with a sheet over his head. The vision contains the same elements as the memory: the appearance of the brother, the sheet, the fright, and its effect. These elements, however, are arranged in different relations and transferred to other people. The obvious motive of the vision, which takes the place of a thought, is her anxiety that her little son, who bore a striking resemblance to his uncle, might share his uncle's fate. Neither of these examples is entirely unrelated to sleep, and they may therefore be unsuitable as proof of my claim. I may instead refer to my analysis of a case of hallucinatory paranoia, and to the results of my as yet unpublished studies on the psychology of the psychoneuroses, in order to stress that in these cases of regressive transformation of thought, one must not overlook the influence of a suppressed or unconscious memory, which in most cases dates from childhood. This memory, so to speak, draws into regression the thought connected with it, a thought that the censorship prevents from finding expression; it draws that thought into the very form of representation in which the memory itself exists psychically. I may mention here, as a finding of my studies of hysteria, that when we succeed in bringing childhood scenes back to consciousness, whether they are memories or fantasies, they are seen as hallucinations and lose this character only once they have been reproduced. It is also known that the earliest childhood memories retain their perceptual vividness until late in life, even in people whose memory is otherwise not visual.

If we now bear in mind the part played in the dream thoughts by childhood memories or by fantasies based on them, how often fragments of these memories surface in the dream content, and how often they even give rise to dream wishes, we cannot deny the likelihood that in dreams, too, the transformation of thoughts into visual images may result from the pull exerted by visually represented memories, which strive for revival, on thoughts that have been cut off from consciousness and are struggling for expression. On this view, we may further describe the dream as a substitute for a childhood scene, modified by being transferred onto recent material. The childhood scene cannot bring about its own revival, and so it must be content to return as a dream.

This reference to the significance of childhood scenes, or of their imaginative repetitions, as in some sense furnishing the pattern for the dream content, makes unnecessary the assumption, advanced by Scherner and his followers, of an internal source of excitation. Scherner posits a state of "visual stimulation," an internal excitation of the organ of sight, whenever dreams display a particular vividness or an unusual abundance of visual elements. We need not object to this assumption; we may simply grant such a state of excitation, but only for the psychical perceptual system of the visual organ. We shall maintain, however, that this state of excitation is created by memory and is merely a revival of a visual excitation that was once actual. From my own experience I cannot offer a good example of such an influence of childhood memory; my own dreams are certainly less rich in sensory elements than I imagine those of other people to be. But in the most beautiful and vivid dream I have had in recent years, I can easily trace the hallucinatory clarity of the dream content to the sensory character of impressions I had recently received. I mentioned earlier a dream in which the dark blue of the water, the brown of the smoke pouring from the ship's funnels, and the somber browns and reds of the buildings I had seen made a deep and lasting impression on me. If any dream is to be attributed to visual stimulation, it is this one. But what had brought my visual organ into this excitable state? A recent impression, joining itself to a series of earlier ones. The colors I saw were those of the toy blocks with which, on the day before the dream, my children had built a grand structure for me to admire. The same somber red covered the large blocks, and the same blue and brown the small ones. Linked to these were the color impressions from my last journey through Italy: the lovely blue of the Isonzo River and the Venetian Lagoon, and the brown tones of the Alpine country. The beautiful colors I saw in the dream were simply a repetition of those preserved in memory.

Let us review what we have learned about the dream's peculiar tendency to transform its content of ideas into plastic, sensory images. We have neither explained this feature of the dream-work nor traced it to any known law of psychology. We have, however, singled it out as a sign of connections not yet understood, and we have named it the "regredient" character of the dream, its tendency to run backward. Wherever such regression has occurred, we have regarded it as an effect of the resistance that blocks a thought on its normal path toward consciousness, and also as a result of the simultaneous pull exerted on that thought by vivid memories already present. In dreams, regression may be further eased by the halting, during sleep, of the forward-moving stream that flows in from the sense organs throughout the day. The other forms of regression lack this auxiliary factor, so they must make up for it through a strengthening of their other motives for regression. We must also remember that in pathological cases of regression, as in the dream, the transfer of energy must proceed differently than in the regressions of normal mental life, since it makes possible a complete hallucinatory occupation of the perceptual systems. What we described in our analysis of the dream-work as "regard for dramatic fitness" may be traced to the selective attraction exerted by visually remembered scenes that the dream thoughts happen to touch.

It is quite possible that this first part of our psychological use of the dream leaves even us not entirely satisfied. We must console ourselves, however, with the knowledge that we are forced to build in the dark. If we have not strayed entirely from the right path, we are bound to reach roughly the same ground from another starting point, and then perhaps we will be better able to see our way.

### (c) The Wish-Fulfillment

The dream of the burning child cited above gives us a welcome occasion to weigh the difficulties facing the theory of wish-fulfillment. The claim that the dream is nothing but the fulfillment of a wish surely struck all of us as strange, and not only because of the contradictions posed by the anxiety dream.

Once our first analytic explanations had taught us that the dream conceals meaning and psychic value, we could hardly have expected that meaning to be so simply determined. According to Aristotle's correct but concise definition, the dream is a continuation of thinking during sleep, insofar as one is asleep. Since our daytime thinking produces such a variety of mental acts, including judgments, inferences, refutations, expectations, and intentions, why should our thinking during sleep be confined to producing wishes? Are there not, on the contrary, many dreams that cast some other mental act into dream form, such as a worry? And is not the father's dream mentioned above, transparent as it is, exactly of this kind? From the glare of light falling on his eyes as he sleeps, the father draws the anxious conclusion that a candle has fallen over and may have set his child's body on fire. He turns this conclusion into a dream by clothing it in a meaningful situation acted out in the present tense. What part does wish-fulfillment play in this dream? And which should we suspect of predominating: the thought carried over from waking life, or the thought prompted by the new sensory impression?

All these objections are fair, and they oblige us to look more closely at the part wish-fulfillment plays in the dream and at the significance of waking thoughts that continue into sleep.

It was wish-fulfillment, in fact, that first led us to divide dreams into two groups. We found some dreams that were openly wish-fulfillments, and others in which no wish-fulfillment could be recognized and in which it was often concealed by every available means. In this second class we recognized the influence of the dream censor. Undisguised wish dreams were found chiefly in children, although brief, frank wish dreams also *seemed* (I stress this word deliberately) to occur in adults.

We may now ask where the wish fulfilled in the dream comes from. But what contrast, or what range of possibilities, do we have in mind when we ask "where"? I believe it is the contrast between conscious daily life and a mental activity that remains unconscious and can make itself felt only at night. I find, accordingly, three possible origins for a wish. First, it may have been aroused during the day and, because of external circumstances, failed to find satisfaction, so that an acknowledged but unfulfilled wish is left over for the night. Second, it may have surfaced during the day but been rejected, leaving behind a wish that is both unfulfilled and suppressed. Third, it may bear no relation to daily life at all and belong to those wishes that emerge from the suppressed material only at night. If we now follow our scheme of the psychic apparatus, we can locate a wish of the first kind in the foreconscious system. We may assume that a wish of the second kind has been pushed back from the foreconscious system into the unconscious system, where alone, if anywhere, it can survive. A wishful impulse of the third kind we consider wholly incapable of leaving the unconscious system. This raises the question of whether wishes from these different sources have the same value for the dream, and whether they have the same power to set a dream in motion.

When we review the dreams available to us for answering this question, we are at once prompted to add a fourth source of the dream-wish: the actual wishful impulses that arise during the night, such as thirst and sexual desire. It then becomes clear that the source of a dream-wish has no bearing on its capacity to instigate a dream. This view is supported by the dream of the little girl who continued the sea trip that had been cut short during the day, and by the other children's dreams already discussed. They are explained by a daytime wish that went unfulfilled but was not suppressed. That a wish suppressed during the day can assert itself in a dream may be shown by a great many examples. I shall mention one very simple instance of this class. A rather sarcastic young woman, whose younger friend has just become engaged, is asked all day long by acquaintances whether she knows the fiancé and what she thinks of him. She answers with unqualified praise and so silences her own judgment, although she would have preferred to tell the truth: that he is an utterly ordinary man, what Germans call a *Dutzendmensch*, literally a "dozen-man," the kind of person who comes by the dozen like stock goods. That night she dreams that the same question is put to her, and that she replies with the formula found in a merchant's catalogue: "For repeat orders, it will suffice to quote the number."

Finally, numerous analyses have taught us that in every dream that has undergone distortion, the wish derives from the unconscious and was unable to reach perception in the waking state. It would seem, then, that all wishes have equal value and equal force for the formation of dreams.

I cannot at present prove that matters really stand otherwise, but I am strongly inclined to assume that the dream-wish is more strictly determined. Children's dreams leave no doubt that an unfulfilled wish from the day can instigate a dream. We must not forget, however, that this is, after all, the wish of a child, a wishful impulse with the strength peculiar to childhood. I seriously doubt whether an unfulfilled wish from the day would be enough to create a dream in an adult. It seems, rather, that as we learn to master our impulses through intellectual activity, we increasingly give up as futile the forming or harboring of such intense wishes as come naturally to children. Individuals may differ in this respect; some retain the infantile type of mental process longer than others. The differences here are the same as those found in the gradual decline of visual imagination, which is so distinct at first.

In general, however, I hold that unfulfilled wishes from the day are not enough to produce a dream in adults. I readily grant that wishful impulses originating in conscious life contribute to instigating dreams, but that is probably all they do. The dream would not come into being if the foreconscious wish were not reinforced from another source.

That source is the unconscious. I believe that a conscious wish instigates a dream only if it succeeds in awakening a similar unconscious wish that reinforces it. Following the indications gained from the psychoanalysis of the neuroses, I believe that these unconscious wishes are always active and ready for expression whenever they find a chance to ally themselves with an impulse from conscious life, and that they transfer their greater intensity to the lesser intensity of that impulse. It may therefore appear that the conscious wish alone has been realized in a dream, but some slight peculiarity in the way the dream is formed will put us on the track of its powerful helper from the unconscious. These ever-active and, so to speak, immortal wishes of the unconscious recall the Titans of legend, on whom the victorious gods long ago rolled massive mountains. The Titans have borne that crushing weight since time immemorial, and even now the mountains tremble from time to time with the convulsions of their mighty limbs. These wishes, held down in repression, are themselves of infantile origin, as the psychological investigation of the neuroses has taught us. I would therefore like to withdraw the opinion I expressed earlier, that it makes no difference where the dream-wish comes from, and replace it with another: the wish represented in a dream must be an infantile one. In the adult it originates in the unconscious. In the child, where no separation and no censorship yet exist between the foreconscious and the unconscious, or where these are only beginning to form, it is an unfulfilled and unrepressed wish from waking life. I am aware that this view cannot be proven universally, but I maintain that it can be demonstrated frequently, even where no one suspected it, and that it cannot be refuted as a general rule.

The wishful impulses left over from conscious waking life are therefore pushed into the background of dream formation. In the content of the dream I shall assign them only the role I assigned earlier to the material of actual sensations during sleep. If I now consider those other mental stimuli left over from waking life that are not wishes, I am simply keeping to the line this train of thought has laid out for me. By deciding to go to sleep, we may succeed in provisionally bringing to a halt the energy invested in our waking thoughts. Whoever can do this is a good sleeper, and Napoleon I is said to have been a model of this kind. But we do not always manage it, or manage it completely. Unsolved problems, tormenting worries, and overwhelming impressions carry our thinking on even into sleep, sustaining mental processes in the system we have called the foreconscious. These processes that continue into sleep may be divided into several groups. The first consists of what was left unfinished during the day because of some chance interruption. The second consists of what remained incomplete because our mental powers temporarily failed, which is to say the unsolved. The third consists of what was rejected and suppressed during the day. To these is joined a powerful fourth group, made up of whatever the work of the foreconscious stirred up in our unconscious during the day. Finally, we may add a fifth group, consisting of the day's indifferent impressions, which for that very reason were left unsettled.

We should not underestimate the mental intensities carried into sleep by these remnants of waking life, especially those from the group of the unsolved. These excitations surely go on striving for expression during the night, and we may assume with equal certainty that the sleeping state makes impossible both their usual continuation in the foreconscious and their resolution through becoming conscious. To the extent that we can become conscious of our mental processes in the normal way, even at night, we are to that extent not asleep. I will not venture to say what change the sleeping state produces in the foreconscious system, but there is no doubt that the psychological character of sleep depends essentially on a change of energy in this very system, which also controls access to motility, the power of movement that is paralyzed during sleep. By contrast, nothing in the psychology of the dream seems to justify the assumption that sleep produces anything more than secondary changes in the conditions of the unconscious system. For the nocturnal excitation in the foreconscious, then, no path remains except the one taken by the wishful excitations from the unconscious. This excitation must seek reinforcement from the unconscious and follow the roundabout routes of unconscious excitations. But what is the relation of the foreconscious day remnants to the dream? There is no doubt that they find their way into dreams in abundance, and that they use the dream content to force themselves upon consciousness even at night. Indeed, they sometimes dominate the dream content and drive it to carry on the work of the day. It is equally certain that the day remnants may have any character at all, not only that of wishes. But it is highly instructive, and even decisive for the theory of wish-fulfillment, to see what conditions they must meet in order to be admitted into the dream.

Let us take one of the dreams cited earlier as an example: the dream in which my friend Otto appears to show the symptoms of Basedow's disease, a disorder of the thyroid gland. During the day, Otto's appearance had caused me some concern, and this worry, like everything else concerning him, affected me. I may also assume that these feelings followed me into sleep. I was probably intent on finding out what was wrong with him. During the night my worry found expression in the dream I have reported, whose content was not only senseless but showed no wish-fulfillment whatever. But I set about investigating the source of this incongruous expression of the concern I had felt during the day, and analysis revealed the connection. I had identified my friend Otto with a certain Baron L., and myself with a Professor R. There was only one explanation for my being driven to choose precisely this substitute for the daytime thought. I must always have been ready, in the unconscious, to identify myself with Professor R., since that identification meant the fulfillment of one of the immortal wishes of childhood: the wish to become great. Ugly ideas about my friend, which I would certainly have repudiated while awake, seized the opportunity to slip into the dream, but the worry of the day also found some form of expression through a substitution in the dream content. The daytime thought, which was no wish in itself but rather a worry, had somehow to establish a connection with the infantile wish, now unconscious and suppressed. That wish then allowed the thought, already suitably prepared, to "originate" for consciousness. The more dominant the worry, the stronger the connection that had to be established. Between the content of the wish and that of the worry there need be no connection at all, nor was there one in any of our examples.

We can now define sharply the significance of the unconscious wish for the dream. It may be granted that there is a whole class of dreams whose instigation comes predominantly or even exclusively from the remnants of daily life. I believe that even my cherished hope of one day becoming a *professor extraordinarius*, a university professor without a full chair, would have let me sleep undisturbed that night if my worry about my friend's health had not still been active. But the worry alone would not have produced a dream. The motive force the dream required had to be supplied by a wish, and it was up to the worry to secure such a wish for itself as the dream's driving force. To put it figuratively, a daytime thought may well play the part of the entrepreneur in the dream. But it is well known that whatever idea the entrepreneur may have in mind, and however eager he may be to put it into practice, he can do nothing without capital. He must rely on a capitalist to cover the necessary costs, and this capitalist, who supplies the mental outlay for the dream, is invariably and indisputably a wish from the unconscious, whatever the nature of the waking thought may be.

In other cases the capitalist is himself the entrepreneur of the dream, and this seems to be the more common arrangement. An unconscious wish is stirred up by the day's activity, and this wish in turn creates the dream. The dream processes, moreover, run parallel to every other possibility in the economic relationship used here as an illustration. The entrepreneur may contribute some capital of his own; several entrepreneurs may turn to the same capitalist; or several capitalists may jointly supply the funds the entrepreneur needs. So too there are dreams produced by more than one dream-wish, along with many similar variations that may easily be passed over and hold no further interest for us. What we have left unfinished in this discussion of the dream-wish we shall be able to develop later.

The common element in the comparisons just used, what logicians call the *tertium comparationis*, is the sum placed at our free disposal and allotted in proper measure. It lends itself to a still finer application in illustrating the structure of the dream. As shown earlier, we can recognize in most dreams a center endowed with special sensory intensity. This center is regularly the direct representation of the wish-fulfillment. For if we reverse the displacements of the dream-work, we find that the psychic intensity of the elements in the dream thoughts has been replaced by the sensory intensity of the elements in the dream content. The elements surrounding the wish-fulfillment often have nothing to do with its meaning; they turn out to be offshoots of painful thoughts opposed to the wish. Yet through their frequently artificial connection with the central element, they have acquired enough intensity to come to expression. The expressive force of the wish-fulfillment is thus diffused over a certain sphere of association, within which it raises every element to expression, including those that are powerless in themselves. In dreams containing several strong wishes, we can readily separate the spheres of the individual wish-fulfillments from one another, and the gaps in the dream can often be explained as the border zones between them.

Although the foregoing remarks have considerably restricted the significance of the day remnants for the dream, it will still be worth our while to give them some attention. They must be a necessary ingredient in dream formation, since experience reveals the surprising fact that every dream shows in its content a connection with some impression from a recent day, often one of the most indifferent kind. So far we have failed to see why this addition to the dream mixture should be necessary. The necessity becomes apparent only when we follow closely the part played by the unconscious wish and then turn for information to the psychology of the neuroses. There we learn that an unconscious idea, as such, is wholly incapable of entering the foreconscious, and that it can exert influence there only by attaching itself to a harmless idea already belonging to the foreconscious, transferring its intensity to that idea and concealing itself behind it. This is the fact of transference, which explains so many surprising occurrences in the mental life of neurotics.

The foreconscious idea that thereby receives an undeserved abundance of intensity may be left unchanged by the transference, or it may have a modification forced upon it by the content of the transferring idea. I hope the reader will forgive my fondness for comparisons drawn from everyday life, but I am tempted to say that the repressed idea finds itself in much the same position as the American dentist in Austria. He is forbidden to practice unless he obtains permission from a licensed physician to display the physician's name on his public signboard, which satisfies the legal requirements. And just as it is naturally not the busiest physicians who enter into such arrangements with dental practitioners, so in mental life the foreconscious or conscious ideas chosen to cover a repressed idea are only those that have not themselves attracted much of the attention at work in the foreconscious. The unconscious entangles in its connections, by preference, either those foreconscious impressions and ideas that were passed over as indifferent, or those that were soon deprived of attention through rejection. It is a familiar fact from association studies, confirmed by all experience, that ideas which have formed close connections in one direction take an almost negative attitude toward whole groups of new connections. I once attempted to build a theory of hysterical paralysis on this principle.

If we assume that the same need for the transference of repressed ideas that we have come to know from the analysis of the neuroses makes itself felt in the dream as well, we can at once explain two riddles of the dream: that every dream analysis reveals a recent impression woven into it, and that this recent element is often of the most indifferent character. We may add what we have already learned elsewhere, that these recent and indifferent elements so often enter the dream content as substitutes for the deepest-lying dream thoughts for the further reason that they have the least to fear from the resisting censorship. But while this freedom from censorship explains only the preference for trivial elements, the constant presence of recent elements points to a need for transference. Both groups of impressions satisfy the repression's demand for material still free of associations: the indifferent ones because they offered no occasion for extensive associations, and the recent ones because they have not yet had time to form them.

We see, then, that the day remnants, among which we may now include indifferent impressions when they take part in dream formation, not only borrow from the unconscious the motive force at the disposal of the repressed wish, but also offer the unconscious something indispensable: the point of attachment that transference requires. If we tried here to penetrate more deeply into these mental processes, we would first have to shed more light on the interplay of emotions between the foreconscious and the unconscious. The study of the psychoneuroses urges us toward this inquiry, but the dream itself offers no help in this respect.

Just one further remark about the day remnants. There is no doubt that these, and not the dream, are the true disturbers of sleep; the dream, on the contrary, strives to protect it. But we shall return to this point later.

We have so far discussed the dream-wish. We have traced it to the realm of the unconscious and analyzed its relation to the day remnants, which may themselves be wishes, psychic impulses of any other kind, or simply recent impressions. We have thus made room for every claim that might be advanced on behalf of conscious thought, in all its variations, as a factor in the formation of dreams. Following our line of reasoning, we would find it by no means impossible to explain even those extreme cases in which the dream, carrying on the work of the day, brings an unsolved problem of waking life to a happy resolution. We do not, however, possess an example whose analysis might reveal the infantile or repressed source of the wish that supplied such an alliance and so successfully reinforced the efforts of preconscious activity. Yet we have not come one step closer to solving the riddle: why can the unconscious supply the motive power for wish-fulfillment only during sleep? The answer to this question must shed light on the psychic nature of wishes, and it will be given with the help of our diagram of the psychic apparatus.

We do not doubt that this apparatus, too, reached its present perfection only through a long course of development. Let us attempt to reconstruct it as it existed at an early stage of its activity. From assumptions that are to be confirmed elsewhere, we know that the apparatus at first strove to keep itself as free from excitation as possible, and that in its earliest form it was therefore built on the plan of a reflex apparatus, able to discharge promptly along the motor pathways any sensory stimulus that reached it from outside. But this simple function was disrupted by the necessities of life, which also supplied the impulse for the apparatus's further development. These necessities first made themselves felt in the form of the great bodily needs. The excitation aroused by an inner need seeks an outlet in movement, which may be described as an "internal change" or an "expression of emotion." The hungry child cries or thrashes about helplessly, yet its situation remains unchanged, for the excitation arising from an inner need calls not for a momentary outburst but for a force that works continuously. A change can come about only when an experience of satisfaction somehow occurs—which, for the child, must come through outside help—and removes the inner excitation. An essential part of this experience is the appearance of a particular perception (in our example, that of food), whose memory image thereafter remains linked with the memory trace of the excitation produced by the need.

Because of this established connection, the next time the need arises a psychic impulse appears that revives the memory image of the earlier perception and so calls up that perception itself; in effect, it re-creates the situation of the first satisfaction. Such an impulse is what we call a wish. The reappearance of the perception is the wish-fulfillment, and the complete revival of the perception by the excitation of the need is the shortest path to that fulfillment. We may suppose a primitive state of the psychic apparatus in which this path really was taken—a state, that is, in which wishing ended in hallucination. This first psychic activity therefore aims at an identity of perception: it seeks to repeat the perception that is bound up with the satisfaction of the need.

Bitter practical experience must have modified this primitive mental activity into a more expedient, secondary one. Establishing an identity of perception by the short regressive route within the apparatus does not, in another respect, bring the result that inevitably follows when the same perception is revived from outside. Satisfaction does not occur, and the need persists. To make the internal expenditure of energy equal to the external one, the internal would have to be sustained continuously, as actually happens in the hallucinatory psychoses and in the deliriums of hunger, which exhaust their entire psychic capacity in clinging to the desired object. To make more appropriate use of psychic force, it becomes necessary to check the regression before it is complete, so that it goes no farther than the memory image; from there it can choose other paths that lead, in the end, to establishing the desired identity through the outer world. This inhibition, and the consequent diversion of the excitation, becomes the task of a second system, one that controls voluntary movement—a system, that is, through whose activity motor expenditure is now put to the service of purposes previously recalled. Yet all of this complicated mental activity, which works its way from the memory image to the establishment of a perceptual identity through the outer world, is merely a detour that experience has forced upon wish-fulfillment. Thinking is, in truth, nothing but a substitute for the hallucinatory wish; and if the dream is called a wish-fulfillment, this becomes self-evident, since nothing but a wish can set our psychic apparatus to work. The dream, which fulfills its wishes by following the short regressive path, has thereby simply preserved for us a specimen of the apparatus's primary mode of working, which was abandoned as inexpedient. What once governed waking life, when the psyche was still young and incapable, seems to have been banished into sleep—just as we find in the nursery the bow and arrow, the discarded primitive weapons of adult humanity. The dream is a fragment of the child's abandoned psychic life. In the psychoses, these modes of operation of the psychic apparatus, which are normally suppressed in waking life, reassert themselves—and then reveal their inability to satisfy our needs in the outer world.

The unconscious wishful impulses evidently strive to assert themselves during the day as well, and the facts of transference and of the psychoses teach us that they try to force their way into consciousness and gain control of movement along the route that leads through the preconscious system. It is therefore the censorship standing between the unconscious and the preconscious—an assumption the dream compels us to make—that we must recognize and respect as the guardian of our psychic health. But is it not careless of this guardian to relax its vigilance at night and allow the suppressed impulses of the unconscious to find expression, thereby once again making hallucinatory regression possible? I think not. For when the critical guardian goes to rest—and we have proof that his sleep is not deep—he takes care to shut the gate to movement. Whatever impulses from the otherwise inhibited unconscious may roam about the stage, they need not be interfered with; they remain harmless, because they cannot set in motion the motor apparatus, which alone can produce a change in the outer world. Sleep guarantees the safety of the fortress under guard.

Matters are less harmless when a shift of forces comes about not through the nightly relaxation of the critical censorship but through a pathological weakening of it, or through a pathological strengthening of the unconscious excitations—and this while the preconscious is charged with energy and the pathways to movement stand open. The guardian is then overpowered. The unconscious excitations subdue the preconscious and through it govern our speech and actions; or else they force hallucinatory regression, taking command of an apparatus not designed for them by virtue of the pull that perceptions exert on the distribution of our psychic energy. This condition we call psychosis.

We are now in the best position to continue our psychological construction, which was interrupted when we introduced the two systems, the unconscious and the preconscious. We still have ample reason, however, to consider further the wish as the sole psychic motive force of the dream. We have explained that the dream is in every case a wish-fulfillment because it is a product of the unconscious, which knows no other aim in its activity than the fulfillment of wishes and has no forces at its disposal other than wishful impulses. If we claim, for a moment longer, the right to build such far-reaching psychological speculations upon the interpretation of dreams, we are obliged to show that in doing so we are placing the dream in a context that can also include other psychic formations. If there exists a system of the unconscious—or something sufficiently like it for the purposes of our discussion—the dream cannot be its only manifestation. Every dream may be a wish-fulfillment, but there must be other forms of abnormal wish-fulfillment besides dreams. And indeed, the whole theory of psychoneurotic symptoms culminates in the proposition that they, too, must be understood as fulfillments of unconscious wishes. Our explanation makes the dream merely the first member of a group of the greatest importance to the psychiatrist, a group whose understanding would amount to solving the purely psychological part of the psychiatric problem. But other members of this group of wish-fulfillments—hysterical symptoms, for example—display one essential feature that I have so far failed to find in the dream. From the investigations I have frequently referred to in this treatise, I know that the formation of a hysterical symptom requires the convergence of both currents of our psychic life. The symptom is not merely the expression of a fulfilled unconscious wish; it must be joined by another wish, from the preconscious, which the same symptom also fulfills. The symptom is thus at least doubly determined, once by each of the two conflicting systems. As in the dream, there is no limit to further overdetermination. The determination that does not come from the unconscious is, as far as I can see, always a train of thought reacting against the unconscious wish—a self-punishment, for example. I may therefore say, in general, that a hysterical symptom arises only where two opposing wish-fulfillments, each originating in a different psychic system, can converge in a single expression. My most recent formulation of the origin of hysterical symptoms appears in an essay published in 1908 in the *Zeitschrift für Sexualwissenschaft*, edited by Hirschfeld and others. Examples would be of little use here, since nothing short of a complete disclosure of the complexities involved would carry conviction. I therefore content myself with simply making the assertion, and I will cite one example, not to convince but to illustrate. A female patient's hysterical vomiting turned out, on the one hand, to fulfill an unconscious fantasy dating from puberty: that she might be continually pregnant and have a great many children—a wish later joined by the further wish that she might have them by as many men as possible. Against this immoderate wish a powerful defensive impulse arose. But since vomiting might spoil the patient's figure and beauty, so that she would no longer find favor in anyone's eyes, the symptom was also in keeping with her punitive train of thought; and being thus acceptable to both sides, it was allowed to become a reality. This is the same manner of granting a wish that the queen of the Parthians chose for the triumvir Crassus. Believing that he had undertaken his campaign out of greed for gold, she had molten gold poured into the throat of his corpse: "Now you have what you longed for." So far we know only that the dream expresses the fulfillment of an unconscious wish, and that the dominant preconscious apparently permits this only after subjecting the wish to certain distortions. We are in no position to demonstrate, as a regular matter, a train of thought opposed to the dream-wish and fulfilled in the dream as its counterpart. Only now and then have we found traces of reaction formations in dreams—for instance, the tenderness toward my friend R. in the "uncle dream." But the contribution from the preconscious that is missing here may be found elsewhere. While the dominant system has withdrawn into the wish to sleep, the dream can give expression, with manifold distortions, to a wish from the unconscious, fulfill that wish by bringing about the necessary changes of energy within the psychic apparatus, and finally sustain it for the entire duration of sleep.

This persistent wish to sleep on the part of the preconscious generally facilitates the formation of dreams. Recall the dream of the father who, from the glow of light coming from the room where his child lay dead, concluded that the body had caught fire. We showed that one of the psychic forces decisive in leading the father to draw this conclusion, rather than to be woken by the light, was the wish to prolong by one moment the life of the child he saw in the dream. Other wishes stemming from repression probably escape us, since we are unable to analyze this dream. But as a second motive force of the dream we may name the father's wish to sleep; for, like the child's life, the father's sleep is prolonged by a moment through the dream. The underlying motive is: "Let the dream go on, or I shall have to wake up." As in this dream, so in all others: the wish to sleep lends its support to the unconscious wish. Earlier we reported dreams that appeared to be dreams of convenience. Strictly speaking, however, all dreams may claim that name. The effectiveness of the wish to go on sleeping is most easily recognized in dreams provoked by an outside stimulus that would otherwise wake us. Such dreams transform the objective sensory stimulus so as to make it compatible with continued sleep, weaving it into the dream in order to strip it of any claim it might make as a signal from the outer world. But this wish to go on sleeping must also take part in forming all other dreams, even those that can disturb sleep only from within. "Go on sleeping—it's only a dream": this, in many cases, is what the preconscious suggests to consciousness when the dream goes too far; and it also describes, in a general way, the attitude of our dominant psychic activity toward dreaming, though the thought remains unspoken. I must conclude that throughout the whole of our sleeping state we know just as surely that we are dreaming as we know that we are asleep. We are obliged to set aside the objection that our consciousness is never directed toward knowledge of the former, and is directed toward knowledge of the latter only on special occasions, when the censorship is taken by surprise. Against this objection we may point out that there are people who remain fully aware that they are sleeping and dreaming, and who apparently possess the conscious ability to steer their dream life. Such a dreamer, dissatisfied with the course a dream is taking, breaks it off without waking and starts it over in order to continue it in a different direction—like a popular playwright who, on request, gives his play a happier ending. Or, on another occasion, if the dream places him in a sexually exciting situation, he thinks in his sleep: "I don't care to continue this dream and exhaust myself with a nocturnal emission; I would rather save it for a real situation."

### (d) Waking Caused by the Dream — The Function of the Dream — The Anxiety Dream

Now that we know the preconscious is suspended during the night by the wish to sleep, we can proceed to investigate the dream process with understanding. But let us first summarize what we have already learned about it. We have shown that waking activity leaves behind day residues from which the charge of energy cannot be entirely withdrawn; or that during the day waking activity reawakens one of the unconscious wishes; or that both occur together—and we have already discovered the many variations that are possible. The unconscious wish has made its way to the day residues, either during the day or at the latest as sleep begins, and has effected a transference onto them. The result is either a wish transferred onto the recent material, or a suppressed recent wish brought back to life through reinforcement from the unconscious. This wish now tries to make its way into consciousness along the normal route of mental processes, through the preconscious, to which it in fact belongs through one of its component elements. There, however, it meets the censorship, which is still active, and it yields to that influence. It now takes on the distortion for which the way has already been prepared by its transference onto the recent material. Up to this point it is on its way to becoming something like an obsession, a delusion, or the like—a thought reinforced by transference and distorted in expression by the censorship. But its further progress is now blocked by the dormant state of the preconscious, which has evidently protected itself against invasion by lowering its excitations. The dream process therefore takes the regressive route, which the peculiar nature of the sleeping state has just opened, and in doing so follows the attraction exerted on it by groups of memories, which themselves exist partly only as visual energy not yet translated into the terms of the later systems. On its regressive path the dream takes on the form of dramatization. The question of compression will be discussed later. The dream process has now completed the second stage of its repeatedly obstructed course. The first stage moved forward, from the unconscious scenes or fantasies toward the preconscious; the second moves back, from the frontier of the censorship toward perception. But once the dream process has become a content of perception, it has, so to speak, slipped past the obstacle that the censorship and the state of sleep had set up in the preconscious. It succeeds in drawing attention to itself and in being noticed by consciousness. For consciousness, which we understand as a sense organ for perceiving psychic qualities, can receive stimuli from two sources: first, from the periphery of the whole apparatus, that is, from the perceptual system; and second, from stimuli of pleasure and pain, which are the only psychic quality produced by the transformation of energy inside the apparatus. All other processes in the Ψ-system, even those in the preconscious, lack any psychic quality, and so are not objects of consciousness, since they supply no pleasure or pain to be perceived. We shall have to assume that these releases of pleasure and pain automatically regulate the discharge of the processes in which energy is invested. Later, however, in order to make more delicate functions possible, it proved necessary to make the course of ideas more independent of signals of pain. To accomplish this, the preconscious system needed qualities of its own that could attract consciousness, and it most probably acquired them by linking preconscious processes with the memory system of verbal signs, which is not devoid of qualities. Through the qualities of this system, consciousness—hitherto a sense organ only for perceptions—becomes also a sense organ for a portion of our thought processes. We now have, as it were, two sensory surfaces: one turned toward perceptions, the other toward the preconscious thought processes.

I must assume that sleep makes the sensory surface of consciousness that faces the preconscious less excitable than the surface facing the perceptual systems. This abandonment of interest in nocturnal thought processes does indeed have a purpose: nothing is to disturb the mind, for the preconscious wants to sleep. But once the dream becomes a perception, it can excite consciousness through the qualities it has thereby acquired. The sensory stimulus then does what it was really meant to do: it directs part of the energy available to the preconscious, in the form of attention, toward the source of stimulation. We must therefore admit that the dream invariably awakens us—that is, it calls into activity part of the dormant force of the preconscious. This force exerts on the dream the influence we have called secondary elaboration, which works toward coherence and intelligibility. The dream is treated by this force like any other content of perception; it is met with the same anticipatory ideas, at least as far as the material allows. As for the direction of movement in this third stage of the dream, it may be said that here once again the movement is progressive.

To avoid misunderstanding, a few words about the temporal characteristics of these dream processes may be useful. In a very interesting discussion, apparently prompted by Maury's puzzling guillotine dream, Goblot tries to show that the dream occupies no more time than the transitional period between sleeping and waking. Awakening takes time, and the dream occurs during that interval.
