We are inclined to believe that the dream's final image is so powerful that it forces the dreamer to wake; in fact, however, the image is powerful only because the dreamer is already very close to waking when it appears. "Un rêve, c'est un réveil qui commence"—a dream is an awakening that is beginning.

Dugas has already pointed out that Goblot was forced to disregard many facts in order to generalize his theory. Moreover, there are dreams from which we do not wake—for instance, some dreams in which we dream that we are dreaming. From what we know of the dream-work, we can by no means accept that it extends only over the period of awakening. On the contrary, we must consider it likely that the first part of the dream-work begins during the day, while we are still under the dominion of the preconscious. The second phase—the modification by the censorship, the attraction exerted by the unconscious scenes, and the push toward perception—must continue throughout the night. And we are probably always right when we say we feel as though we had been dreaming all night, even though we cannot say what. I do not, however, think it necessary to assume that, up to the moment they become conscious, the dream processes actually follow the temporal sequence we have described: first the transferred dream-wish, then the distortion by the censorship, then the reversal of direction into regression, and so on. We were compelled to construct such a sequence for the sake of description. In reality it is much more a matter of simultaneously trying out this path and that, of impulses surging back and forth, until finally, through the most expedient distribution, one particular grouping is achieved and remains. From certain personal experiences, I am myself inclined to believe that the dream-work often requires more than one day and one night to produce its result; if this is true, the extraordinary artistry displayed in the construction of dreams loses all its marvel.

In my view, even the concern for intelligibility, which treats the dream as an object of perception, may begin to take effect before the dream has drawn consciousness to itself. From that point on, admittedly, the process speeds up, since the dream is now handled exactly as any other perception would be. It is like a fireworks display, which takes hours to prepare and only a moment to set off.

Through the dream-work, the dream process now either acquires enough intensity to draw consciousness to itself and rouse the foreconscious, regardless of the hour or the depth of sleep, or, if its intensity falls short, it must wait until it meets the attention that stirs immediately before waking. Most dreams seem to operate with relatively weak psychic intensities, since they wait for the moment of awakening. This also explains why, whenever we are suddenly roused from deep sleep, we regularly find that we have been dreaming. In such cases, as in spontaneous waking, our first glance falls on the perceptual content created by the dream-work, and only our second on the content that comes from outside.

Of greater theoretical interest, however, are the dreams that can wake us in the middle of sleep. The psychic apparatus shows purposefulness everywhere else, and with that in mind we must ask why the dream, or the unconscious wish, should have the power to disturb sleep, which is to say, to disturb the fulfillment of the foreconscious wish. The answer probably lies in certain relations of energy into which we have no insight. If we did have such insight, we would likely find that granting the dream its freedom, and spending a certain amount of detached attention on it, amounts to an economy of energy, given that the unconscious must be held in check at night just as during the day. Experience shows that a dream remains compatible with sleep even when it interrupts sleep several times in the same night. We wake for an instant and at once fall back asleep. It is like brushing away a fly in our sleep: we wake for that one purpose, and when we fall asleep again the disturbance is gone. Familiar examples, such as the sleep of wet nurses who rest soundly yet wake at the first sound from the infant in their care, show that fulfilling the wish to sleep is entirely compatible with keeping a certain amount of attention trained in a particular direction.

At this point, though, we must take account of an objection based on a closer knowledge of unconscious processes. We have ourselves described unconscious wishes as perpetually active, yet we have also maintained that during the day they are not strong enough to make themselves felt. But when we sleep, and the unconscious wish has shown itself strong enough to form a dream and thereby to rouse the foreconscious, why should that strength be exhausted once the dream has been noticed? Would it not seem more likely that the dream would keep renewing itself, like the troublesome fly that, once driven off, delights in returning again and again? What entitles us to claim that the dream removes the disturbance of sleep?

It is quite true that unconscious wishes always remain active. They are paths that can be traveled whenever a sum of excitation makes use of them. Indeed, one remarkable peculiarity of unconscious processes is that they are indestructible. In the unconscious nothing can be brought to an end; nothing ceases and nothing is forgotten. This impression is strongest in the study of the neuroses, especially hysteria. The unconscious current of thought that leads to discharge in a hysterical attack becomes passable again as soon as enough excitation has accumulated. A humiliation suffered thirty years ago, once it has gained access to the unconscious source of affect, goes on working through all those thirty years as though it were fresh. Whenever its memory is touched, it revives and proves to be charged with the excitation that is then discharged in a motor attack. This is precisely where the work of psychotherapy begins, for its task is to bring about settlement and forgetting for these unconscious processes. In fact, the fading of memories and the weakening of emotions, which we tend to take for granted and to explain as the direct effect of time on psychic memories, are really secondary changes produced by painstaking work. It is the foreconscious that carries out this work, and the only course open to psychotherapy is to bring the Unconscious under the rule of the Foreconscious.

There are, then, two outlets for any given unconscious emotional process. Either it is left to itself, in which case it eventually breaks through somewhere and, for that one occasion, discharges its excitation into movement; or it yields to the influence of the foreconscious, and its excitation is contained by that influence instead of being discharged. It is the second of these that occurs in the dream. The energy of the Foreconscious, which meets the dream once the dream has become a perception, is guided by the excitation of consciousness, and it restrains the dream's unconscious excitation and renders it harmless as a source of disturbance. When the dreamer wakes for a moment, he has in fact chased away the fly that threatened to disturb his sleep. We can now see that it is really more expedient and more economical to give the unconscious wish free rein, clearing its path toward regression so that it can form a dream, and then to restrain and adjust that dream with a small outlay of foreconscious labor, than to hold the unconscious in check throughout the entire period of sleep. We should, after all, expect the dream to have acquired some function in the interplay of forces in psychic life, even if it was not originally a purposeful process. We can now see what that function is. The dream has taken on the task of bringing the freed excitation of the Unconscious back under the control of the Foreconscious. In doing so, it gives the Unconscious relief for its excitation and serves it as a safety valve, while at the same time it secures the sleep of the Foreconscious at the cost of only a little wakefulness. Like the other psychic formations of its class, the dream presents itself as a compromise that serves both systems at once, fulfilling both their wishes so far as the two are compatible. A look at Robert's "elimination theory," discussed earlier, will show that we must agree with this author on his main point, namely in defining the function of the dream, although we differ from him in our assumptions and in our account of the dream process.

The qualification just made, "so far as the two wishes are compatible," implies that there may be cases in which the dream fails in its function. The dream process is first admitted as a fulfillment of an unconscious wish. But if this tentative fulfillment disturbs the foreconscious so badly that it can no longer stay at rest, the dream breaks the compromise and fails to carry out the second half of its task. It is then broken off at once and replaced by full wakefulness. Here too, the dream is not really at fault if, though ordinarily the guardian of sleep, it is forced in this case to appear as its disturber, and this should not lead us to doubt its usefulness. This is not the only arrangement in the organism that, though normally effective, becomes ineffective and disruptive as soon as some element in the conditions of its origin is altered. The disturbance then at least serves the new purpose of announcing the change and of calling up the organism's means of adjusting to it. I have in mind here, of course, the anxiety dream, and so that I do not appear to be dodging this evidence against the theory of wish-fulfillment wherever I meet it, I will attempt an explanation of the anxiety dream, or at least offer some suggestions toward one.

We have long since ceased to regard it as a contradiction that a psychic process which produces anxiety may nonetheless be a wish-fulfillment. The explanation is that the wish belongs to one system, the Unconscious, while the other system, the Foreconscious, has rejected and suppressed it. Even in perfect psychic health, the Unconscious is never completely subdued by the Foreconscious, and the extent of this suppression is a measure of our psychic normality. Neurotic symptoms show that the two systems are in conflict. The symptoms are the product of a compromise in that conflict, and for a time they bring it to an end. On the one hand, they give the Unconscious an outlet for discharging its excitation, serving it as a sally port, the gate through which a besieged garrison makes its sorties; on the other, they allow the Foreconscious to dominate the Unconscious to some degree. It is highly instructive to consider the meaning of any hysterical phobia, or of agoraphobia. Suppose a neurotic is unable to cross the street alone, which we rightly call a "symptom." We try to remove the symptom by pressing him to do what he believes he cannot do. The result will be an attack of anxiety, just as an attack of anxiety in the street has often been what first established an agoraphobia. We learn from this that the symptom was formed to guard against the outbreak of anxiety. The phobia is set up in front of the anxiety like a fortress on a frontier.

We cannot carry the discussion further without considering the part that the emotions play in these processes, and that can be done here only imperfectly. Let us therefore propose that the suppression of the unconscious becomes absolutely necessary because, if the discharge of its ideas were left to itself, it would generate an emotion in the Unconscious that originally had the character of pleasure but that, since repression set in, has the character of pain. The aim of the suppression, and also its result, is to prevent this pain from developing. The suppression extends over the unconscious ideas because the release of pain could proceed from them. This lays the groundwork for a quite definite assumption about the nature of emotional development. It is regarded as a motor, or secondary, activity, and the key that releases it lies in the ideas of the Unconscious. Under the rule of the Foreconscious, these ideas are, so to speak, throttled and held back at the very point where the impulses that generate emotion would emerge. The danger arising when the Foreconscious withdraws its charge of energy therefore lies in this: the unconscious excitations release an emotion which, because of the repression that has already occurred, can be felt only as pain or anxiety.

This danger is set loose when the dream process is given free rein. The conditions for its realization are that repressions have taken place and that the suppressed emotional wishes have grown strong enough. These conditions therefore lie entirely outside the psychological framework of dream formation. Were it not that our subject is connected with the development of anxiety through one single factor, namely the freeing of the Unconscious during sleep, I could dispense with discussing the anxiety dream altogether and so avoid all the obscurities attached to it.

As I have said many times, the theory of anxiety belongs to the psychology of the neuroses. I would say that anxiety in dreams is a problem of anxiety, not a problem of dreams. Once we have shown where it touches the subject of the dream process, we have nothing further to do with it. Only one task remains for me. Since I have asserted that neurotic anxiety springs from sexual sources, I can analyze anxiety dreams in order to demonstrate the sexual material in their dream thoughts.

For good reasons, I refrain from citing any of the many examples my neurotic patients have provided, and prefer instead to give anxiety dreams from young people. I myself have not had a real anxiety dream for decades, but I remember one from my seventh or eighth year, which I interpreted some thirty years later. The dream was very vivid. It showed me *my beloved mother, with a peculiarly calm, sleeping expression on her face, being carried into the room and laid on the bed by two (or three) figures with birds' beaks.* I woke up crying and screaming and disturbed my parents. The very tall, strangely draped figures with beaks I had taken from the illustrations in Philippson's Bible; I believe they were deities with the heads of sparrow hawks from an Egyptian tomb relief. The analysis also brought up the memory of an ill-behaved boy, the son of a caretaker, who used to play with us children on the meadow in front of the house; I would add that his name was Philip. I believe it was from this boy that I first heard the vulgar word for sexual intercourse, for which educated people substitute the Latin "coitus." The dream alludes to this word unmistakably through its choice of the birds' heads, since in German the vulgar term is derived from the word for "bird." I must have guessed the word's sexual meaning from the face of my worldly-wise young teacher. My mother's features in the dream were copied from the face of my grandfather, whom I had seen a few days before his death, snoring in a coma. The interpretation supplied by the dream's secondary elaboration must therefore have been that my mother was dying, and the tomb relief fits this as well. I woke in this state of anxiety and could not calm down until I had roused my parents. I remember growing calm all at once when I saw my mother face to face, as if I needed assurance that she was not dead. But this secondary interpretation of the dream had been made only under the influence of anxiety that had already developed. I was not frightened because I dreamed that my mother was dying. Rather, I interpreted the dream this way in its foreconscious elaboration because I was already in the grip of anxiety. That anxiety, in turn, could be traced through repression to an obscure and plainly sexual desire, which had found satisfying expression in the visual content of the dream.

A man of twenty-seven, who had been seriously ill for a year, had had many terrifying dreams between the ages of eleven and thirteen. In them, a man with an axe was chasing him; he wanted to run but felt paralyzed and could not move from the spot. This is a good example of a very common anxiety dream that seems to have nothing to do with sex. In the analysis, the dreamer first thought of a story his uncle had told him, which came later than the dream: the uncle had been attacked at night by a suspicious-looking stranger. From this he concluded that he might already have heard of some similar incident at the time of the dream. In connection with the axe, he remembered that during that period of his life he had once injured his hand with an axe while chopping wood. This led him at once to his relations with his younger brother, whom he used to mistreat and knock down. In particular, he recalled an occasion when he struck his brother on the head with his boot until the boy bled, and his mother remarked, "I'm afraid he will kill him someday." While he seemed to be dwelling on the theme of violence, a memory from his ninth year suddenly came to him. His parents had come home late and gone to bed while he pretended to be asleep. Soon he heard panting and other noises that seemed strange to him, and he could also make out how his parents were positioned in the bed. His further associations showed that he had drawn an analogy between this relation between his parents and his own relation to his younger brother. He classed what happened between his parents under the heading of "violence and wrestling," and so arrived at a sadistic conception of the sexual act, as children often do. The fact that he often noticed blood on his mother's bed confirmed this conception.

That the sexual intercourse of adults strikes children who witness it as strange and frightens them is, I would say, a matter of everyday experience. I have explained this fear by the fact that the sexual excitement involved is beyond their understanding and is probably also unacceptable to them because their parents are involved in it. For the same reason, the excitement is converted into fear. At a still earlier stage of life, sexual feeling directed toward the parent of the opposite sex meets no repression and is expressed freely, as we saw earlier.

I would not hesitate to give the same explanation for the night terrors with hallucinations, known as *pavor nocturnus*, that are so common in children. Here too we are certainly dealing with sexual feelings that are not understood and are rejected. If these attacks were recorded, they would probably show a periodicity over time, since an intensification of the sexual libido can be produced just as well by chance emotional impressions as by the gradual, spontaneous processes of development.

I lack the material from observation needed to support these explanations. Pediatricians, for their part, seem to lack the one point of view that makes the whole series of phenomena intelligible, on the physical as well as the psychic side. To show with a comic example how someone wearing the blinders of medical mythology can miss the meaning of such cases, I will relate one I found in a thesis on *pavor nocturnus* by Debacker, published in 1881. A thirteen-year-old boy in delicate health began to grow anxious and dreamy. His sleep became restless, and about once a week it was broken by an acute attack of anxiety with hallucinations. He always remembered these dreams very distinctly. He reported, for instance, that the devil shouted at him, "Now we have you, now we have you," after which there was a smell of sulfur and fire burned his skin. This dream woke him in terror. At first he was unable to scream; then his voice returned, and he was heard to say clearly, "No, no, not me; why, I haven't done anything," or, "Please don't, I'll never do it again." Sometimes he also said, "Albert hasn't done that." Later he avoided undressing because, as he said, the fire attacked him only when he was undressed. Since these nightmares were threatening his health, he was sent to the country, where he recovered within a year and a half. But at fifteen he once confessed: "I didn't dare admit it, but I constantly felt prickling sensations and overexcitement in my private parts. In the end it got on my nerves so badly that several times I thought of throwing myself out of the dormitory window."

It is surely not hard to guess, first, that the boy had masturbated in earlier years, that he had probably denied it, and that he had been threatened with severe punishment for this misdeed. His confession, "I'll never do it again," and his denial, "Albert has never done that," point to this. Second, that under the pressure of puberty the temptation to touch his genitals was reawakened. Third, that a struggle of repression now arose within him, suppressing the libido and turning it into fear, and that this fear then took the form of the very punishments he had once been threatened with.

Let us, however, quote the conclusions our author draws. This observation shows, he writes:

1. That the influence of puberty may produce in a boy of delicate health a state of extreme weakness, and may lead to a very marked cerebral anemia, that is, an insufficient supply of blood to the brain.

2. That this cerebral anemia produces a change of character, hallucinations of demonic possession, and very violent states of anxiety at night, and perhaps also during the day.

3. That the demonomania and the boy's daytime self-reproaches can be traced to the religious education he received as a child.

4. That all the symptoms disappeared as a result of a long stay in the country, physical exercise, and the return of bodily strength once puberty was over.

5. That a predisposing influence in the origin of the boy's cerebral condition may be attributed to heredity and to his father's chronic syphilis.

The author's concluding remarks read: "We have placed this observation within the category of feverless deliriums caused by inanition, for it is to cerebral ischemia that we attribute this particular condition."

### (e) The Primary and Secondary Processes—Regression

In venturing to penetrate more deeply into the psychology of the dream processes, I have taken on a difficult task, one to which my powers of description are hardly equal. To render in a sequence of words the simultaneity of so complex a chain of events, and to appear impartial throughout the exposition, is rather beyond my abilities. I must now make amends for having been unable, in describing the psychology of dreams, to follow the historical development of my own views. The perspectives that shaped my conception of the dream were reached through earlier investigations into the psychology of the neuroses. I am not supposed to draw on that work here, yet I am repeatedly forced to, whereas I would prefer to proceed in the opposite direction, starting from the dream and building a connection to the psychology of the neuroses. I am well aware of all the inconvenience this causes the reader, but I know of no way to avoid it.

Dissatisfied as I am with this state of affairs, I am glad to dwell on another consideration that seems to lend my efforts greater value. As was shown at the opening of the first chapter, I found myself facing a subject on which the authorities had contradicted one another in the sharpest terms. In the course of working through the problems of the dream, we have found a place for most of these contradictions. We have been forced to reject decisively only two of the views put forward: that the dream is senseless, and that it is a somatic process. Apart from these, we have had to accept every one of the contradictory views at one point or another in our complicated argument, and we have been able to show that each had discovered something correct. That the dream carries on the impulses and interests of waking life has been broadly confirmed by the discovery of the latent dream thoughts. These thoughts concern themselves only with things that seem important to us and of great interest. The dream never busies itself with trifles. Yet we have also agreed with the opposite view, that the dream gathers up the indifferent leftovers of the day, and that an important event of the day cannot be taken up by the dream until it has to some degree been withdrawn from waking activity. We found this to hold true for the dream content, which gives the dream thought an altered expression by means of distortion. We have said that, owing to the nature of the mechanism of association, the dream process more readily takes hold of recent or indifferent material that waking mental activity has not yet seized upon; and because of the censorship, it shifts psychic intensity away from material that is important but disagreeable and onto material that is indifferent. The hypermnesia of the dream, its heightened power of recall, together with its recourse to infantile material, have become main supports of our theory. In that theory we have assigned to the wish originating in infancy the part of an indispensable motor in the formation of the dream. Naturally we could not think of doubting the experimentally demonstrated significance of objective sensory stimuli during sleep; but we have placed this material in the same relation to the dream-wish as the remnants of thought left over from waking activity. There was no need to dispute the fact that the dream interprets objective sensory stimuli in the manner of an illusion; but we have supplied the motive for this interpretation, which the authorities had left undecided. The interpretation proceeds in such a way that the perceived object is rendered harmless as a disturber of sleep and becomes available for wish-fulfillment. Although we do not accept as a special source of dreams the subjective state of excitation in the sense organs during sleep, which Trumbull Ladd seems to have demonstrated, we are nonetheless able to explain this excitation as the regressive revival of the memories that are active behind the dream. A modest part in our conception has also been given to the inner organic sensations that are customarily treated as the cardinal point in explaining the dream. These sensations of falling, of flying, or of being inhibited stand as ever-ready material, which the dream-work can use to express the dream thought as often as the need arises.

That the dream process is rapid and momentary seems to be true of the moment in which consciousness perceives the dream content, once that content has been prepared; the earlier stages of the dream process probably follow a slow and fluctuating course. We have solved the riddle of how so much dream content can be compressed into the briefest moment by explaining that the dream appropriates structures from psychic life that are already almost fully formed. That memory disfigures and distorts the dream we found to be correct, but not troublesome, since this is only the last, manifest operation in a work of disfigurement that has been active from the very beginning of the dream-work. In the bitter and seemingly irreconcilable controversy over whether psychic life sleeps at night or can make the same use of all its capacities as it does during the day, we have been able to agree with both sides, though fully with neither. We have found proof that the dream thoughts represent a highly complicated intellectual activity, one that employs almost every resource the psychic apparatus provides; yet it cannot be denied that these dream thoughts originated during the day, and it is indispensable to assume that there is a sleeping state of psychic life. Thus even the theory of partial sleep has come into play. The characteristics of the sleeping state, however, have been found not in the breakdown of psychic connections but in the suspension of the psychic system that dominates the day, a suspension arising from that system's desire to sleep. Withdrawal from the outer world also retains its significance in our conception; though it is not the only factor, it helps the regression that makes the representation of the dream possible. That we must reject the voluntary guidance of the flow of ideas is beyond dispute; but psychic life does not thereby become aimless, for we have seen that once the desired goal-ideas are abandoned, undesired ones gain the upper hand. We have not only recognized the loose associative connection in the dream, but have placed under its control a far larger territory than anyone could have supposed; we have found it, however, to be merely a feigned substitute for another connection that is correct and meaningful. We too, it is true, have called the dream absurd; but we have been able to learn from examples how wise the dream really is when it simulates absurdity. We do not deny any of the functions that have been attributed to the dream. The view that the dream relieves the mind like a valve, and that, as Robert asserts, all kinds of harmful material are rendered harmless by being represented in the dream, not only coincides exactly with our theory of the twofold wish-fulfillment in the dream, but, in Robert's own wording, becomes even more comprehensible to us than it was to Robert himself. The notion that the psyche freely indulges in the play of its faculties finds its expression in our theory as the preconscious activity's non-interference with the dream. The "return to the embryonic state of psychic life in the dream," and Havelock Ellis's observation of "an archaic world of vast emotions and imperfect thoughts," appear to us as happy anticipations of our own conclusion that primitive modes of operation, suppressed during the day, take part in the formation of the dream; and for us, as for Delage, the suppressed material becomes the mainspring of dreaming. We have fully recognized the role that Scherner ascribes to dream fantasy, and even his interpretation of it; but we have been obliged, so to speak, to move both to a different part of the problem. It is not the dream that produces the fantasy; rather, it is unconscious fantasy that takes the largest part in forming the dream thoughts. We are indebted to Scherner for his clue to the source of the dream thoughts, but almost everything he ascribes to the dream-work belongs to the activity of the unconscious, which is at work during the day and which supplies the incitements not only for dreams but for neurotic symptoms as well. We have had to separate the dream-work from this activity as something entirely different and far more restricted. Finally, we have by no means abandoned the relation of the dream to mental disturbances; on the contrary, we have given it a firmer foundation on new ground.

Held together by the new material of our theory as by a higher unity, the most varied and contradictory conclusions of the authorities thus fit into our structure; some of them are arranged differently, and only a few are rejected outright. But our own structure is still unfinished. Leaving aside the many obscurities we have necessarily encountered in our advance into the darkness of psychology, we now appear to be embarrassed by a new contradiction. On the one hand, we have allowed the dream thoughts to arise from perfectly normal mental operations; on the other, we have found among the dream thoughts a number of entirely abnormal mental processes, which extend likewise to the dream content and which we have consequently retraced in interpreting the dream. Everything we have termed the "dream-work" seems so remote from the psychic processes we recognize as correct that the severest judgments of the authors concerning the low level of psychic activity in dreaming seem to us well founded.

Perhaps only further advance can bring clarity and improvement here. I shall single out one of the constellations of circumstances that lead to the formation of dreams.

We have learned that the dream replaces a number of thoughts derived from daily life, thoughts perfectly formed in their logic. We cannot doubt, therefore, that these thoughts originate in our normal mental life. All the qualities we prize in our mental operations, and which mark them as complicated activities of a high order, we find repeated in the dream thoughts. There is no need, however, to assume that this mental work is performed during sleep, since that would seriously damage the conception of the psychic state of sleep to which we have so far adhered. These thoughts may just as well have originated during the day and, unnoticed by consciousness from their inception, continued to develop until they stood complete at the onset of sleep. If we are to conclude anything from this state of affairs, it will at most prove that the most complex mental operations are possible without the participation of consciousness, which we have already learned independently from every psychoanalysis of persons suffering from hysteria or obsessions. These dream thoughts are surely not in themselves incapable of becoming conscious; if they have not become conscious to us during the day, there may be various reasons. Becoming conscious depends on the exercise of a particular psychic function, namely attention, which seems to be available only in a fixed quantity and which may have been withdrawn from the stream of thought in question by other aims. There is another way in which such streams of thought are kept from consciousness. Our conscious reflection teaches us that when we exercise attention we follow a definite course. But if that course leads us to an idea that does not stand up to criticism, we break off and cease to apply our attention. Now, apparently, the stream of thought thus started and abandoned may continue to spin on without regaining attention, unless it reaches a point of especially marked intensity that compels attention to return. An initial rejection, perhaps brought about consciously by our judgment on the grounds that an idea is incorrect or unsuited to the actual purpose of the mental act, may therefore account for a mental process continuing, unnoticed by consciousness, until the onset of sleep.

To recapitulate: we call such a stream of thought a preconscious one; we believe it to be perfectly correct; and it may equally well be one that was merely neglected or one that was interrupted and suppressed. Let us also state frankly how we conceive this flow of ideas. We believe that a certain sum of excitation, which we call occupation energy, is displaced from a goal-idea along the association paths that this goal-idea selects. A "neglected" stream of thought has received no such charge of energy, and from a "suppressed" or "rejected" one the charge has been withdrawn; both have thus been left to their own excitations. A stream of thought charged with energy from a goal-idea is, under certain conditions, able to draw the attention of consciousness to itself, and by this means it then receives a "surplus of energy." Somewhat later we shall be obliged to clarify our assumptions about the nature and activity of consciousness.

A train of thought set in motion in this way in the preconscious may either die away of its own accord or persist. We conceive the first outcome as follows. The train of thought diffuses its energy along all the association paths that branch out from it and throws the entire chain of ideas into a state of excitation, which, after lasting for a while, subsides as the excitation seeking an outlet is transformed into dormant energy. If this first outcome occurs, the process has no further significance for dream formation. But other goal-ideas lie in wait in our preconscious, ideas that originate in the sources of our unconscious and in its ever-active wishes. These may take possession of the excitations in the circle of thought that has been left to itself, establish a connection between it and the unconscious wish, and transfer to it the energy inherent in that wish. From then on, the neglected or suppressed train of thought is able to sustain itself, although this reinforcement does not help it gain access to consciousness. We may say that the train of thought, until now preconscious, has been drawn into the unconscious.

Other constellations of dream formation would result if the preconscious train of thought had been connected with the unconscious wish from the beginning, and for that reason had been rejected by the dominant charge of the goal-idea; or if an unconscious wish had been activated for other reasons, possibly somatic ones, and had sought on its own accord to transfer itself onto psychic remnants not charged by the preconscious. All three cases ultimately converge on a single outcome: there is established in the preconscious a stream of thought which, having been abandoned by the preconscious charge, receives its charge from the unconscious wish.

From this point on, the stream of thought undergoes a series of transformations that we no longer recognize as normal psychic processes, and these yield a surprising result, namely a psychopathological formation. Let us set these transformations out and group them.

1. The intensities of the individual ideas become capable of being discharged in their entirety, and, passing from one idea to another, they form single ideas endowed with marked intensity. Through the repeated recurrence of this process, the intensity of an entire train of ideas may ultimately be gathered into a single element. This is the principle of compression, or condensation, with which we became acquainted in the chapter on "The Dream-Work." It is condensation that is chiefly responsible for the strange impression the dream makes, for we know of nothing analogous to it in the normal psychic life accessible to consciousness. In normal life, too, we find ideas that carry great psychic significance as junctions or as end-results of whole chains of thought; but this significance does not show itself in any feature conspicuous enough to be perceived inwardly, and so what is represented in such an idea does not become any more intense. In the process of condensation, by contrast, the entire web of psychic connections is transformed into the intensity of the content of a single idea. It is as in a book, where any word on which particular stress is laid for the understanding of the text is spaced out or printed in heavy type. In speech the same word would be pronounced loudly, slowly, and with emphasis. The first comparison leads us at once to an example from the chapter on "The Dream-Work": the word "trimethylamine" in the dream of Irma's injection. Historians of art point out that the most ancient historical sculptures follow a similar principle, expressing the rank of the persons represented through the size of their statues. The king is made two or three times as large as his retinue or his vanquished enemy. A work of art from the Roman period, however, uses subtler means to accomplish the same purpose. The figure of the emperor is placed at the center in a firmly erect posture, special care is taken in modeling his figure, and his enemies are seen cowering at his feet; but he is no longer shown as a giant among dwarfs. Even the bow of a subordinate before his superior in our own day is only an echo of that ancient principle of representation.

The direction taken by the dream's condensations is prescribed on the one hand by the genuine preconscious relations among the dream thoughts, and on the other by the attraction exerted by visual memories in the unconscious. Successful condensation produces the intensities required to break through into the perceptual systems.

2. Through this free transferability of intensities, and in the service of condensation, intermediate ideas are formed that amount to compromises, as the numerous examples show. This, too, is something unheard of in the normal flow of ideas, where the chief concern is to select and retain the "proper" element. On the other hand, composite and compromise formations occur with extraordinary frequency when we are trying to find verbal expression for preconscious thoughts; these we regard as "slips of the tongue."

3. The ideas that transfer their intensities to one another are very loosely connected, and they are joined by kinds of association that our serious thinking scorns and that are put to use only in producing the effects of wit. Among these we find in particular associations based on sound and rhyme.

4. Contradictory thoughts do not try to eliminate one another but remain side by side. They often combine into condensations as though no contradiction existed, or they form compromises of a kind we would never forgive in our thoughts, though we frequently approve of them in our actions.

These are some of the most conspicuous abnormal processes to which thoughts previously formed on rational lines are subjected in the course of the dream-work. As the main feature of these processes we recognize the great importance placed on making the charge of energy mobile and capable of discharge; the content and actual significance of the psychic elements to which these energies are attached become a matter of secondary importance. One might suppose that condensation and compromise formation occur only in the service of regression, when the occasion arises for turning thoughts into pictures. But the analysis, and still more clearly the synthesis, of dreams that lack this regression toward pictures, such as the dream "Autodidasker: Conversation with Court-Councillor N.," reveal the same processes of displacement and condensation as the others.

We cannot, then, refuse to acknowledge that two essentially different kinds of psychic process take part in forming the dream. One produces perfectly correct dream thoughts, equivalent to normal thoughts, while the other treats these ideas in a highly surprising and incorrect manner. The latter process we have already set apart in Chapter VI as the dream-work proper. What can we now put forward concerning this latter psychic process?

We would be unable to answer this question here had we not penetrated a considerable way into the psychology of the neuroses, and especially of hysteria. From that study we learn that the same incorrect psychic processes, along with others not listed here, govern the formation of hysterical symptoms. In hysteria, too, we immediately find a series of perfectly correct thoughts, equivalent to our conscious thoughts, of whose existence in this form, however, we can learn nothing and which we can only reconstruct after the fact. If they have forced their way anywhere into our perception, we discover from analyzing the resulting symptom that these normal thoughts have been subjected to abnormal treatment and transformed into the symptom by means of condensation and compromise formation, through superficial associations, under cover of contradictions, and ultimately by way of regression. Given the complete identity between the peculiarities of the dream-work and those of the psychic activity that forms psychoneurotic symptoms, we feel justified in transferring to the dream the conclusions that hysteria has pressed upon us.

From the theory of hysteria we borrow the proposition that a normal train of thought undergoes such abnormal psychic elaboration only when it has been used as a vehicle for an unconscious wish that dates from infancy and is in a state of repression. In keeping with this proposition, we have built our theory of the dream on the assumption that the dream-wish that sets the dream in motion invariably originates in the unconscious, an assumption which, as we ourselves have admitted, cannot be demonstrated universally, though neither can it be refuted. But in order to explain the real meaning of the term "repression," which we have used so freely, we shall have to make some further additions to our psychological construction.

We have already elaborated the fiction of a primitive psychic apparatus whose work is governed by the effort to avoid an accumulation of excitation and to keep itself, as far as possible, free of excitation. For this reason it was constructed on the plan of a reflex apparatus; motility, originally the path for inner bodily change, formed a channel of discharge at its disposal. We then discussed the psychic consequences of an experience of gratification, and at that point we might also have introduced a second assumption: that an accumulation of excitation, following certain modalities that need not concern us, is felt as pain and sets the apparatus in motion so as to reproduce the experience of gratification, in which the reduction of excitation is felt as pleasure. Such a current in the apparatus, starting from pain and striving toward pleasure, we call a wish. We have said that nothing but a wish can set the apparatus in motion, and that the discharge of excitation within it is regulated automatically by the perception of pleasure and pain. The first wish must have been a hallucinatory charging of the memory of gratification. But this hallucination, unless sustained to the point of exhaustion, proved incapable of bringing the craving to an end, and so of securing the pleasure bound up with gratification.

A second activity was therefore required, in our terminology the activity of a second system, which would not allow the charged memory to advance to perception and thereby tie down the psychic forces, but would instead lead the excitation arising from the stimulus of need along a roundabout path through voluntary movement, a path that would ultimately change the outer world so that the object of gratification could be perceived in reality. So far we have worked out the plan of the psychic apparatus; these two systems are the germ of what we call the Unconscious and the Preconscious in the fully developed apparatus.

To be able to change the outer world successfully through movement, the apparatus needs a large store of experiences accumulated in the memory systems, as well as a manifold fixing of the relations that different goal-ideas call up within this remembered material. We now carry our assumption further. The varied activity of the second system, which tentatively sends out energy and draws it back again, must on the one hand have full command over all the material of memory; on the other hand, it would be a wasteful expenditure for this system to send large quantities of energy along the individual mental paths, where they would flow away to no purpose and diminish the amount available for transforming the outer world. In the interest of efficiency, therefore, I postulate that the second system succeeds in keeping the greater part of its charge of energy in a dormant state and uses only a small portion for purposes of displacement. The mechanism of these processes is entirely unknown to me; anyone who wishes to pursue these ideas must look for the physical analogies and prepare the way for demonstrating the process of motion in the stimulation of the neuron. I hold only to the idea that the activity of the first psychic system, the first Ψ-system, aims at the free outflow of quantities of excitation, and that the second system, through the energies issuing from it, brings about an inhibition of this outflow; that is, it transforms the excitation into dormant energy, probably by raising its level. I therefore assume that under the control of the second system, as compared with the first, the course of excitation is bound to entirely different mechanical conditions. Once the second system has completed its tentative mental work, it lifts the inhibition and the damming-up of the excitations and allows them to flow off into movement.

An interesting train of thought now presents itself if we consider how this inhibition of discharge by the second system relates to regulation by the principle of pain. Let us now look for the counterpart of the primary experience of gratification, namely, the objective experience of fear. A perceptual stimulus acts on the primitive apparatus and becomes the source of a painful emotion. Irregular motor activity follows until one of these movements withdraws the apparatus from the perception, and with it from the pain. When the perception reappears, that movement will immediately repeat itself, perhaps as a movement of flight, until the perception has disappeared once more. In this case, however, no tendency will remain to occupy the perception of the source of pain again, that is, to invest it anew with energy, whether as a hallucination or in any other form. On the contrary, the primary apparatus will tend to abandon the painful memory-image the moment it is in any way awakened, since the overflow of its excitement would surely produce pain, or more precisely, would begin to produce it. This turning away from the memory, which merely repeats the earlier flight from the perception, is made easier by a further fact: unlike a perception, a memory does not possess enough quality to excite consciousness and thereby draw fresh energy to itself. This easy and regularly recurring diversion of the psychic process away from a once-painful memory gives us the model and the first example of psychic repression. As is generally known, much of this turning away from what is painful, much of the behavior of the ostrich that buries its head in the sand rather than face danger, can readily be demonstrated even in the normal mental life of adults.

By virtue of the principle of pain, then, the first system is entirely incapable of bringing anything unpleasant into its mental associations. It can do nothing but wish. If matters remained so, the mental activity of the second system, which ought to have at its disposal all the memories stored up through experience, would be obstructed. Two paths now open. Either the work of the second system frees itself entirely from the principle of pain and continues on its course, paying no heed to the painful recollection, or it contrives to occupy the painful memory in such a way that no pain is released. We may reject the first possibility, since the principle of pain also acts as a regulator of the emotional discharge of the second system. We are therefore directed to the second possibility, namely, that this system occupies a recollection in such a way as to inhibit its discharge, and with it the discharge, comparable to a motor innervation, that would produce pain. We are thus led from two starting points, from a consideration of the principle of pain and from the principle of the smallest expenditure of innervation, to the same hypothesis: that occupation by the second system is at the same time an inhibition of emotional discharge. Let us hold firmly to one fact, for it is the key to the theory of repression: the second system can occupy an idea only when it is in a position to check the development of pain that would emanate from it. Whatever escapes this inhibition also remains inaccessible to the second system, and by virtue of the principle of pain it would soon be abandoned. The inhibition of pain need not, however, be complete. The pain must be allowed to begin, since it signals to the second system the nature of the memory and possibly its unsuitability for the purpose the mind is pursuing.

The psychic process admitted by the first system alone I shall now call the primary process, and the one that results from the inhibition exercised by the second system I shall call the secondary process. I can show from another angle why the second system is obliged to correct the primary process. The primary process strives to discharge the excitement in order to establish, with the sum of excitement thus gathered, an identity of perception. The secondary process has abandoned this aim and taken up instead the task of bringing about an identity of thought. All thinking is merely a roundabout path from the memory of gratification, taken as the end-presentation, to an identical occupation of that same memory, which is to be reached once again by way of motor experience. Thinking must therefore concern itself with the connecting paths between presentations without letting itself be misled by their intensities. Yet it is plain that condensations of presentations, and intermediate or compromise formations among them, obstruct the attainment of this end-identity: by substituting one idea for another, they turn aside from the path that would otherwise have led onward from the original idea. Such processes are therefore carefully avoided in secondary thinking. Nor is it difficult to see that the principle of pain also impedes the progress of the stream of thought in its pursuit of an identity of thought, even though it supplies that stream with its most important points of departure. The thinking process must therefore tend to free itself more and more from exclusive regulation by the principle of pain, and through the work of thought to restrict the development of affect to the minimum required to serve as a signal. This refinement of activity must have been achieved through a further over-occupation of energy, supplied by consciousness. We know, however, that this refinement is seldom completely successful even in the most normal mental life, and that our thoughts always remain open to falsification through the interference of the principle of pain.

This, however, is not the breach in the functional efficiency of our psychic apparatus through which thoughts that form the material of the secondary mental work are able to make their way into the primary psychic process. With that formula we may now describe the work that leads to the dream and to hysterical symptoms. This case of insufficiency arises from the union of two factors in the history of our development. One belongs entirely to the psychic apparatus and has exerted a decisive influence on the relation between the two systems; the other operates in fluctuating degrees and introduces motive forces of organic origin into mental life. Both originate in infancy, and both result from the transformation that our psychic and bodily organism has undergone since that period.

When I called one of the processes in the psychic apparatus the primary process, I did so not only with regard to its rank and capability but also in order to let its temporal relations share in the name. As far as our knowledge extends, no psychic apparatus exists that possesses only the primary process, and to that extent it is a theoretical fiction. But this much rests on fact: the primary processes are present in the apparatus from the beginning, while the secondary processes develop gradually over the course of life, inhibiting and overlaying the primary ones and gaining complete mastery over them perhaps only in the prime of life. Because the secondary processes appear so late, the core of our being, which consists of unconscious wish-impulses, can be neither grasped nor inhibited by the foreconscious, whose role is restricted once and for all to pointing out the most suitable paths for the wish-impulses that arise in the unconscious. These unconscious wishes impose on all later psychic efforts a compulsion to which those efforts must submit, though they may strive, where possible, to divert it from its course and direct it toward higher aims. As a further consequence of this delay in the foreconscious occupation, a large region of the material of memory remains inaccessible.

Among these indestructible and unrestrained wish-impulses arising from infancy there are some whose fulfillment has come to stand in contradiction to the end-presentations of secondary thinking. Fulfilling these wishes would no longer produce an affect of pleasure but one of pain, and it is precisely this transformation of affect that constitutes the essence of what we call "repression." In it we recognize the infantile first step toward passing adverse judgment, toward rejection by reason. To investigate how, and through what motive forces, such a transformation can come about is the problem of repression, which we need only touch on here. It will be enough to note that such a transformation of affect occurs in the course of development (one may think of the appearance in childhood of disgust, which was originally absent) and that it is connected with the activity of the secondary system. The memories from which the unconscious wish brings about its emotional discharge have never been accessible to the foreconscious, and for that reason their emotional discharge cannot be inhibited. It is precisely because of this development of affect that these ideas remain inaccessible even now to the foreconscious thoughts to which they have transferred their wishing power. On the contrary, the principle of pain comes into play and causes the foreconscious to turn away from these thoughts of transference. Left to themselves, the latter are "repressed," and so the existence of a store of infantile memories, withdrawn from the foreconscious from the very beginning, becomes the precondition of repression.

In the most favorable case, the development of pain ceases as soon as the energy has been withdrawn from the thoughts of transference in the foreconscious, and this outcome shows the intervention of the principle of pain to be expedient. Matters are different, however, if the repressed unconscious wish receives an organic reinforcement that it can lend to its thoughts of transference, enabling them to press forward with their excitement even after the foreconscious has withdrawn its occupation from them. A defensive struggle then ensues, as the foreconscious strengthens its opposition to the repressed ideas, and this in turn leads the thoughts of transference, the carriers of the unconscious wish, to break through in some compromise form by means of symptom formation. But from the moment the suppressed thoughts are powerfully occupied by the unconscious wish-impulse and abandoned by the foreconscious occupation, they fall under the sway of the primary psychic process and strive only for motor discharge, or, if the path is open, for a hallucinatory revival of the desired identity of perception. We found earlier, on empirical grounds, that the incorrect processes described above are carried out only on thoughts that lie under repression. We now grasp another part of the connection. These incorrect processes are the ones that are primary in the psychic apparatus. They appear wherever thoughts abandoned by the foreconscious occupation are left to themselves and can fill up with the uninhibited energy that strives for discharge from the unconscious. A few further observations support the view that these so-called "incorrect" processes are not falsifications of normal thinking or mere errors of thought, but the modes of activity of the psychic apparatus once it has been freed from inhibition. We see, for instance, that the transfer of foreconscious excitement to motility follows these same processes, and that the connection of foreconscious presentations with words readily displays the same displacements and confusions that are usually attributed to inattention. Finally, I would offer as proof that the inhibition of these primary processes necessarily entails an increase in work the fact that we obtain a comic effect, a surplus of energy to be discharged in laughter, whenever we allow these streams of thought to reach consciousness.

The theory of the psychoneuroses asserts with complete certainty that only sexual wish-impulses from infancy undergo repression, that is, a transformation of affect, during the developmental period of childhood. These wishes can return to activity at a later stage of development, and they can then be revived either as a consequence of the sexual constitution, which actually grows out of an original bisexuality, or as a result of unfavorable influences in sexual life. In this way they supply the motive power for every psychoneurotic symptom formation. Only by introducing these sexual forces can the gaps that still remain in the theory of repression be filled. I will leave undecided whether this requirement that the wish be sexual and infantile can also be asserted for the theory of the dream. I leave the question unfinished here because I have already gone one step beyond what can be demonstrated in assuming that the dream-wish always originates in the unconscious. Nor will I investigate further the difference in the play of psychic forces between dream formation and the formation of hysterical symptoms, for to do so we would need a more precise knowledge of one of the two terms being compared.

There is, however, another point I regard as important, and I will confess here that it was for the sake of this very point that I undertook the entire foregoing discussion of the two psychic systems, their modes of operation, and repression. It no longer matters whether I have understood the psychological relations in question with approximate correctness or, as may easily happen in so difficult a matter, in a mistaken and fragmentary way. Whatever changes may be made in our interpretation of the psychic censor and of the correct and abnormal elaboration of the dream content, the fact remains that such processes are active in dream formation, and that in their essentials they show the closest analogy to the processes observed in the formation of hysterical symptoms. The dream is not a pathological phenomenon, and it leaves behind no weakening of the mental faculties. The objection that nothing can be inferred about the dreams of healthy people from my own dreams and from those of neurotic patients may be dismissed without comment. When, therefore, we reason from the phenomena back to their motive forces, we recognize that the psychic mechanism the neuroses make use of is not created by a morbid disturbance of mental life but is found ready-made in the normal structure of the psychic apparatus. The two psychic systems, the censorship at the crossing between them, the inhibition and overlaying of one activity by the other, the relation of both to consciousness, or whatever more accurate account of the actual conditions may come to replace these, all belong to the normal structure of our psychic instrument, and the dream shows us one of the roads that lead to a knowledge of this structure. If we wish to content ourselves with a minimum of knowledge that is perfectly established, we shall say that the dream proves that suppressed material continues to exist even in the normal person and remains capable of psychic activity. The dream itself is one of the expressions of this suppressed material. In theory this holds in every case; according to substantial experience, it holds at least in a great number of the dreams that most conspicuously display the characteristic features of dream life. The suppressed psychic material, which in the waking state has been prevented from finding expression and cut off from internal perception by the opposing settlement of its contradictions, finds ways and means during the night, under the dominance of compromise formations, of forcing itself upon consciousness.

"Flectere si nequeo superos, Acheronta movebo": if I cannot bend the powers above, I will stir up the river of the underworld.

The interpretation of dreams is, in any case, the royal road to a knowledge of the unconscious in mental life.

By following the analysis of dreams, we have made some progress toward understanding how this most marvelous and most mysterious of instruments is put together. We have not gone very far, admittedly, but we have made enough of a beginning to push further into the analysis of the unconscious by way of other so-called pathological formations. Disease, at least the kind rightly called functional, does not come from the destruction of this apparatus or from new splits forming inside it. It is better explained dynamically, through the strengthening and weakening of the various components in the play of forces, a play that conceals a great many of its activities while the apparatus is functioning normally. Elsewhere we have shown that because the apparatus is built from two systems, it can refine even its normal activity in ways that no single system could manage.

### (f) The Unconscious and Consciousness—Reality.

On closer inspection, what we find near the motor end of the apparatus is not two systems but two kinds of processes, or two modes of emotional discharge, which we assumed and explained in the psychological discussions of the previous chapter. This makes no difference to us, since we must always be prepared to drop our provisional ideas whenever we can replace them with something that comes closer to the unknown reality. Let us now try to correct certain views that might have been mistakenly formed so long as we pictured the two systems in the crudest and most obvious sense, as two places within the psychic apparatus. These views have left their mark on the terms "repression" and "penetration." When we say that an unconscious idea strives to be transferred into the foreconscious so that it can later penetrate consciousness, we do not mean that a second idea is formed in a new location, like a revised line written between the lines of a manuscript while the original stays where it was. Likewise, when we speak of penetrating into consciousness, we want to avoid any notion of a change of place. When we say that a foreconscious idea is repressed and then taken up by the unconscious, these images, borrowed from the idea of a struggle over territory, might tempt us to suppose that an arrangement is actually dismantled in one psychic location and replaced by a new one in another. For these comparisons we substitute a description that seems to fit the real state of affairs more closely: an occupation of energy, a charge of psychic energy invested in an idea, is shifted onto a certain arrangement or withdrawn from it, so that the psychic formation either falls under the control of a system or is removed from it. Here again we replace a topographical way of describing things with a dynamic one. What appears to us as the moving factor is not the psychic formation itself but the charge of energy that animates it.

I still consider it appropriate and justified, however, to keep working with the illustrative picture of the two systems. We will avoid misusing this way of representing things if we remember that ideas, thoughts, and psychic formations in general should not be located in the organic elements of the nervous system but, so to speak, between them, where resistances and pathways form their physical counterpart. Everything that can become an object of our inner perception is virtual, like the image in a telescope produced by the passage of light rays. But we are justified in assuming that the systems themselves exist. They have nothing psychic about them and never become accessible to our psychic perception, much as the lenses of a telescope, which form the image, are not themselves part of the image. Carrying the comparison further, we may say that the censorship between the two systems corresponds to the refraction that light undergoes as it passes into a new medium.

Until now we have been constructing a psychology on our own responsibility. It is time to examine the theoretical views that govern present-day psychology and to test how they relate to our own. In the authoritative words of Lipps, the question of the unconscious is less a question within psychology than the question of psychology itself. So long as psychology disposed of this question with the verbal formula that the "psychic" simply is the "conscious," and that "unconscious psychic processes" are an obvious contradiction in terms, it was impossible to give any psychological weight to what physicians observed in abnormal mental states. The physician and the philosopher can agree only when both acknowledge that unconscious psychic processes are "the appropriate and well-justified expression for an established fact." The physician can only shrug at the claim that "consciousness is the indispensable quality of the psychic." If his respect for the pronouncements of philosophers is still strong enough, he may conclude that he and they are not dealing with the same subject and do not practice the same science. A single intelligent observation of a neurotic's mental life, or a single analysis of a dream, must convince him beyond any possibility of change that the most complicated and correct mental operations, which no one would deny the name of psychic events, can take place without stirring the person's consciousness at all. It is true that the physician learns of these unconscious processes only once they have produced some effect on consciousness that can be communicated or observed. But this conscious effect may have a psychic character so different from the unconscious process behind it that inner perception cannot possibly recognize one as a stand-in for the other. The physician must reserve the right to work back by deduction from the effect on consciousness to the unconscious psychic process. In this way he learns that the conscious effect is only a distant psychic product of the unconscious process, that the unconscious process itself has not become conscious as such, and that it has existed and operated without betraying itself to consciousness in any way.

A reaction against overvaluing the quality of consciousness is the indispensable precondition for any correct insight into how the psychic behaves. In Lipps's words, the unconscious must be accepted as the general foundation of mental life. The unconscious is the larger circle that contains within it the smaller circle of the conscious. Everything conscious passes through a preliminary stage in the unconscious, whereas the unconscious may stop at that stage and still lay full claim to being a psychic activity. Strictly speaking, the unconscious is the true psychic reality. Its inner nature is as unknown to us as the reality of the external world, and the data of consciousness report it to us just as imperfectly as our sense organs report the external world.

Once the old opposition between conscious life and dream life is abandoned and the unconscious psychic is given its proper place, a whole series of dream problems that intensely occupied earlier writers can be set aside. Many of the achievements of dreams that have excited our admiration are no longer to be credited to the dream at all, but to unconscious thinking, which is active during the day as well. If, as Scherner held, the dream seems to play with a symbolic representation of the body, we now know that this is the work of certain unconscious fantasies, which have probably given way to sexual impulses, and that these fantasies find expression not only in dreams but also in hysterical phobias and other symptoms. If the dream carries on and settles the business of the day, or even brings valuable inspirations to light, we need only strip away the dream's disguise, which is a product of the dream-work and a sign of help from obscure forces in the depths of the mind. The violinist Tartini's dream is a case in point: he dreamed that the devil played him a sonata, and the devil is precisely such a disguise. The intellectual work itself must be credited to the same psychic forces that perform all such work during the day. We are probably far too inclined to overrate the conscious character even of intellectual and artistic production. From the accounts of some of the most productive people, such as Goethe and Helmholtz, we learn that the most essential and original parts of their creations came to them as inspirations and reached their awareness almost finished. In other cases, where all the psychic forces worked together in a concerted effort, there is nothing strange about conscious activity lending its help. But conscious activity enjoys a much-abused privilege: wherever it takes part, it is allowed to hide all the other activities from us.

It is hardly worth treating the historical significance of dreams as a separate subject. Suppose a chieftain is spurred by a dream to undertake some bold venture whose success changes the course of history. This poses a new problem only so long as the dream is regarded as a strange power and set against other, more familiar psychic forces. The problem disappears once we regard the dream as a form of expression for feelings that are weighed down by resistance during the day and can draw reinforcement at night from deep emotional sources. Yet the great reverence the ancients showed for dreams rests on a correct psychological intuition. It is a tribute paid to what is unsubdued and indestructible in the human mind, to the demonic element that supplies the dream-wish and that we rediscover in our unconscious.

I do not use the phrase "in our unconscious" carelessly, for what we mean by it is not the same as the unconscious of the philosophers, nor the unconscious of Lipps. In those usages the term means only the opposite of conscious. The hotly contested and vigorously defended point is that there are unconscious psychic processes alongside conscious ones. Lipps offers the more far-reaching theory that everything psychic exists as unconscious, while some of it may also exist as conscious. But we did not bring forward the phenomena of dreams and of hysterical symptom formation in order to prove this theory; the observation of normal life alone is enough to establish it beyond any doubt. The new fact we have learned from analyzing psychopathological formations, and indeed from the first of them, the dream, is that the unconscious, and therefore the psychic, operates as a function of two separate systems, and that it does so even in normal mental life. There are consequently two kinds of unconscious, which psychologists have not yet distinguished. Both are unconscious in the psychological sense. But in our sense, the first, which we call the Unc., is also incapable of becoming conscious, whereas the second, which we call the Forec., is so named because its impulses can reach consciousness once they have observed certain rules, perhaps only after passing through censorship once more, but independently of the Unc. system. To reach consciousness, these impulses must pass through a fixed sequence of events, a succession of stages, as their alteration by the censor reveals, and this fact has allowed us to borrow a comparison from space. We described the relations of the two systems to each other and to consciousness by saying that the Forec. system stands like a screen between the Unc. system and consciousness. The Forec. system not only blocks access to consciousness but also controls access to voluntary movement, and it can send out a quantity of mobile energy, part of which we know as attention.

We must also steer clear of the distinction between the superconscious and the subconscious that has found such favor in recent writing on the psychoneuroses, because a distinction of exactly this kind seems to reinforce the equation of the psychic with the conscious.

What role, then, remains in our account for consciousness, once all-powerful and overshadowing everything else? Only that of a sense organ for perceiving psychic qualities. In keeping with the basic idea of our schematic approach, we can conceive of conscious perception only as the specific activity of an independent system, for which the abbreviation "Cons." recommends itself. We imagine this system to resemble the perception system P in its mechanical properties: it can be excited by qualities and is incapable of retaining traces of changes, which is to say it has no memory. The psychic apparatus, which faces the outer world through the sense organs of the P-systems, is itself the outer world for the sense organ of Cons., and this relationship is what gives Cons. its purpose. Here we meet once again the principle of a succession of stages, which seems to govern the structure of the apparatus. Excitation flows to the sense organ Cons. from two directions. It comes, first, from the P-system, whose qualitatively determined excitation probably undergoes further elaboration before it becomes conscious perception. It comes, second, from inside the apparatus itself, whose quantitative processes are perceived as a qualitative series of pleasure and pain once they have undergone certain changes.

The philosophers, having learned that correct and highly complicated structures of thought are possible without any help from consciousness, have found it hard to assign consciousness any function at all; it has seemed to them a superfluous reflection of a psychic process already complete. The analogy between our Cons. system and the perception systems frees us from this difficulty. We see that perception through our sense organs directs the occupation of attention toward the pathways along which the incoming sensory excitation spreads. The qualitative excitation of the P-system acts as a regulator for the discharge of the mobile quantity of energy in the psychic apparatus. We may claim the same function for the higher sense organ of the Cons. system. By taking on new qualities, it makes a fresh contribution to guiding and suitably distributing the mobile quantities of occupying energy. Through the perceptions of pleasure and pain, it influences the course of the occupations within the psychic apparatus, which ordinarily works unconsciously and by displacing quantities of energy. The principle of pain probably regulates these displacements of occupation automatically at first. It is quite possible, however, that consciousness of these qualities adds a second and subtler regulation, one that may even oppose the first. This second regulation may perfect the working capacity of the apparatus by enabling it, contrary to its original design, to occupy and develop even material connected with the release of pain. Neuropsychology teaches us that such regulations, which work through the qualitative excitation of the sense organs, play an important part in the functional activity of the apparatus. The automatic control exercised by the primary principle of pain, and the restriction of mental capacity that goes with it, are broken by these sensory regulations, which are themselves automatisms in their turn. We also learn why repression is accomplished so much more easily with memories than with perceptions. Repression is useful in its origins, yet it ends in a harmful surrender of inhibition and psychic control. It works more easily on memories because they receive no additional occupation from the excitation of the psychic sense organs. Once an idea marked for rejection has failed to become conscious because it has succumbed to repression, it can be repressed on later occasions only because it has been withdrawn from conscious perception for other reasons. Therapy uses these clues to undo repressions that have already taken place.

The regulating influence of the conscious sense organ produces an over-occupation of the mobile quantity. From the standpoint of purpose, the value of this over-occupation is shown most clearly by the creation of a new series of qualities, and therefore of a new regulation, which constitutes man's superiority over the animals. Mental processes are in themselves without quality, apart from the excitations of pleasure and pain that accompany them, and these, as we know, must be held in check as possible disturbances of thought.
