To give thought processes a quality, man associates them with verbal memories. The qualitative residues of these memories are enough to draw the attention of consciousness toward them, and consciousness in turn endows thought with a new mobile energy.

The many problems of consciousness can be examined in their entirety only through an analysis of hysterical thought processes. This analysis gives the impression that the passage from the foreconscious to the occupation of consciousness is also bound up with a censorship, similar to the one between the unconscious and the foreconscious. This censorship, too, begins to act only once a certain quantitative degree has been reached, so that thought formations of low intensity escape it. Every possible instance of being held back from consciousness, as well as of penetrating into consciousness under restrictions, appears within the picture of psychoneurotic phenomena, and every instance points to the intimate and twofold connection between the censorship and consciousness. I shall conclude these psychological discussions by reporting two such occurrences.

Some years ago I was called in for a consultation on an intelligent and innocent-looking girl. Her dress was strange. A woman's clothing is usually attended to down to the last fold, yet one of her stockings was hanging down and two buttons of her bodice were undone. She complained of pains in one leg, and without being asked she exposed it. Her chief complaint, however, she put in these words: she had a feeling in her body as if something had been stuck into it that moved back and forth and made her tremble through and through, and sometimes it made her whole body stiff. Hearing this, my colleague in the consultation looked at me; the meaning of the complaint was perfectly plain to him. To both of us it seemed peculiar that the patient's mother thought nothing of the matter, since she herself must repeatedly have been in the situation her child was describing. As for the girl, she had no idea of what her words meant, or she would never have let them pass her lips. Here the censorship had been deceived so successfully that a fantasy, under the mask of an innocent complaint, was admitted to consciousness when it would otherwise have remained in the foreconscious.

Another example. I began the psychoanalytic treatment of a fourteen-year-old boy who was suffering from a convulsive tic, hysterical vomiting, headaches, and other symptoms. I assured him that if he closed his eyes he would see pictures or have ideas, and I asked him to tell me about them. He answered by describing pictures. The last impression he had received before coming to me was revived visually in his memory. He had been playing a game of checkers with his uncle, and he now saw the checkerboard before him. He commented on various positions, some favorable and some unfavorable, and on moves that were not safe to make. He then saw a dagger lying on the checkerboard. It was an object belonging to his father, which his fantasy had transferred to the board. Then a sickle lay on the board, then a scythe was added, and finally he saw the figure of an old peasant mowing the grass in front of the boy's distant family home. A few days later I discovered what this series of pictures meant. Unpleasant family circumstances had made the boy nervous. His father was strict and ill-tempered, lived unhappily with the boy's mother, and brought up his son by means of threats. The father had then separated from the tender and delicate mother and remarried, and one day he brought home a young woman as the boy's new mother. The boy's illness broke out a few days later. It was his suppressed anger against his father that had arranged these pictures into intelligible allusions, and a memory from mythology supplied the material. The sickle was the one with which Zeus castrated his father. The scythe and the figure of the peasant represented Kronos, the violent old man who devours his children and on whom Zeus takes vengeance in so unfilial a manner. The father's marriage gave the boy an opportunity to return the reproaches and threats his father had once made against him because, as a child, he had played with his genitals. The checkerboard, the forbidden moves, and the dagger with which a person may be killed all point to this. Here we have long-repressed memories, and unconscious remnants of them, that slipped into consciousness disguised as meaningless pictures, by roundabout paths that had been left open to them.

I would therefore expect the theoretical value of the study of dreams to lie in its contribution to psychological knowledge and in the groundwork it lays for an understanding of the neuroses. Who can foresee how important a thorough knowledge of the structure and workings of the psychic apparatus may become, when even our present knowledge has a beneficial therapeutic effect on the curable forms of the psychoneuroses? Someone may ask about the practical value of this study for psychological insight and for uncovering the hidden peculiarities of individual character. Do the unconscious impulses revealed by the dream not have the value of real forces in psychic life? Should we take lightly the ethical significance of suppressed wishes which, just as they now create dreams, may someday create other things?

I do not feel entitled to answer these questions, since I have not thought further about this side of the dream problem. I believe, however, that the Roman emperor who had one of his subjects executed for dreaming that he had killed the emperor was in any case in the wrong. He ought first to have tried to find out what the dream meant, and most probably it did not mean what it appeared to mean. And even if a dream with different content had carried the significance of this offense against the sovereign, it would still have been fitting to remember Plato's words, that the virtuous man is content to dream what the wicked man actually does. I am therefore of the opinion that dreams are best left free. Whether any reality is to be attributed to unconscious wishes, and in what sense, I am not prepared to say offhand. Reality must of course be denied to all transitional and intermediate thoughts. Even if we had the unconscious wishes before us, carried to their final and truest expression, we would still do well to remember that psychic reality must be granted more than one single form of existence. For the practical purpose of judging a man's character, his actions and the conscious expression of his thoughts are usually enough. Action, above all, deserves to be ranked first. Many of the impulses that penetrate into consciousness are neutralized by real forces in psychic life before they turn into action. Indeed, they often meet no psychic obstacle on their way precisely because the unconscious is certain they will meet resistance later. In any case, it is instructive to become acquainted with the much-churned soil, turned over again and again, from which our virtues proudly spring. Human character is complicated and moves dynamically in every direction, and it very rarely lends itself to a simple either-or judgment, as our antiquated moral philosophy would have it.

And what of the dream's value for knowing the future? That, of course, is out of the question. One would rather say instead that it is valuable for knowing the past, since the dream springs from the past in every sense. The ancient belief that dreams reveal the future is admittedly not entirely without truth. By presenting a wish to us as fulfilled, the dream certainly leads us into the future. But this future, which the dreamer takes for the present, has been shaped by the indestructible wish into the likeness of that past.
